Two slips. 108 is the triangle before the flower bed goes in. And 200 comes from taking the bed away from the whole courtyard, forgetting that only half was painted.
Go in the order of the story: the whole rectangle, half of it, then take away the piece on top.
Kavya's family drive fast on the highway, then slowly up the mountain. We want the average speed for the whole journey.
The number halfway between 60 and 30 is 45. Before we work anything out: will the average speed be 45, more than 45, or less?

ask.ifNot: They drive at 60 for 2 hours, but at 30 for only 1 hour. More of the trip is fast, so the average is pulled up above 45.

beats.say: Let's prove it. Average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time.

board.text: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time

beats.say: Distance is speed times time. Highway: 60 times 2 is 120 kilometres. Mountain road: 30 times 1 is 30 kilometres.
Whole distance: 120 plus 30 is 150 kilometres. Whole time: 2 hours plus 1 hour is 3 hours.
150 divided by 3 is 50. The average speed is 50 kilometres an hour, and yes, it is more than 45.
Here is another way to see it. List the speed for each hour of the trip: 60, 60, then 30. Add them and share by 3, and you get 50 again.
So average speed is whole distance divided by whole time. A speed kept up for longer counts for more.
Ravi buys 3.5 kilograms of mangoes at 48.60 rupees a kilogram, and pays with a 200 rupee note. How much change should he get?
First the cost. 3.5 kilograms is 3 whole kilograms and half a kilogram more. So we can split the multiplying into two easy parts.
The 3 whole kilograms: 3 times 48.60 is 145.80.
Now the half kilogram. What does it cost?

choices: half of the price of 1 kilogram
ask.ifNot: 0.5 means one half. So half a kilogram costs half of what a whole kilogram costs.

beats.say: Half of 48.60 is 24.30.
Add the two parts. 145.80 plus 24.30 is 170.10. That is the cost of the mangoes.
Careful: 170.10 is the bill, not the change. Take it from the 200 rupee note. 200 minus 170.10 is 29.90 rupees.
Check: the bill and the change should make the note again. 170.10 plus 29.90 is 200.
So when a weight has a decimal, split it into whole kilograms and the bit left over. Cost each part, add, and then find the change.

Kabir and Sahil scored runs in the ratio 3 to 5, and their coach shares 480 rupees between them in that same ratio. How much does Sahil get? It is the money we are sharing, so the 96 runs are not needed.
A ratio of 3 to 5 means equal parts: 3 parts for Kabir and 5 parts for Sahil. Here they are as boxes.

spec.note: All the boxes together: ₹480

beats.say: So how many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 5 make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. So the 480 rupees are shared into 8 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 480 divided by 8 is 60, so each part is 60 rupees. Careful: we divide by all 8 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Sahil has 5 parts. Which sum gives that share?

ask.ifNot: Sahil has 5 parts. One part is 60 rupees, so we want 5 lots of 60.

beats.say: 5 times 60 is 300. So Sahil gets 300 rupees.
That is our answer: 300 rupees for Sahil.
Check the sharing. Kabir has 3 parts, and 3 times 60 is 180. 180 plus 300 is 480, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So every time: total parts first, then the size of one part, then the share. And read the last line of the story to see what is still left to do.
Two lines cross in Riya's rangoli, and one angle is 65 degrees. Then a third line splits the angle next to the 65 into two equal parts. We want the size of each part.

board.text: One angle = 65°. The angle next to it is cut in half.

beats.say: Notice that the third line does not touch the 65 degrees. So first we need the angle next to it, and then we halve that.

board.text: 1. Find the angle next door.  2. Halve it.

beats.say: Job one. The 65 degrees and the angle next to it sit together on a straight line. What do they add up to?

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So the two angles next to each other share 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the angle next door is whatever takes 65 up to 180. Count up from 65. A hop of 5 reaches 70, then 110 more reaches 180. The two hops together make 115.
Job two. The third line cuts this 115 degree angle into two equal parts. Which sum gives each part?

ask.ifNot: The line cuts the angle next door, the 115 degrees, not the 65 degrees we started with. And two equal parts means dividing by 2.

beats.say: Half of 110 is 55, and half of 5 is 2.5. Together that makes 57.5.
So each part is 57.5 degrees.
Watch for two slips. One is to halve the 65 we were given. The other is to stop at 115 and forget the cutting.
Check. 57.5 plus 57.5 is 115, and 115 plus 65 is 180. Everything fits on the straight line.
So: straight line first, to get the angle next door. Then halve it. Two small steps, in the right order.
Riya puts 2500 rupees in a bank that pays 8 percent simple interest a year. Later she receives 3100 rupees in total, with her deposit included. For how many years did she keep the money there?

board.text: P = ₹2500, R = 8% a year, Amount = ₹3100, T = ?

beats.say: She got back 3100 rupees in total. How much of that is interest?

ask.ifNot: The total is the deposit plus the interest. Take the deposit away, and what remains is the interest.

beats.say: 3100 minus 2500 is 600. So the bank added 600 rupees of interest.
Now think about 1 year. 2500 is 25 hundreds, and each hundred earns 8 rupees a year. 25 times 8 is 200.
So every year adds 200 rupees. The interest was 600 altogether. How do we find the number of years?

ask.ifNot: Each year brings the same 200 rupees. So we ask how many lots of 200 fit into 600. That is a division.

beats.say: 600 divided by 200 is 3, because 3 times 200 is 600. So Riya kept her money in the bank for 3 years.
Check with the formula: principal times rate times time, divided by 100. 2500 times 8 times 3, divided by 100, is 600. It matches.
The trap is dividing the whole 3100 by 200. Only the 600 of interest was earned by waiting. The rest was hers from the start.
First separate the interest from the deposit. Then it is 1 year's interest, and how many of those.
Ravi and Sanjay scored 84 runs together. For every 3 runs Ravi scored, Sanjay scored 4. That is a ratio in disguise: Ravi to Sanjay is 3 to 4. We want Sanjay's runs.
Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 3 parts for Ravi and 4 parts for Sanjay.

spec.note: All the boxes together: 84 runs

beats.say: First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 4 make 7 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 3 plus 4 makes 7. All 84 runs sit in those 7 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 84 divided by 7 is 12, so each part is 12 runs. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 7 parts.
Sanjay has 4 parts. Which sum gives that share?

ask.ifNot: Sanjay has 4 parts. One part is 12 runs, so we want 4 lots of 12.

beats.say: 4 times 12 is 48. So Sanjay gets 48 runs.
That is our answer: 48 runs for Sanjay.
Check the sharing. Ravi has 3 parts, and 3 times 12 is 36. 36 plus 48 is 84, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So remember three moves: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. Then do whatever else the story asks.
Vikram buys ingredients for 250 rupees and sells samosas worth 350 rupees in total. He donates 20 per cent of his profit to a charity for planting trees. How much does he donate?

board.text: Spent ₹250, sold for ₹350; gives 20% of profit

beats.say: First we need the profit: money earned, take away money spent. 350 minus 250 is 100 rupees.
Now the donation: 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: The story says 20 per cent of his profit. So the donation is worked out on the 100 rupees, not on the 350 rupees he took in.

beats.say: Per cent means out of every 100. And his profit is exactly 100 rupees, which makes this a friendly one.
20 per cent of 100 is 20. Vikram donates 20 rupees.
Here is the trap. 20 per cent of the 350 rupees he earned would be 70 rupees, and that is one of the choices. But the gift comes out of the profit.
Check that it makes sense: 100 minus 20 leaves him 80 rupees of profit. He gives the small share and keeps the big one.
So work in order: the cost, the sales, the profit, and only then the percentage. And always ask: a percentage of which amount?
Ravi spends 600 rupees on ingredients and makes 200 samosas to sell at 5 rupees each. At the end, 40 samosas are still unsold. What percentage profit or loss does he make on the money he spent?
To find a profit we need two amounts: the money Ravi spent, and the money he earned. Profit is earned, take away spent.
The money going out is quick this time. Ravi spent 600 rupees on ingredients, and that is the whole cost.
Ravi made 200 samosas. How many of them brought in money?

ask.ifNot: Look at the story again: 40 samosas stayed unsold. They bring in no money, so they come off. 200 minus 40 is 160.

beats.say: 200 minus 40 is 160, so 160 samosas were sold. The cost does not shrink, though: all 200 were paid for.
Now the money coming in. 160 samosas at 5 rupees each: 160 times 5 is 800 rupees. That is the money earned.
He earned more than he spent, so it is a profit. 800 minus 600 is 200 rupees.
Now the percentage. We compare that 200 rupees of profit with which amount?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for the percentage on his investment, the money he put in. That is the 600 rupees he spent.

beats.say: So write the profit over the cost: 200 over 600. Both numbers divide by 200, so that fraction is one third.
one third of 100 per cent is 33 and a third per cent. Ravi makes a profit of 33 and a third per cent.
Check: one third of 600 is 200, and 200 rupees is exactly his profit.
So for a profit percentage: find the profit, put it over the cost, and turn that fraction into a percentage.
Rohan's bathroom floor is a square with a side of 50 centimetres. He covers it with small square tiles of side 5 centimetres. How many tiles?

board.text: Square floor of side 50 cm, square tiles of side 5 cm

beats.say: Tiles cover a surface, so we need areas. The floor is a square, so its area is side times side: 50 times 50 is 2,500 square centimetres.
Now the tile. It is a square with a side of 5 centimetres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 5 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. So each tile covers 25 square centimetres.
The floor is 2,500 square centimetres and each tile covers 25. How do we find the number of tiles?

ask.ifNot: We want to know how many tile areas fit into the floor area. So we divide area by area: 2,500 by 25, not by the side of the tile.

beats.say: 25 times 100 is 2,500. So 2,500 divided by 25 is 100. Rohan needs 100 tiles.
Check by picturing the tiles. 50 divided by 5 is 10, so 10 tiles fit in a row. And there are 10 rows. 10 times 10 is 100.
That shows the trap. 10 is only the number of tiles along 1 edge. The floor needs row after row of them.
For tiling: floor area, divided by the area of 1 tile.
Priya's rangoli has 4 straight lines crossing at O, making 8 angles. Three of them in a row are 35, 70 and 55 degrees. We want the angle directly opposite the 70.

board.text: 4 lines through O. In a row: 35°, 70°, 55°. Opposite 70° = ?

beats.say: That is a lot of lines and numbers. So ask: which do we really need? The 70 degree angle is the opening between two of the lines. Which lines make its opposite angle?

ask.ifNot: Follow the two lines that make the 70 degree angle straight through O. On the far side they open out again. That opening is the opposite angle.

beats.say: So forget the other lines for a moment. We have just two lines crossing, with 70 degrees on one side.
And when two lines cross, what do we know about the angles straight across from each other?

ask.ifNot: Adding up to 180 is for angles next door on a line. Angles straight across are made by the same two lines, opened by the same amount. So they are equal.

beats.say: Here is why. Next door to the 70 is 180 minus 70, which is 110. The opposite angle is next door to that 110, so it is 180 minus 110. That is 70 again.
So the angle opposite the 70 is also 70 degrees.
The 35 and the 55 were never needed. Extra numbers are sometimes there just to tempt you. And 110 is the angle next door, not the one opposite.
A check that uses everything. Four angles in a row fill a straight line: 35, 70, 55 and 20 more. The four opposite them are the same again.
However many lines cross at a point, the angle straight across is always equal. Find the two lines that make your angle, and look across.
Two sticks stand on a plank and lean in until they meet, making a triangle. The left stick makes 65 degrees with the plank, and the right stick makes 48 degrees. What is the angle at the top?
Every triangle keeps one rule about its angles. What do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: 90 degrees is one square corner, and 360 is a full turn. The three angles of a triangle together make a half turn.

beats.say: 180 degrees. Always, for every triangle.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: We know two of the angles, so add them. 65 plus 48 is 113.
So 113 of the 180 degrees are used up. How do we find the third angle?

ask.ifNot: The three angles share 180 degrees between them. Two of them have used 113, so the third is whatever is left.

beats.say: 180 minus 113 is 67. So the two sticks meet at 67 degrees.
Check by adding all three: 65 plus 48 plus 67 is 180. A full set.
The trap is to stop at 113. That is the two angles we were given, added together. The question wants the angle that is left.
So for a missing angle in a triangle: add the two you know, and take the total away from 180.
Meera's card is 24 centimetres long and 18 centimetres wide. A square photo of side 10 centimetres is pasted in the centre. Glitter paint for the rest costs 2 rupees for each square centimetre.

board.text: Card 24 cm × 18 cm, square photo of side 10 cm
Glitter paint: ₹2 per sq. cm. Cost = ?

beats.say: Before any cost, we need an area. Which area gets glitter paint?

ask.ifNot: No glitter goes on the photo. So the photo's area has to come off the card's area.

beats.say: The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the card: split the 18 into 10 and 8. 24 times 10 is 240, and 24 times 8 is 192. Together, 432.
So the card has an area of 432 square centimetres.
Now the photo. It is a square, so its area is side times side: 10 times 10 is 100 square centimetres.
Now take the photo away from the card. 432 minus 100 is 332 square centimetres.
Each square centimetre costs 2 rupees. How do we find the cost of 332 square centimetres?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 332 square centimetres costs 2 rupees. 332 lots of 2 is a multiplication.

beats.say: 332 times 2 is 664. Meera spends 664 rupees.
If you forget the photo, you get 432 times 2, which is 864. But no glitter goes on the photo.
So: the area that is really painted, times the price of 1 square centimetre.
Riya's room is 12 metres long and 8 metres wide, with a square rangoli of side 3 metres in one corner. The rest of the floor gets small square tiles of side 50 centimetres. How many tiles?

board.text: Room 12 m × 8 m, square rangoli of side 3 m
Square tiles of side 50 cm. How many?

beats.say: Two jobs. First the area to tile: the room, take away the rangoli. Then count how many tiles fill it.
The area of a rectangle is length times breadth. For the room, 12 times 8 is 96 square metres.
Now the rangoli. It is a square with a side of 3 metres. What is its area?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 4 is the distance all the way round the square. For the space inside it, we multiply side by side.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9. So the rangoli covers 9 square metres.
Now take the rangoli away from the room. 96 minus 9 is 87 square metres.
Now one tile. Its side is 50 centimetres, which is 0.5 of a metre. So its area is 0.5 times 0.5. What is that?

ask.ifNot: Half of a half is a quarter. And a quarter, written as a decimal, is 0.25.

beats.say: 0.25 of a square metre, a quarter. So 4 tiles cover 1 whole square metre.
87 square metres, with 4 tiles in each. 80 times 4 is 320, and 7 times 4 is 28. That makes 348 tiles.
The big trap is the units. If you divide 87 by 50, you are mixing metres with centimetres. Always change the tile into metres first.
And remember the rangoli. Without taking it away you would get 96 times 4, which is 384.
So: area to tile, in square metres, times the number of tiles in 1 square metre.
Priya's father borrowed 24000 rupees and paid back 31200 after 3 years. Her mother deposits some money at the same rate, and after 5 years her interest is 6000. How much did the mother deposit?

board.text: Father: ₹24000 loan, pays back ₹31200 after 3 years
Mother: same rate, 5 years, interest ₹6000, P = ?

beats.say: The mother's deposit depends on the rate. Where can we get the rate from?

ask.ifNot: For the father we know the loan, the time and what he paid back. That is a complete story, so it can give us the rate.

beats.say: The extra he paid back is the interest. 31200 minus 24000 is 7200. That built up over 3 years, the same each year, so 1 year is 2400.
24000 is 240 hundreds. Share 2400 among 240 hundreds and each hundred earns 10 rupees a year. So the rate is 10 percent.
Now the mother. Her 6000 of interest built up over 5 years. 6000 divided by 5 is 1200 rupees a year.
At 10 percent, every 100 rupees she deposited earns 10 rupees a year. She earns 1200 a year. How many hundreds did she deposit?

ask.ifNot: Each hundred brings in 10 rupees. So count how many lots of 10 there are in 1200: that is how many hundreds she has.

beats.say: 1200 divided by 10 is 120. So she deposited 120 hundreds, which is 12000 rupees.
Check with the formula: principal times rate times time, divided by 100. 12000 times 10 times 5, divided by 100, is 6000.
Notice the deposit is much bigger than the interest it earns in a year. At 10 percent, it is 10 times as big. That is a quick way to sense-check your answer.
Rate first, from the complete story. Then 1 year's interest, and from that, work back to the deposit.
Priya puts 6000 rupees in a bank that pays 4 percent simple interest a year. After some years the interest has grown to 1440 rupees. For how many years did she leave the money there?

board.text: P = ₹6000, R = 4% a year, Interest = ₹1440, T = ?

beats.say: First, what does 4 percent a year mean?

ask.ifNot: Percent means out of 100. So the bank pays 4 rupees for every 100 rupees kept there, and it pays that again every year.

beats.say: So for 1 year: 6000 is 60 hundreds, and each hundred earns 4 rupees a year. 60 times 4 is 240.
So every year adds 240 rupees. The interest was 1440 altogether. How do we find the number of years?

ask.ifNot: Each year brings the same 240 rupees. So we ask how many lots of 240 fit into 1440. That is a division.

beats.say: 1440 divided by 240 is 6, because 6 times 240 is 1440. So Priya kept her money in the bank for 6 years.
Check with the formula: principal times rate times time, divided by 100. 6000 times 4 times 6, divided by 100, is 1440. It matches.
Careful not to stop at 240. That is the interest for 1 year, and the question asks for the number of years.
The interest grows by the same step every year. Find the step, then count the steps.
Sameer has 122 samosas. He packs them 9 to a packet, and 5 are left over. How many full packets did he make?

board.text: 122 samosas, 9 in a packet, 5 left over

beats.say: Let p be the number of full packets, so the packets hold 9 times p samosas. Where do the 5 leftover ones go in the equation?

ask.ifNot: The 122 is everything: the samosas in packets and the 5 left over. So packets plus leftovers gives 122. That is 9 p plus 5.

beats.say: Samosas in packets, plus the 5 left over, make all 122.
The 9 p is not alone yet. Which move clears away the 5 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 5 is undone by taking 5 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: Take away 5 on the left, and 5 on the right as well. That leaves 9 p equals 122 minus 5, which is 117.
Now 9 p is 9 lots of p. To find just one p, we divide both sides by 9.
117 divided by 9 is 13, because 9 times 13 is 117. Sameer made 13 full packets.
Check: 13 packets of 9 is 117, and 5 more makes 122. Just right.
Notice we did not divide 122 by 9 straight away. The leftovers come off first, and then we share into packets.

Meena has two square frames. One has a side of the square root of 49 centimetres, the other the square root of 144 centimetres. She puts one light every 1 centimetre along both borders. How many lights?

board.text: Sides: √49 cm and √144 cm. One light per cm of border

beats.say: First turn those square roots into plain numbers. Which number times itself is 49? 7 times 7. So the first frame has a side of 7 centimetres.
And 12 times 12 is 144, so the second frame has a side of 12 centimetres.
The lights go along the border. So what do we need for each frame?

ask.ifNot: The border is the edge all the way round, and a square has 4 equal sides. So we need 4 times the side. Area would be for lights filling the inside.

beats.say: First frame: 4 times 7 is 28 centimetres of border, so 28 lights.
Second frame: 4 times 12 is 48 centimetres of border, so 48 lights.
Together, 28 plus 48 is 76 lights.
Two traps. Adding the sides, 7 plus 12, gives 19: that is one side of each frame and nothing more. And using 49 and 144 as the sides forgets the square roots.
That 19 gives us a check, though. One side of each is 19 centimetres, and there are 4 sides. 4 times 19 is 76.
So take the square roots first to get the sides. Then a border means perimeter: 4 times the side.
Riya lists the factors of 720 that are prime numbers, and adds them up. What total does she get?
To find the prime factors, we break 720 down until only prime numbers are left. 720 is 72 times 10. That is a friendly start.
10 is 2 times 5. And 72 is 8 times 9.
8 is 2 times 2 times 2, and 9 is 3 times 3. Now every piece is prime.
Riya writes each prime factor once in her list. Which list is hers?

ask.ifNot: A list of factors names each number once, however many times it is used. And 1 is not a prime number. So her list is 2, 3 and 5.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 plus 5 is 10.
Check that each one really divides 720. It is even, so 2 works. It ends in 0, so 5 works. And its digits add to 9, so 3 works.
Careful not to add every 2 and every 3 in the long line. Break the number into primes, then count each prime once.
Each gift box has 3 layers, each layer has 4 rows, and each row has 7 sweets. Grandmother made 15 boxes, gave 2 away, and sold every sweet in the rest for 12 rupees.

board.text: Box: 3 layers × 4 rows × 7 sweets. 15 boxes − 2. ₹12 each

beats.say: Start small, with one layer. 4 rows of 7 is 28 sweets.
A box has 3 layers. 3 times 28 is 84 sweets in one box.
She made 15 boxes but gave 2 away. How many boxes does she sell?

ask.ifNot: Boxes that were given away earn no money. 15 minus 2 leaves 13 boxes to sell.

beats.say: 13 boxes of 84. 10 boxes hold 840, and 3 boxes hold 252. Together, 1092 sweets.
Careful: 1092 is among the choices, but that counts sweets, not rupees. Each sweet sells for 12 rupees.
1092 times 10 is 10,920, and 1092 times 2 is 2,184. Together, 13,104 rupees.
Selling all 15 boxes would bring 15,120, which is also among the choices. But the 2 gift boxes earn nothing.
Use that as a check. The 2 gift boxes would have earned 2,016. And 15,120 minus 2,016 is 13,104.
So build it up in layers: one box, then the boxes sold, then the money.
Rohan's father has 7500 rupees in his wallet. He buys firecrackers at 3 shops: 2475 at the first, 1368 at the second and 2157 at the third. How much is left in the wallet?
He paid at 3 different shops. Before we can see what is left, what do we need?

choices: the amount at the first shop only
the total spent at all 3 shops
ask.ifNot: All 3 payments came out of the same wallet. So add the 3 amounts to see how much left the wallet altogether.

beats.say: First, the total spent. 2475 plus 1368 is 3843, and 2157 more makes 6000.
Now take that from the 7500 Rohan's father started with. 7500 minus 6000 is 1500.
So 1500 rupees are left in the wallet.
Careful not to stop at 6000. That is the money that was spent. The question asks for the money that is left.
Check by adding back. 1500 plus the 6000 that went out is 7500, the money Rohan's father began with.
So for a what-is-left question: add up everything spent, then take that total from the money at the start.
Priya goes from one perfect square of diyas to the very next one, and needs exactly 45 extra diyas to do it. How many diyas are in the larger square?

board.text: Smaller square of diyas + 45 more = the next square

beats.say: Picture a square of diyas. To grow it into the very next square, we add one more row along the bottom and one more column down the side.
The new row is as long as a side of the small square. So is the new column. And 1 more fills the corner where they meet.
There are 45 extra diyas, and one of them is the corner. How many are left for the new row and the new column together?

ask.ifNot: The 45 extra ones are a row, a column and 1 corner piece. Take the corner away, and what is left is the row and the column.

beats.say: 45 minus 1 is 44. That is the row and the column together.
The row and the column are the same length, so we halve. 44 divided by 2 is 22. The small square has 22 diyas on each side.
But the question asks about the larger square. Its side is 1 more: 22 plus 1 is 23.
So the larger square holds 23 times 23. 23 times 20 is 460, and 23 times 3 is 69. 460 plus 69 is 529.
The larger square has 529 diyas.
Check: the smaller square is 22 times 22, which is 484. And 529 minus 484 is 45, just as the story says.
Careful: 484 is among the choices too, but that is the smaller square. Always look back at which square the question asks for.
So the jump from one square to the next is always a row, a column and 1 corner. Take off the 1, halve, and you have the side.

Meera's mother put 8000 rupees in a bank and got back 9920 after 3 years. She then puts only the interest into a second bank, at 8 percent a year, for 2 years. How much interest does the second bank pay?

board.text: Second bank: the interest only, at 8% for 2 years

beats.say: What goes into the second bank?

choices: only the interest from the first bank
ask.ifNot: Read that line again: she deposits the interest she had earned. So the second bank's principal is just the extra money, not the whole amount.

beats.say: So first we find that interest. 9920 minus 8000 is 1920 rupees. That is the new principal.
The second bank pays 8 rupees on every 100, each year. So for 1 year we want 1920 times 8, divided by 100. First, 1920 times 8 is 15360.
Now divide 15360 by 100. What happens to the digits?

ask.ifNot: Dividing by 100 makes a number 100 times smaller. Every digit slides 2 places to the right, so a decimal point appears before the last 2 digits.

beats.say: 15360 divided by 100 is 153.60. That is 153 rupees and 60 paise of interest for 1 year.
For 2 years, double it. 153.60 times 2 is 307.20. That is 307 rupees and 20 paise.
A rough check: 8 percent of about 2000 rupees, for 2 years, is 320. Our 307.20 is close, and a little less, as it should be, because 1920 is a little less than 2000.
The first bank's 3 years are not needed at all. And the tempting slip is using 8000 or 9920 as the new principal.
Work out exactly what money goes into the bank. Then it is the usual interest: 1 year first, then times the years.
Riya ordered 74,208 packets of coloured powder. How many times the face value of the 8 is the place value of the 7?
Two different values are mixed here, so go slowly. First the 7: which place is it in?

ask.ifNot: Count from the right, one digit at a time: 8 is in the ones, 0 in the tens, 2 in the hundreds, 4 in the thousands, and 7 in the ten-thousands.

beats.say: So the 7 means 7 ten-thousands. 7 times 10,000 is 70,000.
Now the 8. The question asks for its face value, and face value is just the digit itself, wherever it sits. So that is 8.
Now, how many times 8 is 70,000? Which operation tells us?

ask.ifNot: How many times asks how many lots of 8 fit into 70,000. Counting how many fit is dividing, not subtracting.

beats.say: Dividing by 8 is the same as halving 3 times. Half of 70,000 is 35,000.
Half of 35,000 is 17,500, and half of 17,500 is 8,750.
So 70,000 divided by 8 is 8,750. The place value of the 7 is 8,750 times the face value of the 8.
Check by multiplying back: 8,750 times 8 is 70,000.
So: read which value is wanted for each digit, place or face. And how many times always means divide.
Arjun has 126 samosas and 90 gulab jamuns. Every plate must have the same number of samosas and the same number of gulab jamuns, with nothing left over. What is the greatest number of plates?
Every plate gets the same share of each pile. So the number of plates has to divide 126 and 90 exactly. We want the greatest number that does. What is it called?

ask.ifNot: A common multiple is at least as big as the biggest of these numbers, so it could never divide them all. We need a factor of both numbers, and the greatest one: the highest common factor.

beats.say: So our job is to find the highest common factor of 126 and 90.
Let's break each number into its prime factors, smallest first. 126 is 2 times 3 times 3 times 7.
And 90 is 2 times 3 times 3 times 5.
Now look at the 7. It is a factor of 126, but not of 90. Does 7 go into the highest common factor?

choices: Yes, it is a prime factor
No, it must be in both lists
ask.ifNot: A common factor has to divide every number. 7 does not divide 90, so it stays out.

beats.say: So we mark only what both lists share: 2, 3 and 3. Every other prime is missing from at least one list.
Now multiply the shared primes. 2 times 3 times 3 is 18. So the highest common factor is 18.
That is our answer. Arjun can make 18 plates.
Check. 126 divided by 18 is 7, and 90 divided by 18 is 5. Nothing is left over.
And 7 and 5 have no common factor bigger than 1, so no greater number of plates would work.
Remember the plan: prime factors, keep only what every list shares, and multiply. That gives the greatest number of equal plates.
Coach Sharma has 64 players standing in a square. Then 17 more join. What is the least number of extra players needed so that everyone can stand in a perfect square again?

board.text: 64 players in a square, 17 more join. How many more needed?

beats.say: First, how many players are there now? 64 plus 17 is 81.
Before we add anyone else, what should we check about 81?

choices: whether 81 is already a square number
ask.ifNot: The least number to add could be none at all. So first we test whether 81 players can already make a square.

beats.say: Is there a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 81? Yes: 9 times 9 is 81.
So the 81 players can already stand in 9 rows of 9. Nobody else is needed, and the answer is 0.
This question is a little sneaky. 17 and 81 are both among the choices, and both appear in our working. But the question asks how many more are needed, and that is none.
Here is why it worked out so neatly. The old square was 8 by 8. A row of 8, a column of 8 and 1 for the corner make 17, exactly what the next square needs.
So before adding anything to reach a square, always check whether you are standing on one already.
Kavya is given 1,200 rupees. She saves 25 percent in her piggy bank. From the rest she buys 8 packets of sparklers at 45 rupees each. How much is left?
Kavya puts 25 percent of the money in her piggy bank. Is that the same as 25 rupees?

choices: No: it is a share of the ₹1,200
ask.ifNot: Percent means out of every 100. So 25 percent is 25 rupees from every 100 rupees, and Kavya has more than 100. It is a share of the whole 1,200.

beats.say: 25 percent is one quarter, so we divide by 4. 1,200 divided by 4 is 300.
So 300 rupees went into the piggy bank. What do we do with that 300?

ask.ifNot: That 300 is money put away in the piggy bank. The question asks what is left, so it comes off the 1,200.

beats.say: 1,200 minus 300 is 900. That is what Kavya has after saving.
Next, the sparklers: 8 of them at 45 rupees each. 8 times 45 is 360.
Take that away too: 900 minus 360 is 540. So Kavya has 540 rupees left.
Check: 300 for the piggy bank, 360 for the sparklers, and 540 left over. Together they make 1,200, all the money from the start.
So: turn the percent into rupees, take it off, and then take off what was spent. Money saved and money spent both leave the purse.
Arjun puts 4000 rupees in a bank that pays 5 per cent simple interest a year, for 3 years. Then he buys a bat for 4500. We want what he has left.

board.text: ₹4,000 at 5% a year for 3 years. Bat costs ₹4,500.

beats.say: 5 per cent a year means every 100 rupees earns 5 rupees in a year. So how many hundreds are in 4000? 4000 divided by 100 is 40.
Each of those 40 hundreds earns 5 rupees. 40 times 5 is 200. So 1 year brings 200 rupees of interest.
The money stays in the bank for 3 years. So what is the interest altogether?

ask.ifNot: Simple interest pays the same 200 rupees every single year. So 3 years means 3 lots of 200.

beats.say: 3 lots of 200 is 600. That is all the interest Arjun earns.
Careful here: the bank gives back his 4000 as well as the interest. 4000 plus 600 is 4600.
Now the bat. 4600 minus 4500 leaves 100 rupees.
Check by going back. The bat, 4500, plus the 100 left over, is 4600. That is exactly what the bank gave him.
So the plan is: interest for 1 year, times the years, add it to the deposit, and only then do the shopping.
Rohit bats for 2 sessions. We know the overs and the runs per over in each. How many runs does he score altogether?
Runs per over, times the number of overs, gives the runs. So each session is one multiplication, and then we add the two.
First session: 12.5 times 6.4. Split 12.5 into 10 and 2.5. 10 times 6.4 is 64.
And 2.5 times 6.4? Here is a hint: 2.5 is a quarter of 10.

ask.ifNot: 10 times 6.4 was 64. And 2.5 is a quarter of 10, so we want a quarter of 64. 4 times 16 is 64, so a quarter of 64 is 16.

beats.say: 64 plus 16 is 80 runs in the first session.
Second session: 7.5 times 8.2. 7 times 8.2 is 57.4, and half of 8.2 is 4.1.
57.4 plus 4.1 is 61.5 runs in the second session.
Altogether: 80 plus 61.5 is 141.5 runs.
Check the second session another way. 7.5 times 8 is 60, and 7.5 times 0.2 is 1.5. That makes 61.5 again.
Careful not to drop the 0.5 at the end of 61.5: one of the choices is waiting for that slip. Split an awkward decimal into easy pieces, multiply each, and add.
Team A scored 248 and 176 in its two innings. Team B scored 195 and 213. We want to know by how many runs the winning team won.

board.text: Team A: 248 and 176.   Team B: 195 and 213.

beats.say: Team A scored more in the first innings, and Team B scored more in the second. Can we name the winner yet?

choices: No: add each team's two innings
Yes: Team A, it has the top score
Yes: Team B, it won the last innings
ask.ifNot: A match is decided by the runs over both innings together. One good innings is not enough, so add up each team's two scores.

beats.say: Team A first. 248 plus 176 is 424.
Now Team B. 195 plus 213 is 408.
424 is more than 408, so Team A wins. By how many? Mind the borrowing here: 424 minus 408 is 16.
So Team A won by 16 runs.
Careful: comparing just one innings gives a different gap. Only the totals decide a match.
Check by adding on. Team B's 408 plus 16 is 424, which is Team A's total.
So to find a winning margin: total each team, see which is bigger, and subtract the smaller from it.
Ravi and his grandfather walk once round a park that is 400 metres long and 200 metres wide, at 3 kilometres an hour. We want the time in minutes.

board.text: Park 400 m by 200 m, speed 3 km/hr, time in minutes?

beats.say: One full round means walking along the boundary. So what do we find first?

ask.ifNot: Walking round the park means going along all 4 sides. Two sides are 400 metres and two are 200 metres, so we need the perimeter.

beats.say: One long side and one short side make 400 plus 200, which is 600. There are two of each, so 2 times 600 is 1200. One round is 1200 metres.
Now the trap. The distance is in metres, but the speed is in kilometres an hour. Before we divide, the units have to match.
3 kilometres is 3000 metres, and an hour is 60 minutes. So they walk 3000 metres in 60 minutes.

board.text: 3 km in 1 hr = 3000 m in 60 min

beats.say: How many metres do they walk in just 1 minute?

ask.ifNot: The 3000 metres are spread equally over 60 minutes. So we share 3000 by 60 to find the metres in one minute.

beats.say: 3000 divided by 60 is 50. They walk 50 metres every minute.
So how many minutes for 1200 metres? 1200 divided by 50 is 24. One round takes 24 minutes.
Check: 24 minutes at 50 metres a minute is 24 times 50, which is 1200 metres. That is exactly one round.
So the plan is: find the distance, make the units match, and then time is distance divided by speed.
Ravi has a paper triangle. He measures two of its angles: 60 degrees and 70 degrees. What kind of triangle is it, going by its angles?
We cannot name the triangle until we know all three angles. So first, the rule: the three angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: Add the two we know. 60 plus 70 is 130.
Now, which sum gives the third angle?

ask.ifNot: The three angles share 180 degrees. Two of them use up 130, so the third is what is left over.

beats.say: 180 minus 130 is 50. So the third angle is 50 degrees.
Now we can name the triangle by its angles. If all three angles are less than 90 degrees, it is acute. If one is exactly 90, it is right. If one is more than 90, it is obtuse.

board.text: Acute: all three angles less than 90°
Obtuse: one angle is more than 90°

beats.say: Our angles are 60, 70 and 50. Is any of them 90 degrees or more?

ask.ifNot: Compare each angle with 90, one at a time: 60, then 70, then 50. Is any of them as big as 90?

beats.say: None of them. All three angles are less than 90 degrees, so this is an acute triangle.
Check the angles: 60 plus 70 plus 50 is 180.
With only two angles you cannot be sure. The hidden third angle might have been the big one! That is why we found it first.
So: find the third angle from 180, then compare all three angles with 90.
Arjun's dad buys 50 kilograms of mangoes at 40 rupees a kilogram, and pays 200 rupees for transport. He sells all the mangoes at 52 rupees a kilogram. What is his profit?

board.text: 50 kg at ₹40, transport ₹200; sold at ₹52 per kg

beats.say: Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out. The mangoes: 50 times 40 is 2,000 rupees.
Now add the transport. 2,000 plus 200 is 2,200 rupees. That is everything Arjun's dad spent.
Now the money coming in. 50 kilograms at 52 rupees a kilogram: 50 times 52 is 2,600 rupees. That is all the money earned.
Arjun's dad took in 2,600 rupees. Is all of that profit?

ask.ifNot: Part of that 2,600 rupees only pays back the 2,200 rupees Arjun's dad spent. Profit is what is left after the cost comes off.

beats.say: Last step: 2,600 minus 2,200 is 400. Arjun's dad makes a profit of 400 rupees.
The slip to watch for is forgetting the transport. Bringing the mangoes to the stall cost money, so it joins the cost.
Check by adding back. 400 plus 2,200 is 2,600, exactly the money that came in.
So the method is: total cost first, total sales next, and profit is sales take away cost.
Ankit's family sold 1,548 cups of chai at 12 rupees each. Each cup cost 8 rupees to make. We want the profit for the day.

board.text: 1,548 cups sold at ₹12. Each cup costs ₹8 to make

beats.say: The story also says each pot makes 36 cups. Do we need that to find the profit?

ask.ifNot: We already know how many cups were sold: 1,548. The pots do not change the money, so the 36 is extra information.

beats.say: The profit on one cup is what it sells for, minus what it costs. 12 minus 8 is 4 rupees.
So every cup brings 4 rupees of profit, and there are 1,548 cups.
Split 1,548 into 1500 and 48. 1500 times 4 is 6000. 48 times 4 is 192.
6000 plus 192 is 6192. The profit is 6,192 rupees.
The trap is stopping at the sales. 1,548 times 12 is all the money taken in, but 8 rupees of every 12 went on milk, sugar and tea leaves.
Check the long way. Money in is 18,576. Money out is 12,384. And 18,576 minus 12,384 is 6,192.
So find the profit on one cup, then multiply by the number of cups. And leave out numbers the question does not need.
Ananya's garden is a triangle. The distance round it is 72 metres, and its sides are in the ratio 3 to 4 to 5. We want its area.

board.text: Triangle: perimeter 72 m, sides in ratio 3 : 4 : 5

beats.say: A ratio is about equal parts. The sides are 3 parts, 4 parts and 5 parts. How many parts make up the whole 72 metres?

ask.ifNot: The 72 metres is all three sides put together. So we add the parts: 3 and 4 and 5.

beats.say: 3 plus 4 plus 5 is 12 parts. So 1 part is 72 divided by 12, which is 6 metres.
Now the sides. 3 parts is 18 metres, 4 parts is 24 metres, and 5 parts is 30 metres.
The question hints that this triangle is special. Test it: 18 times 18 is 324, and 24 times 24 is 576. Together, 900. And 30 times 30 is 900 as well.
When the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side, the triangle has a right angle. So 18 and 24 meet at a square corner: they are the base and the height.
So which sum gives the area of this right-angled triangle?

ask.ifNot: A right-angled triangle is half of a rectangle, so we must halve. And we use the two sides that meet at the right angle, 18 and 24, not the slanted side.

beats.say: 18 times 20 is 360, and 18 times 4 is 72, so 18 times 24 is 432. Half of 432 is 216 square metres.
A quick check on the sides: 18 plus 24 plus 30 is 72, the perimeter we were given.
So: share the perimeter by the ratio to get the sides, spot the right angle, then take half of base times height. The answer is 216 square metres.
Deepa has 360 rupees for her art project. She spends 25 percent on paint brushes, and then 95 rupees on a sketch pad. How much is left?

board.text: ₹360. 25% on brushes, then ₹95 on a sketch pad.

beats.say: The paint brushes cost 25 percent of the money. Is that the same as 25 rupees?

choices: No: it is a share of the ₹360
ask.ifNot: Percent means out of every 100. So 25 percent is 25 rupees from every 100 rupees, and Deepa has more than 100. It is a share of the whole 360.

beats.say: 25 percent is one quarter, so we divide by 4. 360 divided by 4 is 90.
So 90 rupees went on the paint brushes. What do we do with that 90?

ask.ifNot: That 90 is money that has been spent. The question asks what is left, so it comes off the 360.

beats.say: 360 minus 90 is 270. That is what Deepa has after the paint brushes.
Then the sketch pad: 270 minus 95 is 175. So Deepa has 175 rupees left.
Check: 90 for the paint brushes, 95 for the sketch pad, and 175 left over. Together they make 360, all the money from the start.
Remember: a percent is a share, not a number of rupees. Change it into rupees, and the rest is plain subtraction.
Ravi takes 500 rupees to the Diwali mela. He buys sparklers for 127, rangoli colours for 89 and sweets for 156. Going home, he finds 20 rupees and keeps it. How much does he have now?
Sort the amounts before adding anything. Which ones did Ravi pay out?

ask.ifNot: He paid for sparklers, colours and sweets, so 127, 89 and 156 went out. The 20 he found came in.

beats.say: Add up the spending first. 127 plus 89 is 216, and 156 more makes 372.
Now take that from the 500 Ravi started with. Careful: borrowing across those zeros is where slips happen.
So here is a trick: take 1 off both numbers, and the gap between them stays the same. 499 minus 371 needs no borrowing, and it is 128.
So 128 rupees are left after the shopping. Is that our final answer?

ask.ifNot: The story carries on after the mela. He found 20 rupees and kept it, so his money grows by 20.

beats.say: 128 plus 20 is 148. So Ravi has 148 rupees now.
Check by walking backwards. Take away the 20 that came in, and we are at 128. Put back the 372 that went out, and we are at 500, where Ravi began.
So in a money story, sort the amounts first. Add up what goes out, take it from the start, then add what comes in.
Rohan's team made 48 runs, then 5 batsmen made 12 each, the rest made 15, and 3 runs were taken off 2 times as a penalty. Here is the line.
Don't rush in from the left. Which piece of this line has to be done first?

ask.ifNot: Times is stronger than plus and minus, so it goes first, wherever it sits in the line. Here that is 5 times 12.

beats.say: Starting on the left with 48 plus 5 is the classic slip. Times goes before plus, so 5 times 12 is first, and that makes 60.
There is another times waiting: 3 times 2 is 6. Write the line again with 60 and 6 in place.
Only plus and minus are left now, so we go left to right: 48 plus 60 is 108.
Keep going: 108 plus 15 is 123.
And 123 minus 6 is 117. The team's total is 117 runs.
Let's check by undoing our steps. 117 plus 6 is 123, and 123 minus 15 is 108, just as it says on the board.
So remember: times and divide go first, wherever they sit in the line. Then plus and minus, from left to right.
Ravi deposits 4500 rupees at 6 per cent. Priya deposits 3500 at 8 per cent. We want to know when their interest will be the same.
Let's see what each of them earns in 1 year. Ravi first. 4500 is 45 hundreds, and each hundred earns 6 rupees. 45 times 6 is 270.
Now Priya. 3500 is 35 hundreds, and each hundred earns 8 rupees. 35 times 8 is 280.
So every year Ravi gets 270 and Priya gets 280. As the years go by, what happens to the gap between them?

choices: It shrinks until they are level
ask.ifNot: Each year Priya adds 10 rupees more than Ravi does. So she is 10 ahead after 1 year, and every year after that puts another 10 on the gap.

beats.say: Here are the first 3 years in a table. After 3 years Ravi has 810 and Priya has 840. Priya is ahead in every row.
They both start from 0, and Priya pulls ahead in the very first year. Ravi never catches up, so their interest can never be equal.

board.text: Never equal: Priya always earns more

beats.say: The trap is to look at only one thing. Ravi has more money in the bank, but Priya has the higher rate. Only the interest for a year settles it.
So to compare two deposits, work out 1 year for each. If one earns more every year, it stays ahead for good.
Sneha has 15.6 kilograms of besan. She uses 2.35 kilograms a day for 4 days, and on day 5 she uses all that is left. How much is that?

board.text: 15.6 kg of besan. Uses 2.35 kg a day for 4 days.

beats.say: What do we need before we can find day 5?

ask.ifNot: She uses 2.35 kilograms on each of 4 days, not just once. And day 5 is not an equal share: it is whatever is left. So first find what the 4 days used.

beats.say: 4 times 2.35. Double it: 4.70. Double again: 9.40. So 9.40 kilograms are gone after 4 days.
Now subtract from 15.6. Write it as 15.60, so the decimal points line up.
15.60 minus 9.40 is 6.20. On day 5 she uses 6.20 kilograms.
Check: 9.40 used in 4 days, plus 6.20 on day 5, is 15.60. That is all the besan.
Notice that day 5 uses far more than the other days. That is fine: the story says she uses whatever is left.
So multiply for the equal days, then subtract from the start. And write in a zero when one number has fewer decimal places.
Team Lotus has the code 63,242. The digit 2 is there twice, in the hundreds place and in the units place. How many times as big is the place value of the first 2?
Same digit, different seats. The 2 in the hundreds place means 2 hundreds: 2 times 100 is 200.
The 2 at the end is in the units place. 2 times 1 is just 2.
How many times 2 is 200? Which operation tells us?

ask.ifNot: How many times asks how many lots of 2 fit into 200. Counting how many fit is dividing, not subtracting.

beats.say: 200 divided by 2 is 100. The 2 in the hundreds place is worth 100 times the 2 in the units place.
Here is why. Each step to the left makes a digit 10 times bigger. From units to hundreds is 2 steps, and 10 times 10 is 100.
Check by multiplying back: 100 times 2 is 200.
So the same digit can be worth very different amounts. Its seat decides, and how many times means divide.
Riya writes 76,258 on the board. We want the difference between the place value of the 6 and the place value of the 2.
Place value depends on where a digit sits. Start with the 6: which place is it in?

ask.ifNot: Count from the right, one digit at a time: 8 is in the ones, 5 in the tens, 2 in the hundreds, and 6 in the thousands.

beats.say: So the 6 means 6 thousands. 6 times 1,000 is 6,000.
Now the 2. It sits in the hundreds place, so it means 2 times 100, which is 200.
Which subtraction gives the difference between the place values?

ask.ifNot: The question asks about place values, so we use what each digit is worth: 6,000 and 200, not the bare digits 6 and 2.

beats.say: 6,000 minus 200 is 5,800. Take care with the zeros: we are taking away 2 hundreds.
Check by adding back: 5,800 plus 200 is 6,000.
So: find the place of each digit first. The 6 here was in the thousands, not the ten-thousands. Then subtract the place values.
Kavya's dad buys 8 cups of chai at 15 rupees each, and 12 samosas at 20 rupees each. He gets 10 percent off the total bill. How much does he pay?
Start with the chai. 8 cups at 15 rupees each: 8 times 15 is 120.
Now the samosas. 12 of them at 20 rupees each: 12 times 20 is 240.
Add the two for the whole bill. 120 plus 240 is 360.
Now the 10 percent discount. What do we do with it?

choices: find 10% of 360: that is the answer
ask.ifNot: 10 percent is not 10 rupees. It is one tenth of the bill. And a discount is taken off, so we subtract it from the 360.

beats.say: 10 percent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 360 divided by 10 is 36.
Take the discount off the bill. 360 minus 36 is 324, so Kavya's dad pays 324 rupees.
Check: the 324 he pays and the 36 he saves should make the full bill of 360. And they do.
So with a discount on a whole bill: add up the bill first, find the percent of that total, and take it off.
Priya's line for the samosas she sold has two pairs of brackets, and one of them has a times hiding inside it.
Don't rush in from the left. Which piece of this line has to be done first?

ask.ifNot: Look for the brackets. Whatever sits inside them is worked out before anything else, so 6 plus 2 goes first.

beats.say: Brackets come first, and there are two pairs. In the first pair, 6 plus 2 is 8.
In the second pair, times goes before minus, so 3 times 4 is 12. Write the line again with those in place.
Now finish the bracket: 15 minus 12 is 3.
No brackets are left, so now we look for times and divide. 8 times 3 is 24.
There is another times waiting: 5 times 2 is 10. Write the line again with 24 and 10 in place.
Only plus and minus are left: 150 minus 24 plus 10. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we read from left to right, like a sentence. That means 150 minus 24 comes first.

beats.say: Left to right it is: 150 minus 24 is 126.
And 126 plus 10 is 136. Priya sold 136 samosas.
Check by walking backwards. 136 minus 10 is 126, and 126 plus 24 is 150, right where that line started.
So every time: clear the brackets, then do times and divide as you meet them, then finish with plus and minus, left to right.
A train leaves at 7:30 in the morning and arrives at 12:30. It runs at 60 kilometres an hour for 2 hours, stops for 30 minutes, then runs at 90 kilometres an hour. How far is the whole trip?

board.text: 7:30 to 12:30: 60 km/hr for 2 hr, stop 30 min, 90 km/hr

beats.say: The first part is ready to go. 60 kilometres an hour for 2 hours is 60 times 2, which is 120 kilometres.
For the second part we know the speed, 90, but not the time. So first: how long is the whole trip, from 7:30 to 12:30?

ask.ifNot: The minutes are the same at both ends, so just count the hours from 7 up to 12. That is 5 hours.

beats.say: The whole trip is 5 hours. Take away the 2 hours of the first part, and the half hour at the station. 5 minus 2 minus a half leaves 2.5 hours, that is 2 and a half hours.
Careful here: the 30 minutes at the station use up time, but the train covers no distance while it stands still.
Now the second part: 90 kilometres an hour for 2.5 hours. How do we find its distance?

ask.ifNot: Distance is speed times time. The speed is 90, and the time for this part is 2.5 hours, not the whole 5.

beats.say: 2 hours at 90 is 180 kilometres. The extra half hour adds half of 90, which is 45. So the second part is 225 kilometres.
Add the two parts. 120 plus 225 is 345. The whole trip is 345 kilometres.
Check the time: 2 hours, plus half an hour, plus 2.5 hours makes 5 hours, from 7:30 to 12:30. It fits.
So when a trip comes in parts: find the time for each part, use speed times time for each distance, then add the distances.
Neha and Kavitha run towards each other from the two ends of a 600 metre track. Neha runs 5 metres a second and Kavitha 3. When they meet, Neha turns and runs back to her start at 4 metres a second.

board.text: 600 m track: Neha 5 m/s, Kavitha 3 m/s; Neha back at 4 m/s

beats.say: There are two stretches of time to find: the time until they meet, and the time Neha takes to run back. Then we add them.
Each second, Neha covers 5 metres and Kavitha covers 3. By how much does the gap between them shrink each second?

ask.ifNot: They run towards each other, so both of them eat into the gap. Neha takes 5 metres off it and Kavitha takes 3, so it shrinks by 8 metres each second.

beats.say: The gap starts at 600 metres and shrinks by 8 metres a second. 600 divided by 8 is 75, so they meet after 75 seconds.
How far has Neha run by then? 5 metres a second for 75 seconds is 5 times 75, which is 375 metres.
Now she turns and runs back to her start. How far does she have to run?

ask.ifNot: She goes back the way she came. She is 375 metres from her starting point, so that is how far she runs back.

beats.say: 375 metres at 4 metres a second means 375 divided by 4. Half of 375 is 187.5, and half of that is 93.75. The run back takes 93.75 seconds.
Add the two times. 75 plus 93.75 is 168.75 seconds.
The trap is stopping at 75 seconds. That is only when the girls meet. The question asks for the time until Neha is back where she started.
Check the run back: 93.75 seconds at 4 metres a second is 375 metres, exactly as far as she ran out.
So when two runners come towards each other, add their speeds to see how fast the gap closes. Then take the story one stretch at a time.
Team India scored 247 and 189 in their two innings. Team Australia scored 312 in their first. How many runs does Team Australia need in the second innings to tie?

board.text: Team India: 247 and 189.   Team Australia: 312 and ?

beats.say: Start with Team India's two innings. 247 plus 189 is 436.
To tie the match, what must Team Australia's total be at the end?

ask.ifNot: A tie means both teams finish on exactly the same total. So Team Australia must end on 436, no more and no less.

beats.say: Team Australia already has 312 from the first innings, so the second innings must bring the rest. 436 minus 312 is 124.
So the second innings for Team Australia must be 124 runs.
Careful not to answer 436. That is the whole total Team Australia needs, and 312 of it is already on the scoreboard.
Check: 312 plus 124 is 436, level with Team India. A tie.
So a target question has two steps: build the total to be matched, then take away the runs already scored.
Some money is in a bank at simple interest. After 3 years it has become 6500 rupees, and after 5 years, 7500. We want the money first put in, and the interest after 7 years.
Between year 3 and year 5 the amount grew. What made it grow?

ask.ifNot: Nothing new was put in. The only thing added between year 3 and year 5 is the interest for those 2 extra years.

beats.say: So 2 years of interest is 7500 minus 6500, which is 1000.
Simple interest is the same every year. So 1 year is half of 1000, which is 500 rupees.
After 3 years the amount was 6500. How do we get back to the money first put in?

ask.ifNot: The 6500 is the starting money with 3 years of interest on top. To get back to the start, peel those 3 years off.

beats.say: 3 years of interest is 3 times 500, which is 1500. And 6500 minus 1500 is 5000. So the principal is 5000 rupees.
Now 7 years of interest. 7 times 500 is 3500.
Check with the other fact. 5 years of interest is 5 times 500, which is 2500. And 5000 plus 2500 is 7500, just as the question says.
So when you know the amount at two different times, the difference is pure interest. Find 1 year of it, then peel the interest off to reach the principal.
Arjun's samosas go into groups of 2, or 3, or 5, with none left over each time. He has more than 50 but fewer than 80.

board.text: Groups of 2, 3 or 5: none left over

beats.say: Nothing left over in 2s, 3s or 5s. So the number is a multiple of 2, and of 3, and of 5, all at the same time.
What is the smallest number that 2, 3 and 5 all divide?

ask.ifNot: 10 splits into 2s and 5s, but not into 3s. 15 splits into 3s and 5s, but not into 2s. We need all three at once, and that first happens at 30.

beats.say: 2 times 3 times 5 is 30. Every number that works is a multiple of 30.
Which one is more than 50 and fewer than 80? 30 is too small and 90 is too big. Only 60 fits.
Check. 60 divided by 2 is 30. 60 divided by 3 is 20. 60 divided by 5 is 12. No remainders.
Careful with the other choices. 70 will not split into 3s, 75 will not split into 2s, and 72 will not split into 5s. Each one passes two tests but not all three.
So when a number must split into several group sizes, find the smallest number they all share, then count in that.
Anita's grandmother sells rangoli powder at 8 rupees for every 100 grams. The shopkeeper orders 48 red bags, 36 yellow bags and 64 green bags, and each colour has its own bag size.

board.text: Red 48 × 125 g, yellow 36 × 250 g, green 64 × 75 g

beats.say: The price is for grams, not for bags. So what must we find before we can work out the cost?

ask.ifNot: Look at the price again: 8 rupees for every 100 grams. It is all about weight, so first we need the total grams of powder.

beats.say: Red first: 48 bags of 125 grams. 40 bags weigh 5000 grams and 8 bags weigh 1000 grams, so red is 6000 grams.
Yellow: 36 bags of 250 grams. 4 of those bags make 1000 grams, and 36 bags is 9 lots of 4. So yellow is 9000 grams.
Green: 64 bags of 75 grams. 60 bags weigh 4500 grams and 4 bags weigh 300 grams, so green is 4800 grams.
Now add the three colours. 6000 plus 9000 is 15,000, and 4800 more makes 19,800 grams of powder.
Now the money. 8 rupees pays for a whole 100 grams. What do we do with 19,800?

ask.ifNot: The 8 rupees pays for 100 grams, not for 1 gram. So first count how many hundreds of grams there are, then multiply by 8.

beats.say: 19,800 divided by 100 is 198. So there are 198 lots of 100 grams.
Each lot costs 8 rupees. 200 times 8 is 1600, and we have 2 lots fewer, so take off 16. That leaves 1584 rupees.
Check it the long way. 198 times 8 really is 1584. And notice that adding up the bags would not have helped, because the bags are different sizes.
So when a price is for a weight: find the total weight, count how many lots of that weight you have, then multiply by the price.
Priya has 100 rupees. She buys 6 boxes of sparklers at 9 rupees each, then shares what is left equally between her 2 cousins.
What do we need to find first?

ask.ifNot: The cousins only share what is left after the shopping. So first we need to know what the sparklers cost: 6 boxes at 9 rupees each.

beats.say: 6 times 9 is 54. The sparklers cost 54 rupees.
Take that away from her 100 rupees. 100 minus 54 is 46, so 46 rupees are left.
Now share the 46 rupees between the 2 cousins. 46 divided by 2 is 23, so each cousin gets 23 rupees.
As one line it looks like this. The brackets say: finish the shopping first, and only then share.
Careful: 46 is one of the choices, but 46 is the money left over. The question asks for one cousin's share, so there is still a divide to do.
Check: 23 plus 23 is 46, and 46 plus 54 is 100. Every rupee is accounted for.
So follow the story in order: spend first, see what is left, then share it out.
Deepa's mom spends 250 rupees on silk threads, 150 on decorative stones and 100 on packaging. She makes 25 rakhi sets, gives 5 away as gifts, and sells the rest at 40 rupees each.
Profit is the money that comes in, take away the money that goes out. So we need two totals: what Deepa's mom spent, and what she earned.
Start with the money going out: the silk threads, the stones and the packaging. 250 plus 150 plus 100 is 500 rupees, and that is everything Deepa's mom spent.
She made 25 rakhi sets. But how many were actually sold?

ask.ifNot: Look at the story again: 5 sets were given as gifts. They bring in no money, so they come off. 25 minus 5 is 20.

beats.say: 25 minus 5 is 20, so 20 sets were sold. The cost does not shrink, though: all 25 were paid for.
Now the money coming in. 20 rakhi sets at 40 rupees each: 20 times 40 is 800 rupees. That is all the money earned.
Last step: 800 minus 500 is 300. Deepa's mom makes a profit of 300 rupees.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 300 plus 500 is 800. It fits.
So in a story like this: all the costs count, but only the things really sold bring money in. Then subtract.
Coach Sharma shares 84 balls between Team Sixer and Team Boundary in the ratio 3 to 4. Later, 5 balls move from Team Boundary to Team Sixer. We want the new ratio.

board.text: Then 5 balls go from Boundary to Sixer

beats.say: Read the ratio as parts: 3 parts for Team Sixer and 4 parts for Team Boundary, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.

spec.note: All the boxes together: 84 balls

beats.say: Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 4 make 7 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 4 is 7. So the 84 balls are shared into 7 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 84 divided by 7 is 12, so each part is 12 balls. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 7 parts.
Team Sixer has 3 parts: 3 times 12 is 36. Team Boundary has 4 parts: 4 times 12 is 48.
Now 5 balls move from Team Boundary to Team Sixer. What happens to the two numbers?

ask.ifNot: The 5 balls leave Team Boundary, so Boundary loses 5. They arrive at Team Sixer, so Sixer gains 5. Both numbers change.

beats.say: 36 plus 5 is 41 for Team Sixer. 48 minus 5 is 43 for Team Boundary.
So the new ratio is 41 to 43. No number bigger than 1 divides both 41 and 43, so it cannot be made any simpler.
Check: no ball was lost, they only changed teams. 41 plus 43 is still 84.
So the plan: share in the ratio first to get real numbers, make the change the story describes to those numbers, then write the new ratio.
Sanya's flag is a triangle with exactly two equal sides, and the angle between those two sides is 40 degrees. We want each of the other two angles.

board.text: Two equal sides, angle between them = 40°

beats.say: A triangle with two equal sides is called isosceles. Its special trick: the two angles opposite the equal sides are equal to each other.

board.text: The other two angles are equal

beats.say: Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So the 40 and the two equal angles make 180. Take the 40 away: 180 minus 40 is 140.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: That 140 is for both of the equal angles together. So how big is each one?

ask.ifNot: The 140 is shared by two angles of the same size. Sharing equally between 2 means dividing by 2.

beats.say: 140 divided by 2 is 70. Careful: this is where many people stop at 140, but that is two angles, not one.
So each of the other two angles is 70 degrees.
Check: 40 plus 70 plus 70 is 180. It fits.
So for a triangle with two equal sides: take the angle between them from 180, then halve what is left.
Aarav and his mother are tiling two walls, one 120 centimetres wide and one 90 centimetres wide. They want the largest square tile that fits across both walls with no cutting.

board.text: Walls: 120 cm and 90 cm wide. Largest square tile?

beats.say: Whole tiles must fit across each wall, with no cutting. So the side of a tile has to divide 120 and 90 exactly. We want the greatest number that does. What is it called?

ask.ifNot: A common multiple is at least as big as the biggest of these numbers, so it could never divide them all. We need a factor of both numbers, and the greatest one: the highest common factor.

beats.say: So our job is to find the highest common factor of 120 and 90.
The sure way is prime factors. Break each number down, smallest prime first. 120 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
And 90 is 2 times 3 times 3 times 5.
Now count how many times 2 appears. In 120 it appears 3 times, and in 90 it appears once. How many times can 2 go into the highest common factor?

ask.ifNot: A common factor has to fit inside every one of the numbers. In 90, 2 appears only once, so once is all we can take.

beats.say: So we mark only what both lists share: 2, 3 and 5.
Now multiply the shared primes. 2 times 3 times 5 is 30. So the highest common factor is 30.
So the largest tile has a side of 30 centimetres. That is our answer.
Check. 120 divided by 30 is 4, and 90 divided by 30 is 3. Nothing is left over.
And 4 and 3 have no common factor bigger than 1, so no bigger tile would fit both.
The largest tile that fits two widths exactly is the highest common factor of the widths.
Riya writes 72,508. She swaps the digit in the thousands place with the digit in the tens place. What is the difference between the original number and the new one?
Which two digits change seats?

ask.ifNot: Count from the right, one digit at a time: 8 is in the ones, 0 in the tens, 5 in the hundreds, and 2 in the thousands. So the 2 and the 0 change seats.

beats.say: Swap them. The 0 goes to the thousands place and the 2 goes to the tens place. Every other digit stays, so the new number is 70,528.
We could subtract the long way. But look closer: only the 2 really moved, because the 0 is worth nothing in any seat.
In the thousands place the 2 was worth 2,000. In the tens place it is worth only 20.
So the number lost 2,000 and got 20 back. 2,000 minus 20 is 1,980.
Careful: the difference is not 2,000. The 2 did not vanish. It still counts for 20 in its new seat.
Check by adding back: 70,528 plus 1,980 is 72,508, the number Riya started with.
So when digits swap seats, ask what each one was worth before and after. The change in worth is the change in the number.
Meera's uncle buys 80 diyas at 5 rupees each. He spends 120 rupees on paint and glitter, and 80 rupees on packaging. He sells 60 diyas at 12 rupees each and gives the other 20 away as gifts.

board.text: 80 diyas at ₹5, paint ₹120, packaging ₹80; 60 sold at ₹12

beats.say: Profit is the money that comes in, take away the money that goes out. So we need two totals: what Meera's uncle spent, and what he earned.
Start with the money going out. The diyas: 80 times 5 is 400 rupees.
Now add the paint and glitter and the packaging. 400 plus 120 plus 80 is 600 rupees. That is everything Meera's uncle spent.
Now the money coming in. 60 diyas at 12 rupees each: 60 times 12 is 720 rupees. That is all the money earned.
720 rupees came in. So is the profit 720 rupees?

ask.ifNot: Part of that 720 rupees only pays back the 600 rupees Meera's uncle spent. Profit is what is left after the cost comes off.

beats.say: Now subtract. 720 minus 600 is 120. Meera's uncle makes a profit of 120 rupees.
Notice the 20 diyas he gave away. They earn nothing, yet he paid for all 80. So the cost uses 80 diyas, and the sales use only 60.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 120 plus 600 is 720. It fits.
So the method is: total cost first, total sales next, and profit is sales take away cost.
Priya's rangoli has 5 dots in row 1, 8 in row 2 and 11 in row 3, growing by the same amount each time, up to row 15. How many dots does she use across all 15 rows?
First, the jump. 8 minus 5 is 3, and 11 minus 8 is 3 as well. So each row has 3 more dots than the row before.
Adding 15 numbers one by one is slow, so we will use a shortcut. For it we need the last one, row 15. How many jumps of 3 is that from row 1?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps, not the rows. From row 1 to row 2 is 1 jump, and to row 3 is 2 jumps. The jumps are always one fewer than the row number.

beats.say: 15 minus 1 is 14 jumps. And 14 jumps of 3 is 42.
Add that to row 1. 5 plus 42 is 47, so row 15 is 47.
Careful: 47 is only row 15, and it is one of the choices. We want all 15 rows together.
Here is the shortcut. Pair the first with the last: 5 plus 47 is 52. Now pair the second with the second last, 8 and 44. What will they make?

ask.ifNot: 8 is 3 more than 5, and 44 is 3 less than 47. One goes up by 3 and the other comes down by 3, so the total stays the same.

beats.say: 8 plus 44 is 52 as well. Every pair, working inwards, makes 52.
15 numbers make 7 pairs, with one number left over in the middle. 7 pairs of 52 is 364.
The middle one sits exactly halfway between 5 and 47, so it is half of 52, which is 26.
364 plus 26 is 390. Priya uses 390 dots across all 15 rows.
Let's check the slow way. The first 8 rows add up to 124, the other 7 add up to 266, and 124 plus 266 is 390. It matches.
So remember the shortcut: last number first, then first plus last, then times the number of pairs.
Meera goes to a Diwali mela with 500 rupees. She spends 30 percent on bangles, and then 40 percent of the remaining money on sweets. How much does she have left?

board.text: ₹500. 30% on bangles, then 40% of the rest.

beats.say: We take the story one step at a time, in order. First, the bangles: 30 percent of 500.
Start small, with 10 percent. That is one tenth, so 500 divided by 10 is 50.
Now build up. 30 percent is 3 times as much, and 3 times 50 is 150.
500 minus 150 is 350. That is the money left after the bangles.
Next, 40 percent of the remaining money goes on sweets. 40 percent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: Listen for the words about what is left. After the bangles, only 350 remains. So this percent is taken from 350, not from 500.

beats.say: That is the trap here: taking both percents of 500. The second percent is of the 350 that is left.
Find 10 percent first, because that is easy: one tenth. 350 divided by 10 is 35.
Now build up. 40 percent is 4 times as much, and 4 times 35 is 140.
So 140 rupees go on the sweets. 350 minus 140 leaves Meera with 210 rupees.
Check: 150 for the bangles, 140 for the sweets, and 210 left. Add them, and we are back at 500.
With two percents, always ask, percent of what? The first was of all the money. The second was only of what was left.
Rohan has two trays. One holds a perfect square number of samosas, and the other holds the very next perfect square number. Together they hold 85. How many are on the larger tray?
Let's write out the square numbers, so we can see the neighbours side by side.
The two trays hold nearly the same amount, and 85 together. Roughly how big is each one?

ask.ifNot: Two numbers that are close together and add up to 85 must each be near half of 85, which is a little over 40.

beats.say: So we want neighbours in the list that sit either side of 40 or so. That points at 36 and 49.
Test them. 36 plus 49 is 85. That's our pair.
36 is 6 times 6 and 49 is 7 times 7, so they really are squares next door to each other. The larger tray holds 49 samosas.
Careful: 36 is among the choices too. It is the smaller tray, and the question asks for the larger one.
Check the pairs on either side. 25 plus 36 is 61, too small. 49 plus 64 is 113, too big. Only 36 and 49 work.
So when two neighbouring squares add up to a total, look near half of the total, then test the pair.
Meera's father buys 80 boxes of sweets at 125 rupees each. He spends 400 rupees on ribbons and 200 rupees on gift bags. He sells 60 boxes at 200 rupees each, and the other 20 at 150 rupees each.

board.text: 80 boxes at ₹125, ribbons ₹400, bags ₹200; 60 and 20 sold

beats.say: Profit is the money that comes in, take away the money that goes out. So we need two totals: what Meera's father spent, and what he earned.
Start with the money going out. The boxes: 80 times 125 is 10,000 rupees.
Now add the ribbons and the gift bags. 10,000 plus 400 plus 200 is 10,600 rupees. That is everything Meera's father spent.
Now the money coming in. 60 boxes at the full price of 200 rupees: 60 times 200 is 12,000 rupees.
Then 20 boxes at the lower price of 150 rupees: 20 times 150 is 3,000 rupees.
Put the sales together: 12,000 plus 3,000 is 15,000 rupees. That is the money earned.
15,000 rupees came in. So is the profit 15,000 rupees?

ask.ifNot: Part of that 15,000 rupees only pays back the 10,600 rupees Meera's father spent. Profit is what is left after the cost comes off.

beats.say: Last step: 15,000 minus 10,600 is 4,400. Meera's father makes a profit of 4,400 rupees.
A quick check: 4,400 plus 10,600 is 15,000, and that is the money earned. It works.
So the method is: total cost, then the money from each batch, then earned take away spent.
Priya's train covers 120 kilometres at 60 kilometres an hour, then 80 at 40, then 100 at 50. Deepa's bus does the whole 300 kilometres at one steady speed and arrives at exactly the same time.

board.text: Train: 120 km at 60, 80 km at 40, 100 km at 50. Bus: 300 km

beats.say: For the bus's speed we need its distance, 300, and its time. Where will the time come from?

ask.ifNot: Both arrive at the same moment, so the bus takes exactly as long as the train. So we find the train's time for each part and add them up.

beats.say: Time is distance divided by speed. First part: 120 divided by 60 is 2 hours.
Second part: 80 divided by 40 is 2 hours. Third part: 100 divided by 50 is 2 hours as well.
So the train takes 2 plus 2 plus 2, which is 6 hours. The bus takes 6 hours too.
The bus covers 300 kilometres in 6 hours. 300 divided by 6 is 50, so the bus travels at 50 kilometres an hour.
A word of warning. Never find a steady speed by just mixing the speeds 60, 40 and 50 together. Always use the whole distance divided by the whole time.
Check: 50 kilometres an hour for 6 hours is 50 times 6, which is 300 kilometres. It fits.
So: arriving together means taking the same time. Find the total time, and then speed is distance divided by time.
Riya buys 3 boxes of diyas and 7 loose ones. Ankit buys 5 of the same boxes but gives 9 diyas away. They end up with the same number. How many diyas are in a box?
Let x be the number of diyas in one box. Riya has 3 boxes and 7 extra, so that is 3 x plus 7.
Ankit has 5 boxes but gives away 9, so that is 5 x minus 9. Careful: those 9 are taken off, not added.
They end up with the same number, so the two expressions are equal.
Now there are x terms on both sides. Let's collect them on one side. Which is the tidy move?

ask.ifNot: The left has 3 x and the right has 5 x. Take the smaller lot, 3 x, from both sides. Then the left has no x at all, and the balance stays level.

beats.say: Take 3 x from both sides. The left is just 7. On the right, 5 x minus 3 x is 2 x.
Now the 2 x has 9 taken off it. What should we do about that?

ask.ifNot: Taking off 9 is undone by adding 9. And we add it to both sides to keep the balance level.

beats.say: Add 9 to both sides. 7 plus 9 is 16, so 16 equals 2 x.
2 x means 2 times x, so we divide both sides by 2. 16 divided by 2 is 8. Each box holds 8 diyas.
Check both. Riya: 3 times 8, plus 7, is 31. Ankit: 5 times 8, minus 9, is 31. The same! It works.
When the letter is on both sides, collect it on one side first. After that it is an ordinary two step equation.
Priya cycles 24 kilometres to the library at 12 kilometres an hour, and comes back the same way at 8 kilometres an hour. We want her average speed for the whole trip.

board.text: 24 km there at 12 km/hr, 24 km back at 8 km/hr

beats.say: What do we work out to get an average speed?

ask.ifNot: It is tempting to take the number halfway between 12 and 8. But she spends longer riding at the slow speed, so we need the whole distance divided by the whole time.

beats.say: Average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time. The whole distance is there and back: 24 plus 24 is 48 kilometres.

board.text: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time

beats.say: Going: 24 kilometres at 12 an hour takes 24 divided by 12, which is 2 hours.
Coming back: 24 divided by 8 is 3 hours. Slower, so it takes longer.
The whole time is 2 plus 3, which is 5 hours.
Now 48 kilometres in 5 hours. 48 divided by 5 is 9.6, so her average speed is 9.6 kilometres an hour.
See the trap? Halfway between 12 and 8 is 10, but the true answer is a little less. She rides at 8 for 3 hours and at 12 for only 2, so the slow speed pulls the average down.
Check: 9.6 times 5 is 48, the whole distance.
So for an average speed, never average the speeds. Add up the distances, add up the times, and divide.
Arjun's triangle has sides of 9, 12 and 15 centimetres. Meena doubles every side. By how much does the area go up?

board.text: Every side doubled. Increase in area = ?

beats.say: First, what kind of triangle is it? Test for a right angle. 9 times 9 is 81, 12 times 12 is 144, and together they make 225. And 15 times 15 is 225 too.
They match, so it is a right-angled triangle. The two shorter sides, 9 and 12, meet at the right angle. They are the base and the height.
The area is half of base times height. 9 times 12 is 108, and half of 108 is 54 square centimetres.
Now double every side. The new triangle is 18, 24 and 30. Its base is 18 and its height is 24.
Before we work it out, have a guess. When every side is doubled, what happens to the area?

ask.ifNot: It is natural to say it doubles. But the base doubles and the height doubles too, so the area is doubled twice. Let's work it out and see.

beats.say: 18 times 20 is 360, and 18 times 4 is 72, so 18 times 24 is 432. Half of 432 is 216 square centimetres.
216 is 4 times 54. But the question asks for the increase: 216 minus 54 is 162 square centimetres.
Three traps in the choices. 54 is the old area, 216 is the new area, and 108 comes from thinking the area only doubles. The increase is the gap between new and old.
Double every side and the area becomes 4 times as big. So the increase is 3 times the old area: 3 times 54 is 162.
Meena's mother spends 8 rupees on ingredients for each samosa, and sells each one for 12 rupees. She makes and sells 25 samosas. What is her total profit?

board.text: Each samosa costs ₹8, sells for ₹12; 25 sold

beats.say: Every samosa costs the same and sells for the same. So we can find the profit on just one samosa first.
Selling price, take away cost price: 12 minus 8 is 4. Each samosa earns Meena's mother 4 rupees.
