Watch the two counts in this story. The 12 is mangoes bought, the 20 is glasses sold. Each goes with its own price.
A quick check: 120 plus 240 is 360, and that is the money earned. It works.
So remember the plan: every cost goes into one total, the sales go into another, and the gap is the profit.
Ravi's grandmother gives him some money. Before spending, he lends 750 to Arjun. Then he spends 1275 on crackers, 850 on sweets and 1460 on clothes, and has 2165 left. How much was he given?
Start with what went out. 1275 plus 850 is 2125, and 1460 more makes 3585.
He spent 3585 and still has 2165. How do we get back to what he had before the shopping?

ask.ifNot: Think of it backwards. What went out and what is left were once all together. To rebuild the start, add them.

beats.say: The spent part and the left part together make what he had before the shopping. 3585 plus 2165 is 5750.
So 5750 is what he had before the shopping. Is that everything grandmother gave him?

ask.ifNot: The 750 he lent to Arjun came out of grandmother's gift too, and it has not come back. So it has to be added on.

beats.say: 5750 plus 750 is 6500. Grandmother gave him 6500 rupees.
That lent money is the trap. It is not spent and it is not in the piggy bank, so it is easy to lose. But it was part of the gift.
Check it forwards. From 6500, lend 750, then spend 3585, and 2165 is left. It matches.
So to rebuild the start, add back everything that left: what was spent, what was lent, and what is still there.
Arjun sells samosas at x rupees each: 3 in the first innings and 5 in the second. A happy customer tips him 10 rupees, and he earns 50 rupees in all.
He sold 3 and then 5, so 8 samosas, each bringing in x rupees. Which equation matches his earnings?

ask.ifNot: 8 samosas at x rupees is 8 x. The tip is extra money on top, so it is added. 8 x plus 10 makes 50.

beats.say: 8 x from the samosas, plus the tip of 10, equals 50.
We want the 8 x by itself. So what should we do about the 10 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 10 is undone by taking 10 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: So we take 10 from both sides. That leaves 8 x on the left, and 50 minus 10, which is 40, on the right.
8 x means 8 times x. So to undo the times, we divide both sides by 8.
40 divided by 8 is 5. One samosa costs 5 rupees.
Check. 8 samosas at 5 rupees is 40 rupees, and the tip makes 50. It works.
The tip did not come from samosas. So we take it off first, and then share the rest among the 8 samosas.
Raju's grandfather has a square garden. He adds 5 metres to each side, and the new square garden has an area of 576 square metres. How long was a side of the first garden?

board.text: Square garden, each side + 5 m → area 576 sq m

beats.say: Which do we find first?

choices: the side of the new garden
ask.ifNot: The 5 metres were added to a side, not to the area. So we need the new side first, and then we can step back 5.

beats.say: The new garden is a square, so its side times itself is 576. 20 times 20 is 400 and 30 times 30 is 900, so the side is between 20 and 30.
576 ends in 6, so the side ends in 4 or 6. Try 24: 24 times 20 is 480, 24 times 4 is 96, and 480 plus 96 is 576. The new side is 24 metres.
The new side is the old side plus 5. So step back: 24 minus 5 is 19. The first garden had a side of 19 metres.
The trap is stopping at 24. That is the side after the garden grew. And adding another 5 would be going the opposite way.
Check: 19 plus 5 is 24, and 24 times 24 is 576. It fits.
So work backwards: a square root gives the new side, then undo the change to get the old side.
Ankit's mother puts 2000 rupees in Bank A at 10 per cent and 3000 rupees in Bank B at 6 per cent, saving for his school trip. After 2 years all the money is taken out. How much is that?

board.text: Bank A: ₹2,000 at 10%.  Bank B: ₹3,000 at 6%.  2 years.

beats.say: Take Bank A first. 2000 is 20 hundreds, and each hundred earns 10 rupees a year. 20 times 10 is 200 a year.
The money stays for 2 years, so Bank A pays 200 times 2, which is 400.
Bank B the same way. 3000 is 30 hundreds, each earning 6 rupees. 30 times 6 is 180 a year, so 360 in 2 years.
Now all the money is withdrawn from both banks. What comes back?

ask.ifNot: A bank hands back what was put in, with the interest on top. So there are 4 things to add: 2 deposits and 2 lots of interest.

beats.say: The deposits: 2000 plus 3000 is 5000. The interest: 400 plus 360 is 760.
Altogether, 5000 plus 760 is 5760 rupees.
Check it bank by bank. Bank A gives back 2400, Bank B gives back 3360, and together that is 5760 again.
So treat each bank on its own: 1 year's interest, times the years. Then remember that the deposits come back too.
Red and yellow paint are mixed in the ratio 3 to 5, and 24 litres of yellow paint were used. We want the litres of red.
The ratio means equal parts: 3 parts of red for every 5 parts of yellow.
Here is the trap in this question. What is the 24 litres?

ask.ifNot: Read it once more: they used 24 litres of yellow paint. So 24 is not the total. It is the yellow on its own.

beats.say: So this time we do not add 3 and 5. The 24 litres fill yellow's 5 parts, and nothing else.
One part is 24 divided by 5. A neat way to divide by 5 is to double, then divide by 10. Double 24 is 48, and 48 divided by 10 is 4.8.
So each part is 4.8 litres. Red has 3 parts. Which sum gives the red paint?

ask.ifNot: Each part is 4.8 litres, and red has 3 parts. So we want 3 lots of 4.8.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12, and 3 times 0.8 is 2.4. Add them: 12 plus 2.4 is 14.4.
So they used 14.4 litres of red paint.
Check: red has fewer parts than yellow, and 14.4 is less than 24, so that fits. And 5 parts of 4.8 give back the 24 litres of yellow.
So before you share in a ratio, ask what the number in the story belongs to. If it is one share, divide by that share's parts, not by all the parts.
Priya and Sneha share 270 packets of coloured sand in the ratio 4 to 5. Afterwards Sneha gives one third of her packets back to the art teacher. How many does she have now?
Read the ratio as parts: 4 parts for Priya and 5 parts for Sneha, and every part is the same size. Look at the boxes.

spec.note: All the boxes together: 270 packets

beats.say: First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 4 and 5 make 9 parts.

beats.say: 4 plus 5 is 9. So the 270 packets are shared into 9 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 270 divided by 9 is 30, so each part is 30 packets. Careful: we divide by all 9 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Sneha has 5 parts, and each part is 30 packets. 5 times 30 is 150, so Sneha gets 150 packets.
Sneha gives back one third of her 150 packets. To find one third, we divide by 3, and 150 divided by 3 is 50.
So 50 packets go back to the teacher. How many does Sneha have now?

ask.ifNot: The 50 packets are the ones she gave back, not the ones she kept. Take them away from her 150 to see what is left.

beats.say: 150 minus 50 is 100.
So Sneha has 100 packets now.
Check the sharing. Priya has 4 parts, and 4 times 30 is 120. 120 plus 150 is 270, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So every time: total parts first, then the size of one part, then the share. And read the last line of the story to see what is still left to do.
Arjun has 500 rupees, spends 4 lots of 35, and gets 150 from his uncle. The brackets hold all of that, because the whole amount is then shared among 5 people.
Don't rush in from the left. Which piece of this line has to be done first?

ask.ifNot: Brackets go first. And inside the brackets, times goes before minus, so 4 times 35 is the very first job.

beats.say: The brackets get done first. In there the same order holds, so times goes before minus: 4 times 35 is 140.
Still inside the brackets, we go left to right: 500 minus 140 is 360.
That bracket has one job left: 360 plus 150 is 510.
Just one job left: 510 divided by 5 is 102. Each person gets 102 rupees.
Check the last step backwards: 102 times 5 is 510. It fits.
So every time: clear the brackets, then do times and divide as you meet them, then finish with plus and minus, left to right.
Ravi buys 5 boxes of sweets and pays 45 rupees for decorations. Meena buys 3 of the same boxes and pays 129 rupees for fireworks. They spend exactly the same. What does one box cost?
Each box costs x rupees. So Ravi spends 5 x plus 45, and Meena spends 3 x plus 129. Equal spending means the two are equal.
Now x is on both sides. Which move collects the x terms on one side?

ask.ifNot: Take the smaller lot of x, which is 3 x, from both sides. The right side then has no x at all, and the balance stays level.

beats.say: Take 3 x from both sides. On the left, 5 x minus 3 x is 2 x. The right is just 129.
That line tells a little story of its own. Ravi's 2 extra boxes, plus his 45, match Meena's 129. Careful not to add the 45 and the 129: they sit on opposite sides.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. What gets rid of the 45 that is added on and keeps the balance level?

ask.ifNot: Adding 45 is undone by taking 45 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: So we take 45 from both sides. That leaves 2 x on the left, and 129 minus 45, which is 84, on the right.
Now 2 x is 2 lots of x. To find just one x, we divide both sides by 2.
84 divided by 2 is 42, because 2 times 42 is 84. One box of sweets costs 42 rupees.
Check both. Ravi: 5 times 42, plus 45, is 255. Meena: 3 times 42, plus 129, is 255. The same! It works.
When the letter is on both sides, take the smaller lot from both sides first. Then it is a two step equation.
Arjun goes to a stationery shop with 250 rupees. He buys a geometry box for 90 rupees, and then spends 40 percent of the money he has left on coloured pens. How much remains?
Go in the order of the story. First the geometry box: 250 minus 90 is 160.
Next, the pens cost 40 percent of the money he has left. 40 percent of which amount?

choices: 90, the price of the geometry box
ask.ifNot: Listen to the words again: 40 percent of the money he has left. After the geometry box, Arjun has 160. So the percent is taken from 160, not from 250.

beats.say: That is the trap in this question: taking the percent of 250. But only 160 is left, so we want 40 percent of 160.
Find 10 percent first, because that is easy: one tenth. 160 divided by 10 is 16.
Now build up. 40 percent is 4 times as much, and 4 times 16 is 64.
So the pens cost 64 rupees. Take that from the 160. 160 minus 64 leaves Arjun with 96 rupees.
Check: 90 for the geometry box, 64 for the pens, and 96 left. Add them, and we are back at 250.
So: follow the story in order, and always ask, percent of what? Here it was the money left, not the money at the start.
Rohan's train covers 360 kilometres in 5 hours. It runs at 90 kilometres an hour at first, then slows to 60 kilometres an hour for the rest. How many kilometres does it do at the slower speed?

board.text: 360 km in 5 hr: part at 90 km/hr, the rest at 60 km/hr

beats.say: We don't know how long the train spent at each speed. So let's try a pretend trip: what if it had kept to 90 for the whole 5 hours?
5 hours at 90 would be 5 times 90, which is 450 kilometres.
But the real trip is only 360. The pretend trip is too long by 450 minus 360, which is 90 kilometres.
Every hour the train goes at 60 when we pretended 90, how many kilometres does it lose?

ask.ifNot: In one hour at 90 it would cover 90 kilometres. At 60 it covers only 60. The gap between those two is what each slow hour loses.

beats.say: 90 minus 60 is 30. Every slow hour loses 30 kilometres.
We have 90 kilometres to lose, 30 at a time. 90 divided by 30 is 3, so the train spent 3 hours at the slower speed.
3 hours at 60 kilometres an hour is 3 times 60, which is 180 kilometres at the slower speed.
Careful: the 3 is hours, and the question asks for kilometres. That is why we needed one more step.
Check: the other 2 hours were at 90, which is 180 kilometres as well. 180 plus 180 is 360, the whole trip.
So when you know the total but not the split: pretend it was all one speed, see how far off you are, and put it right one hour at a time.
Ananya and Bhavna share a profit of 360 rupees in the ratio 5 to 4. Ananya buys gift boxes that cost 30 rupees each with her share. How many boxes can she buy?
A ratio of 5 to 4 means equal parts: 5 parts for Ananya and 4 parts for Bhavna. Here they are as boxes.

spec.note: All the boxes together: ₹360

beats.say: First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 5 and 4 make 9 parts.

beats.say: 5 plus 4 is 9. So the 360 rupees are shared into 9 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 360 divided by 9 is 40, so each part is 40 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 9 parts.
Ananya has 5 parts, and each part is 40 rupees. 5 times 40 is 200, so Ananya gets 200 rupees.
Each gift box costs 30 rupees, so count in 30s. 6 boxes cost 6 times 30, which is 180. 7 boxes would cost 210.
Ananya has 200 rupees. So how many boxes can she buy?

ask.ifNot: 7 boxes cost 210 rupees, and she only has 200, so 7 is too many. And a shop will not sell part of a box. 6 is the most she can buy.

beats.say: 6 boxes use up 180 rupees. 200 minus 180 leaves 20 rupees, which is not enough for another box.
So Ananya can buy 6 gift boxes, with 20 rupees left over.
Check the sharing. Bhavna has 4 parts, and 4 times 40 is 160. 200 plus 160 is 360, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So the plan: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. And when you are buying whole things, leftover money that cannot buy one more is simply left over.
Arjun's bamboo triangle has one angle of 90 degrees and another of 35 degrees. We want the third angle.
Here is the fact we need. What do the three angles of a triangle always add up to?

ask.ifNot: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: Add the two angles we know. 90 plus 35 is 125.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: The three angles must make 180, and the ones we know use up 125. How do we find the third?

ask.ifNot: The third angle is whatever is left of the 180 once the other two are taken out. Finding what is left is a take away. So it is 180 minus 125.

beats.say: 180 minus 125 is 55. Careful not to stop at 125: that is the two angles we already had, not the missing one.
So the third angle of Arjun's triangle is 55 degrees.
Check: 90 plus 35 plus 55 is 180. And here is a bonus: in a right-angled triangle the other two angles always make 90, and 35 plus 55 is 90.
So to find the third angle of any triangle: add the two you know, and take the total from 180.
Ravi sells 6 cups of chai in over 1, 10 cups in over 2, 14 cups in over 3, and the pattern continues. How many cups does he sell in total in the first 5 overs?
First, the jump. 10 minus 6 is 4, and 14 minus 10 is 4 as well. So each over he sells 4 more cups than the over before.
The question asks for a total. What do we need before we can add anything up?

choices: Only the amounts in the story
ask.ifNot: A total means every over put together. The story only tells us some of them, so first we find all 5.

beats.say: Keep adding 4 each time: 18, 22. Now we have all 5.
Careful: 22 is only over 5, and it is one of the choices. We want all 5 overs together.
Here is a quick way to add them. Pair the first with the last: 6 plus 22 is 28. Now the second with the second last, 10 and 18. What will they make?

ask.ifNot: 10 is 4 more than 6, and 18 is 4 less than 22. One goes up by 4 and the other comes down by 4, so the total stays the same.

beats.say: 10 plus 18 is 28 too. That is 2 pairs worth 28, and the 14 in the middle is left on its own.
2 times 28 is 56, and 56 plus the 14 in the middle is 70. Ravi sells 70 cups in the first 5 overs.
Let's check the slow way. The first 3 overs add up to 30, the other 2 add up to 40, and 30 plus 40 is 70. It matches.
So for a total like this: find the jump, write out every number, then pair them from the outside in and add.
Kavitha's small box holds x sweets. A large box holds 2 x plus 3. She makes 4 small boxes and 3 large ones, and x is 6. How many sweets in all?

board.text: Small box: x.   Large box: 2x + 3.   x = 6

beats.say: The 4 small boxes hold 4 x. The 3 large boxes hold 3 times the whole bracket, 2 x plus 3.
3 times that bracket. What does it open out to?

ask.ifNot: The 3 outside multiplies both things inside. 3 times 2 x is 6 x, and 3 times 3 is 9.

beats.say: The 3 multiplies the 2 x, and it multiplies the 3 as well. Each large box has 3 extra sweets and there are 3 boxes, so 9 extras.
That is the classic slip in this question: multiplying the 2 x but leaving the 3 alone. Every large box has those 3 extras.
Now gather the x's. 4 x and 6 x make 10 x.
Put in x as 6. 10 times 6 is 60, and 60 plus 9 is 69. Kavitha has 69 sweets.
Check by counting boxes. A small box holds 6 sweets. A large box holds 2 times 6, plus 3, which is 15.
4 small boxes hold 24, and 3 large boxes hold 45. 24 plus 45 is 69. It matches.
A number outside a bracket multiplies everything inside. Open the bracket, gather the like terms, then put in the value.
Ravi's father fills 48 crates, and every crate holds 35 mangoes. We want to know how many mangoes he packed.
Which sum gives the total?

ask.ifNot: Every crate holds the same 35 mangoes, and there are 48 crates. 48 equal lots means we multiply.

beats.say: 35 times 48 looks hard. But 48 is only 2 less than 50, and 50 is friendly. So we find 35 times 50, then take away 35 times 2.
35 times 50 is 1750. And 35 times 2 is 70.
1750 minus 70 is 1680. He packed 1680 mangoes.
Here is the slip to watch for. We counted 50 crates, which is 2 crates too many. So the 70 mangoes come off. They are not added on.
Check by splitting 48 another way, into 40 and 8. 35 times 40 is 1400, 35 times 8 is 280, and together they make 1680 again.
So to multiply by a number just under a round one, multiply by the round number, then take off the extra.
48 students each collect 375 rupees to buy cricket kits. After buying the kits, 1800 rupees are left over. We want to know what the kits cost.

board.text: 48 students × ₹375 collected; ₹1,800 left after the kits

beats.say: First, the money collected: 48 times 375. 375 is 25 less than 400, so we find 48 times 400 and take off 48 times 25.
48 times 400 is 19,200. And 48 times 25 is 1200.
19,200 minus 1200 is 18,000. So the class collected 18,000 rupees.
They collected 18,000 rupees, and 1800 was left over. How do we find what the kits cost?

ask.ifNot: The money collected is the money spent plus the money left. So to find the spending, take the leftover away from the collection.

beats.say: 18,000 minus 1800 is 16,200. The kits cost 16,200 rupees.
Two things to watch. 18,000 is among the choices, but that is the money collected. And the snacks at the end of the story are extra: nobody asked about them.
Check by adding back. 16,200 for the kits plus 1800 left over is 18,000, the money they collected.
So read to the very end to see what is asked. Here it was collected money, take away leftover money.
Priya and Kiran start from the same point on a 600 metre round track and run in opposite directions. Priya runs 5 metres a second and Kiran 3. When do they meet for the third time?

board.text: 600 m round track, opposite ways: 5 m/s and 3 m/s

beats.say: They set off in opposite directions, so they come round to meet on the far side. Between them, they must cover one whole lap of 600 metres before they meet.
Each second, how many metres do the two of them cover between them?

ask.ifNot: Priya covers 5 metres of the lap, and Kiran covers 3 metres of it from the other side. Together that uses up 8 metres of the lap every second.

beats.say: Together they cover 8 metres a second. 600 divided by 8 is 75, so they first meet after 75 seconds.
They pass each other and keep running. When do they meet again?

ask.ifNot: From the moment they pass, it is the same story again: side by side, heading opposite ways, with one whole lap to cover between them. That takes 75 seconds again.

beats.say: So they meet every 75 seconds. The first meeting is at 75 seconds, and the second is at 150.
The third meeting is 75 seconds later still. 3 times 75 is 225 seconds.
The trap is stopping at 75. That is the first meeting, and the question asks for the third.
Check: in 225 seconds Priya runs 1125 metres and Kiran runs 675. Together that is 1800 metres, which is exactly 3 laps of 600.
So on a round track, running opposite ways: add the speeds, find the time for one lap between you, and count one meeting for each lap.
In Meera's banner, the first angle is 15 degrees more than the second, and the third is 25 degrees more than the second. We want the type of triangle.
Both clues lean on the second angle, so let's call it x. Then the first angle is x plus 15, and the third is x plus 25.

spec.note: The three angles together make the whole triangle

beats.say: Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: A square corner is 90 degrees and a full turn is 360. The three angles of a triangle always make a half turn, a straight line, which is 180 degrees.

beats.say: So our three angles together make 180: x plus 15, plus x, plus x plus 25.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: There are 3 x's, and 15 plus 25 is 40. So 3 x plus 40 equals 180. Take 40 from both sides, and 3 x equals 140.
Now, 140 does not divide by 3 exactly. 3 times 46 is 138 and 3 times 47 is 141, so x is somewhere between 46 and 47 degrees.
That is fine, because we only need the type of triangle. Which angle decides the type?

ask.ifNot: If the largest angle is under a right angle, the other two must be as well. So the largest one, x plus 25, decides the type.

beats.say: x is less than 47, so the largest angle is less than 47 plus 25, which is 72.
72 is well under 90, the size of a right angle. So all three angles are smaller than a right angle.
A triangle whose angles are all less than 90 degrees is an acute-angled triangle. That is Meera's banner.
Check another way. If the largest angle were 90, the second would be 65 and the first 80. Those add up to 235, far more than 180, so the real angles must be smaller.
So the method: write every angle using x and make them add up to 180. And when you only need the type, you just need to know which side of 90 the largest angle falls.
Meera's family needs one sweet for each of 1250 people. The sweets come in boxes of 48. What is the smallest number of boxes that will do?

board.text: 1250 people, 1 sweet each; boxes of 48 sweets

beats.say: How do we find the number of boxes?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many groups of 48 are needed to cover 1250. Making equal groups is dividing.

beats.say: 48 is close to 50, and 25 fifties make exactly 1250. So let's try 25 boxes. 25 times 48 is 1200. Not enough yet.
One more box, the 26th, adds 48 and brings us to 1248. That is still 2 sweets short of 1250.
With 26 boxes, 2 people are left without a sweet. So how many boxes must the family buy?

ask.ifNot: With 26 boxes, 2 people get nothing. The shop will not sell part of a box, so the family needs one whole extra box.

beats.say: 26 boxes and 1 more is 27 boxes.
Check: 27 boxes hold 1296 sweets. That is more than 1250, so everyone gets one, with a few to spare.
So when everybody must get one, divide. If anything is left over, go up to the next whole box.
Six months of results, in thousands of rupees. Priya's father imagines swapping the worst month's result for the best month's result, and asks how much the total would go up.
Which is the worst month, the smallest number of all?

ask.ifNot: The worst month is the biggest loss. Among the negative numbers, the one furthest below 0 is the smallest: that is minus 12.

beats.say: The worst is minus 12, in January. And the best is the largest number, plus 22, in May.
Now think about the swap. Every other month stays the same. Only January changes, from minus 12 to plus 22.
So the total goes up by the distance from minus 12 to plus 22. How far is that?

ask.ifNot: Minus 12 and plus 22 are on opposite sides of 0. First it takes 12 steps to get up to 0, and then 22 more.

beats.say: 12 steps to get up to 0, then 22 more. 12 plus 22 is 34. The total goes up by 34 thousand rupees.
Let's check with the totals. The old total is 19. With plus 22 in January's place, the new total is 53. And 53 minus 19 is 34.
The tempting answer is 22, just the best month. But we also got rid of a loss of 12, and losing a loss is a gain.
When one number in a list is swapped, the total changes by exactly the difference between the new number and the old one.
Riya has some rupees saved, and Arjun has exactly 3 times as much. Their mother gives each of them 15 rupees. Now they have 142 rupees together. What did Riya have at first?

board.text: Riya x, Arjun 3 times x, ₹15 each, total ₹142

beats.say: Call Riya's savings x. Then Arjun's are 3 x. After the gift, Riya has x plus 15, and Arjun has 3 x plus 15.
Together that is 142.
Gather the like terms. x and 3 x make 4 x. And how much gift money is there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Each of them gets 15 rupees, and there are 2 children. 15 and 15 make 30.

beats.say: Careful: the gift comes twice, once for each child. So the equation is 4 x plus 30 equals 142.
We want the 4 x by itself. So what should we do about the 30 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 30 is undone by taking 30 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: So we take 30 from both sides. That leaves 4 x on the left, and 142 minus 30, which is 112, on the right.
Now 4 x is 4 lots of x. To find just one x, we divide both sides by 4.
112 divided by 4 is 28, because 4 times 28 is 112. Riya had 28 rupees at first.
Check. Arjun had 3 times 28, which is 84. After the gifts they have 43 and 99, and 43 plus 99 is 142.
So: write each person's money with the same letter, add, gather like terms, and undo one step at a time.
Kavya's class spends 600 rupees on ingredients and makes 200 samosas to sell at 8 rupees each. They sell 90 per cent of the samosas and give the rest away. What is their profit?
To find a profit we need two amounts: the money Kavya's class spent, and the money they earned. Profit is earned, take away spent.
The money going out is quick this time. Kavya's class spent 600 rupees on ingredients, and that is the whole cost.
They sold 90 per cent of the 200 samosas. How many samosas is that?

ask.ifNot: 10 per cent of 200 is 20. And 90 per cent is 9 lots of that, so 9 times 20, which is 180 samosas.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 200 is 20 samosas. So 90 per cent is 9 times as many, and that is 180 samosas sold.
Now the money coming in. 180 samosas at 8 rupees each: 180 times 8 is 1,440 rupees. That is the money earned.
Money earned, take away money spent: 1,440 minus 600 is 840. Kavya's class makes a profit of 840 rupees.
Did you spot the trap? Selling all 200 would bring in more money, but 20 samosas were given away and earned nothing.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 840 plus 600 is 1,440. It fits.
So the method is: total up every cost, count only what was really sold, then take the cost away from the money earned.
Ravi's line for the cricket balls has two pairs of brackets, with a times in front of one and a divide in front of the other.
Before we work anything out, look along the whole line. Which piece do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Look for the brackets. Whatever sits inside them is worked out before anything else, so 12 minus 4 goes first.

beats.say: Brackets are always the first job, and there are two pairs. In the first pair, 12 minus 4 is 8.
In the second pair, 3 plus 6 is 9. Write the line again with 8 and 9 where the brackets were.
With the brackets gone, times and divide come next. 5 times 8 is 40.
The divide goes early too: 36 divided by 9 is 4.
And the last one: 2 times 3 is 6. Write the line again with 40, 4 and 6 in place.
Only plus and minus are left now, so we go left to right: 40 plus 4 is 44.
And 44 minus 6 is 38. Ravi needs 38 cricket balls.
Check by walking backwards. 38 plus 6 is 44, and 44 minus 4 is 40, right where that line started.
So every time: clear the brackets, then do times and divide as you meet them, then finish with plus and minus, left to right.
Team A scored 2748 runs. Team B scored 1965 runs more than Team A. Team C scored 3210 runs fewer than Team A and Team B put together. We want Team C's runs.
Team B scored 1965 runs more than Team A. So how many runs did Team B score?

ask.ifNot: 1965 is not Team B's score. It is how far ahead of Team A they finished. So start from Team A's 2748 and add 1965.

beats.say: 2748 plus 1965 is 4713. That is Team B's score. Look at the bars: Team B's bar is Team A's bar with 1965 more on the end.
Next we need Team A and Team B combined. Which sum is that?

ask.ifNot: Combined means both whole scores together. Team A's score is 2748 and Team B's whole score is 4713, so add those two.

beats.say: 2748 plus 4713 is 7461. Careful: 2748 plus 1965 was only Team B's score. The combined total counts Team A's runs as well.
Team C scored 3210 fewer than that. Fewer means take away. 7461 minus 3210 is 4251.
So Team C scored 4251 runs.
Check by adding back. 4251 plus 3210 is 7461, the combined score of Team A and Team B.
So take a chain of clues one link at a time. More than means add, fewer than means subtract, and each answer feeds the next step.
Priya has diyas arranged in a square. With 45 more diyas, she can form the next bigger perfect square. How many diyas does she have now?

board.text: A square of diyas + 45 more = the next bigger square

beats.say: Think how a square grows into the next one up. It gets one more row along the bottom, and one more column down the side.
The new row is as long as a side of the small square. So is the new column. And 1 more fills the corner where they meet.
There are 45 extra diyas, and one of them is the corner. How many are left for the new row and the new column together?

ask.ifNot: The 45 extra ones are a row, a column and 1 corner piece. Take the corner away, and what is left is the row and the column.

beats.say: 45 minus 1 is 44. That is the row and the column together.
The row and the column are the same length, so we halve. 44 divided by 2 is 22. The small square has 22 diyas on each side.
So the small square holds 22 times 22. 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44. 440 plus 44 is 484.
Priya has 484 diyas now.
Check: the next square is 23 times 23, which is 529. And 529 minus 484 is 45, just as the story says.
Two traps to name. 529 is the bigger square, not the one she has. And 22 is only the side: the question asks for all the diyas, so we had to square it.
So when you are told the gap between two squares that are neighbours: take away 1 for the corner, halve, and you have the smaller side.
Ananya buys packets of chai masala for 35 rupees each, and ties a ribbon that costs 5 rupees on each one. She sells them for 56 rupees each, and sells 12 packets. What is her total profit?

board.text: Packet ₹35 + ribbon ₹5; sells at ₹56; 12 packets sold

beats.say: Every packet costs the same and sells for the same. So we can find the profit on just one packet first.
What does one finished packet really cost Ananya?

ask.ifNot: She pays 35 rupees for the packet, and then 5 rupees more for its ribbon. Both are money spent on that one packet.

beats.say: The packet and its ribbon together: 35 plus 5 is 40 rupees. Leaving out the ribbon is the trap in this story.
Selling price, take away cost: 56 minus 40 is 16. Each packet earns her 16 rupees.
She sells 12 packets, so we multiply. 12 times 16 is 192. Ananya's total profit is 192 rupees.
Check the long way. She took in 12 times 56, which is 672 rupees, and spent 12 times 40, which is 480 rupees.
672 minus 480 is 192. Both ways agree.
So when every item has the same cost and the same price, find the full cost of one, then the profit on one, then multiply.
Priya sells chai at x rupees a cup and biscuit packets at 3 rupees each. She sells 5 cups and 4 packets, and earns 47 rupees.
The chai brings in 5 x. The biscuits bring in 4 times 3 rupees. Together they make 47.
We can work out the biscuit money straight away. How much is it?

ask.ifNot: 4 packets at 3 rupees each means 4 times 3, which is 12 rupees. We multiply, because every packet costs 3.

beats.say: So the equation is 5 x plus 12 equals 47.
We want the 5 x by itself. So what should we do about the 12 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 12 is undone by taking 12 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: Take away 12 on the left, and 12 on the right as well. That leaves 5 x equals 47 minus 12, which is 35.
Now 5 x is 5 lots of x. To find just one x, we divide both sides by 5.
35 divided by 5 is 7. One cup of chai costs 7 rupees.
Check. 5 cups at 7 rupees is 35 rupees, and the biscuits add 12. 35 plus 12 is 47. It works.
Work out anything you can first, like the biscuit money. Then the equation is a simple two step one.
Riya and Karan share 360 rupees in the ratio of their ages. Riya spends her share on diyas that cost 12 rupees each. How many diyas can she buy?
Riya is 9 years old and Karan is 6. So the ratio of their ages, Riya to Karan, is 9 to 6.
Those numbers can be made simpler. What is the biggest number that divides both 9 and 6 exactly?

ask.ifNot: 9 is 3 times 3, and 6 is 2 times 3. Nothing bigger goes into both.

beats.say: 9 divided by 3 is 3, and 6 divided by 3 is 2. So 9 to 6 is the same ratio as 3 to 2, just in smaller numbers.
A ratio of 3 to 2 means equal parts: 3 parts for Riya and 2 parts for Karan. Here they are as boxes.

spec.note: All the boxes together: ₹360

beats.say: Before sharing anything, count. How many equal parts altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 2 make 5 parts.

beats.say: Add the ratio numbers: 3 plus 2 makes 5. All 360 rupees sit in those 5 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 360 divided by 5 is 72, so each part is 72 rupees. The classic slip is to divide by just one ratio number, but the total belongs to all 5 parts.
Riya has 3 parts, and each part is 72 rupees. 3 times 72 is 216, so Riya gets 216 rupees.
Each diya costs 12 rupees, so we need the number of 12s in 216. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 8 is 96. Together that makes 216, so 12 goes in 18 times.
So Riya can buy 18 diyas.
Check the sharing. Karan has 2 parts, and 2 times 72 is 144. 216 plus 144 is 360, the whole amount, so the shares are right.
So remember three moves: count the parts, find one part, multiply for the share. Then do whatever else the story asks.
Ananya's tile shows 63,842. She wonders how many times bigger the place value of the 3 is than the place value of the 2.
Look at the chart. The 3 is in the thousands column. What is it worth there?

ask.ifNot: Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. So this 3 means 3 thousands, and that is 3000.

beats.say: 3 times 1000 is 3000. That is the place value of the 3.
Now the 2. It is in the units column, so it is worth just 2.
How many times 2 is 3000? Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: How many times means divide. So we divide what the digits are worth: 3000 by 2.

beats.say: 3000 divided by 2 is 1500. That is just half of 3000. Careful: dividing the bare digits, 3 by 2, forgets that the 3 stands for thousands.
Check by multiplying back: 1500 times 2 is 3000. It works.
So the place value of the 3 is 1500 times the place value of the 2.
So for how many times: find what each digit is worth, then divide the bigger value by the smaller.
Riya's number is 73809. We want the difference between the place value of the 8 and the place value of the 3. Let's start with the 3, because it sits further left.
A digit is worth more the further left it sits. In the chart, the 3 is in the thousands column. So what is it worth?

ask.ifNot: Count the columns from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands. So this 3 means 3 thousands, and that is 3000.

beats.say: So the 3 is worth 3 times 1000, which is 3000.
And the 8 sits in the hundreds column. 8 times 100 is 800.
Now, the difference between 3000 and 800. Which sum gives it?

ask.ifNot: Difference means subtract. And we subtract what the digits are worth, 3000 and 800, not the bare digits.

beats.say: 3000 minus 800 is 2200. Careful: 8 is the bigger digit, but the 3 is worth more, because it sits further left. So the 800 comes off the 3000.
Let's check by putting it back: 2200 plus 800 is 3000, just where we started.
So her friend should answer 2200.
So: the place value of each digit first, from its column. Only then do we subtract.
Ravi has 17 rupees saved and earns 8 rupees each week. After w weeks he has exactly 73 rupees. We need the equation, and then w.

board.text: ₹17 saved, ₹8 each week, ₹73 after w weeks

beats.say: Which equation matches Ravi's savings?

ask.ifNot: He earns 8 rupees every week, so the 8 goes with w. The 17 he already had is added on top. Together they make 73.

beats.say: 8 w from the weeks, plus the 17 he started with, equals 73.
The 17 is added on, so to undo it we take 17 from both sides. That leaves 8 w equals 73 minus 17, which is 56.
Now 8 w means 8 lots of w. How do we get down to just one w?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So we divide both sides by 8.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 8.
56 divided by 8 is 7. Ravi worked for 7 weeks.
Check. 7 weeks at 8 rupees is 56 rupees, and 17 more makes 73. It works.
So the choice we want is 8 w plus 17 equals 73, with w equal to 7. Two choices share that equation, so only solving it tells them apart.
Coach Sharma buys jerseys at 8 rupees each, and a set of stumps for 19 rupees. The bill is 91 rupees. How many jerseys did he buy?
Let x be the number of jerseys. They cost 8 times x rupees. Add the stumps, and we have the whole bill.
The 8 x is not alone yet. Which move clears away the 19 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 19 is undone by taking 19 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: Take away 19 on the left, and 19 on the right as well. That leaves 8 x equals 91 minus 19, which is 72.
Now 8 x means 8 lots of x. How do we get down to just one x?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So we divide both sides by 8.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 8.
72 divided by 8 is 9. The coach bought 9 jerseys.
Check. 9 jerseys at 8 rupees is 72 rupees. Add the stumps at 19, and the bill is 91. It works.
The stumps are bought once, so their cost comes off first. Then the rest is shared out at 8 rupees a jersey.
Aman tiles a square courtyard. The outermost ring of tiles, the border, has 76 tiles. How many tiles cover the whole courtyard?

board.text: Square courtyard. Border ring: 76 tiles. Total?

beats.say: We need the number of tiles along one side. But count the border one side at a time, and something odd happens at the corners.
If we count all 4 sides in full, how many times is each corner tile counted?

ask.ifNot: A corner tile sits at the end of two sides: the one going across and the one going down. So it gets counted with both of them.

beats.say: Each corner is counted 2 times, and there are 4 corners. So 4 full sides come to 4 more than the border: 76 plus 4 is 80.
4 full sides make 80, so one side is 80 divided by 4, which is 20 tiles.
The whole courtyard is 20 rows of 20. 20 times 20 is 400 tiles.
The trap is 76 divided by 4, which is 19, and then 19 times 19, which is 361. That forgets that the corners are shared.
Check: 4 sides of 20 is 80. Take off the 4 corners that were counted double, and we get 76, just what Aman counted.
So for the border of a square: add 4 for the shared corners, divide by 4 to get the side, then square the side for the total.
Priya's rangoli is a rectangle, 9 metres long and 5 metres wide. Each packet of coloured powder covers 3 square metres. How many packets fill the whole rangoli?

board.text: Rangoli 9 m × 5 m, 1 packet covers 3 sq. m

beats.say: Powder fills the space inside the rangoli. Which sum measures that space?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides only measures along the edges. The space inside is the area: 5 rows of 9 square metres.

beats.say: 9 times 5 is 45. The rangoli covers 45 square metres.
Each packet covers 3 of those square metres. So we need to know how many 3s there are in 45. That is a division.
30 divided by 3 is 10, and the 15 left over, divided by 3, is 5. So 45 divided by 3 is 15 packets.
Check: 15 packets, 3 square metres each. 15 times 3 is 45. The whole rangoli is filled, with nothing left over.
Don't stop at 45. That is how many square metres there are, not how many packets. And 14 comes from adding 9 and 5, which is not an area.
So: find the area, then divide by what 1 packet covers.

Deepa and Rohan have two ribbon rolls, 180 centimetres and 252 centimetres long. They cut both into equal pieces, as long as possible, with none left over. How long is a piece, and how many pieces are there?

board.text: Rolls: 180 cm and 252 cm. Longest equal pieces?

beats.say: Every piece is the same length, with nothing left over. So that length has to divide 180 and 252 exactly. Is that a factor of these numbers, or a multiple of them?

ask.ifNot: A multiple of these numbers is at least as big as the biggest of them, so it cannot divide them all exactly. A number that divides exactly is a factor.

beats.say: A factor of both, and we want the greatest one. So we need the highest common factor of 180 and 252.
The sure way is prime factors. Break each number down, smallest prime first. 180 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 3 times 5.
And 252 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 3 times 7.
Now look at the 5. It is a factor of 180, but not of 252. Does 5 go into the highest common factor?

choices: Yes, it is a prime factor
No, it must be in both lists
ask.ifNot: A common factor has to divide every number. 5 does not divide 252, so it stays out.

beats.say: So we mark only what both lists share: 2, 2, 3 and 3. Every other prime is missing from at least one list.
Multiply them together. 2 times 2 times 3 times 3 is 36. So the highest common factor is 36.
So each piece is 36 centimetres long. Now count the pieces.
180 divided by 36 is 5, and 252 divided by 36 is 7.
Careful: the pieces come from both rolls, so we add them all. 5 plus 7 is 12.
So each piece is 36 centimetres long, and there are 12 pieces in all.
Check. 12 pieces of 36 centimetres make 432 centimetres. And 180 plus 252 is 432 too.
Longest equal pieces with nothing wasted means the highest common factor. Then divide to count the pieces.
Priya buys 48 packets of sparklers with 125 in each packet. She puts all of them into gift bags of 25. How many bags can she fill?
First, all the sparklers. Here is a fact worth keeping: 8 times 125 is 1000. And 48 is 6 lots of 8, so 48 times 125 is 6 thousands, 6000.
6000 sparklers go into bags of 25. Which sum gives the number of bags?

ask.ifNot: We are making equal groups of 25 out of 6000. Making equal groups is dividing.

beats.say: 4 lots of 25 make 100, so every 100 sparklers fill 4 bags. 6000 is 60 hundreds, and 60 times 4 is 240 bags.
Careful: 6000 is among the choices too. But 6000 is the number of sparklers, and the question asks for bags.
Check a second way. One packet of 125 fills 5 bags. So 48 packets fill 48 times 5, which is 240 bags.
So in a pack and repack story, find the total first, then divide by the size of the new group.
A long story! Groups of 108, 144 and 180 players are split into squads, and then Arjun buys jerseys in packs of 8. Let's read right to the end to see what is asked.
The question asks for the number of jersey packs, so that every player gets a jersey. What do we need to know for that?

choices: how many players there are in all
ask.ifNot: Every player needs one jersey, whichever squad they are in. So what matters is how many players there are altogether.

beats.say: Let's look at the squads anyway. The biggest squad size is the highest common factor, which is 36. 108 is 36 times 3, 144 is 36 times 4, and 180 is 36 times 5.
That makes 3 plus 4 plus 5, which is 12 squads of 36. But sorting players into squads does not add or remove a single player.
So count the players. 108 plus 144 is 252, and 252 plus 180 is 432.
432 players, and 8 jerseys in a pack. How do we find the number of packs?

ask.ifNot: Each pack covers 8 players. So we ask how many 8s are in 432, and that is 432 divided by 8.

beats.say: 8 times 50 is 400, and 8 times 4 is 32. So 432 divided by 8 is 54 packs, with no jerseys spare.
Careful: 36 and 12 are tempting, but they are the squad size and the number of squads. The question asked for packs of jerseys.
Check. 54 packs of 8 is 432 jerseys, one for each player. And 12 squads of 36 is 432 players too.
In a long word problem, find the final question first. Then use the numbers that answer it.
Ravi's 4500 rupees becomes 5310 in 3 years. Meena puts 6000 in the same bank, at the same rate, for 4 years. We want Meena's interest.

board.text: Meena: ₹6,000 for 4 years, same rate. Interest = ?

beats.say: We do not know the rate yet, but Ravi's money can tell us. His interest is 5310 minus 4500, which is 810.
That is for 3 years. So in 1 year Ravi earns 810 divided by 3, which is 270.
Ravi's 4500 is 45 hundreds, and together they earn 270 a year. What does each hundred earn?

ask.ifNot: The 270 rupees is shared equally among the 45 hundreds. So divide 270 by 45.

beats.say: 270 divided by 45 is 6. Every hundred earns 6 rupees a year, so the rate is 6 per cent.
Now Meena. Her 6000 is 60 hundreds, and each one earns 6 rupees. 60 times 6 is 360 a year.
Careful with the years: Meena's money stays for 4 years. The 3 years belonged to Ravi. 360 times 4 is 1440 rupees.
Check the rate on Ravi. 45 hundreds, 6 rupees each, for 3 years: 45 times 6 times 3 is 810. That is his interest, so the rate is right.
So when two people share a rate, use the one you know to find what each hundred earns in a year. Then give that rate to the other.
Priya and her friends buy 5 packets of red powder and 3 of blue, each costing x rupees. They get 18 rupees off, pay 32 rupees for stencils, and pay 174 rupees in all.
5 packets and 3 packets make 8 packets, so the powder costs 8 x. The discount comes off, and the stencils go on.
Tidy the plain numbers first: minus 18, then plus 32. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: 18 comes off and 32 goes on. More goes on than comes off, by 32 minus 18, which is 14. So together they add 14.

beats.say: So the equation is 8 x plus 14 equals 174. Careful with the signs: a discount is taken off, and a charge is added on.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. What gets rid of the 14 that is added on and keeps the balance level?

ask.ifNot: Adding 14 is undone by taking 14 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: So we take 14 from both sides. That leaves 8 x on the left, and 174 minus 14, which is 160, on the right.
8 x means 8 times x. So to undo the times, we divide both sides by 8.
160 divided by 8 is 20, because 8 times 20 is 160. Each packet costs 20 rupees.
Check. 8 packets at 20 rupees is 160. Take off 18 and add 32, and we get 174. It works.
So: count the packets, put a minus on what comes off and a plus on what goes on, tidy the numbers, then solve.
Sanjay's kite is a triangle with sides of 15, 20 and 25 centimetres, and his friend says one angle is 90 degrees. Cloth costs 2 rupees for each square centimetre. What does the cloth cost?
Let's test what the friend said. In a right-angled triangle, the squares of the two shorter sides add up to the square of the longest side.

board.text: Right angle test: short² + short² = longest²

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225. 20 times 20 is 400. Add them: 625. And 25 times 25 is 625 as well. It matches, so the triangle really is right-angled.
The right angle sits between two of the sides. Those two are the base and the height. Which two are they?

ask.ifNot: The longest side, 25, always lies opposite the right angle, on a slant. The two shorter sides, 15 and 20, are the ones that meet at the square corner.

beats.say: 15 and 20. Now, a right-angled triangle is exactly half of a rectangle. So its area is half of base times height.
15 times 20 is 300. Half of 300 is 150. So the kite needs 150 square centimetres of cloth.
Each square centimetre costs 2 rupees. 150 times 2 is 300 rupees.
Notice that 300 turned up twice: first as the area of the whole rectangle, then as the cost. The slips here are forgetting to halve, and using the slanted side, 25, as a height.
Right-angled triangle: half of the two short sides multiplied together. Then area times price.
Ananya's mother buys 5.75 litres of milk in the morning and 3.25 litres in the evening. Each cup of chai needs 0.125 litres of milk and sells for 12.50 rupees. How much does she earn?

board.text: Each cup: 0.125 litres of milk, sold for ₹12.50

beats.say: First, all the milk together. 5.75 plus 3.25 is 9 litres.
Each cup takes 0.125 litres. How many cups come out of 1 litre?

ask.ifNot: 0.125 is one eighth. Count up in steps of 0.125, and the 8th step lands exactly on 1. So 1 litre makes 8 cups.

beats.say: Every litre makes 8 cups. So 9 litres make 9 times 8, which is 72 cups.
Careful: do not multiply the litres by the price. The 12.50 rupees is for a cup, not for a litre. That is why we needed the number of cups.
Now the money. 72 cups at 12.50 each. 72 times 12 is 864, and 72 halves are 36.
864 plus 36 is 900 rupees.
Check by going back. 900 rupees at 12.50 a cup is 72 cups, and 72 cups of 0.125 litres is 9 litres. It fits.
Milk, then cups, then money. Each step needs the one before it, so take them in order.
Ravi's uncle has boxes that hold 12, 36 and 108 ladoos. Each box holds 3 times as many as the one before. He wants an extra large box that carries the pattern on, and he needs 15 of them.

board.text: Boxes hold 12, 36, 108, ?   He needs 15 of the next size

beats.say: Let's see the pattern on the board first. 12 times 3 is 36, and 36 times 3 is 108.
So how many ladoos does the extra large box hold?

ask.ifNot: The boxes grow by times 3 at each step, not by adding. So the next box holds 108 times 3.

beats.say: 100 times 3 is 300, and 8 times 3 is 24. So the extra large box holds 324 ladoos.
He needs 15 of these boxes, so we want 324 times 15. 15 is 10 plus 5, so we find 324 times 10 and 324 times 5.
324 times 10 is 3240. And 5 is half of 10, so 324 times 5 is half of 3240, which is 1620.
3240 plus 1620 is 4860. He needs 4860 ladoos.
Careful: 1620 is one of the choices. But that is only 5 boxes' worth, half way through the sum.
A rough check: 300 times 15 is 4500. Our box holds a little more than 300, so 4860 is just what we should expect.
So first carry the pattern on to find the new box. Then multiply by the number of boxes.

Ravi spends 1245 on firecrackers, 876 on sweets and 1389 on clothes, and has 2490 left. The money he began with included 500 from his uncle and 750 from his aunt. How much came from grandmother alone?
First, total what went out. 1245 plus 876 is 2121, and 1389 more makes 3510.
He spent 3510 and still has 2490. How do we get back to all the money he began with?

ask.ifNot: Think of it backwards. What went out and what is left were once all together. To rebuild the start, add them.

beats.say: The spent part and the left part together make everything he began with. 3510 plus 2490 is 6000.
He began with 6000. Did all of that come from grandmother?

choices: No: take off uncle's and aunt's
ask.ifNot: The story says the 500 from his uncle and the 750 from his aunt were already inside that total. So they must come off.

beats.say: Uncle and aunt together gave 500 plus 750, which is 1250.

board.text: The start includes uncle's ₹500 and aunt's ₹750

beats.say: Take that from the 6000. Careful: the zeros in 6000 make the borrowing fiddly.
A neat way round it: slide both numbers down by 1. The gap does not change, and 5999 minus 1249 needs no borrowing at all. It is 4750.
So grandmother alone gave him 4750 rupees.
Check by putting the three gifts together. 4750 plus 500 plus 750 is 6000, everything he began with.
So rebuild the whole starting amount first, by adding. Then take away the parts that came from other people.
Vikram buys 3 packets of red powder and 4 of blue, each costing x rupees. He pays 15 rupees for glitter, and the bill comes to 85 rupees.
The red costs 3 x, the blue costs 4 x, and the glitter is 15. Together they make 85.
3 x and 4 x are like terms. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: 3 packets and 4 packets make 7 packets, each costing x. So we add the 3 and the 4, and keep the x: 7 x.

beats.say: So 7 x plus 15 equals 85. Red and blue cost the same, so we can count all the packets together.
The 15 is added on, so to undo it we take 15 from both sides. That leaves 7 x equals 85 minus 15, which is 70.
Nearly there. 7 x means 7 times x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So we divide both sides by 7.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 7.
70 divided by 7 is 10. Each packet costs 10 rupees.
Check. 7 packets at 10 rupees is 70 rupees, and 15 for the glitter makes 85. It works.
Like terms first, then the loose number, then divide. Three small steps.
Neha sells 24 friendship bands at 15 rupees each. She gives 20 percent of her earnings to charity. How much money does she have left?
First, what did she earn? That is 24 times 15. Split the 15 into 10 and 5, to make it easy.
24 times 10 is 240, and 24 times 5 is half of that, 120. Together, 360 rupees earned.
Now the charity gets 20 percent of the 360.
Start small, with 10 percent. That is one tenth, so 360 divided by 10 is 36.
Now build up. 20 percent is 2 times as much, and 2 times 36 is 72.
So 72 rupees go to charity. Is 72 our answer?

ask.ifNot: 72 is the money Neha gives away. The question asks what she has left, so we take it from her 360.

beats.say: 360 minus 72 is 288. Neha has 288 rupees left.
Check: the 288 she keeps and the 72 she gives should make 360 again. And they do.
So: find the total, turn the percent into rupees, and then read the question once more. It asked for what is left, not what was given.
Priya adds diyas to her rangoli every day, following the pattern 5, 11, 17, 23, 29, and so on, for 12 days. How many does she add on day 12, and how many are there in total?
First, the jump. 11 minus 5 is 6, and 17 minus 11 is 6 as well. So each day she adds 6 more diyas than the day before.
Adding 12 numbers one by one is slow, so we will use a shortcut. For it we need the last one, day 12. How many jumps of 6 is that from day 1?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps, not the days. From day 1 to day 2 is 1 jump, and to day 3 is 2 jumps. The jumps are always one fewer than the day number.

beats.say: 12 minus 1 is 11 jumps. And 11 jumps of 6 is 66.
Add that to day 1. 5 plus 66 is 71, so day 12 is 71.
That answers the first part: she adds 71 diyas on day 12. Hold on to that number. Now for the total of all 12 days.
Now the clever part. Put the first and the last together: 5 plus 71 is 76. Then take the second and the second last, 11 and 65. What will they make?

ask.ifNot: 11 is 6 more than 5, and 65 is 6 less than 71. One goes up by 6 and the other comes down by 6, so the total stays the same.

beats.say: 11 plus 65 is 76 too. Keep pairing inwards and every pair makes 76.
12 numbers make 6 pairs, and each pair is worth 76. 6 times 76 is 456. So the complete rangoli has 456 diyas.
Let's check the slow way. The first 6 days add up to 120, the other 6 add up to 336, and 120 plus 336 is 456. It matches.
So the two answers are: 71 diyas on day 12, and 456 diyas in total.
Look carefully at the choices. Two of them have the right number for day 12, but only one has the right total as well. Check both parts before you choose.
So find the last number with the jumps, then pair first with last for the total. And answer every part of the question.
Deepa and Farhan play 4 rounds each. Deepa: plus 12, minus 5, minus 9, plus 6. Farhan: minus 3, plus 8, plus 4, minus 7. We want Deepa's total minus Farhan's total.
Deepa first. Her gains are 12 and 6, which make 18. Her losses are 5 and 9, which make 14.
18 minus 14 is 4. Deepa finishes with 4 rupees.
Now Farhan: minus 3, plus 8, plus 4, minus 7. What is his total?

ask.ifNot: Collect his gains, 8 and 4, and his losses, 3 and 7. Then see which pile is bigger, and by how much.

beats.say: His gains are 8 and 4, which make 12. His losses are 3 and 7, which make 10. And 12 minus 10 is 2.
The question wants Deepa's total minus Farhan's total. Which sum is that?

ask.ifNot: Deepa's total comes first, because the question says Deepa's minus Farhan's. Deepa has 4 and Farhan has 2.

beats.say: 4 minus 2 is 2. The answer is positive, so Deepa has 2 rupees more than Farhan.
Check Deepa round by round: 12, then 7, then minus 2, then 4. Yes, 4.
The order matters in a subtraction. 2 minus 4 would give minus 2, and that would say Deepa has less. Put first whoever the question names first.
Total each player on their own, then subtract in the order the question asks for.
Kavya's mother buys 3 bundles of paper at 160 rupees each, glue and stickers for 120 rupees, and pays 80 rupees stall rent. She sells 40 bags at 25 rupees each. What is her profit?
Profit is the money that came in, take away all the money that went out. So we need two totals.
Start with the paper. How much did the paper cost her?

ask.ifNot: 160 rupees is the price of one bundle, and she buys 3 of them. So the paper costs 3 times 160.

beats.say: 3 times 160 is 480. So the paper costs 480 rupees.
Now add up everything she spent: 480 for paper, 120 for glue and stickers, and 80 for rent. That makes 680 rupees.
Next, the money that came in. 40 bags at 25 rupees each is 40 times 25, which is 1000 rupees.
Now take the money out away from the money in. 1000 minus 680 is 320. Her profit is 320 rupees.
The trap is leaving out a cost. Take off only the paper and you get 520, which is one of the choices. The glue and the rent are costs too.
Check by adding back. Her costs of 680, plus her profit of 320, should make the 1000 she took in. And they do.
So for profit: add up every cost, work out everything earned, then take the costs away from the earnings.
Here is the coach's line for Aarav's score. No brackets, but there is a divide and a times side by side.
Don't rush in from the left. Which piece of this line has to be done first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide go before plus and minus. And when they sit side by side, we take them from left to right, so 12 divided by 3 goes first.

beats.say: It is tempting to start on the left with 15 plus 12. But divide is stronger than plus, so 12 divided by 3 goes first: that makes 4.
Keep going with that same piece: 4 times 2 is 8.
Only plus and minus are left now, so we go left to right: 15 plus 8 is 23.
And 23 minus 5 is 18. Aarav's total score is 18.
Let's check by undoing our steps. 18 plus 5 is 23, and 23 minus 8 is 15, right where that line started.
So the plan is: hunt for the times and divide signs first. When only plus and minus are left, read from left to right.
Neha's bookmark has two angles of 70 degrees each. She says it is both an acute triangle and an isosceles triangle. We must find the third angle and decide if she is right.
Before we go on: what do the three angles of any triangle add up to?

ask.ifNot: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line, and a straight line is 180 degrees.

beats.say: 70 plus 70 is 140, and 180 minus 140 leaves 40. So the third angle is 40 degrees.

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: Now test Neha's word isosceles. A triangle is isosceles when two of its angles are equal. Here two angles are both 70, so yes.
Now her other word, acute. What must be true for a triangle to be acute?

ask.ifNot: Every triangle has some angles under 90 degrees, so one is not enough. A triangle is acute only when all three of its angles are less than 90 degrees.

beats.say: Look at each one: 70, 70 and 40 are all less than 90. So it is acute as well.
So Neha is correct on both counts, and the third angle is 40 degrees.
Check: 70 plus 70 plus 40 is 180. It fits.
So find the missing angle from 180 first. Then test each name on its own: equal angles for isosceles, all angles under 90 for acute.
Team A scored 247 and 189. Team B scored 198 and 215. The team with the higher total wins, and we want to know by how many runs.

board.text: Team A: 247 and 189.   Team B: 198 and 215.

beats.say: Team A scored more in the first innings, and Team B scored more in the second. Can we name the winner yet?

choices: Yes: Team A, it has the top score
No: add each team's two innings
Yes: Team B, it won the last innings
ask.ifNot: A match is decided by the runs over both innings together. One good innings is not enough, so add up each team's two scores.

beats.say: Team A first. 247 plus 189 is 436.
Now Team B. 198 plus 215 is 413.
436 is more than 413, so Team A wins. By how many? 436 minus 413 is 23.
So Team A won by 23 runs.
Careful: comparing just one innings gives a different gap. Only the totals decide a match.
Check by adding on. Team B's 413 plus 23 is 436, which is Team A's total.
So add each team's innings first. The margin is the bigger total minus the smaller one.
Arjun has 180 coins and 240 notes for prize bags. Each bag gets 3 coins, 4 notes and 5 pencils. How many pencils does he need altogether?

board.text: 180 coins, 240 notes. Each bag: 3 coins, 4 notes, 5 pencils

beats.say: To count the pencils, we first need the number of bags. Which sum gives it?

ask.ifNot: 180 coins are shared out 3 to a bag. So the number of bags is how many 3s are in 180: 180 divided by 3.

beats.say: 180 divided by 3 is 60. So there are 60 bags.
Let's make sure with the notes. 240 divided by 4 is also 60. Good, the two agree.
Is 60 really the greatest possible number of bags? 180 is 60 times 3, and 240 is 60 times 4.
3 and 4 have no common factor bigger than 1, so no bigger number divides both. 60 is the highest common factor, just as the story says.
Now the pencils. 60 bags with 5 pencils in each is 60 times 5, which is 300.
Careful: 5 is the pencils in one bag, and 60 is the number of bags. The question wants the pencils for all the bags together.
Check. 300 pencils shared among 60 bags gives 5 each.
Find the number of groups first. Then multiply by how many each group gets.
Priya has diyas in a square. With 45 more, she can make a bigger square that has 23 diyas on each side. How many diyas are in her first square?

board.text: square + 45 = a bigger square with 23 on each side

beats.say: Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: We know everything about the bigger square: 23 on each side. So we can count its diyas, and then step back to the first square.

beats.say: 23 times 20 is 460, and 23 times 3 is 69. 460 plus 69 is 529. The bigger square has 529 diyas.
The bigger square is the first square plus 45. So how do we get back to the first square?

ask.ifNot: The 45 were added to make the bigger square. To go back to the first square, take them off again.

beats.say: 529 minus 45 is 484. Her first square has 484 diyas.
The story says the first arrangement is a square too, so 484 should be a square number. 22 times 20 is 440, 22 times 2 is 44, and 440 plus 44 is 484. It is 22 times 22.
Careful: 529 is among the choices. That is the bigger square, after the 45 were added.
So when you know the bigger square, build it first, then take away what was added. And check that what is left is a square too.
Meera buys 40 boxes of sparklers at 75 rupees each, and gets 20 percent off the bill. She sells every box for 80 rupees, then pays 200 rupees stall rent. Does she end with a profit or a loss?
First, the bill before any discount. 40 times 75 is 3000 rupees.
The wholesaler takes 20 percent off that bill. How much is 20 percent of 3000 rupees?

ask.ifNot: 20 percent means 20 rupees off for every hundred rupees on the bill. And 3000 rupees is a lot of hundreds, so the discount is much more than 20.

beats.say: 3000 is 30 hundreds, and each hundred gets 20 rupees off. 30 times 20 is 600, so the discount is 600 rupees.
So Meera really pays 3000 minus 600, which is 2400 rupees for the sparklers.
The rent is money out as well. 2400 plus 200 is 2600 rupees spent in all.
Now the money in. 40 boxes at 80 rupees each is 3200 rupees.
More came in than went out, so it is a profit. 3200 minus 2600 is 600 rupees.
Careful: forget the rent and you get 800 rupees, which is one of the choices. Every rupee she pays out counts.
Check by adding back: 2600 spent, plus 600 profit, makes 3200, the money she took in.
So take the discount off the bill first, add every other cost, and only then compare with the money that came in.
This one has two parts. First, a crossing where one angle is 3 times the angle next to it. Then a triangle that borrows the smaller of those angles, and has another angle of 50 degrees.

board.text: Crossing: one angle = 3 × the next. Triangle: small, 50°, ?

beats.say: Start with what we know for sure. Two angles side by side on a straight line add up to how much?

ask.ifNot: A straight line is half of a full turn. A full turn is 360 degrees, so the two angles share 180 degrees.

beats.say: Neither angle is given, only how they compare. So let's use equal parts. Call the small angle 1 part. Then the big angle is 3 parts.

board.text: small angle = 1 part,  big angle = 3 parts

beats.say: Look at the bar. How many equal parts fill the whole 180 degrees?

ask.ifNot: Count both angles. The small one is 1 part and the big one is 3 parts. 1 plus 3 makes 4 parts.

beats.say: That is the trap in this question. It says 3 times, so it is tempting to divide by 3. But the small angle needs a part of its own too.
So 180 degrees is shared among 4 equal parts. Halve 180 to get 90, then halve again to get 45. That is one part.
One part is 45 degrees, so that is the small angle. The big angle is 3 parts: 3 times 45 is 135.
Now the triangle. One of its angles equals the smaller crossing angle, 45 degrees. Another is 50 degrees. We want the third.
The three angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees. 45 plus 50 is 95, and 180 minus 95 is 85.
So the third angle of the triangle is 85 degrees.
Careful to use the smaller angle, 45. With 135 the triangle could not even close: 135 and 50 together are already more than 180.
Check the triangle: 45 plus 50 plus 85 makes 180.
Two facts did all the work, and both are about 180. Angles on a straight line make 180, and so do the angles of a triangle.
Deepa buys garlands at 15 rupees each and a kolam stencil for 22 rupees. A coupon takes 7 rupees off, and she pays 120 rupees. How many garlands did she buy?
Let g be the number of garlands. The garlands cost 15 g, and the stencil adds 22. What does the coupon do to the bill?

ask.ifNot: A coupon is a discount. It makes the bill smaller, so the 7 rupees is taken off.

beats.say: So the equation is 15 g, plus 22, minus 7, equals 120.
Tidy the plain numbers. 22 minus 7 is 15. So 15 g plus 15 equals 120.
We want the 15 g by itself. So what should we do about the 15 that is added on?

ask.ifNot: Adding 15 is undone by taking 15 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: So we take 15 from both sides. That leaves 15 g on the left, and 120 minus 15, which is 105, on the right.
15 g means 15 times g. So to undo the times, we divide both sides by 15.
105 divided by 15 is 7, because 15 times 7 is 105. Deepa bought 7 garlands.
Check. 7 garlands at 15 rupees is 105 rupees. Add 22 and take off 7, and she pays 120. It works.
A coupon comes off, a purchase goes on. Get the signs right, tidy up, and the rest is two steps.
Deepa spends 400 rupees on tea and 200 rupees on milk. She sells 120 cups of chai at 8 rupees each, but 15 teachers get 25 percent off their cup. What is her profit?

board.text: Costs ₹400 + ₹200.  120 cups at ₹8, 15 of them 25% off

beats.say: Money out first. 400 plus 200 is 600 rupees.
Now the teachers' price. 25 percent is one quarter, and a quarter of 8 rupees is 2 rupees. So a teacher pays 8 minus 2, which is 6 rupees.
15 cups go to teachers. So how many cups are sold at the full price?

ask.ifNot: The 15 teacher cups are part of the 120, not extra ones. So take them away from 120 to find the cups sold at full price.

beats.say: 120 minus 15 is 105 cups at the full price.
The teachers pay 15 times 6, which is 90 rupees. Everyone else pays 105 times 8, which is 840 rupees.
Together that is 90 plus 840, so 930 rupees came in.
Profit is money in, take away money out. 930 minus 600 is 330 rupees.
The trap is selling all 120 cups at 8 rupees. That brings in 960 rupees, but each teacher really paid 2 rupees less.
And that gives us a check. 15 teachers saving 2 rupees each is 30 rupees, and 960 minus 30 is 930. The same money in.
So when some things sell at a different price, split the sales into groups, total each group, and then take away the costs.
Priya buys 7 packets of gulal and spends 35 rupees on water balloons. A coupon takes 20 rupees off, and she pays 120 rupees. What does one packet cost?
Call the price of a packet x. Then 7 packets cost 7 x. The balloons add 35, and the coupon takes off 20.
Let's tidy the plain numbers. Plus 35 and minus 20: what do they make together?

ask.ifNot: 35 goes on and 20 comes off. 35 minus 20 leaves 15, and it is still added on.

beats.say: So 7 x plus 15 equals 120.
The 15 is added on, so to undo it we take 15 from both sides. That leaves 7 x equals 120 minus 15, which is 105.
Nearly there. 7 x means 7 times x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So we divide both sides by 7.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 7.
105 divided by 7 is 15, because 7 times 15 is 105. Each packet of gulal costs 15 rupees.
Check. 7 packets at 15 rupees is 105 rupees. Add 35 for the balloons, take off the coupon of 20, and she pays 120. It works.
Careful with a coupon: it is money off, so it goes in with a minus. Then tidy, clear and divide.
Meera starts with 53 sachets. She fills 4 packets with the same number in each, and 9 sachets are left over. How many did she put in each packet?
Let x be the number of sachets in one packet. Which equation fits the story?

ask.ifNot: The 53 is everything she started with. Some went into the 4 packets, and 9 were left. So the packets and the leftovers together make 53.

beats.say: 4 packets of x, plus 9 left over, equals 53. Careful: sharing all 53 among 4 packets would not even come out whole. The leftovers must come off first.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. What gets rid of the 9 that is added on and keeps the balance level?

ask.ifNot: Adding 9 is undone by taking 9 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: So we take 9 from both sides. That leaves 4 x on the left, and 53 minus 9, which is 44, on the right.
4 x means 4 times x. So to undo the times, we divide both sides by 4.
44 divided by 4 is 11, because 4 times 11 is 44. Each packet has 11 sachets.
Check. 4 packets of 11 is 44, and 9 left over makes 53. It works.
The total is the packets plus the leftovers. Take the leftovers off, then share among the packets.
Priya's two lines cross at the centre, and one of the 4 angles is 65 degrees. A third line splits the angle directly opposite into two equal parts. We want each part.

board.text: One angle = 65°. The opposite angle is cut in half.

beats.say: Before any cutting, we need the size of the opposite angle. What is it?

ask.ifNot: Taking away from 180 gives the angle next door. The angle straight across is made by the same two lines, opened by the same amount. So it is equal.

beats.say: Here is why. The angle next door is 180 minus 65, which is 115. The opposite angle sits next to that 115 on the other line, so it is 180 minus 115. Back to 65.
Angles straight across a crossing are called vertically opposite angles, and they are always equal. So the opposite angle is 65 degrees.
Now the third line cuts that 65 degree angle into two equal parts. Which sum do we need?

ask.ifNot: The line cuts the opposite angle, which is 65 degrees, not the 115 next door. Two equal parts means dividing by 2.

beats.say: Half of 60 is 30, and half of 5 is 2.5. Together that makes 32.5.
So each part is 32.5 degrees.
Careful: the word opposite matters. Had the line cut the angle next door, we would be halving 115 instead.
Check: 32.5 plus 32.5 gives back 65.
So ask yourself: across, or next door? Across means equal. Next door means the two make 180. Then halve.
Coach Sharma buys jerseys at 200 rupees each and a kit bag for 250 rupees. He hands over 2000 rupees and gets 150 rupees back. How many jerseys did he buy?

board.text: ₹200 a jersey, ₹250 bag. Gave ₹2000, got ₹150 back.

beats.say: First things first. How much did the coach actually spend?

ask.ifNot: He handed over 2000 rupees, but 150 came back to him. So the shop kept 2000 minus 150, which is 1850 rupees.

beats.say: He spent 1850 rupees. Careful: 2000 is only what he handed over. It is not the bill.
Now the equation. x jerseys at 200 rupees each cost 200 x. Add the bag at 250, and that is the 1850 he spent.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. What gets rid of the 250 that is added on and keeps the balance level?

ask.ifNot: Adding 250 is undone by taking 250 away, and the balance only stays level if both sides lose the same. The dividing comes later.

beats.say: Take away 250 on the left, and 250 on the right as well. That leaves 200 x equals 1850 minus 250, which is 1600.
200 x means 200 times x. So to undo the times, we divide both sides by 200.
1600 divided by 200 is 8, because 200 times 8 is 1600. The coach bought 8 jerseys.
Check. 8 jerseys at 200 rupees is 1600. Add the bag and we get 1850. And 2000 minus 1850 is the 150 change. It all fits.
So: find what was really spent, write the equation, then undo one thing at a time.
Arjun's profit line, in rupees, has a bracket near the front, and a divide and a times side by side at the end.
Before we work anything out, look along the whole line. Which piece do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Look for the brackets. Whatever sits inside them is worked out before anything else, so 15 plus 5 goes first.

beats.say: Brackets come first. Inside them, 15 plus 5 is 20, so we write 20 where the bracket was.
No brackets are left, so now we look for times and divide. 3 times 20 is 60.
Now look at 48 divided by 6 times 2. Divide and times sit side by side. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are equal partners, so neither one is stronger. We take them from left to right, and 48 divided by 6 is on the left.

beats.say: Left to right it is: 48 divided by 6 is 8. Write the line again with 60 and 8 in place.
Carry on along that piece: 8 times 2 is 16.
Only plus and minus are left now, so we go left to right: 200 minus 60 is 140. Careful: the 60 comes off before the 16 goes on, because we read left to right.
And 140 plus 16 is 156. Arjun's profit is 156 rupees.
Check by walking backwards. 156 minus 16 is 140, and 140 plus 60 is 200, right where that line started.
So every time: clear the brackets, then do times and divide as you meet them, then finish with plus and minus, left to right.
Ananya's cost line, in rupees, has one bracket, a times, a divide, a minus and a plus.
Don't rush in from the left. Which piece of this line has to be done first?

ask.ifNot: Look for the brackets. Whatever sits inside them is worked out before anything else, so 3 plus 7 goes first.

beats.say: The brackets get done first. Inside them, 3 plus 7 is 10, so we write 10 where the bracket was.
No brackets are left, so now we look for times and divide. 4 times 10 is 40.
The divide goes early too: 60 divided by 5 is 12. Write the line again with 40 and 12 in place.
Only plus and minus are left: 120 minus 40 plus 12. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are equal partners, so we read from left to right, like a sentence. That means 120 minus 40 comes first.

beats.say: Left to right it is: 120 minus 40 is 80.
And 80 plus 12 is 92. Ananya needs to spend 92 rupees.
Let's check by undoing our steps. 92 minus 12 is 80, and 80 plus 40 is 120, right where that line started.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Brackets, then times and divide, then plus and minus, always reading left to right.
Ravi's uncle packs 48 mangoes in a crate. He filled 125 crates on Monday and 78 on Tuesday, and sold every mango for 15 rupees. How much did he earn?

board.text: 48 mangoes a crate; 125 + 78 crates; ₹15 a mango

beats.say: Where shall we start?

ask.ifNot: Monday's crates and Tuesday's crates are being put together. Putting together is adding.

beats.say: 125 plus 78 is 203 crates.
Each crate holds 48, so we want 48 times 203. 203 is 200 plus 3, which makes this easy.
48 times 200 is 9600. And 48 times 3 is 144.
9600 plus 144 is 9744. That is 9744 mangoes.
Each mango sells for 15 rupees. Times 15 is times 10 and times 5 together. How do we get times 5 quickly from times 10?

ask.ifNot: 5 is half of 10. So 5 lots is half as much as 10 lots.

beats.say: 9744 times 10 is 97,440. Half of that is 48,720, and that is 9744 times 5.
Add the two: 97,440 plus 48,720 is 1,46,160. He earned 1,46,160 rupees.
The slip to avoid is stopping early. 9744 is mangoes, not rupees: the price still has to be multiplied in.
Check another way. One crate of 48 mangoes earns 720 rupees. And 203 crates at 720 rupees each comes to 1,46,160 again.
So work in stages: crates, then mangoes, then rupees. And know what each number is counting.
Riya has a square rangoli of tiles. With 7 more rows and 7 more columns, the bigger square would need 225 tiles in total. How many tiles are in the rangoli she has now?

board.text: her square with 7 more rows and columns = 225 tiles

beats.say: The bigger rangoli is a square of 225 tiles, so its side times itself is 225. 15 times 10 is 150, 15 times 5 is 75, and 150 plus 75 is 225. Its side is 15.
The bigger square has 7 more rows and 7 more columns than hers. So what is the side of her square?

ask.ifNot: 7 more rows make it 7 taller, and 7 more columns make it 7 wider. Each side grew by 7 just once, so step each side back by 7.

beats.say: 15 minus 7 is 8. Her rangoli is 8 by 8.
So how many tiles does she have now?

ask.ifNot: 8 is only one side. The tiles fill the whole square, 8 rows of 8, so we multiply 8 by 8.

beats.say: 8 times 8 is 64. Her rangoli has 64 tiles.
The trap is 7 times 7, which is 49. The 7 changes the side of the square. It is not a little square of tiles to take away.
Check: 8 plus 7 is 15, and 15 times 15 is 225. It fits.
So work backwards from the bigger square: square root for its side, step the side back, then square again.
Riya's number has 6 digits and six clues. Some clues give a digit straight away, and some depend on other digits. We start with the ones that are simply given.
