Meena's family spent 86,473 rupees. We swap the digits 6 and 4, and ask by how much the number changes.
Here it is in the chart. The 6 is in the thousands place and the 4 is in the hundreds place. After the swap, what is the new number?

ask.ifNot: Only the 6 and the 4 change places. The 8 in front and the 7 and 3 at the end stay where they are. So it reads 8, 4, 6, 7, 3.

beats.say: The new number is 84,673. The 4 has moved up to the thousands and the 6 has moved down to the hundreds.
Is the new number bigger or smaller than 86,473?

ask.ifNot: Compare the thousands place. The old number has 6 thousands there, and the new one has only 4. So the new number is smaller.

beats.say: Smaller. So the change is the old number minus the new one. The 8 in front and the 7 and 3 at the end are the same in both, so only the middle matters.
In the middle, the old number has 6 thousands and 4 hundreds, which is 6400. The new one has 4 thousands and 6 hundreds, which is 4600.
6400 minus 4600 is 1800. So the number goes down by 1800 rupees.
Careful: the answer is not 2000. The 6 and the 4 do differ by 2 in the thousands place, but the swap hands 2 hundreds back in the hundreds place.
Check by adding: 84,673 plus 1800 is 86,473, the number we began with.
So when two digits swap, write the new number, see which one is bigger, and subtract. Only the places that changed matter.
Raju's 15000 rupees is split: 9000 in Bank A at 6 per cent, and the rest in Bank B at 10 per cent, for 2 years. He buys a bat for 2000 from the interest. How much interest is left?

board.text: ₹15,000: ₹9,000 at 6% (Bank A), the rest at 10% (Bank B)
2 years. Then a ₹2,000 bat, paid from the interest.

beats.say: First, the rest. 15000 minus 9000 is 6000, so Bank B holds 6000 rupees.
Bank A: 9000 is 90 hundreds, each earning 6 rupees a year. 90 times 6 is 540. Careful, the money stays 2 years, so double it: 1080.
Bank B: 6000 is 60 hundreds, each earning 10 rupees a year. 60 times 10 is 600, and for 2 years that is 1200.
Raju pays for the bat. Which money does he pay from?

ask.ifNot: The story says he uses the total interest earned from both banks. The 15000 itself is not touched.

beats.say: So add the two lots of interest. 1080 plus 1200 is 2280.
Now buy the bat. 2280 minus 2000 leaves 280 rupees.
Check by adding back. The 280 left, plus the 2000 for the bat, is 2280, all the interest he earned.
So split the money first, work out each bank's interest for all the years, add them, and only then spend.
Priya's family starts the week with 3,500 rupees in the cash box. Over four days, money comes in three times and goes out once. Let's follow it day by day.
On Wednesday they spent 1,345 rupees on milk, tea leaves and sugar. What does spending do to the cash box?

ask.ifNot: Money that is spent leaves the cash box. So Wednesday is the one day we take away. On every other day we add.

beats.say: Start with Monday's earnings. 3,500 plus 2,475 makes 5,975 rupees in the box.
Tuesday brings in 1,860 more. 5,975 plus 1,860 is 7,835.
Now Wednesday, the spending day. Careful here: this one comes off. 7,835 minus 1,345 is 6,490.
On Thursday they earn again. 6,490 plus 2,190 is 8,680. So the cash box holds 8,680 rupees at the end of Thursday.
The trap in this story is adding all five numbers, just because they are all money. Ask of each amount: did it come in, or did it go out?
Check another way. All the money that came in adds up to 10,025. Take off the 1,345 that was spent, and we get 8,680 again.
So in a money story, start with what was there. Add what comes in, take away what goes out, one step at a time.
Grandma's tablecloth is 120 centimetres by 80 centimetres, with a border 10 centimetres wide all round the inside edge. We want the area of the border only.

board.text: Cloth 120 cm × 80 cm, border 10 cm wide inside the edge

beats.say: The border is like a picture frame. The easy way to find a frame is the whole cloth, minus the middle piece.
The whole cloth is 120 times 80, which is 9600 square centimetres.
Now the middle piece. The border is 10 centimetres wide at each end. So how long is the middle?

ask.ifNot: There is border at the left end and at the right end. So the length loses 10, and then another 10. That leaves 100.

beats.say: That is the trap: the 10 comes off both ends. For the length, 120 minus 10 minus 10 is 100. For the width, 80 minus 10 minus 10 is 60.
So the middle piece is 100 times 60, which is 6000 square centimetres.
The border is what is left. 9600 minus 6000 is 3600 square centimetres.
Let's check it another way, strip by strip. Two long strips, 120 by 10, make 2400. Two short strips, 60 by 10, make 1200. Together that is 3600 again.
So for a border, find the whole, find the middle, and subtract. And remember the width comes off at both ends.
Aarav's line for the chai stall has two pairs of brackets, and a divide, two times signs, a minus and a plus.
Before we work anything out, look along the whole line. Which piece do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Look for the brackets. Whatever sits inside them is worked out before anything else, so 4 plus 2 goes first.

beats.say: Brackets are always the first job, and there are two pairs. In the first pair, 4 plus 2 is 6.
In the second pair, 8 minus 6 is 2. Write the line again with 6 and 2 where the brackets were.
Now look at 120 divided by 6 times 3. Divide and times sit side by side. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are equal partners, so neither one is stronger. We take them from left to right, and 120 divided by 6 is on the left.

beats.say: Left to right it is: 120 divided by 6 is 20.
The times goes early too: 5 times 2 is 10. Write the line again with 20 and 10 in place.
Carry on along that piece: 20 times 3 is 60.
Only plus and minus are left now, so we go left to right: 60 minus 10 is 50. Careful: the 10 comes off before the 15 goes on, because we read left to right.
And 50 plus 15 is 65. The expression is worth 65.
Let's check by undoing our steps. 65 minus 15 is 50, and 50 plus 10 is 60, right where that line started.
So here is the plan for a line like this. Brackets, then times and divide, then plus and minus, always reading left to right.
Arjun's ground is 120 metres by 80 metres, with a track 5 metres wide all round the outside. Grass on the track costs 12 rupees for each square metre.

board.text: Ground 120 m × 80 m, track 5 m wide round the outside
Grass on the track: ₹12 per sq m. Cost = ?

beats.say: The track is a frame round the ground. So its area is the big outer rectangle, minus the ground.
The track adds 5 metres at each end of the ground. So how long is the outer rectangle?

ask.ifNot: There is track at both ends of the ground. So the length grows by 5, and then by 5 again. That makes 130.

beats.say: The outer length is 120 plus 5 plus 5, which is 130. The outer breadth is 80 plus 5 plus 5, which is 90.
So the outer rectangle is 130 times 90, which is 11700. And the ground itself is 120 times 80, which is 9600.
Take the ground away. 11700 minus 9600 is 2100 square metres of track.
Now the cost, 2100 times 12. 2100 times 10 is 21000, and 2100 times 2 is 4200.
21000 plus 4200 is 25200. The grass costs 25200 rupees.
The classic slip is adding the 5 only once. A track all the way round adds its width twice to the length, and twice to the breadth.
So for a path round the outside: make the outer rectangle, subtract the inner one, then multiply by the price.
Ravi bought crackers, sweets and gifts, and still had 2,350 rupees left. Part of his money was 500 rupees from an old envelope. We want only what Grandmother gave him.
This is a work backwards story: we know the end and we want the start. First, the spending. 1,245 plus 867 plus 1,538 is 3,650 rupees.
He spent 3,650 and still had 2,350 left. How do we find what he had before he started spending?

ask.ifNot: Before the shopping, he was holding the money he spent and the money he kept. So we put the two back together: 3,650 plus 2,350.

beats.say: 3,650 plus 2,350 is 6,000. So Ravi had 6,000 rupees before he bought anything.
Careful here. 6,000 is one of the choices, but it did not all come from Grandmother. 500 of it came from the envelope.
So what do we do with the 500?

ask.ifNot: The 6,000 already has the envelope money inside it. To leave only Grandmother's gift, we take the 500 out.

beats.say: 6,000 minus 500 is 5,500. Grandmother gave him 5,500 rupees.
Check by playing the story forwards. 5,500 plus 500 is 6,000. Take away the 3,650 he spent, and 2,350 is left, just as the story says.
So when a story gives you the end, walk backwards. Put back what was spent, then take out anything that came from somewhere else.
Coach Sharma buys jerseys, and a kit bag for 350 rupees. The bill is 2030 rupees. He returns 3 jerseys, and after the refund his spending is 1670 rupees. What does one jersey cost?
We are not told how many jerseys he bought. But his spending dropped. What made it drop?

ask.ifNot: Only the 3 jerseys went back to the shop. So the whole drop in spending is the price of exactly 3 jerseys.

beats.say: So how big is the drop? 2030 minus 1670 is 360 rupees. That is the refund.
Call the price of one jersey x. The refund is for 3 jerseys, so 3 x equals 360.
3 x means 3 times x. What undoes times 3?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 3, we divide both sides by 3.

beats.say: Divide both sides by 3. 360 divided by 3 is 120. Each jersey costs 120 rupees.
Check with the first bill. Take off the bag: 2030 minus 350 is 1680. And 1680 is exactly 14 jerseys at 120 rupees. A whole number of jerseys, so it fits.
Careful: the kit bag is a distraction here. The clue is the change. When a total changes, look at the difference and ask what caused it.
Arjun puts 3 rupees in his piggy bank on Monday, 7 on Tuesday, 11 on Wednesday and 15 on Thursday. If the pattern carries on, how much goes in on Sunday, which is day 7?
Before we jump ahead, look at how the pattern grows. What happens from one day to the next?

ask.ifNot: Look at the gap between neighbours, not at the numbers themselves. How far is it from 3 up to 7?

beats.say: 7 minus 3 is 4, and 11 minus 7 is 4 too. So each day he puts in 4 rupees more than the day before.
Day 1 is 3. To get from day 1 to day 7, how many jumps of 4 do we make?

ask.ifNot: Count the jumps, not the days. From day 1 to day 2 is 1 jump, and to day 3 is 2 jumps. The jumps are always one fewer than the day number.

beats.say: So we need 7 minus 1, which is 6 jumps. And 6 jumps of 4 is 6 times 4, which is 24.
Now add that 24 to the 3 we started with. 3 plus 24 is 27. So on Sunday, day 7, Arjun puts in 27 rupees.
Here is the trap: making 7 jumps, just because it is day 7. That gives 31, which is really day 8.
Check by counting on, 4 at a time, from 15: 19, 23, 27. That is day 7, and it lands on 27.
So when a pattern grows by the same amount each time: find the jump, count the jumps, which are one fewer than the place you want, multiply, and add to the start.
Here is the earnings line from Ravi's family chai stall. Watch the middle: a divide, then a bracket, then a times.
There are several jobs in this line. Which one comes first?

ask.ifNot: Look for the brackets. Whatever sits inside them is worked out before anything else, so 2 plus 6 goes first.

beats.say: Brackets come first. Inside them, 2 plus 6 is 8, so we write 8 where the bracket was.
Now look at 48 divided by 8 times 3. Divide and times sit side by side. Which goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are equal partners, so neither one is stronger. We take them from left to right, and 48 divided by 8 is on the left.

beats.say: Left to right it is: 48 divided by 8 is 6.
Carry on along that piece: 6 times 3 is 18.
Only plus and minus are left now, so we go left to right: 120 minus 18 is 102. Careful: the 18 comes off before the 15 goes on, because we read left to right.
And 102 plus 15 is 117. The expression is worth 117.
Let's check by undoing our steps. 117 minus 15 is 102, and 102 plus 18 is 120, right where that line started.
So every time: clear the brackets, then do times and divide as you meet them, then finish with plus and minus, left to right.
Riya buys 25 packets of gulal, pink to yellow in the ratio 3 to 2. A pink packet costs 15 rupees and a yellow packet costs 20 rupees. How much does she spend altogether?
Think of the ratio as equal boxes: 3 parts for pink and 2 parts for yellow.

spec.note: All the boxes together: 25 packets

beats.say: First job: how many equal parts are there in all?

ask.ifNot: Count the boxes in all the rows together: 3 and 2 make 5 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5. So the 25 packets are shared into 5 equal parts.
To find one part, we divide: 25 divided by 5 is 5, so each part is 5 packets. Careful: we divide by all 5 parts, not by one of the ratio numbers on its own.
Pink has 3 parts: 3 times 5 is 15 packets. Yellow has 2 parts: 2 times 5 is 10 packets.
Now the money. There are 15 pink packets at 15 rupees each. Which sum gives their cost?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 15 pink packets costs 15 rupees. 15 lots of 15 is 15 times 15.

beats.say: 15 times 15 is 225 rupees for pink. And 10 yellow packets at 20 rupees each cost 10 times 20, which is 200 rupees.
Add the two costs: 225 plus 200 is 425.
So Riya spends 425 rupees altogether.
Check the sharing: 15 plus 10 is 25, the whole amount. The shares are right.
So the plan: use the ratio to find how many of each kind, multiply each kind by its own price, then add the two costs.
Ananya has 76,482 rupees in her piggy bank. Her father asks: the place value of the 7 is how many times the face value of the 8?
Look at the chart. The 7 is in the ten-thousands column. What is it worth there?

ask.ifNot: Count the columns from the right: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. So this 7 means 7 ten-thousands, and that is 70,000.

beats.say: 7 times 10,000 is 70,000. That is the place value of the 7.
Now the face value of 8. In this number the 8 sits in the tens column, so its place value is 80. But face value is just the digit as it looks, so it is simply 8.
How many times 8 is 70,000? Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: How many times means divide. And we divide by the face value of the 8, which is 8, not by 80.

beats.say: Here is a neat way to divide by 8: halve, halve again, and halve once more. That works because 2 times 2 times 2 is 8.
70,000 halved is 35,000. Halve again: 17,500. And once more: 8750.
So 70,000 divided by 8 is 8750. Careful: dividing by 80, the place value of the 8, would give a much smaller answer.
Check by multiplying back: 8750 times 8 is 70,000. It works.
So Ananya should say 8750 times.
So remember: place value depends on the column, and face value is just the digit. Find both, then divide.
Meera's tablecloth is 90 centimetres by 60 centimetres. She cuts a piece, 30 centimetres by 20 centimetres, out of one corner. How much cloth is left?

board.text: Piece cut from a corner: 30 cm × 20 cm

beats.say: How do we find the area that is left?

ask.ifNot: Cutting a piece out makes the cloth smaller. So we take the area of the piece away from the area of the whole cloth.

beats.say: First the whole cloth, 90 times 60. 9 times 6 is 54, and the two zeros go on the end: 5400 square centimetres.
Now the piece. 30 times 20 is 600 square centimetres.
Take it away. 5400 minus 600 is 4800 square centimetres.
Careful not to subtract the sides first. That would give 60 by 40, which is only 2400. It slices off a whole strip, not just one corner.
Check by putting the piece back. 4800 plus 600 is 5400, the whole cloth.
So when a piece is cut out, work out both areas first, and then subtract the areas, never the sides.
Arjun's team has 11 players. In each match, every player scores an average of 35 runs, and they play 18 matches. The principal gives one certificate for every 50 runs. How many certificates?

board.text: 11 players × 35 runs, 18 matches; 1 certificate per 50 runs

beats.say: Start with one match. How many runs does the whole team score in a match?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 11 players makes 35 runs. 11 lots of 35 is 11 times 35.

beats.say: 10 players make 350 runs, and 1 more player makes it 385 runs in a match.
They play 18 matches, so we want 385 times 18. 18 is 2 less than 20, so find 385 times 20 and take off 385 times 2.
385 times 20 is 7700. And 385 times 2 is 770.
7700 minus 770 is 6930. The team scores 6930 runs in all.
Now the certificates, one for every 50 runs. 100 runs earn 2 certificates, and 6930 is 69 hundreds with 30 left over.
69 hundreds earn 69 times 2, which is 138 certificates. And 30 runs are still left.
30 runs are left over. Do they earn one more certificate?

choices: No, a certificate needs a full 50
ask.ifNot: A certificate is given only for a complete 50 runs. 30 is not a full 50, so it earns nothing.

beats.say: So 138 certificates are given out.
Check: 138 certificates use up 6900 runs, and the 30 spare runs make 6930. Notice 6930 is in the choices too, but that is the runs, not the certificates.
So multiply up to the total, divide by 50, and here the left over runs are simply dropped.
Arjun has a square sheet of side 20 centimetres. He cuts a 4 centimetre square from each corner and folds up the sides to make a tray. We want the area of the flat base.

board.text: A 4 cm square is cut from each corner

beats.say: When the flaps fold up, the flat middle is the base. So first we need to know how long the base is.

board.text: Base = the middle that stays flat

beats.say: Look along one edge of the sheet. There is a corner cut at both ends. How long is the base along that edge?

ask.ifNot: One corner takes 4 off the left end, and another takes 4 off the right end. 20 minus 4, and minus 4 again, leaves 12.

beats.say: That is the trap. Take off 4 only once and you get 16. But there is a corner at each end, so it is 20 minus 4 minus 4, which is 12.
The sheet was a square, so the very same thing happens the other way. The base is a square, 12 by 12.
12 times 12 is 144. The base is 144 square centimetres.
Let's check that every bit of the sheet is counted. The whole sheet is 20 times 20, 400. The four corners are 4 times 16, which is 64.
Each flap is 12 by 4, which is 48, and four of them make 192. Then 144 plus 64 plus 192 is 400, the whole sheet.
So when corners are cut from a sheet, each side of the base loses the cut twice. Then the base is just length times breadth.
Meera plays 5 rounds: plus 6, minus 9, plus 4, minus 3, plus 5. Her friend Deepa finished on minus 2. How many more points does Meera have than Deepa?
Collect Meera's gains: 6, 4 and 5 make 15. And her losses: 9 and 3 make 12.
Gains of 15, losses of 12. What is Meera's total?

ask.ifNot: This time the gains are bigger than the losses, by 3. So Meera's total is above 0.

beats.say: 15 minus 12 is 3. Meera finishes on 3 points.
Meera has 3 and Deepa has minus 2. How many more points does Meera have?

ask.ifNot: Deepa is below 0 and Meera is above it. From minus 2 up to 0 is 2 points, and then from 0 up to 3 is 3 more.

beats.say: 2 points to climb up to 0, then 3 more to reach Meera. 2 plus 3 is 5. Meera has 5 more points.
As a subtraction it is 3 minus minus 2. Taking away a negative is the same as adding, so it becomes 3 plus 2.
The slip to avoid is 3 take away 2, which gives 1. That would be right if Deepa had plus 2, but she is below 0.
Find the total first. Then, for scores on opposite sides of 0, add their distances from 0.
At the school fair, the ring toss costs 3 rupees to enter, and then 4 rupees for each ring. Rohan spent 31 rupees. How many rings did he toss?
Let x be the number of rings. Which number gets multiplied by x?

ask.ifNot: The 4 rupees is paid again for every ring, so it is 4 times x. The 3 rupees is paid just once, to get in.

beats.say: 3 to enter, plus 4 x for the rings, equals 31.
The 3 is added on, so to undo it we take 3 from both sides. That leaves 4 x equals 31 minus 3, which is 28.
Nearly there. 4 x means 4 times x. What undoes times 4?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So we divide both sides by 4.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide by 4.
28 divided by 4 is 7. Rohan tossed 7 rings.
Check. 7 rings at 4 rupees is 28 rupees. Add the 3 to enter, and he spent 31. It works.
Once only, or every time? The every time number goes with the letter. The once only number comes off first.
Riya has a big square of 625 tiles. She takes a small square out of one corner, and 576 tiles are left. We want the side of the square she can make from the tiles she took out.

board.text: 625 tiles − a small square = 576 tiles. Its side?

beats.say: First, how many tiles did she take out? Which sum tells us?

ask.ifNot: She started with 625, and 576 are still there. The missing tiles are the difference between those two numbers.

beats.say: 625 minus 576. Let's count up. From 576, 24 more gets us to 600. Then 25 more gets us to 625.
24 and 25 make 49. So she took out 49 tiles.
Now those 49 tiles make a new square. The question asks for its side, not the number of tiles. Which number times itself makes 49?

ask.ifNot: 49 is how many tiles are in the whole square. The side is the number that, multiplied by itself, makes 49. Think of the 7 times table.

beats.say: 7 times 7 is 49. So the new square has 7 tiles on each side.
Check that no tile has gone missing. The 576 left, plus the 49 taken out, make 625.
The trap is to stop at 49. That is how many tiles there are. The side is its square root.
So: subtract to find what was removed, then take the square root to find the side.

Suresh buys 30 cricket balls at 45 rupees each, and pays 150 rupees for a banner and 75 rupees for carry bags. He sells 24 balls at 70 rupees each and gives the other 6 away. Profit or loss, and how much?
He only sold 24 balls. But how many balls did he pay for?

ask.ifNot: The wholesaler was paid for every ball Suresh took, even the 6 he later gave away. So the cost is for all 30.

beats.say: 30 times 45 is 1350 rupees for the balls.
Add the banner and the bags. 1350 plus 150 is 1500, and 75 more makes 1575 rupees spent.
Now the money in. Only the 24 balls he sold count here. 24 times 70 is 1680 rupees.
1575 rupees went out and 1680 rupees came in. Is that a profit or a loss?

ask.ifNot: Compare the two amounts. More money came in than went out, and that is a profit.

beats.say: It is a profit. 1680 minus 1575 is 105 rupees.
The trap is forgetting the banner and the bags. That gives 1680 minus 1350, which is 330, one of the choices.
Check: 1575 spent, plus 105 profit, makes 1680, the money he took in.
So pay for everything that was bought, earn only on what was sold, and take one total from the other.
Sameer starts at minus 8. Round 1, he climbs 12. Round 2, he slides down 5. Round 3, he climbs twice the distance he slid in Round 2.

board.text: Start −8: up 12, down 5, up twice the slide

beats.say: Round 1, up 12. Minus 8 plus 12 is 4. 8 of those steps bring us up to 0, and then 4 more above it.
Round 2, down 5. 4 minus 5 is minus 1. 4 of those steps take us down to 0, and then 1 more below it.
Round 3: he climbs twice the distance he slid down in Round 2. How far is that climb?

ask.ifNot: Look back at Round 2. The slide was 5 metres, and twice 5 is 10. It is the slide we double, not the place where he is standing.

beats.say: Twice 5 is 10, so in Round 3 he climbs 10 metres.
Up 10 from minus 1. Minus 1 plus 10 is 9. Sameer finishes at plus 9.
Check with totals. Up 12, up 10 and down 5 is 17 up overall. And minus 8 plus 17 is 9. It matches.
The trap here was the word twice. It doubles the slide of 5, not Sameer's position.
So: keep track of the position after every round, and read carefully what each round's move depends on.
Ravi puts 5000 rupees in a bank at 6 per cent simple interest a year, for 3 years. With just the interest he buys cricket balls at 150 rupees each. How many can he buy?

board.text: ₹5,000 at 6% a year for 3 years. A ball costs ₹150.

beats.say: 6 per cent a year means every 100 rupees earns 6 rupees in a year. So how many hundreds are in 5000? 5000 divided by 100 is 50.
Each of those 50 hundreds earns 6 rupees. 50 times 6 is 300. So 1 year brings 300 rupees of interest.
The money stays for 3 years. 300 times 3 is 900. So the interest is 900 rupees.
He spends only the interest on balls that cost 150 each. Which sum tells us how many balls?

ask.ifNot: Only the interest is being spent, and that is 900 rupees. Each ball uses up 150 of it, so we count how many 150s fit into 900.

beats.say: 2 balls cost 300. And 900 is 3 lots of 300, so that is 3 lots of 2 balls: 6 balls.
Check by multiplying. 6 balls at 150 each is 900, which uses up the interest exactly.
Notice his 5000 is still safe in the bank. The question only let him spend the interest, so only the interest gets divided.
So: 1 year's interest, times the years, and then share that interest out by the price of 1 ball.
Ravi's family set aside 5,000 rupees for Diwali shopping. They bought crackers, sweets and decorations, and shared what was left between 2 charity boxes.
What do we need to find first?

ask.ifNot: Only the leftover money is shared. And we cannot know the leftover until we know what the three things cost altogether.

beats.say: Add the crackers and the sweets first. 2,475 plus 1,368 is 3,843.
Now the decorations. 3,843 plus 957 is 4,800. So they spent 4,800 rupees.
Take that from the 5,000 they set aside. 5,000 minus 4,800 leaves 200 rupees.
Careful: 200 is one of the choices, but that is the whole leftover. It still has to be split between the 2 boxes.
200 divided by 2 is 100. Each charity box gets 100 rupees.
Check it. 2 boxes of 100 make 200, and 200 plus the 4,800 they spent is 5,000. Every rupee is accounted for.
So follow the story in order: total the spending, find what is left, then share it out.
Riya's grandfather uses 375 millilitres of milk for each cup of chai. He sold 48 cups on Monday and 64 on Tuesday. Milk comes in 5 litre packets. What is the smallest number of packets he needs?

board.text: 375 ml a cup; 48 + 64 cups; milk in 5 litre packets

beats.say: First the cups. 48 plus 64 is 112 cups.
Each cup takes 375 millilitres. 100 cups take 37,500, and the other 12 cups take 4500. Altogether that is 42,000 millilitres.
The milk is in millilitres, but the packets are in litres. How do we change millilitres into litres?

ask.ifNot: 1 litre holds 1000 millilitres. So we count how many thousands there are, and that means dividing by 1000.

beats.say: 42,000 divided by 1000 is 42. He needs 42 litres of milk.
Now the 5 litre packets. 8 packets hold 40 litres, and that leaves 2 litres still needed.
8 packets give 40 litres, but he needs 42. How many packets must he buy?

ask.ifNot: 8 packets leave him 2 litres short, and the shop does not sell part of a packet. So he has to buy one more whole packet.

beats.say: 8 packets and 1 more is 9 packets.
Check: 9 packets hold 45 litres, which covers the 42 he needs. 8 packets would not.
So get the total, change it into the packet's unit, divide, and go up to the next whole packet when some is still needed.
We are hunting for the number whose digits add up to 20. Here are the four to choose from.

ask.ifNot: Digit sum is just what it says. Take each digit of the number and add them all together.

beats.say: First, what does 'digit sum' ask us to do?
So we test the numbers one at a time. A tip: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip straight over any zeros.
Try 6516. 6 plus 5 plus 1 plus 6 makes 18. That is too small, so we cross it out.
Take 5052. 5 plus 0 plus 5 plus 2 makes 12. Not 20 either, so out it goes.

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time: 8, 0, 5, 7. Keep a running total as you go.

beats.say: Now 8057. Add its digits yourself before I do. What do you get?
8 plus 0 plus 5 plus 7 makes 20. We have found it!
Let's make sure of the others. First 8296. 8 plus 2 plus 9 plus 6 makes 25, which is too big. Cross it out.
So the number with a digit sum of 20 is 8057.
Digit sum means add the digits, nothing more. Test each choice calmly and cross out the ones that miss.
Let's write the number down: 26051. We want the place value of the 6 sitting in the thousands place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. So that is where our 6 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: A digit in the thousands column counts thousands. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 6 of those. 6 times 1000 makes 6000.
Careful: 6 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 6000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 20000 plus 6000 plus 50 plus 1. There is our 6000, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 6 in the thousands place is 6000.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Here is our number, 46180. The question points at the 8 in the tens place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens. There is our 8.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: A digit in the tens column counts tens. So what is each one in that column worth?
So the 8 means 8 lots of 10. That is 80.
Careful: 8 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 80. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 40000 plus 6000 plus 100 plus 80. There is our 80, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 8 in the tens place is 80.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Let's write the number down: 31471. We want the place value of the 3 sitting in the ten-thousands place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. There is our 3.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called ten-thousands, so each one in it stands for 10000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the ten-thousands place?
Our digit says there are 3 of those. 3 times 10000 makes 30000.
Careful: 3 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 30000. The 4 zeros are there because 4 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 30000 plus 1000 plus 400 plus 70 plus 1. And look, 30000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 3 in the ten-thousands place is 30000.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
Let's write the number down: 81615. We want the place value of the 1 sitting in the thousands place.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. Careful, this number has more than one 1. We want the one in the thousands column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: A digit in the thousands column counts thousands. So what is each one in that column worth?
We have just 1 of them. 1 times 1000 is 1000.
Careful: 1 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 1000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 80000 plus 1000 plus 600 plus 10 plus 5. There is our 1000, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 1 in the thousands place is 1000.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Let's write the number down: 54827. We want the place value of the 2 sitting in the tens place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens. So that is where our 2 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the tens place?
So the 2 means 2 lots of 10. That is 20.
Careful: 2 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 20. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 50000 plus 4000 plus 800 plus 20 plus 7. There is our 20, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 2 in the tens place is 20.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Here is our number, 26004. The question points at the 4 in the units place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
The units place is the very last column, on the right. There is our 4.

ask.ifNot: The units column counts single ones. So each one in that column is worth just 1.

beats.say: The units column is the smallest of them all. What is each one in that column worth?
We have 4 ones. 4 times 1 is just 4.
Here is something neat. In the units place, the place value and the face value are the same: 4.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 20000 plus 6000 plus 4. There is our 4, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 4 in the units place is 4.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
Here is our number, 68748. The question points at the 8 in the thousands place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. Careful, this number has more than one 8. We want the one in the thousands column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the thousands place?
We have 8 of them. So 8 times 1000 is 8000.
Careful: 8 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 8000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 60000 plus 8000 plus 700 plus 40 plus 8. And look, 8000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 8 in the thousands place is 8000.

Here is our number, 37814. The question points at the 8 in the hundreds place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds. There is our 8.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the hundreds place?
So the 8 means 8 lots of 100. That is 800.
Careful: 8 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 800. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 30000 plus 7000 plus 800 plus 10 plus 4. And look, 800 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 8 in the hundreds place is 800.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Here is our number, 83710. The question points at the 7 in the hundreds place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds. There is our 7.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the hundreds place?
We have 7 of them. So 7 times 100 is 700.
Careful: 7 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 700. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 80000 plus 3000 plus 700 plus 10. And look, 700 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 7 in the hundreds place is 700.
So, find the column, then multiply the digit by what the column is worth. That works for any number.
Here is 88510. We are comparing two digits: the 8 in the ten-thousands place, and the 5 in the hundreds place.

ask.ifNot: It is 8 in the ten-thousands column, so it stands for 8 lots of 10000. That makes 80000.

beats.say: Here they are in the chart. Start with the 8 in the ten-thousands column. What is it worth?
8 times 10000 is 80000. So that 8 is worth 80000.
Now the 5 in the hundreds place. 5 times 100 is 500.

ask.ifNot: 'How many times' asks how many lots of 500 fit into 80000. Fitting in means dividing the place values, not taking away.

beats.say: Now for the words 'how many times'. Which sum answers that?
80000 divided by 500 is 160.
Good mathematicians check. 160 times 500 is 80000, just as it should be.
So the 8 in the ten-thousands place is worth 160 times the 5 in the hundreds place.
The plan: find each place value first, then divide. Never just divide the digits as they look.
Here is our number, 29916. The question points at the 1 in the tens place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens. And there sits our 1.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: A digit in the tens column counts tens. So what is each one in that column worth?
We have just 1 of them. 1 times 10 is 10.
Careful: 1 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 10. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 20000 plus 9000 plus 900 plus 10 plus 6. There is our 10, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 1 in the tens place is 10.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
This is 87298. One of its digits, the 8 in the units place, has a value for us to find.
The units place is the very last column, on the right. Careful, this number has more than one 8. We want the one in the units column.

ask.ifNot: The units column counts single ones. So each one in that column is worth just 1.

beats.say: The units column is the smallest of them all. What is each one in that column worth?
We have 8 ones. 8 times 1 is just 8.
Here is something neat. In the units place, the place value and the face value are the same: 8.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 80000 plus 7000 plus 200 plus 90 plus 8. And look, 8 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 8 in the units place is 8.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
One of these four numbers has a digit sum of 10. Let's find out which.

ask.ifNot: Digit sum is just what it says. Take each digit of the number and add them all together.

beats.say: First, what does 'digit sum' ask us to do?
So we test the numbers one at a time. Add slowly, one digit at a time, and nothing can go astray.

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time: 3, 3, 4. Keep a running total as you go.

beats.say: Start with 334. Add its digits yourself before I do. What do you get?
3 plus 3 plus 4 makes 10. There it is!
Let's make sure of the others. First 666. 6 plus 6 plus 6 makes 18. That is too big, so we cross it out.
Then 369. 3 plus 6 plus 9 makes 18. Not 10 either, so out it goes.
And last, 977. 9 plus 7 plus 7 makes 23, which is too big. Cross it out.
So the number with a digit sum of 10 is 334.
Digit sum means add the digits, nothing more. Test each choice calmly and cross out the ones that miss.
This is 92203. One of its digits, the 2 in the thousands place, has a value for us to find.
Count the columns from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. Careful, this number has more than one 2. We want the one in the thousands column.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called thousands, so each one in it stands for 1000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the thousands place?
We have 2 of them. So 2 times 1000 is 2000.
Careful: 2 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 2000. The 3 zeros are there because 3 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 90000 plus 2000 plus 200 plus 3. And look, 2000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 2 in the thousands place is 2000.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Here is our number, 72816. The question points at the 7 in the ten-thousands place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. So that is where our 7 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called ten-thousands, so each one in it stands for 10000.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the ten-thousands place?
Our digit says there are 7 of those. 7 times 10000 makes 70000.
Careful: 7 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 70000. The 4 zeros are there because 4 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 70000 plus 2000 plus 800 plus 10 plus 6. And look, 70000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 7 in the ten-thousands place is 70000.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
Let's write the number down: 30578. We want the place value of the 3 sitting in the ten-thousands place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. So that is where our 3 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called ten-thousands, so each one in it stands for 10000.

beats.say: A digit in the ten-thousands column counts ten-thousands. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 3 of those. 3 times 10000 makes 30000.
Careful: 3 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 30000. The 4 zeros are there because 4 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 30000 plus 500 plus 70 plus 8. There is our 30000, right where it should be.

Here is our number, 77441. The question points at the 4 in the hundreds place, and asks what that digit is really worth.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: A digit in the hundreds column counts hundreds. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 4 of those. 4 times 100 makes 400.
Careful: 4 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 400. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.

6 pencils, and every one costs 3 rupees. How much does Siya pay altogether?
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one pencil, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 6 pencils costs 3 rupees. That is 3 rupees, 6 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 6 times, so it is a times sum. 6 times 3 is 18.
So the total cost is 18 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 18 rupees, in lots of 3 rupees, gives 6 pencils. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Now you try one!
Vivek buys 5 books at 8 rupees each, and hands over 65 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 books at Rs.8 each. Pays Rs.65.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 65 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 5 books at 8 rupees each: that is 5 times 8. 5 times 8 is 40.
Careful: 40 is only the cost, not the answer. Vivek paid 65. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 40 away from 65.

beats.say: 65 take away 40 leaves 25.
So Vivek gets 25 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 40 plus 25 is 65. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Isha pays 120 rupees for a book. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 120 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 120 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 120 divided by 10 is 12.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 12 is 6.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 12 plus 6 makes 18. That is the profit.
So the profit is 18 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 120 plus 18 is 138. So the selling price is 138 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 138 is 18 more than 120. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Rohan is sharing out 72 marbles in the ratio 3 is to 5. Our job is to find the larger group.

board.text: 72 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 72 to share. The ratio is 3 is to 5. And the question only wants the larger group.
A ratio of 3 is to 5 means this. One side gets 3 equal parts, and the other gets 5 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 5 together make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 and 5 make 8. That means the 72 is spread over 8 equal parts.
Careful with this next step, it is the one that trips people up. What is one part worth?

ask.ifNot: The 72 fills all 8 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 72 by 8.

beats.say: 72 divided by 8 is 9. Now we can write 9 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 9

beats.say: The larger group has 5 of these parts. 5 times 9 is 45.
So the larger group has 45 marbles. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is 3 times 9, which is 27. And 27 plus 45 is 72, just what we started with.
So, to share in a ratio: count the parts, find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as you need.
54 is being shared out in the ratio 2 is to 7. We are after the smaller share.

board.text: Divide 54 in the ratio 2 : 7. Smaller share = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 54 to share. The ratio is 2 is to 7. And the question only wants the smaller share.
A ratio of 2 is to 7 means this. One side gets 2 equal parts, and the other gets 7 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 7 together make 9 parts.

beats.say: 2 and 7 make 9. That means the 54 is spread over 9 equal parts.
Here comes the turning point. Which sum tells us what a single part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 54 fills all 9 parts, not just the 7 parts of one bar. So we divide 54 by 9.

beats.say: 54 divided by 9 is 6. Now we can write 6 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 6

beats.say: We want the smaller share, and that is 2 parts. 2 times 6 makes 12.
So the smaller share is 12. There it is!
Let's check. The larger share is 7 times 6, which is 42. And 12 plus 42 is 54, just what we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
Kavya is sharing out 49 toffees in the ratio 2 is to 5. Our job is to find the larger group.

board.text: 49 toffees in the ratio 2 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Before any sum, let's be sure what we know. The total is 49. The ratio is 2 is to 5. And we want the larger group only.
Let's draw the ratio. 2 is to 5: one bar with 2 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 5 together make 7 parts.

beats.say: 2 and 5 make 7. That means the 49 is spread over 7 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 49 fills all 7 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 49 by 7.

beats.say: 49 divided by 7 is 7. Now we can write 7 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 7

beats.say: The larger group has 5 of these parts. 5 times 7 is 35.
So the larger group has 35 toffees. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is 2 times 7, which is 14. And 14 plus 35 is 49, just what we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
The ages of Kavya and Karan are in the ratio 4 is to 7. Karan is 56 years old, and we want Kavya's age.
Look at the order carefully. Kavya is named first, so Kavya goes with the 4. Karan is second, and goes with the 7.
As bars: Kavya's age is 4 equal parts, and Karan's is 7 parts of the same size. We know Karan's whole bar is 56 years.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: So how do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 56 years belong to Karan alone, and Karan's bar has 7 parts. So we divide 56 by 7.

beats.say: 56 divided by 7 is 8, so each part is 8 years. Notice we did not add 4 and 7 this time, because 56 is not the total of both ages.

spec.note: Each piece is 8 years

beats.say: Kavya has 4 of these parts. 4 times 8 is 32.
So Kavya is 32 years old.
Check. Take 32 is to 56, and divide both by 8. We get 4 is to 7, the ratio in the question.
Here is the plan to keep. Find one part from the age you know, then take as many parts as the other person has.
Diya is 39 years old and Nikhil is 20. We want the sum of their ages after 10 years.

board.text: Diya is 39, Nikhil is 20. Sum after 10 years = ?

beats.say: Read the last part again: after 10 years. So we don't add the ages they have today. We add the ages they will have then.
Here is a bar for each of them. In 10 years, each bar grows by a piece of 10.

spec.note: Both bars grow by the same piece

beats.say: Who gets older in those 10 years?

ask.ifNot: Time passes for everybody. Diya gets 10 years older, and so does Nikhil.

beats.say: Diya will be 39 plus 10, which is 49. Nikhil will be 20 plus 10, which is 30.
Now add the two new ages. 49 plus 30 is 79.
So after 10 years, their ages add up to 79.
Here is a quick check. Today they add up to 59. Two people each gain 10 years, so the sum gains 20. And 59 plus 20 is 79.
The slip to avoid is adding the 10 only once. Two people means the years are added two times.
Arjun is 47 years old and Riya is 42. The question asks for the difference in their ages 7 years ago.

board.text: Arjun is 47, Riya is 42. Difference 7 years ago = ?

beats.say: Difference means the gap between the two ages: how much older one of them is than the other.
Think about this before any sum. 7 years ago, was the gap between them bigger, smaller, or the same as today?

ask.ifNot: Both of them were 7 years younger then. They step back together, so the gap between them does not move.

beats.say: Here is a fact worth keeping: the gap between two ages never changes. Every year, both people get exactly one year older.

spec.note: The extra piece is the gap between them

beats.say: So we only need the gap today. Arjun's bar is Riya's bar plus an extra piece. 47 minus 42 is 5.
Don't just take my word for it. Go back 7 years: Arjun was 47 minus 7, that is 40. Riya was 42 minus 7, that is 35.
And 40 minus 35 is 5. The very same gap!
So 7 years ago, the difference in their ages was 5 years.
The 7 years was only there to tempt us into extra sums. For a difference in ages, past or future, just subtract the ages you are given.
Arjun is at the shop, buying 15 sharpeners. Each one costs 7 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one sharpener, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 15 sharpeners costs 7 rupees. That is 7 rupees, 15 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 15 is 10 and 5. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 7 is 70.
And 5 times 7 is 35.
Put the two bites together. 70 plus 35 makes 105. So 15 times 7 is 105.
So Arjun pays 105 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 105 rupees, in lots of 7 rupees, gives 15 sharpeners. It fits.
Remember it like this: price of one, times the number you buy, is the total cost. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 6 books at 3 rupees each, and Siya pays with 43 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 6 books at Rs.3 each. Pays Rs.43.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 43 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 6 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 6 books at 3 rupees each: that is 6 times 3. 6 times 3 is 18.
Careful: 18 is only the cost, not the answer. Siya paid 43. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 18 away from 43.

beats.say: From 43, take off the 18. That leaves 25.
So Siya gets 25 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 18 plus 25 is 43. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Isha pays 250 rupees for a tablet. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 250 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 250 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 250 divided by 10 gives 25.
20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 25 is 50. That is the loss.
So the loss is 50 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 250 take away 50 is 200. So the selling price is 200 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 200 is 50 below 250. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!

Meera has 2 bags of lentils, and each bag weighs 10 kilograms 750 grams. We want the weight of all the bags together, in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of lentils, each 10 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 10 kg 750 g

beats.say: One bag is written in two units at once, kilograms and grams, and those do not mix. We want grams, so let's turn the kilograms into grams. How many grams are in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. A gram is much smaller than a kilogram, so we need many more of them: that is why we multiply. 10 times 1000 is 10000 grams.
Now put back the 750 grams that were already there. 10000 plus 750 makes 10750 grams. That is one bag, all in grams.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 10 kg 750 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 10750 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 10750 grams. So we need 2 lots of 10750: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 10000 is 20000, and double 750 is 1500.
Add the two pieces: 20000 plus 1500 is 21500. So the 2 bags together weigh 21500 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 20000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 750 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.

beats.say: Let's multiply in two easy pieces. 5 times 10000 is 50000, and 5 times 750 is 3750.
Add the two pieces: 50000 plus 3750 is 53750. So the 5 bags together weigh 53750 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 50000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 750 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
That is the whole method. Change the kilograms into grams, add the loose grams, then multiply by how many bags there are.
Here is a rectangle, 23 centimetres long and 13 centimetres wide. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides takes you along the edges, and that is the perimeter, the walk around. For the space inside we count rows of squares: length times width.

beats.say: Picture little squares, 1 centimetre each way. Every row holds 23 of them, and there are 13 rows. 13 rows of 23 is 23 times 13.
Split 13 into 10 and 3. 23 times 10 is 230, and 23 times 3 is 69. Together that makes 299.
That gives an area of 299 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area counts squares that cover the shape.
Check by undoing it. 299 shared into 13 rows gives 23 in each row, and that is our length. It fits.
Remember: area means the space inside, so multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the walk around the edge.

Our rectangle is 21 centimetres long and 19 centimetres wide, and the question asks for the perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round, like an ant walking along the edge. Which sides does the ant walk along?

ask.ifNot: Trace the edge with your finger: along the top, down the side, back along the bottom, up the other side. That is 2 lengths and 2 widths.

beats.say: One length and one width take the ant halfway round. So we add them, then double.
Halfway round first. 21 plus 19 is 40 centimetres.
Careful: 40 is only half the walk, and stopping here is the slip to watch for. Double it for the whole way round. 2 times 40 is 80.
So the perimeter is 80 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because it is a distance along a line.
Check by walking it side by side. 21, then 19, then 21, then 19. That adds up to 80.
Remember: perimeter is the walk around. Length plus width gets you halfway, so double it.
Here is Priya's shopping. 12 sharpeners, at 3 rupees each. We want the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one sharpener, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 12 sharpeners costs 3 rupees. That is 3 rupees, 12 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 12 is 10 and 2. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 3 is 30.
And 2 times 3 is 6.
Put the two bites together. 30 plus 6 makes 36. So 12 times 3 is 36.
So the total cost is 36 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 36 rupees, in lots of 3 rupees, gives 12 sharpeners. It fits.
Remember it like this: price of one, times the number you buy, is the total cost. Now you try one!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 8 pens at 8 rupees each, and Rohan pays with 114 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 8 pens at Rs.8 each. Pays Rs.114.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 114 rupees pays for the pens, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the pens
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 pens, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 pens at 8 rupees each: that is 8 times 8. 8 times 8 is 64.
Careful: 64 is only the cost, not the answer. Rohan paid 114. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 64 away from 114.

beats.say: From 114, take off the 64. That leaves 50.
So Rohan gets 50 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 64, plus the change, 50, should make the 114 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
The bag costs Meera 250 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 10 per cent. What is the selling price?
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 250 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 10 per cent. But 10 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 250 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is a friendly one: it is one tenth. So we divide by 10. 250 divided by 10 is 25. That is the profit.
So the profit is 25 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 250 plus 25 is 275. So the selling price is 275 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 275 is 25 more than 250. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!

The bicycle costs Aarav 500 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a loss of 25 per cent. What is the selling price?
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 500 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 500 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
4 lots of 25 make 100, so 25 per cent is one quarter. A quarter is half of a half. First, half of 500 is 250.
And half of 250 is 125. So 25 per cent of 500 is 125 rupees. That is the loss.
So the loss is 125 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 500 take away 125 is 375. So the selling price is 375 rupees.
Does that make sense? A loss should drop the selling price below the cost price, and 375 is 125 less than 500. It fits.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!
One of these four numbers has a digit sum of 16. Let's find out which.

ask.ifNot: Digit sum is just what it says. Take each digit of the number and add them all together.

beats.say: First, what does 'digit sum' ask us to do?
So we test the numbers one at a time. A tip: a zero adds nothing, so you can skip straight over any zeros.
Take 3528. 3 plus 5 plus 2 plus 8 makes 18. That is too big, so we cross it out.
Take 7406. 7 plus 4 plus 0 plus 6 makes 17. Not 16 either, so out it goes.

ask.ifNot: Go one digit at a time: 7, 4, 4, 1. Keep a running total as you go.

beats.say: Next is 7441. Your turn: add up its digits. What do they make?
7 plus 4 plus 4 plus 1 makes 16. That is the one!
Let's make sure of the others. First 3062. 3 plus 0 plus 6 plus 2 makes 11, which is too small. Cross it out.
So the number with a digit sum of 16 is 7441.
That is the whole method: add the digits of each choice, and keep the one that hits the target.
Let's write the number down: 41055. We want the place value of the 4 sitting in the ten-thousands place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands. So that is where our 4 lives.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called ten-thousands, so each one in it stands for 10000.

beats.say: A digit in the ten-thousands column counts ten-thousands. So what is each one in that column worth?
Our digit says there are 4 of those. 4 times 10000 makes 40000.
Careful: 4 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 40000. The 4 zeros are there because 4 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 40000 plus 1000 plus 50 plus 5. And look, 40000 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 4 in the ten-thousands place is 40000.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Here is our number, 45380. The question points at the 3 in the hundreds place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds. There is our 3.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: Now think about the column itself. What is a single 1 worth when it sits in the hundreds place?
So the 3 means 3 lots of 100. That is 300.
Careful: 3 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 300. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 40000 plus 5000 plus 300 plus 80. And look, 300 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 3 in the hundreds place is 300.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Here is our number, 29500. The question points at the 0 in the units place, and asks what that digit is really worth.
The units place is the very last column, on the right. Careful, this number has more than one 0. We want the one in the units column.

ask.ifNot: The units column counts single ones. So each one in that column is worth just 1.

beats.say: The units column is the smallest of them all. What is each one in that column worth?
And how many of them do we have? Zero. 0 times 1 is 0, so this digit is worth nothing at all.
Zero is special. Wherever it sits, its place value is 0, because zero lots of anything is nothing.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 20000 plus 9000 plus 500. No units part at all, so the 0 really adds nothing.
So the place value of the 0 in the units place is 0.
The plan every time: find the digit's column, see what that column is worth, and multiply.
Let's write the number down: 32813. We want the place value of the 8 sitting in the hundreds place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens, hundreds. And there sits our 8.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called hundreds, so each one in it stands for 100.

beats.say: A digit in the hundreds column counts hundreds. So what is each one in that column worth?
So the 8 means 8 lots of 100. That is 800.
Careful: 8 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 800. The 2 zeros are there because 2 more places sit to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 30000 plus 2000 plus 800 plus 10 plus 3. There is our 800, right where it should be.
So the place value of the 8 in the hundreds place is 800.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!
Let's write the number down: 87868. We want the place value of the 6 sitting in the tens place.
Every digit lives in its own column. Counting from the right: units, tens. And there sits our 6.

ask.ifNot: Look at the chart again. The column is called tens, so each one in it stands for 10.

beats.say: A digit in the tens column counts tens. So what is each one in that column worth?
We have 6 of them. So 6 times 10 is 60.
Careful: 6 on its own is only the face value, the digit as it looks. Its place value is 60. The zero on the end is there because 1 more place sits to its right.
Let's check by breaking the number into its parts: 80000 plus 7000 plus 800 plus 60 plus 8. And look, 60 is one of the parts.
So the place value of the 6 in the tens place is 60.
Remember it like this: place value is the digit times the worth of its column. Your turn next!

spec.note: Each bag weighs 4 kg 500 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 4500 grams, and there are 5 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 5 bags, and each one is the full 4500 grams. So we need 5 lots of 4500: a multiplication.

beats.say: Let's multiply in two easy pieces. 5 times 4000 is 20000, and 5 times 500 is 2500.
Add the two pieces: 20000 plus 2500 is 22500. So the 5 bags together weigh 22500 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 20000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 500 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.

board.text: 5 bags of flour, each 10 kg 250 g

That is the whole method. Change the kilograms into grams, add the loose grams, then multiply by how many bags there are.

Find the H C F of 91 and 52. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 91 and 52 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both 91 and 52: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into its prime factors.
Take 91. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 7, and 13 is left. So 91 is 7 times 13.
52 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 52 is 2 times 2 times 13.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 91 and 52 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have a 13. The 7 belongs only to 91 and the 2 belongs only to 52, so they stay out.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share: just the 13. So the H C F is 13.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 91 divided by 13 is 7, and 52 divided by 13 is 4, with nothing left over. And 7 and 4 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
Find the H C F of 33 and 55. H C F stands for highest common factor: the biggest number that divides both 33 and 55 exactly.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 33?

choices: No, it has to fit into 33
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 33, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. We break each number into prime factors, the building blocks that cannot be split any further.
Take 33. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 3, and 11 is left. So 33 is 3 times 11.
Take 55. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 5, and 11 is left. So 55 is 5 times 11.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 33 and 55 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Let's ring them. Both lines have an 11. The 3 belongs only to 33 and the 5 belongs only to 55, so they stay out.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share: just the 11. So the H C F is 11.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 33 divided by 11 is 3, and 55 divided by 11 is 5, with nothing left over. And 3 and 5 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
Remember the three moves: split into primes, ring what is shared, multiply. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.
We need the H C F of 6 and 8. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both of them with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 6?

choices: No, it has to fit into 6
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 6, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. We break each number into prime factors, the building blocks that cannot be split any further.
Take 6. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, and 3 is left. So 6 is 2 times 3.
8 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 8 is 2 times 2 times 2.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 6 and 8 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 2. Careful: 8 has three 2s, but 6 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share: just the 2. So the H C F is 2.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 8 divided by 2 is 4, with nothing left over. And 3 and 4 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 4, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: Here is the plan. We break each number into prime factors, the building blocks that cannot be split any further.
4 is even, so 2 comes out first. That leaves 2, so 4 is 2 times 2.
6 is even, so 2 comes out first. That leaves 3, so 6 is 2 times 3.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 4 and 6 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 4 divided by 2 is 2, and 6 divided by 2 is 3. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 3 have nothing more in common.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
