Arjun has 104 marbles and shares them into two groups, in the ratio 3 is to 5. We want to know how many are in the larger group.

board.text: 104 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: First, what are we given? A total of 104, and a ratio, 3 is to 5. And what are we asked for? Just the larger group.
Let's draw the ratio. 3 is to 5: one bar with 3 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 5 together make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 plus 5 is 8. So the whole 104 is cut into 8 equal parts.
Careful with this next step, it is the one that trips people up. What is one part worth?

ask.ifNot: The 104 fills all 8 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 104 by 8.

beats.say: 104 divided by 8 is 13. So every single part is worth 13 marbles.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 13

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 5 parts. 5 times 13 makes 65.
So the larger group has 65 marbles. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is 3 times 13, which is 39. And 39 plus 65 is 104, just what we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
Here is a proportion. 5 is to 3, equals 20 is to x. Two ratios that are equal, with one number, x, in hiding.
Before any sum, look at what is given. The first ratio is whole: 5 is to 3. The second has its first number, 20, and a gap where x sits.
Compare the two first numbers, 5 and 20. What happened to 5 to turn it into 20?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 5 times 4 gives 20, so it was multiplied by 4.

beats.say: 20 divided by 5 is 4. So the first number was multiplied by 4.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 3?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 5 was multiplied by 4, so 3 is multiplied by 4 as well.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12. Careful: we multiply here. Adding would break the ratio.
That makes x equal to 12.
Let's check. Divide 20 and 12 by 4, and we get 5 and 3 again. The two ratios match.
So in a proportion, find what the first number was multiplied by, then do the very same to the second.
We have to divide 28 in the ratio 2 is to 5, and find the smaller share.

board.text: Divide 28 in the ratio 2 : 5. Smaller share = ?

beats.say: Before any sum, let's be sure what we know. The total is 28. The ratio is 2 is to 5. And we want the smaller share only.
Let's draw the ratio. 2 is to 5: one bar with 2 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 5 together make 7 parts.

beats.say: 2 plus 5 is 7. So the whole 28 is cut into 7 equal parts.
Here comes the turning point. Which sum tells us what a single part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 28 fills all 7 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 28 by 7.

beats.say: 28 divided by 7 is 4. So every single part is worth 4.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 4

beats.say: We want the smaller share, and that is 2 parts. 2 times 4 makes 8.
So the smaller share is 8. There it is!
Let's check. The larger share is 5 times 4, which is 20. And 8 plus 20 is 28, just what we started with.
Remember the three moves. Add the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the share you want.
Here is Diya's shopping. 8 sharpeners, at 10 rupees each. We want the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one sharpener, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 8 sharpeners costs 10 rupees. That is 10 rupees, 8 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 8 times 10 is 80.
So the total cost is 80 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 80 rupees, in lots of 10 rupees, gives 8 sharpeners. It fits.

Here is a shop sum with two parts. 6 crayons at 6 rupees each, and Arjun pays with 46 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 6 crayons at Rs.6 each. Pays Rs.46.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 46 rupees pays for the crayons, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the crayons
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 6 crayons, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 6 crayons at 6 rupees each: that is 6 times 6. 6 times 6 is 36.
Careful: 36 is only the cost, not the answer. Arjun paid 46. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 36 away from 46.

beats.say: Count up from 36 to 46. That is 10 more.
So Arjun gets 10 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 36 plus 10 is 46. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Now you try one!
The toy costs Siya 60 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 30 per cent. What is the selling price?
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 60 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 30 per cent. But 30 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 60 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 60 divided by 10 is 6.
30 per cent is 3 lots of 10 per cent. 3 times 6 is 18. That is the profit.
So the profit is 18 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 60 plus 18 is 78. So the selling price is 78 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 78 is 18 above 60. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!

Here is our story. 51 marbles, split into two groups in the ratio 1 is to 2. How many marbles land in the larger group?

Let's draw the ratio. 1 is to 2: one bar with 1 equal part, and one bar with 2. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 1 and 2 together make 3 parts.

This says 2 is to 9, equals 6 is to x. So the second ratio is the first one in disguise, and x is its missing number.

Sahil is sharing out 91 toffees in the ratio 2 is to 5. Our job is to find the larger group.

board.text: 91 toffees in the ratio 2 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 91 to share. The ratio is 2 is to 5. And the question only wants the larger group.
Let's draw the ratio. 2 is to 5: one bar with 2 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 5 together make 7 parts.

beats.say: 2 plus 5 is 7. So the whole 91 is cut into 7 equal parts.
Here comes the turning point. Which sum tells us what a single part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 91 fills all 7 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 91 by 7.

beats.say: 91 divided by 7 is 13. So every single part is worth 13 toffees.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 13

beats.say: The larger group has 5 of these parts. 5 times 13 is 65.
So 65 toffees are in the larger group.
Let's check. The smaller group is 2 times 13, which is 26. And 26 plus 65 is 91, just what we started with.
So, to share in a ratio: count the parts, find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as you need.
This says 2 is to 7, equals 6 is to x. So the second ratio is the first one in disguise, and x is its missing number.
What do we have? A complete ratio, 2 is to 7. The second ratio shows only its first number, 6. We must find its partner.
Compare the two first numbers, 2 and 6. What happened to 2 to turn it into 6?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 2 times 3 gives 6, so it was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: 6 divided by 2 is 3. So the first number was multiplied by 3.

So x is 21. There is our missing number!
Let's check. Divide 6 and 21 by 3, and we get 2 and 7 again. The two ratios match.
That is the trick for any proportion. Spot the multiplier between the first numbers, and use it on the second numbers.

Neha is at the shop, buying 7 pens. Each one costs 5 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one pen, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 7 pens costs 5 rupees. That is 5 rupees, 7 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 7 times 5 is 35.
So Neha pays 35 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 35 rupees, in lots of 5 rupees, gives 7 pens. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Your turn next!
Nikhil buys 5 markers at 9 rupees each, and hands over 50 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 markers at Rs.9 each. Pays Rs.50.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 50 rupees pays for the markers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the markers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 markers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 5 markers at 9 rupees each: that is 5 times 9. 5 times 9 is 45.
Careful: 45 is only the cost, not the answer. Nikhil paid 50. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 45 away from 50.

beats.say: Count up from 45 to 50. That is 5 more.
So Nikhil gets 5 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 45 plus 5 is 50. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Riya pays 50 rupees for a toy. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 10 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 50 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 10 per cent. But 10 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 50 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 out of every 100 is one tenth. To find a tenth, divide by 10. 50 divided by 10 is 5. That is the profit.
So the profit is 5 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 50 plus 5 is 55. So the selling price is 55 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 55 is 5 above 50. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Find the H C F of 40 and 70. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 40 and 70 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both 40 and 70: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into its prime factors.
Take 40. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, and 5 is left. So 40 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 5.
Take 70. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 5, and 7 is left. So 70 is 2 times 5 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 40 and 70 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 2 and a 5. Careful: 40 has three 2s, but 70 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 5 is 10. So the H C F is 10.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 40 divided by 10 is 4, and 70 divided by 10 is 7, with nothing left over. And 4 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

beats.say: Let's check. 16 divided by 8 is 2, and 56 divided by 8 is 7, with nothing left over. And 2 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.

7 x, plus 18, equals 95. Someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 7, then added 18, and got 95. Let's work backwards and find that number.
The two sides are worth the same, like a level see-saw. To get x alone we undo things, last one first. The plus 18 was done last. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 18, we take away 18.

beats.say: And here is the rule of the balance: whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So 18 comes off both sides.
On the left, plus 18 and minus 18 cancel each other out. On the right, 95 minus 18 makes 77.
It is tempting to stop here and say 77. But that is 7 x, and we want just x. 7 x means 7 times x. What undoes times 7?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 7, we divide by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7.
77 divided by 7 is 11. So x equals 11. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 11 back in place of x. 7 times 11 is 77, and 77 plus 18 is 95. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Look at this one. 5 x, minus 3, equals 47. We want x standing all on its own, so we can see what it is worth.
An equation is like a balance: both sides weigh the same, and we must keep it that way. What should we do first?

ask.ifNot: If we divided first, the 3 would have to be divided as well, and that gets messy. It is easier to clear the minus 3 first, by doing the opposite.

beats.say: We add 3 to both sides. Plus is the opposite of minus, so that clears the minus 3 away.
On the left the minus 3 has gone, and only 5 x is there. On the right, 47 plus 3 is 50. So 5 x equals 50.
It is tempting to stop here and say 50. But that is 5 x, and we want just x. 5 x means 5 times x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide both by 5.
50 divided by 5 is 10. So x equals 10. There is our hidden number!
Let's test it in the equation we started with. 5 times 10 is 50. Then 50 minus 3 gives 47, just as it should.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Here is our equation. 8 x, plus 9, equals 41. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.
The two sides are worth the same, like a level see-saw. To get x alone we undo things, last one first. The plus 9 was done last. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 9, we take away 9.

beats.say: So 9 comes off. But if we only did that on the left, the balance would tip. So we take 9 from both sides.
On the left the plus 9 has gone, and only 8 x is there. On the right, 41 minus 9 is 32. So 8 x equals 32.
Careful, we are not finished. 32 is what 8 x is worth, not x. How do we get from 8 lots of x down to one x?

ask.ifNot: 8 x is 8 equal lots of x. To find one lot, we share 32 into 8 equal parts. That is dividing by 8.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide both by 8.
32 divided by 8 is 4. So x equals 4. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 4 back in place of x. 8 times 4 is 32, and 32 plus 9 is 41. It works.

ask.ifNot: Use the 8 times table. 8 times 6 is 48, so the bottom was multiplied by 6.

beats.say: 8 times 6 is 48. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 6 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 6 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 6.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 3 times 6 is 18.
So 3 over 8 equals 18 over 48. The missing number is 18.
Check it backwards. Divide 18 and 48 by 6, and we are back at 3 over 8.
So for equal fractions: whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by the same number.
Here is Aditya's shopping. 4 rulers, at 7 rupees each. We want the total cost.
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One ruler costs 7 rupees, and there are 4 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 4 rulers costs 7 rupees. That is 7 rupees, 4 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 4 times 7 is 28.
So Aditya pays 28 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 28 rupees, in lots of 7 rupees, gives 4 rulers. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 4 rulers at 4 rupees each, and Tara pays with 21 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 4 rulers at Rs.4 each. Pays Rs.21.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 21 rupees pays for the rulers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the rulers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 4 rulers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 4 rulers at 4 rupees each: that is 4 times 4. 4 times 4 is 16.
Careful: 16 is only the cost, not the answer. Tara paid 21. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 16 away from 21.

beats.say: Count up from 16 to 21. That is 5 more.
So Tara gets 5 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 16, plus the change, 5, should make the 21 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Ananya pays 300 rupees for a bicycle. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 25 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 300 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
25 per cent is one quarter, because 4 lots of 25 make 100. To find a quarter, halve it, then halve it again. Half of 300 is 150.
And half of 150 is 75. So 25 per cent of 300 is 75 rupees. That is the loss.
So the loss is 75 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 75 is 225. So the selling price is 225 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 225 is 75 below 300. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
Which is greater, one third or 1 over 6? Let's find out.
Let's draw them as two bars, both the same length. One has 3 pieces with 1 shaded, and the other has 6 pieces with 1 shaded.
Both tops are 1. Does that mean the two fractions are equal?

choices: Yes, same top means same amount
No, the pieces are different sizes
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Thirds and sixths are different sizes, so 1 of one is not the same as 1 of the other.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. 3 goes into 6, so we can turn the thirds into sixths.
For one third, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 2 as well: 1 times 2 is 2. That makes 2 over 6. And 1 over 6 stays as it is.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all sixths. Which is greater, 2 over 6 or 1 over 6?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 2 pieces is more than 1 pieces.

beats.say: 2 is more than 1, so 2 over 6 is greater. And 2 over 6 is just one third cut into smaller pieces.
Did you notice? Both tops were 1, but thirds are bigger pieces than sixths. Same top, smaller bottom, greater fraction.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
Arjun has 90 marbles and gives away 4 over 5 of them. We want to know how many are left.
Let's draw all 90 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 5, so we cut it into 5 equal parts.
How many marbles are in each part?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 90 marbles equally into 5 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 90 divided by 5.

beats.say: 90 divided by 5 is 18. So each part holds 18 marbles.
The top number is 4, so 4 parts go to the friend. 4 times 18 is 72 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 72?

ask.ifNot: 72 is how many marbles went to the friend. Arjun started with 90, so what is left is 90 take away 72.

beats.say: 90 minus 72 is 18. So Arjun has 18 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 part was not given away, and one part is 18 marbles. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
Two equal fractions, but one top number is hiding. 3 over 7 equals something over 42.
Here is 3 over 7 as a bar: 7 equal pieces, with 3 shaded. To get 42 pieces, each one has to be cut into smaller pieces.
Start with the bottoms. What was 7 multiplied by to make 42?

ask.ifNot: Use the 7 times table. 7 times 6 is 42, so the bottom was multiplied by 6.

beats.say: 7 times 6 is 42. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 6 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 6 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 6.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 3 times 6 is 18.
So 3 over 7 equals 18 over 42. The missing number is 18.
Check it backwards. Divide 18 and 42 by 6, and we are back at 3 over 7.
So for equal fractions: whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by the same number.
2 over 5 of 90. That little word, of, means we are taking a part of the 90.
A picture helps. This bar is the whole 90, and the bottom number, 5, says cut it into 5 equal parts.
So what is our first job with the 90?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 5, tells us how many equal parts to make. Sharing into 5 equal parts means dividing by 5.

beats.say: 90 divided by 5 is 18. So each part is worth 18.
Now the top number, 2. It tells us how many of those parts to take. So what is 2 over 5 of 90?

ask.ifNot: One part is 18, and the top number says take 2 of them. So we need 2 times 18.

beats.say: 2 parts of 18. 2 times 18 is 36.
So 2 over 5 of 90 is 36.
Let's check our parts were fair. 5 parts of 18 should give back 90, and 5 times 18 is 90. They were.
So, for a fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.
Two fractions, two thirds and 3 over 5. We want the greater one.
Here they are as two bars of the same length. The first is cut into 3 pieces with 2 shaded. The second is cut into 5 pieces with 3 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 2 and 3?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Thirds and fifths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 3 and 5 both go into, and the smallest one is 15.
For two thirds, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 5 as well: 2 times 5 is 10. That makes 10 over 15.
And for 3 over 5, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 3 as well: 3 times 3 is 9. That makes 9 over 15.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all fifteenths. Which is greater, 10 over 15 or 9 over 15?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 10 pieces is more than 9 pieces.

beats.say: 10 is more than 9, so 10 over 15 is greater. And 10 over 15 is just two thirds cut into smaller pieces.
And look: two thirds has the smaller top, yet it is the greater fraction. That is why we never compare tops until the pieces match.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
Here is our story. Ananya has 24 marbles, and 1 over 6 of them go to a friend. How many does Ananya keep?
Let's draw the 24 marbles. The bottom number is 6, so we share them into 6 equal groups.
How many marbles are in each group?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 24 marbles equally into 6 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 24 divided by 6.

beats.say: 24 divided by 6 is 4. So each group holds 4 marbles.
Ananya gives away 1 of those groups, so 4 marbles go to the friend.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 4?

ask.ifNot: 4 is how many marbles went to the friend. Ananya started with 24, so what is left is 24 take away 4.

beats.say: 24 minus 4 is 20. So Ananya has 20 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. 5 groups were not given away, and 5 times 4 is 20. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
Here is our question. What is 1 over 6 of 84?
A picture helps. This bar is the whole 84, and the bottom number, 6, says cut it into 6 equal parts.
What do we do to the 84 first?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 6, tells us how many equal parts to make. Sharing into 6 equal parts means dividing by 6.

beats.say: 84 divided by 6 is 14. So each part is worth 14.
The top number is 1, so we take just 1 of those parts.
There it is. 1 over 6 of 84 is 14.
Let's check our parts were fair. 6 parts of 14 should give back 84, and 6 times 14 is 84. They were.
So, for a fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top. When the top is 1, the dividing does it all.
Here is our story. Isha has 72 marbles, and three quarters of them go to a friend. How many does Isha keep?
Let's draw all 72 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 4, so we cut it into 4 equal parts.
How many marbles are in each part?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 72 marbles equally into 4 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 72 divided by 4.

beats.say: 72 shared into 4 equal parts gives 18 in each. So one part is 18 marbles.
The top number is 3, so 3 parts go to the friend. 3 times 18 is 54 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 54?

ask.ifNot: 54 is how many marbles went to the friend. Isha started with 72, so what is left is 72 take away 54.

beats.say: 72 take away 54 leaves 18. Isha keeps 18 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 part was not given away, and one part is 18 marbles. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
Here is our story. Aditya has 72 marbles, and 5 over 8 of them go to a friend. How many does Aditya keep?
Let's draw all 72 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 8, so we cut it into 8 equal parts.
So how many marbles does one part hold?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 72 marbles equally into 8 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 72 divided by 8.

beats.say: 72 shared into 8 equal parts gives 9 in each. So one part is 9 marbles.
The top number is 5, so 5 parts go to the friend. 5 times 9 is 45 marbles.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 45?

ask.ifNot: 45 is how many marbles went to the friend. Aditya started with 72, so what is left is 72 take away 45.

beats.say: 72 take away 45 leaves 27. Aditya keeps 27 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. 3 parts were not given away, and 3 times 9 is 27. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
Two fractions, 3 over 5 and three quarters. We want the greater one.
Here they are as two bars of the same length. The first is cut into 5 pieces with 3 shaded. The second is cut into 4 pieces with 3 shaded.
Both tops are 3. Does that mean the two fractions are equal?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, same top means same amount
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Fifths and quarters are different sizes, so 3 of one is not the same as 3 of the other.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 5 and 4 both go into, and the smallest one is 20.
For 3 over 5, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 4 as well: 3 times 4 is 12. That makes 12 over 20.
And for three quarters, whatever we do to the bottom we do to the top. So we multiply the top by 5 as well: 3 times 5 is 15. That makes 15 over 20.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all twentieths. Which is greater, 12 over 20 or 15 over 20?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 15 pieces is more than 12 pieces.

beats.say: 15 is more than 12, so 15 over 20 is greater. And 15 over 20 is just three quarters cut into smaller pieces.
Did you notice? Both tops were 3, but quarters are bigger pieces than fifths. Same top, smaller bottom, greater fraction.
So to compare fractions: make the pieces the same size, then compare the tops.
Arjun has 90 marbles and gives away 3 over 5 of them. We want to know how many are left.
Let's draw all 90 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 5, so we cut it into 5 equal parts.
How many marbles are in each part?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 90 marbles equally into 5 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 90 divided by 5.

beats.say: 90 shared into 5 equal parts gives 18 in each. So one part is 18 marbles.
Arjun gives away 3 of those parts. 3 times 18 is 54 marbles.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 54?

ask.ifNot: 54 is how many marbles went to the friend. Arjun started with 90, so what is left is 90 take away 54.

beats.say: 90 minus 54 is 36. So Arjun has 36 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. 2 parts were not given away, and 2 times 18 is 36. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
Here is our question. What is 7 over 9 of 90?
A picture helps. This bar is the whole 90, and the bottom number, 9, says cut it into 9 equal parts.
What do we do to the 90 first?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 9, tells us how many equal parts to make. Sharing into 9 equal parts means dividing by 9.

beats.say: 90 divided by 9 is 10. So each part is worth 10.
Now the top number, 7. It tells us how many of those parts to take. So what is 7 over 9 of 90?

ask.ifNot: One part is 10, and the top number says take 7 of them. So we need 7 times 10.

beats.say: 7 parts of 10. 7 times 10 is 70.
There it is. 7 over 9 of 90 is 70.
Let's check our parts were fair. 9 parts of 10 should give back 90, and 9 times 10 is 90. They were.
So, for a fraction of an amount: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top number.
Two fractions, 2 over 4 and 4 over 5. We want the greater one.
A picture first. Two equal bars: the top one cut into 4 with 2 shaded, the bottom one cut into 5 with 4 shaded.
Is it fair to compare the tops, 2 and 4, straight away?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Quarters and fifths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 4 and 5 both go into, and the smallest one is 20.
For 2 over 4, the bottom was multiplied by 5, so the top must be too. 2 times 5 is 10, so 2 over 4 is 10 over 20.
And for 4 over 5, the bottom was multiplied by 4, so the top must be too. 4 times 4 is 16, so 4 over 5 is 16 over 20.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all twentieths. Which is greater, 10 over 20 or 16 over 20?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 16 pieces is more than 10 pieces.

beats.say: 16 pieces beat 10 pieces. And 16 over 20 is only another name for 4 over 5, so 4 over 5 is the greater fraction.
The picture agrees. The bar for 4 over 5 has more of it shaded.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
We are adding two fractions. 1 over 5, plus 2 over 5.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 5 equal pieces. The first has 1 shaded, and the second has 2.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all fifths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, this is the classic slip. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, fifths. Adding more fifths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 5.

beats.say: So we only count the pieces. 1 piece and 2 pieces make 3 pieces.
Can we make 3 over 5 simpler? 3 and 5 share no factor except 1, so it is already in its simplest form.
So 1 over 5 plus 2 over 5 is 3 over 5.
Quick check with the picture. Count the shaded pieces in the first two bars: 1 and 2 make 3. It matches.
Remember it like this. Same size pieces? Just count them: add the tops, and the bottom stays as it is.
Here is our story. Aarav has 48 marbles, and 6 over 8 of them go to a friend. How many does Aarav keep?
Let's draw the 48 marbles. The bottom number is 8, so we share them into 8 equal groups.
How many marbles are in each group?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 48 marbles equally into 8 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 48 divided by 8.

beats.say: 48 divided by 8 is 6. So each group holds 6 marbles.
Aarav gives away 6 of those groups. 6 times 6 is 36 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 36?

ask.ifNot: 36 is how many marbles went to the friend. Aarav started with 48, so what is left is 48 take away 36.

beats.say: 48 take away 36 leaves 12. Aarav keeps 12 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. 2 groups were not given away, and 2 times 6 is 12. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
Three bags hold 24 apples between them. We know two totals for pairs of bags, and we want the first and third bags together.
All three bags hold 24. The first and second together hold 11. What does that tell us about the third bag?

ask.ifNot: The three bags make 24. Take away the first two, which hold 11 between them, and what is left must be in the third bag.

beats.say: 24 minus 11 is 13. The third bag holds 13 apples.
Now the same idea from the other end. The second and third together hold 18, so the first bag holds 24 minus 18, which is 6.
First and third together: 6 plus 13 is 19.
Let's check with the second bag. It must hold 24 minus 19, which is 5. Then 6 plus 5 is 11, and 5 plus 13 is 18. Both clues fit.
When you know the whole and one part, subtract to find the rest. Here we simply did that twice.
How many whole numbers lie between 4 squared and 4 cubed? We need those two numbers first.

board.text: Between 4² and 4³: how many whole numbers?

beats.say: 4 squared is 4 times 4: a square of tiles, 4 rows of 4. That is 16.
And 4 cubed? The little 3 tells us how many 4s to use. So what is 4 cubed?

ask.ifNot: The little 3 does not mean times 3. It means three 4s multiplied together: 4 times 4 times 4.

beats.say: 4 times 4 is 16, and 16 times 4 is 64. So 4 cubed is 64.
So we count the whole numbers between 16 and 64. Between means 16 and 64 themselves stay out. The first is 17 and the last is 63.
How many numbers are there from 17 to 63?

ask.ifNot: 63 minus 17 is 46, but that counts the steps. Count the starting number too, and it is 1 more.

beats.say: 63 minus 17 is 46 steps, and 1 more for the number we start on. That makes 47.
Another way to check: 64 minus 16, minus 1, is also 47.
Work out the powers first. Then count carefully, leaving out both ends.
A watch with only an hour hand. The hand is 4 over 5 of the way from 12 to 1, and we must tell the time.

board.text: Hour hand: 4/5 of the way from 12 to 1

beats.say: How long does the hour hand take to go from 12 to 1? One whole hour, and that is 60 minutes.
The hand has gone 4 over 5 of the way. So what do we need to find?

ask.ifNot: The whole trip from 12 to 1 is 60 minutes. The hand has done 4 over 5 of that trip, so we want 4 over 5 of 60 minutes.

beats.say: The bottom number is 5, so we share the 60 minutes into 5 equal parts. 60 divided by 5 is 12.
The top number is 4, so we take 4 of those parts. 4 times 12 is 48.
So 48 minutes have passed since 12 o'clock. The time is 48 minutes past 12.
Does that feel right? 4 over 5 is nearly the whole way, and 48 minutes is nearly the whole hour. Yes.
So a fraction of an hour is that fraction of 60 minutes: divide by the bottom number, then multiply by the top.
36 is 12 per cent of some number. So we have a part, and we want the whole number.
Per cent means out of every 100. So the whole number is 100 per cent, and 36 is only 12 of those 100 parts.

spec.note: The 12% piece is 36

beats.say: What is the easiest thing to find first?

ask.ifNot: We know that 12 per cent is 36. Share that 36 into 12 equal parts, and each part is 1 per cent. That is a lovely stepping stone.

beats.say: 12 per cent is 36. So 1 per cent is 36 divided by 12, which is 3.
Careful: a common slip is to find 12 per cent of 36. But 36 is already the 12 per cent. We are climbing up to the whole, not down to a smaller part.
The whole is 100 per cent, so we need 100 lots of 3. 100 times 3 is 300.
Check it. 10 per cent of 300 is 30, and 1 per cent is 3. So 12 per cent is 30 plus 3 plus 3, which is 36. It works.
So when you know a per cent of a number and want the whole number, find 1 per cent first, then multiply by 100.
A worker earns 3 rupees an hour for his first 40 hours. After that comes overtime, which pays twice as much. In all he was paid 168 rupees.

board.text: ₹3 an hour for the first 40 hours
Overtime pays twice as much. Total pay ₹168

beats.say: What are we hunting for? The number of overtime hours. So picture his pay as one bar with two pieces: regular pay and overtime pay.
Which of the two pieces can we work out straight away?

ask.ifNot: We know everything about the regular time: 40 hours, at 3 rupees an hour. So we start there.

beats.say: 40 hours at 3 rupees an hour. 40 times 3 is 120, so 120 rupees is his regular pay.
The rest of the 168 rupees must be overtime pay. 168 minus 120 is 48.
Now, how much does one hour of overtime pay? Remember, it is twice the regular 3 rupees.

ask.ifNot: Twice means 2 times. 2 times 3 rupees is 6 rupees for each overtime hour.

beats.say: 2 times 3 is 6. Careful here: the trap is to divide the 48 rupees by the regular 3. Overtime hours earn 6 rupees each.
So how many times does 6 go into 48? 48 divided by 6 is 8.
He worked 8 hours of overtime.
Check it. 8 hours at 6 rupees is 48. Add the regular 120, and we get 168, exactly what he was paid.
So when pay comes in two parts, work out the part you know, take it away, and then deal with what is left.
Here is a sequence: 2, 7, 14, 23, 34. We want the 10th term. Let's see how it grows.
From 2 to 7 is plus 5. What is the jump from 7 to 14?

ask.ifNot: 14 minus 7 is 7. So this jump is plus 7, not plus 5 again.

beats.say: Plus 5, plus 7, then plus 9, then plus 11. The jumps are not the same this time. They are changing.
So let's look at the jumps themselves: 5, 7, 9, 11. What is happening to them?

ask.ifNot: 7 minus 5 is 2. 9 minus 7 is 2. 11 minus 9 is 2. Each jump is 2 bigger than the one before.

beats.say: Each jump is 2 bigger than the last. So the next jumps are 13, 15, 17, 19 and 21.
We have 5 terms and want the 10th, so 5 more jumps. 34 plus 13 is 47. 47 plus 15 is 62.
62 plus 17 is 79. 79 plus 19 is 98. That is the 9th term. One more jump to go: which is it?

ask.ifNot: The new jumps go 13, 15, 17, 19, and then 21. We have used the first four of them.

beats.say: 98 plus 21 is 119. So the 10th term is 119.
Here is the whole list. Count along it: 10 terms, ending on 119.
When the jumps are not equal, write the jumps in a row of their own and look for the pattern in them.
Here is our equation. 3 x, minus 4 times the bracket x plus 6, equals 0. The bracket is the tricky part, so we open it first.
The minus 4 multiplies both things in the bracket. Minus 4 times x is minus 4 x. What is minus 4 times plus 6?

ask.ifNot: 4 times 6 is 24, and the minus sign in front of the 4 comes along too. So it is minus 24. This is the slip to watch for.

beats.say: So the bracket opens into minus 4 x, minus 24.
Now gather the x terms. 3 x take away 4 x: we have 3 and we need to take 4, so we are one x short. That is minus x.
We want a plain x, standing on its own. What could we do to both sides?

ask.ifNot: The x has a minus in front of it. Adding x to both sides undoes that minus x, and puts a plain x on the right.

beats.say: Add x to both sides. On the left, minus x and plus x cancel, leaving minus 24. On the right, 0 plus x is just x.
So x equals minus 24. A negative answer is perfectly fine.
Check it. 3 times minus 24 is minus 72. Inside the bracket, minus 24 plus 6 is minus 18, and minus 4 times minus 18 is plus 72. Minus 72 plus 72 is 0.
The plan: open the bracket, taking the minus sign to every term inside. Then gather the x terms and keep the balance.
A boy played for 1 hour and 15 minutes. We want that as a decimal number of hours.
It is tempting to put the 15 straight after the point. Why does that not work?

ask.ifNot: A decimal counts in tenths and hundredths. But minutes are sixtieths of an hour. So 15 minutes is 15 out of 60, not 15 out of 100.

beats.say: So 15 minutes is 15 out of 60 of an hour. 15 goes into 60 exactly 4 times, so that is one quarter of an hour.

spec.note: A quarter of the way round

beats.say: And one quarter is 25 hundredths, which we write as 0.25.
So the time is 1 whole hour plus 0.25 of an hour. That is 1.25 hours.
Check it backwards. 0.25 of 60 minutes is 15 minutes. Just right.
To turn minutes into hours, divide by 60 first. Never just write the minutes after the point.
Three numbers this time. The H C F is the biggest number that divides all three of them exactly.
Split each into primes. 18 is even, so 2 comes out, and 3 times 3 is left.
24 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3. And 36 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 3.
A prime only counts if it is on all three lines. So what do all three share?

ask.ifNot: 18 has only one 2, so only one 2 is shared by all three. 24 has only one 3, so only one 3 is shared.

beats.say: Ring one 2 and one 3 on every line.
Multiply them: 2 times 3 is 6. So the H C F is 6.
Check: 18 divided by 6 is 3, 24 divided by 6 is 4, and 36 divided by 6 is 6. All exact.
Careful with 12. It goes into 24 and 36, but 18 is 12 plus 6 left over. The H C F must go into every number.
With three numbers the method is the same: split into primes, and keep only what every line has.
We want a fraction that is greater than one third, but less than 7 over 8.
The four choices are one quarter, 23 over 24, 11 over 12 and 17 over 24. Let's write them down.
The bottoms are all different: 3, 8, 4, 12 and 24. What should we do before we compare?

ask.ifNot: Pieces of different sizes cannot be compared fairly. 3, 8, 4 and 12 all go into 24, so we can turn every fraction into twenty-fourths.

beats.say: First the two fences. One third: 3 times 8 is 24, so the top is 1 times 8. And 7 over 8: 8 times 3 is 24, so the top is 7 times 3, which is 21.
So, written in twenty-fourths, our fraction needs a top between 8 and 21.

spec.note: counting in twenty-fourths

beats.say: Now the choices. One quarter is 6 over 24, and 11 over 12 is 22 over 24. The other two are in twenty-fourths already.
So the four tops are 6, 23, 22 and 17. Which one sits between 8 and 21?

ask.ifNot: We need more than 8 and less than 21. 6 is too small, and 22 and 23 are too big. Only 17 fits.

beats.say: 17 over 24 it is. It is more than 8 over 24, and less than 21 over 24.
So to find a fraction between two others: give them all the same bottom number, then just look at the tops.
Amar walks from A to B and rides back, and that takes 37 minutes. Walking both ways takes 55 minutes. We want the time to ride both ways.
We are never told how far it is, and we will not need it. Here is a neat idea: imagine Amar does his walk and ride trip twice. What has he done altogether?

ask.ifNot: Each trip is 1 walk and 1 ride. Do the trip twice and you get 2 walks and 2 rides.

beats.say: Twice 37 minutes is 74 minutes. So 2 walks and 2 rides together take 74 minutes.
But we already know how long 2 walks take: 55 minutes. Take the 2 walks away, and only the 2 rides are left.
74 minus 55 is 19. So riding both ways takes 19 minutes.
A tempting slip is to take 37 away from 55 straight off. That only tells you how much longer a walk is than a ride, not the time for two rides.
Check with single trips. Half of 55 is 27.5 minutes for one walk, and half of 19 is 9.5 for one ride. 27.5 plus 9.5 is 37 minutes. It matches.
So the trick here: build the first fact up until it holds the piece you already know, then take that piece away.
A fruit seller buys oranges in two lots: 4 dozen at 12 rupees a dozen, and 2 dozen at 16 rupees a dozen. He wants a profit of 20 per cent. What price per dozen must he sell at?

board.text: 4 dozen at Rs.12, 2 dozen at Rs.16. Profit 20%.

beats.say: Let us write his buying as a bill, and add it up line by line.
4 dozen at 12 rupees: 4 times 12 is 48. And 2 dozen at 16 rupees: 2 times 16 is 32.
Altogether he paid 48 plus 32, which is 80 rupees. That is his cost price, for 4 plus 2, which is 6 dozen.
He wants a profit of 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, on all the money he paid. That is 80 rupees.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 80 is 8, so 20 per cent is twice that: 16. His profit must be 16 rupees.
So he must collect 80 plus 16, which is 96 rupees, for all the oranges.
Careful: the question asks for the price per dozen. What do we do with the 96?

ask.ifNot: The 96 rupees is for all the oranges, and there are 6 dozen altogether. So we share 96 among 6.

beats.say: 96 divided by 6 is 16. So he sells at 16 rupees per dozen.
Check: 6 dozen at 16 rupees brings in 96 rupees. That is 16 more than the 80 he paid, and 16 is 20 per cent of 80. It fits.
So the plan was: total cost first, then add the profit worked on the cost price, then share by the number of dozens.

board.text: Rectangle: one side 8 cm, perimeter 40 cm

spec.note: Perimeter = 40 cm

beats.say: Here is a rectangle. One side is 8 centimetres and the perimeter is 40 centimetres. We want the area.
For the area we need both sides, and we only have one. The perimeter will give us the other. Remember, the perimeter is the walk all the way round: 2 lengths and 2 breadths.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth take us exactly halfway round. So it is half of 40. Dividing by 4 only works for a square.

beats.say: The whole walk is 40. So how far is just one length plus one breadth?
One length and one breadth are halfway round. Half of 40 is 20.
The two sides together make 20, and one of them is 8. So the other side is 20 take away 8, which is 12 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Area is the space inside, rows of little squares. So we multiply the length by the breadth. Adding is for the walk round the edge.

beats.say: Now we have both sides, 12 and 8. Which sum gives the area?
Area is length times breadth. 12 times 8 is 96.
So the area is 96 square centimetres.
Check the walk round. 12 plus 8 is 20, and double 20 is 40. That is the perimeter we were given.
So: halve the perimeter to get length plus breadth, take away the side you know, then multiply the two sides. The trap is to treat the perimeter as if it were a side.
How many natural numbers below 2009 can be divided by both 4 and 6? First we need to know what such numbers look like.

board.text: Below 2009: divisible by both 4 and 6. How many?

beats.say: Here are both tables. Where do they meet?

ask.ifNot: Look along both lists. 12 is in both, and so is 24. They first meet at 12, the L C M, and then at every multiple of 12.

beats.say: They meet at 12, then 24, and so on. Trap alert: 4 times 6 is 24, but counting only in 24s would skip 12.
So we count the multiples of 12. Below 2009 means up to 2008.

board.text: Count the multiples of 12 up to 2008

beats.say: How many 12s fit into 2008? 12 times 100 is 1200, which leaves 808. 12 times 60 is 720, which leaves 88.
12 times 7 is 84, with 4 left over. So 100 plus 60 plus 7 makes 167 twelves.
There are 4 left over. Do they give us one more multiple of 12?

ask.ifNot: A left over of 4 is not a whole 12. Only complete twelves count, so we ignore the remainder.

beats.say: So there are 167 such numbers.
Divisible by both means divisible by the L C M. Then divide the limit by the L C M and keep only the whole part.
40 grams of talc powder costs 12 rupees. We want the cost of 70 grams of the same powder.
Same powder, so every gram costs the same. But 70 grams is not double 40 grams, or any neat number of times 40. So there is no quick jump.
So what is the smart thing to find first?

ask.ifNot: When the numbers don't fit neatly, find the cost of 1 first. From 1, we can reach any number.

beats.say: One gram costs 12 rupees shared over 40 grams. Careful: that is 12 divided by 40, not 40 divided by 12. We are sharing rupees among grams.
12 divided by 40 is 0.30. So 1 gram costs 0.30 rupees, which is 30 paise.
We have one. Now, how do we get to 70 grams?

ask.ifNot: Each gram costs 0.30 rupees, and there are 70 of them. 70 lots of the same amount means multiply.

beats.say: 70 times 0.30 is 21. Think of it as 7 times 3.
So 70 grams costs 21 rupees.
Check another way. 10 grams cost 10 times 0.30, which is 3 rupees. 70 grams is 7 lots of 10 grams, and 7 times 3 is 21. Same answer.
That is the unitary method: find one, then find many.
One crore. That is a huge number, and we want to know how many tens are inside it.
One crore is 1 followed by 7 zeros. In the Indian system we put the commas like this.

ask.ifNot: 'How many tens' asks how many groups of 10 fit in. Making equal groups is dividing.

beats.say: How do we find how many tens fit into a number?
Dividing by 10 takes one zero off the end. So 7 zeros become 6 zeros.
Now read what is left, the Indian way. The lakhs come after the thousands. A 1 with 6 zeros is ten lakh.
Check by going back. Ten lakh tens, times 10, puts the zero back and gives one crore.
So there are ten lakh tens in one crore.
To count the tens in a number, divide by 10. Then read the answer carefully, group by group.
First we build the smallest 5 digit odd number from 1, 8, 4, 0 and 7. Then we see what its 4 is worth.
Odd means the last digit is odd. Our odd digits are 1 and 7, so one of them goes last.

choices: No, it would not have 5 digits
ask.ifNot: A number that starts with 0 really has only 4 digits. So the front digit must be the smallest digit that is not 0.

beats.say: For the smallest number we want a small digit at the front. Can 0 go first?
So 1 should lead, and that means 7 is the odd digit at the end. Fill the middle with the smallest first: 0, 4, 8. That gives 10487.
If we had put 1 at the end instead, the smallest we could make is 40781. Much bigger.
Now find the 4. Units, tens, hundreds. It is in the hundreds place.
4 hundreds: 4 times 100 is 400.
So the place value of the 4 is 400. Build the number first, then read the place.
A vendor buys 6 toffees for 1 rupee. He wants to gain 20 per cent. So how many toffees should he give for 1 rupee when he sells?

board.text: Buys 6 toffees for Rs.1. Wants a gain of 20%.

beats.say: A single rupee is awkward to cut up, so let us use paise. 1 rupee is 100 paise. So the 6 toffees cost him 100 paise.
He wants a gain of 20 per cent. 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A gain is always measured on the cost price, the money he paid. Here that is 100 paise.

beats.say: 20 per cent of 100 is simply 20. So for those 6 toffees he must get 100 plus 20, which is 120 paise.
So 6 toffees must sell for 120 paise. One toffee sells for 120 divided by 6, which is 20 paise.
Each toffee sells for 20 paise. How many toffees is that for 1 rupee, which is 100 paise?

ask.ifNot: How many twenties make 100? 5 twenties. So 100 paise buys 5 toffees.

beats.say: 100 divided by 20 is 5. So he must sell 5 toffees for a rupee.
Does it make sense? He buys 6 for a rupee, and sells only 5 for a rupee. Fewer toffees for the same money: that is where his gain comes from.
So when the prices are fiddly, switch to paise, find the selling price of one, and see how many fit in a rupee.
We have three expressions, and sum means add them all. So I write them in one long line.
Look for partners that cancel. Which term cancels the very first a?

ask.ifNot: a and minus a are opposites. Put together, they make nothing at all.

beats.say: So a and minus a cancel. I cross them both out.
Now the b terms. There is a b, another b, and a minus 2 b. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: b and b make 2 b. Then minus 2 b takes both of them away again. Nothing is left.

beats.say: One b and another b make 2 b, and then minus 2 b takes them away. So the b terms vanish too.
Only the plain numbers are left: minus 1, plus 1, and plus 1. Minus 1 and plus 1 cancel, so 1 remains.
So the whole sum is just 1. All those letters, and they disappear completely!
Let's test with real numbers. Say a is 2 and b is 3. The three parts become 4, 2 and minus 5. And 4 plus 2 minus 5 is 1.
To add expressions: write them in a line, then gather each family. a with a, b with b, numbers with numbers.
A line with decimals in it, and four different signs. The order matters just as much with decimals.
Which parts do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Divide and times come before plus and minus. So the 4.2 divided by 6 and the 0.3 times 0.4 are both done first.

beats.say: First the divide. 42 divided by 6 is 7, so 4.2 divided by 6 is 0.7.
Now the times. 3 times 4 is 12. There are two decimal places in the question, one in each number, so the answer has two as well: 0.12.
Write the line again with those two answers in place.
Now left to right. 8 minus 0.7 is 7.3.
7.3 is the same as 7.30. Add 0.12 and we get 7.42.
Same rule as always: times and divide first, then plus and minus from left to right. And count the decimal places when you multiply.
Here are the digits of 2138574, spread out so we can see each position clearly.

ask.ifNot: Ascending means going up, like climbing stairs. So we start with the smallest digit, which is 1.

beats.say: We must arrange them in ascending order. Ascending means smallest first. So which digit comes first?
In order they are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8. I have written them right underneath, so each digit sits below the one in the same position.
Now compare, position by position. First position: 2 on top, 1 below. Different. Second: 1 and 2. Different again.
Third position: 3 on top and 3 below. The same!
Fourth: 8 and 4, different. Fifth: 5 and 5, the same. Sixth: 7 and 7, the same. Last: 4 and 8, different.
Count the rings: the 3, the 5 and the 7. Three digits kept their positions.
Write the two arrangements one under the other, then compare place by place. The picture does the work.

board.text: 2000: a multiple of 8.   2001: a multiple of 7.

beats.say: Two clues about Mr. Sam's age. In 2000 it was a multiple of 8, and in 2001 it was a multiple of 7.
From 2000 to 2001 he grows exactly 1 year older. So we want a multiple of 8 whose very next number is a multiple of 7.
Here are the multiples of 8. For each one, think about the number that comes just after it.

ask.ifNot: 41 and 57 are not in the 7 times table. But 49 is 7 times 7. So the pair is 48 and 49.

beats.say: Which multiple of 8 is followed by a multiple of 7?
48 is 8 times 6, and 49 is 7 times 7. So he was 48 in the year 2000.
He was born 48 years before 2000. 2000 minus 48 is 1952.
Check the second clue. In 2001 he is 2001 minus 1952, which is 49. Both clues fit.
So Mr. Sam was born in 1952. One year apart means two numbers next to each other: that was the key.
A cafe puzzle. Toast and tea cost 4 rupees. 2 toasts and 2 sandwiches cost 9. A sandwich and 2 teas cost 2. We want the cost of one of each.
Look at the middle line. 2 toasts and 2 sandwiches cost 9 rupees. So what do 1 toast and 1 sandwich cost?

ask.ifNot: Half as much food costs half as much money. Half of 9 rupees is 4 and a half rupees.

beats.say: Half of 9 is 4 and a half. So a toast and a sandwich together cost 4 and a half rupees.
Compare two lines. Toast and tea cost 4. Toast and sandwich cost 4 and a half. The toast is the same in both. So which costs more, the sandwich or the tea?

choices: the sandwich, by half a rupee
the tea, by half a rupee
ask.ifNot: Only one thing changed: the tea became a sandwich. And the price went up by half a rupee. So the sandwich costs half a rupee more than the tea.

beats.say: 4 and a half, minus 4, is a half. So a sandwich is a tea plus half a rupee.
Now use the last line: a sandwich and 2 teas cost 2 rupees. Swap the sandwich for a tea plus a half. That gives 3 teas, plus a half, making 2.
Take the half away from both sides, and 3 teas cost 1 and a half rupees. Share that by 3, and one tea costs half a rupee.
A sandwich is half a rupee more than that, so 1 rupee. And toast plus tea is 4, so the toast is 4 minus a half, which is 3 and a half.
Now add one of each: 3 and a half, plus 1, plus a half. That is 5 rupees.
Check the middle line. 2 toasts are 7 rupees and 2 sandwiches are 2 rupees. 7 plus 2 is 9. It fits.
So with a puzzle like this: compare two lines that share something, see what changed, and work out one price at a time.
Jim buys a cat and a dog for 600 rupees each. He sells the dog at a profit of 20 per cent, and the cat at a loss of 25 per cent. How much does he get altogether?

board.text: Dog: Rs.600, profit 20%. Cat: Rs.600, loss 25%.

beats.say: Two pets, so two little sums. We find the selling price of each one, and then add them.
Start with the dog. 10 per cent of 600 is 60, so 20 per cent is 2 times 60, which is 120. That is the profit.
The dog made a profit of 120 rupees. So what did the dog sell for?

ask.ifNot: A profit means he got more than he paid. So we add the 120 on to the 600.

beats.say: 600 plus 120 is 720. The dog sold for 720 rupees.
Now the cat. 25 per cent is one quarter. Half of 600 is 300, and half of 300 is 150. So the loss is 150 rupees.
A loss means he got less than he paid. 600 take away 150 is 450. The cat sold for 450 rupees.
Now, what does the question want?

ask.ifNot: Read the last line again. It asks how much he got altogether when he sold them. So we add the two selling prices.

beats.say: 720 plus 450 is 1170. He got 1170 rupees altogether.
Check: he paid 1200 for both. He gained 120 and lost 150, so he is 30 down. And 1200 minus 30 is 1170. It agrees.
So take one pet at a time. A profit is added to the cost price, a loss is taken away. Then answer exactly what is asked.
Four fractions in one line. One half, take away one quarter, take away one third, plus 1 over 6.
The bottoms are 2, 4, 3 and 6. Which number can all four go into?

ask.ifNot: 6 is close, but 4 does not go into 6. The smallest number that 2, 4, 3 and 6 all go into is 12.

beats.say: So we change every fraction into twelfths. One half is 6 over 12, because 2 times 6 is 12. One quarter is 3 over 12, because 4 times 3 is 12.
One third is 4 over 12, and 1 over 6 is 2 over 12. Here are all four as bars of twelfths.
Now they are all twelfths, so we only work with the tops. Careful: each sign stays with the number that follows it.
6, take away 3, take away 4, plus 2. What is left?

ask.ifNot: Gather what we add: 6 and 2 make 8. Gather what we take away: 3 and 4 make 7. And 8 take away 7 is 1.

beats.say: We add 6 and 2, which makes 8. We take away 3 and 4, which makes 7. And 8 take away 7 leaves 1 piece.
1 piece, and the pieces are twelfths. So the answer is 1 over 12.
With several fractions: find one bottom number for all, change each fraction, then do the adding and taking away on the tops.
This list looks strange: a fraction, then a whole number, then a fraction again. And one place is blank.
When a list keeps flipping like that, it is often two patterns woven together. Take every second number: 4, 16, 64.
What takes 4 to 16, and then 16 to 64?

ask.ifNot: 4 plus 12 is 16, but 16 plus 12 is not 64. Multiplying works both times: 4 times 4 is 16, and 16 times 4 is 64.

beats.say: Times 4, each time. 4 times 4 is 16, and 16 times 4 is 64.
Now the other strand: 1 half, then 1 eighth, then our blank.
From 1 half to 1 eighth, the bottom number went from 2 to 8. So what happened to the fraction?

ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. The bottom number became 4 times bigger, so each piece is 4 times smaller. The fraction was divided by 4.

beats.say: 1 half divided by 4 is 1 eighth. So one strand multiplies by 4, and the other divides by 4.
The blank is 1 eighth divided by 4. 8 times 4 is 32, so the blank is 1 over 32.
If a list keeps flipping between two kinds of number, split it into two lists, every other term, and solve each one.
Four little sums made of 9s and 3s. We want the one with the least value, so let's work out each.
The first one. Times goes first: 9 times 3 is 27, and 27 plus 3 is 30.
The second. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 plus 9 is 18.
The fourth has a bracket, so that goes first. 9 plus 3 is 12, and 12 times 3 is 36.
Now the third one, 9 minus 3 times 3. Which part goes first?

ask.ifNot: Times comes before minus. So 3 times 3 goes first, even though the minus is on the left.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 minus 9 is 0.
So the values are 30, 18, 0 and 36. Nothing here is smaller than 0, so the third one is the least.
Work out every choice in the proper order before you compare. One slip in the order can change which one wins.
A shirt priced at 700 rupees is sold for 651 rupees in a sale. We want the discount as a per cent.
Two bars. The top is the price on the shirt, 700 rupees. The bottom is what it sold for, 651. The gap between them is the discount.
First the discount in rupees. 700 minus 651 is 49.
Now we need 49 rupees as a per cent. A per cent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: A discount is always measured against the price before the sale. That is the 700 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. The per cent is taken on the 700, the starting price, never on the 651.
Per cent means out of every 100, and 700 is 7 hundreds. So share the 49 rupees over the 7 hundreds: 49 divided by 7 is 7.
So every 100 rupees of price gets 7 rupees off. That is a discount of 7 per cent.
Check: 1 per cent of 700 is 7, so 7 per cent is 7 times 7, which is 49. That is our discount.
So for a discount per cent: find the rupees off, then ask how many that is for every 100 of the starting price.
A man bought 27 eggs. We want to say that in dozens, as a decimal.
How many full dozens fit into 27?

ask.ifNot: Count in 12s. Two 12s still fit inside 27, but a third 12 would go past it.

beats.say: 2 dozens use up 24 eggs. That leaves 3 eggs over.
Those 3 left-over eggs are only part of a dozen. What fraction of a dozen are they?

ask.ifNot: A dozen has 12 eggs, so 3 eggs are 3 out of 12, not 3 out of 10. This is exactly where the decimal trap hides.

beats.say: 3 out of 12 is one quarter. And one quarter, as a decimal, is 0.25.
So 27 eggs are 2 dozens and 0.25 of a dozen. That is 2.25 dozen.
Check: 2.25 times 12 should take us back to 27 eggs. It does.
The leftovers become a fraction of the group size, here twelfths. Then turn that fraction into a decimal.
12 buckets can hold 108 litres of water. How many buckets do we need to store 162 litres?
What do we want? A number of buckets, not litres. And every bucket is the same size, so let's line up what we know.
What should we find first?

ask.ifNot: Find one first. Once we know what 1 bucket holds, any number of litres is easy.

beats.say: 108 litres shared equally among 12 buckets. 108 divided by 12 is 9. So one bucket holds 9 litres.
Now we have 162 litres to store, at 9 litres to a bucket. What do we do?

ask.ifNot: We are asking how many times 9 litres fits into 162 litres. Counting how many times it fits is a division.

beats.say: 162 divided by 9 is 18.
So we need 18 buckets.
Check: 18 buckets with 9 litres in each. 18 times 9 is 162. And more water needed more buckets than 12, which makes sense.
So here is the plan. Find what one holds, then see how many of those you need.
Five gifts, costing 21 rupees in all. And we know four pair totals. We want A and E together.
Look at two of the pairs: A with B, and C with D. Together they cover four gifts. Which gift is left out?

ask.ifNot: A, B, C and D are all inside those two pairs. The only gift not counted is E.

beats.say: So take those two pairs away from the total, and what is left is E. 21 minus 6 minus 7 is 8.
Now we want A. Which two pairs leave only A out?

ask.ifNot: We need two pairs that cover B, C, D and E, with no A in them. That is B with C, together with D and E.

beats.say: B and C cost 10, and D and E cost 9. 21 minus 10 minus 9 is 2. So A costs 2 rupees.
A is 2 and E is 8. Together, 2 plus 8 is 10 rupees.
Let's check with the others. B is 6 minus 2, which is 4. C is 10 minus 4, which is 6. D is 7 minus 6, which is 1. And D plus E is 1 plus 8, which is 9. It all fits.
When you know a total and some pairs, take away pairs that do not overlap. Whatever is left out is what you have found.
An angle and its supplement sit together on a straight line. We are told the supplement is 3 times as big as the angle. How big is the angle?
We do not know the angle, so let's give it a name: x. Then the supplement, which is 3 times as big, is 3 x.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Look at the drawing. x and 3 x lie along a straight line. So what do they add up to?
A straight line is a half turn, 180 degrees. So x, plus 3 x, equals 180.
1 x and 3 more x's make 4 x. So 4 x equals 180.

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. To undo times 4, we divide by 4, on both sides.

beats.say: 4 x means 4 times x. How do we undo times 4?
Divide both sides by 4. To divide by 4, halve and halve again. Half of 180 is 90, and half of 90 is 45.
So x equals 45. The angle is 45 degrees.
Let's check. The supplement is 3 times 45, which is 135. And 45 plus 135 makes 180, a straight line. It works.
So when a question gives a link between an angle and its supplement, call the angle x, write both on a straight line, and make them add up to 180.
Here is a triangle whose sides are written with the letter a: 2 a plus 6, 3 a plus 5, and a plus 7. We are told a is 3, and we want the perimeter.

ask.ifNot: A number written right next to a letter means times. So 2 a is 2 times 3, not 23.

beats.say: Wherever we see a, we put 3. But first: what does 2 a mean when a is 3?
The first side is 2 times 3, plus 6. 2 times 3 is 6, and 6 plus 6 is 12 centimetres.
The second side is 3 times 3, plus 5. 3 times 3 is 9, and 9 plus 5 is 14 centimetres.
The third side is the easy one: 3 plus 7 is 10 centimetres. Now every side has a real length.

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along every side, and a triangle has 3 of them. So we add all 3 lengths.

beats.say: Perimeter is the walk all the way round the triangle. Which sum gives it?
Add them one at a time. 12 plus 14 is 26. Then 26 plus 10 is 36.

spec.note: Perimeter = 36 cm

beats.say: So the perimeter is 36 centimetres.
Here is another way to check. Add the letters first: the 3 sides together are 6 a plus 18. And 6 times 3, plus 18, is 36 too.
So: put the number in place of the letter to get each side, then add all the sides for the walk round.
Some money is put away at 10 per cent simple interest per annum, for 5 years. It grows to 4500 rupees. How much was put in at the start?

board.text: 10% per annum for 5 years. Amount = Rs.4500.

beats.say: Think of the starting sum as 100 per cent. Each year, it earns 10 per cent of itself.
It earns 10 per cent every year, for 5 years. How much interest is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Simple interest earns the same each year. 10 per cent, 5 times over, is 50 per cent.

beats.say: 5 times 10 is 50. So the interest is 50 per cent of the starting sum: exactly half of it.

spec.note: Starting sum (100%) + interest (50%) = amount

beats.say: Careful now. Is 4500 the starting sum, the interest, or both together?

ask.ifNot: Amount means everything at the end: the starting sum and the interest together.

beats.say: So 4500 is the starting sum plus half as much again. That is 150 per cent: 3 equal pieces of 50 per cent.
3 equal pieces make 4500. So one piece is 4500 divided by 3, which is 1500.
The starting sum is 2 of those pieces. 2 times 1500 is 3000. So 3000 rupees was put in.
Check: 10 per cent of 3000 is 300 a year. 5 years gives 1500. And 3000 plus 1500 is 4500. It works.
So when you are given the amount, remember it is the starting sum and the interest together. Work out what per cent that is, then go back to 100 per cent.

board.text: (f − 9) is even. The 25th odd number after it?

beats.say: This one looks like algebra, but it is really about counting along a line of numbers.
We do not know f, and we do not need to. Think of f minus 9 as one even number, and walk forward from it.

ask.ifNot: Even and odd numbers take turns. So the number right next to it, 1 more, is odd.

beats.say: What is the first odd number after any even number?
So the 1st one is 1 more. After that, each new odd number is 2 further on: 3 away, then 5 away.
To get from the 1st to the 25th takes 24 more jumps of 2. Careful: 24 jumps, not 25, because the 1st one is already counted.
24 jumps of 2 cover 48. Add the first step of 1, and we have gone 49 in all.
So the 25th odd number is 49 more than our starting number, f minus 9.
Minus 9 and plus 49 together make plus 40. So we have f plus 40.
Try it with a real number. If f is 11, then f minus 9 is 2. Going on by 49 lands on 51. And 11 plus 40 is 51 too.
So the answer is f plus 40. Remember: 1 step to reach the first one, then jumps of 2 for all the rest.
Five people, and their ages add up to 105. We know four pair totals. We need the youngest, so we have to find everyone.
A and B make 39, and C and D make 38. Those two pairs cover four people. Who is left out?

ask.ifNot: A, B, C and D are all inside those two pairs. The only person not counted is E.

beats.say: So E is the total, minus those two pairs. 105 minus 39 minus 38 is 28.
The same trick finds A. B and C make 40, D and E make 44, and only A is left out. 105 minus 40 minus 44 is 21.
Now we know A is 21. Which fact gives us B straight away?

ask.ifNot: We want a fact with B and one other person whose age we already know. A and B make 39, and we know A.

beats.say: B is 39 minus 21, which is 18. Then C is 40 minus 18, which is 22. And D is 38 minus 22, which is 16.
Line them up: A is 21, B is 18, C is 22, D is 16 and E is 28. The smallest is 16.
Check the one pair we did not use. D and E are 16 plus 28, which is 44. Just what the question said.
So with a total and some pairs: remove pairs that do not overlap to find one person, then walk along the chain. The youngest is 16.
A tank is 5 over 6 full. We take out 30 litres, and now it is 4 over 5 full. How much does the full tank hold?
Think about what those 30 litres really are. They are the gap between 5 over 6 of the tank and 4 over 5 of the tank.
To take 4 over 5 away from 5 over 6, what do we need first?

ask.ifNot: Sixths and fifths are different sizes of piece. Before we can take one from the other, both must be cut into pieces of the same size.

beats.say: 6 and 5 both go into 30. So 5 over 6 becomes 25 over 30, and 4 over 5 becomes 24 over 30.
25 over 30, take away 24 over 30, is just 1 over 30. One tiny piece of the tank!
So 1 over 30 of the tank is 30 litres. How do we get the whole tank?

ask.ifNot: The whole tank is 30 of those pieces, and every piece holds 30 litres. So we need 30 lots of 30.

beats.say: The full tank is 30 pieces of 30 litres each. 30 times 30 is 900 litres.
Let's check. 5 over 6 of 900 is 750, and 4 over 5 of 900 is 720. And 750 take away 720 is 30 litres. It works.
So the full tank holds 900 litres. When two fractions of one thing differ by a known amount, find what fraction that amount is, then build up to the whole.
A retailer buys from a wholesaler at 20 per cent off the list price. He then sells at 8 per cent off the list price. We want his profit per cent.

board.text: Retailer buys at 20% off the list price,
and sells at 8% off the list price.

beats.say: No price is given, so we may choose one. Let us make the list price 100 rupees, because per cents of 100 are so easy.
He buys at 20 per cent off. 20 per cent of 100 is 20, so he pays 100 minus 20, which is 80 rupees. That is his cost price.
He sells at 8 per cent off the list price. 8 per cent of 100 is 8, so he gets 100 minus 8, which is 92 rupees. That is his selling price.
His profit is the gap between the two bars: 92 minus 80, which is 12 rupees.
Now the profit per cent. 12 rupees is a profit on which amount?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, the money he paid. He paid 80 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. 12 on 100 would be 12 per cent, but he did not pay 100. He paid 80, so we compare 12 with 80.
12 out of 80. Divide both by 4: that is 3 out of 20. Now multiply both by 5: 15 out of 100. So the profit is 15 per cent.
Check: 10 per cent of 80 is 8, and 5 per cent is 4. Together, 15 per cent of 80 is 12. That is our profit.
So when no price is given, choose 100. And always take the profit per cent on the cost price.

board.text: Clock shows 11:00 a.m. Hour hand turns 165°.

beats.say: The clock shows 11 o'clock in the morning. Then the hour hand, the short one, turns through 165 degrees. What time is it now?

board.text: Hour hand: full turn = 360° in 12 hours

beats.say: Here is the key fact. The hour hand goes right round the clock face, one full turn, in 12 hours. And a full turn is 360 degrees.

ask.ifNot: 360 degrees are shared equally among 12 hours, so we divide 360 by 12. Dividing by 60 is for the minute hand.

beats.say: So how far does the hour hand turn in just 1 hour?
360 divided by 12 is 30. So every hour, the hour hand moves 30 degrees, from one number to the next.
Now, how many 30s are there in 165? 5 thirties make 150. That leaves 15 degrees over.

ask.ifNot: 30 degrees is a whole hour, and 15 is half of 30. So it is half an hour. The trap is to read 15 degrees as 15 minutes.

beats.say: The 150 degrees are 5 whole hours. What about the 15 degrees left over?
15 is half of 30, so it is half an hour, which is 30 minutes. Altogether the hand has moved for 5 hours and 30 minutes.
Now add that to 11 o'clock. 1 hour takes us to 12 noon, and 4 more hours take us to 4 in the afternoon.
Then the extra 30 minutes. The time is 4:30 in the afternoon.
So remember: the hour hand turns 30 degrees every hour. Divide the turn by 30 for the hours, and change what is left over into minutes.
Four children, and their ages add up to 20. We want Anil's age, so let's call Anil's age a.
Anil is 3 years younger than Chetan. So how do we write Chetan's age?

ask.ifNot: If Anil is 3 years younger, then Chetan is 3 years older than Anil. Older means we add: a plus 3.

beats.say: So Chetan is a plus 3. David is 5 years older than Chetan, so David is a plus 3 plus 5, which is a plus 8.
David is 3 years older than Bunty, so Bunty is 3 years younger than David. That makes Bunty a plus 8 minus 3, which is a plus 5.
Now add all four ages, and that must be 20.
Gather the like terms. There are 4 lots of a. And the plain numbers, 5 and 3 and 8, make 16.
Now it is an equation we know. What do we do first?

ask.ifNot: The 4 a has a plus 16 hanging on to it. We clear that first, by taking 16 from both sides.

beats.say: Take 16 from both sides. 20 minus 16 is 4, so 4 a equals 4.
Divide both sides by 4. 4 divided by 4 is 1. So Anil is just 1 year old.
Check the story. Anil is 1, so Chetan is 4, David is 9 and Bunty is 6. 1 plus 6 plus 4 plus 9 is 20. It fits.
So in a word problem: give a letter to the thing you want, write everyone else using that letter, and build one equation.
A seagull flew 16500 miles from Finland to Australia, covering 125 miles every day. How many days did it take?

spec.note: 125 miles every day

beats.say: Each day uses up 125 miles of the journey. So what are we really asking?

ask.ifNot: Every day the seagull covers one more lot of 125 miles. Counting how many lots fit into 16500 is a division.

beats.say: So it is 16500 divided by 125. That looks scary, but here is a friendly fact: 125 times 8 is exactly 1000. So every 1000 miles takes 8 days.
Now split 16500 into 16000 and 500. 16000 is 16 thousands, and each thousand takes 8 days. 16 times 8 is 128 days.
What about the last 500 miles? How many days is that?

ask.ifNot: 8 lots of 125 make 1000, and 500 is half of 1000. So we need half of 8, which is 4.

beats.say: 125 times 4 is 500, so the last stretch takes 4 more days.
128 days plus 4 days makes 132 days. That is how long the seagull took.
Check by multiplying back. 125 times 132 is 16500 miles. Exactly the whole journey.
So, how many days means how many day sized pieces fit into the distance, and that is division. A friendly fact, like 125 times 8, can tame a big one.
72 men can do a piece of work in 40 hours. How many hours will 9 men take to do the same work?

board.text: 72 men do the work in 40 hours

beats.say: Think before any sum. With fewer men on the same job, will it take more time or less?

ask.ifNot: Picture it: fewer hands, the same job. Each man has more to do, so it takes longer. More time.

beats.say: So our answer must be bigger than 40. Keep that in your head. It will protect you from the trap in this question.
