beats.say: 97. Working the same way, the others are 89, 83, 79 and 73.
The drops are 8, 6, 4, and then 6. No steady rule there. So let's look at the numbers themselves instead.
97, 89, 83, 79, 73. None is even, and none ends in 5. Which family do they belong to?

ask.ifNot: They are odd, but many odd numbers in between are missing. Only the primes are here, counting downwards.

beats.say: Primes, going down. After 73 comes 71: the 6th term. 69 is 3 times 23, so skip it. 67 is prime: the 7th term.
65 is 5 times 13 and 63 is 7 times 9, so skip both. 61 is prime: the 8th term. And 59 is prime: the 9th term.
Now back into Roman numerals. 59 is 50 and 9. 50 is L. How is 9 written?

ask.ifNot: 9 is 1 less than 10, so the I goes before the X. With the I after the X, it would be 1 more than 10.

beats.say: So the 9th term is 59, written L, then I, X.
When a pattern is in disguise, change it into ordinary numbers, solve it, and then change the answer back.

board.text: Triangle: two sides 16 cm and 7 cm

beats.say: Two sides of a triangle are 16 centimetres and 7 centimetres. We do not know the third side, but we have to say what the perimeter could be.
The third side cannot be just anything. Picture the 7 side as a door, hinged to one end of the 16 side. Swing it wide open, flat, and the far ends are 16 plus 7 apart: 23.
Swing the door shut, flat against the 16 side, and the gap between the far ends is 16 take away 7: 9.

choices: No: the triangle would be flat
ask.ifNot: At exactly 23 or exactly 9 the door lies flat along the line, and there is no triangle left. The third side has to be in between.

beats.say: Can the third side be exactly 23, or exactly 9?
So the third side is more than 9 and less than 23. That is true for every triangle: more than the difference of the other two sides, less than their sum.
Now the perimeter. The two known sides make 23. Add the smallest and the largest third side: 23 plus 9 is 32, and 23 plus 23 is 46.

ask.ifNot: 31 is below 32. And 46 is the flat edge itself, which is not allowed. Only 34 lies properly in between.

beats.say: The choices are 34, 31 and 46. Which one lies between 32 and 46?
34 is between 32 and 46. It gives a third side of 34 take away 23, which is 11, safely between 9 and 23.
So a possible perimeter is 34 centimetres.
Remember the door. The third side of a triangle is always less than the sum of the other two, and more than their difference.
We are given 4 pairs of angles, all with decimals. We have to find the pair that is supplementary.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Supplementary angles fit together on a straight line, like this. So what must the pair add up to?

board.text: Supplementary: the pair adds up to 180°

beats.say: The pair must make exactly 180 degrees. So we add each pair. Here is a tip: look at the decimal parts first.
First pair: 127.5 and 53.5. The two point 5s make 1 whole, and the total comes to 181. One too many.
Second pair: 83.6 and 95.4. Point 6 and point 4 make 1 whole, and the total is 179. One short.
Third pair: 111.8 and 68.2. Point 8 and point 2 make 1 whole, and this time the total is exactly 180.
Check the last pair too: 115.7 and 65.3 make 181. So only one pair works.
The supplementary pair is 111.8 degrees and 68.2 degrees.
Notice how close the other pairs came: 179 and 181. Supplementary means exactly 180, so add carefully, decimals and all.

board.text: Square: side 56 cm. Rectangle: breadth 49 cm.

beats.say: A square has a side of 56 centimetres. A rectangle with a breadth of 49 centimetres has the same area. We want the perimeter of the rectangle.
The area of the square is side times side: 56 times 56. That comes to 3136 square centimetres, a big number. Keep it as 56 times 56 for a moment.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times breadth. So to get back from the area to the length, we divide by the breadth.

beats.say: The rectangle has that same area, and its breadth is 49. How do we find its length?
So the length is 56 times 56, divided by 49. Here is a neat way to do it. 49 is 7 times 7, and 56 is in the 7 times table: 56 divided by 7 is 8.
So divide each 56 by one of the 7s. We are left with 8 times 8, which is 64. The length is 64 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 64 plus 49 is only one length and one breadth, which is halfway round. We double it for the whole walk.

beats.say: Now the perimeter of the rectangle, the walk all the way round. Which sum gives it?
64 plus 49 is 113, and that is halfway. Double it: 2 times 113 is 226 centimetres.
Now look at the choices: 230, 224 and 222. Our 226 is not among them. Check the length before deciding: 64 times 49 is 3136, the same as the square. So it is right.

spec.note: Perimeter = 226 cm

beats.say: So the answer is: none of these.
So: the square's area, then the rectangle's length, then its perimeter. And when careful working gives an answer that is not on the list, none of these is the one to pick.
An article sold at 440 rupees gives a profit of 10 per cent. We want the selling price that would give a profit of 17 per cent.
Both selling prices belong to the same article. So the bridge between them is the cost price. Call the cost price 100 per cent.
With a 10 per cent profit, the selling price, 440, is what per cent of the cost price?

ask.ifNot: The selling price is the whole cost price, 100 per cent, with the 10 per cent profit on top. That makes 110 per cent.

beats.say: 100 per cent plus 10 per cent is 110 per cent. So 110 per cent of the cost price is 440 rupees.
Find 1 per cent: 440 divided by 110. 110 times 4 is 440, so 1 per cent of the cost price is 4 rupees.
Careful: the trap is to add 7 per cent of 440. But every profit per cent is taken on the cost price, not on the old selling price.
For a profit of 17 per cent, the selling price is 100 plus 17, which is 117 per cent of the cost price.
So we need 117 lots of 4. 100 times 4 is 400, and 17 times 4 is 68. Together, 468.
So it should be sold at 468 rupees.
Check: the cost price is 400 rupees. 17 per cent of 400 is 68, and 400 plus 68 is 468.
So to change from one profit per cent to another, go back to the cost price first, then build the new selling price.
A long line with no brackets at all. It looks scary, but it breaks into pieces.
The minus and the plus split the line into three chunks. What do we do first: the chunks, or the minus and plus between them?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide come before plus and minus. So each chunk is worked out on its own first.

beats.say: First chunk, left to right. 21 goes into 84 exactly 4 times, so 21 divided by 84 is one quarter. And a quarter of 16 is 4.
Second chunk: 7 times 3 is 21.
Third chunk: 306 divided by 17. 17 times 10 is 170 and 17 times 8 is 136. Together they make 306, so the answer is 18.
The line is now 4 minus 21 plus 18. But 4 minus 21 dips below zero. Is there a friendlier way?

ask.ifNot: The minus belongs only to the 21. So we may bring the plus 18 forward: 4 plus 18, and then take away 21.

beats.say: 4 plus 18 is 22, and 22 minus 21 is 1.
Split a long line at its plus and minus signs. Work out each chunk, then put the chunks together.

board.text: Clock at 7:20. Angle between the hands = ?

beats.say: The clock shows 7:20. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.
Here is the plan. We measure how far each hand has turned from the 12 at the top, one hand at a time. The whole clock face is a full turn, 360 degrees.
The minute hand first. It goes all the way round, 360 degrees, in 60 minutes. That is 6 degrees every minute. So at 20 minutes it has turned 20 times 6, which is 120 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand never stops. By 20 minutes past, it has crept on from the 7 towards the 8.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. At 7:20, where exactly is it pointing?
It is a little past the 7. Take the 7 first. Each hour is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees. So from the 12 round to the 7 is 7 times 30, which is 210 degrees.
Now the creep. The hour hand moves 30 degrees in 60 minutes, so half a degree each minute. In 20 minutes that is 10 degrees more. The hour hand is at 220 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The angle between the hands is the gap between their two positions, so we subtract. And we use 220, not 210, because the hour hand has moved past the 7.

beats.say: The minute hand is at 120 degrees and the hour hand is at 220 degrees. How do we get the angle between them?
220 take away 120 is 100. The angle between the hands is 100 degrees.
So work the two hands separately: 6 degrees a minute for the minute hand, 30 degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute for the hour hand. Forget the creep, and you are 10 degrees out.
We add a small number to 4618 and must land on a perfect square.
Do we want a square above 4618 or below it?

ask.ifNot: Adding makes a number bigger. So the square we land on has to be above 4618, and we want the first one.

beats.say: 60 times 60 is 3600, and 70 times 70 is 4900. So the root is between 60 and 70, and 4618 is nearer to 4900.
Let's try 68. 68 times 70 is 4760. That is 2 lots of 68 too many, so we take away 136. We get 4624.
4624 is just above 4618. To be sure it is the first square above, look at the one before: 67 times 67 is 4489, far below.
So how much do we add to 4618 to reach 4624?

ask.ifNot: Find the gap going up: 4624 minus 4618.

beats.say: 4624 minus 4618 is 6. So we add 6.
Check: 4618 plus 6 is 4624, and that is 68 times 68.
Trap the number between two tens, test a root near the top, and find the gap up to the first square above.

board.text: (7th odd number after 54) + (12th even number before 65)

beats.say: Two little hunts, then one addition. First the 7th odd number after 54, then the 12th even number before 65.
The odd numbers after 54 are short enough to list: 55, 57, 59, 61, 63, 65, 67. The 7th one is 67.
Now the even numbers before 65. Counting backwards, they start at 64 and go down in jumps of 2.

ask.ifNot: The 1st is already there with no jump at all. Each jump after that gives one more, so the 12th needs 11 jumps.

beats.say: 64 is the 1st. How many jumps back do we need to reach the 12th?
11 jumps of 2 is 22. And 64 minus 22 is 42.
Now add the two answers. 67 plus 42 is 109.
So the sum is 109.
When you count along a list, the jumps are always one fewer than the position.
Nirav travels 680 kilometres from A to B in 8 hours. Coming back, he drives 17 kilometres per hour slower. How long does the return journey take?

board.text: A to B: 680 km in 8 hours
B to A: 17 km/hr slower. Time = ?

beats.say: To slow a speed down, we first need to know the speed. Speed means how far in one hour. How do we find his speed from A to B?

ask.ifNot: The 680 kilometres are spread evenly over 8 hours. One hour's share is 680 split into 8 equal parts.

beats.say: 680 is 640 and 40. 640 divided by 8 is 80, and 40 divided by 8 is 5. So he drives 85 kilometres every hour.
On the way back he is 17 kilometres per hour slower. 85 minus 17 is 68 kilometres per hour.

spec.note: 68 km in every hour

beats.say: It is the same road, so the distance back is still 680 kilometres. Now he covers 68 kilometres each hour. How many hours will it take?

ask.ifNot: Each hour takes care of 68 kilometres. Count how many lots of 68 fit into 680.

beats.say: 68 times 10 is 680. So the return journey takes 10 hours.
Careful, we are not finished: the choices are in minutes. 1 hour is 60 minutes, so 10 hours is 10 times 60, which is 600 minutes.
Sense check. He drove slower on the way back, so it should take longer than the 8 hours going. 10 hours is longer. Good.
So: find the first speed, change it, then use the new speed with the same distance. And always read which unit the choices want.
A bracket, times A, equals 9 over 4. If we work out the bracket first, finding A will be easy.
Inside the bracket: three quarters divided by 9 over 4. To divide by a fraction, we flip it and multiply.
Three quarters times 4 over 9. Tops together, bottoms together. What do we get?

ask.ifNot: Multiply top by top: 3 times 4. Then bottom by bottom: 4 times 9.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12, and 4 times 9 is 36. And 12 goes into both of those, so 12 over 36 is one third.
So the puzzle is now: one third of A is 9 over 4.
If one third of A is 9 over 4, how do we get all of A?

ask.ifNot: A is made of 3 equal thirds, and each third is 9 over 4. So A is 3 lots of 9 over 4.

beats.say: 3 lots of 9 over 4. 3 times 9 is 27, and the bottom stays 4. So A is 27 over 4.
Let's check. One third of 27 over 4 is 9 over 4, because 27 divided by 3 is 9. It works.
Simplify the bracket first. Then ask what undoes it: if a third of A is known, A is 3 times as much.
Four decimals built from 8s and 0s. They look alike, so the danger is letting a digit slip into a place where it does not belong.
We will give every number three decimal places, so the points line up. What does 0.08 become?

ask.ifNot: Padding means writing zeros at the end, after the last digit. So 0.08 becomes 0.080. A zero slipped in front of the 8 would change its value.

beats.say: Here they are, padded and lined up on the point.
Add two at a time. 8.008 plus 0.08 is 8.088.
Add 80.8 to that. The 8 tenths drop into the empty tenths place, and we get 88.888. All eights!
Last, add 80.08. Take care: 8 tens and 8 tens make more than 10 tens, so 1 goes into the hundreds place. We get 168.968.
A rough check. 8 plus 80 plus 80 is 168, and our answer is just a little more than that. Good.
With decimals, line up the points, pad with zeros at the end, and add place by place.
Three steps: find the greatest 2 digit prime, square it, and then find what the 4 in the answer is worth.

ask.ifNot: 99 can be divided by 9, and 93 by 3. 97 cannot be divided by anything, so it is the greatest 2 digit prime.

beats.say: Which is the greatest 2 digit prime?
So we must square 97. That means 97 times 97.
97 is 3 less than 100. So take 97 hundreds, 9700, and take away 3 lots of 97, which is 291. That leaves 9409.
So the square is 9409. Now find the 4.
Units, tens, hundreds. The 4 is in the hundreds place, so it is worth 4 times 100, which is 400.
So the place value of the 4 is 400.
Find the number, do the sum, then read the place. Take one step at a time and a long question becomes easy.
d is 6. We must find which statement is true. True means the left side and the right side are worth the same.
Put 6 in place of d on both sides. For A, the left is 5 times 6, plus 19, which is 49. The right is 7 times 6, minus 17, which is 25. Nowhere near.
Now B. The left side is 8, plus 4 times 6, which is 32. What is the right side, 6 d minus 6?

ask.ifNot: 6 d means 6 times 6. Take 6 away from that, and we get 30.

beats.say: The right side is 30, but the left side was 32. Close, but not equal. B is out.
Now C. The left is 12 times 6, minus 14, which is 58. The right is 16, plus 7 times 6, which is also 58. They match!
So the true statement is 12 d minus 14 equals 16 plus 7 d.
One of them worked, so we do not need none of these. But we only knew that because we tested every one.
To check whether a statement is true: put the number in on both sides, work each side out, and compare.
How many natural numbers less than 3009 can be divided by both 6 and 9? Let's see where the two tables meet.

board.text: Below 3009: divisible by both 6 and 9. How many?

beats.say: Here are both tables. Numbers in both of them are multiples of which number?

ask.ifNot: Look along both lists. 18 is the first number in both, and 36 comes next. 54 is in both tables too, but it is not the first.

beats.say: The tables meet at 18, then 36: every multiple of 18. So we count multiples of 18.
Less than 3009 means up to 3008. So how many 18s fit into 3008?

board.text: Count the multiples of 18 up to 3008

beats.say: 18 times 100 is 1800, which leaves 1208. 18 times 60 is 1080, which leaves 128.
18 times 7 is 126, with 2 left over. So 100 plus 60 plus 7 makes 167 eighteens.
2 is left over. Does it count as another multiple?

ask.ifNot: The left over 2 is not a full 18. We count complete eighteens only.

beats.say: So there are 167 such numbers.
Divisible by both means divisible by the L C M, not the product. Then divide the limit by the L C M and keep the whole part.
Here is our equation. 6 x minus 9, equals 4 x plus 30, all over 2. Let's tidy the right side first.
All over 2 means the whole bracket is halved. What is half of 4 x plus 30?

ask.ifNot: The 2 divides both parts. Half of 4 x is 2 x, and half of 30 is 15. Halving only one of them is the slip to avoid.

beats.say: So half of 4 x is 2 x, and half of 30 is 15.
x is on both sides. Take the smaller lot, 2 x, from both sides. 6 x take away 2 x leaves 4 x.
What is in the way of the 4 x now?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side. The 4 x has a minus 9 hanging on to it. That is what we clear next.

beats.say: To undo minus 9 we add 9 to both sides. 15 plus 9 is 24. So 4 x equals 24.
Divide both sides by 4. 24 divided by 4 is 6. So x equals 6.
Check. Left: 6 times 6 is 36, and 36 minus 9 is 27. Right: 4 times 6, plus 30, is 54, and half of 54 is 27. Both sides are 27.
So: tidy any fraction first, bring the x terms together, clear the plain number, then divide.
28 per cent of a number is 196. We want 43 per cent of that same number.

spec.note: We know the 28% piece. We want a 43% piece.

beats.say: We need a stepping stone between 28 per cent and 43 per cent. What is the handiest one?

ask.ifNot: 196 is already 28 per cent of the number. Share it into 28 equal parts and each part is 1 per cent. From 1 per cent we can reach any per cent.

beats.say: So how many 28s make 196? Let us try 7. 20 times 7 is 140, and 8 times 7 is 56.
140 plus 56 is 196. It fits exactly. So 1 per cent of the number is 7.
Careful: do not take 43 per cent of 196. 196 is only a part of the number, not the number itself.
43 per cent is 43 lots of 1 per cent. 40 times 7 is 280, and 3 times 7 is 21. Together, 301.
So 43 per cent of the number is 301.
Check: the whole number is 100 times 7, which is 700. Half of 700 is 350, and 43 per cent should be a bit less than half. 301 is. Sensible.
So to go from one per cent of a number to another, drop down to 1 per cent, then climb back up.
The series goes 3, 7, 11, 15, 19. We need two far away terms, the 11th and the 18th, and then their sum.
What is the jump from each number to the next?

ask.ifNot: 7 minus 3 is 4. 11 minus 7 is 4. 15 minus 11 is 4.

beats.say: Plus 4, every time.
To reach a term we start at 3 and make jumps of 4. The 2nd term needs 1 jump. The 3rd needs 2 jumps.
So how many jumps for the 11th term, and how many for the 18th?

ask.ifNot: Always 1 fewer than the term number: 10 jumps for the 11th term, and 17 jumps for the 18th.

beats.say: The 11th term: 10 jumps of 4 is 40, and 3 plus 40 is 43.
The 18th term: 17 jumps of 4 is 68, and 3 plus 68 is 71.
Now add the two terms. 43 plus 71 is 114.
We got 114. But the choices are 116, 108, 124, or none of these. Which do we pick?

ask.ifNot: Our working gives 114, and 114 is not on the list. Close is not the same as equal, so we choose none of these.

beats.say: 114 is not offered. So the right choice is none of these.
Find each term with 1 fewer jumps than its number. And if your answer is not offered, check it once, then choose none of these.
Medha borrowed 3500 rupees from a friend at simple interest. After 3 years she repaid the loan with 4340 rupees. What was the rate of interest per annum?

board.text: Borrowed Rs.3500. Repaid Rs.4340 after 3 years.

beats.say: 4340 rupees is called the amount. It is the 3500 rupees that was borrowed, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 4340 minus 3500 is 840. So the interest is 840 rupees, for all 3 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 3. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 840 divided by 3, which is 280.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 3500 divided by 100 is 35, so the money is 35 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 35 hundreds earn 280 rupees a year. Try 8: 30 times 8 is 240, and 5 times 8 is 40. Together that is 280, so each hundred earns 8 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 8 rupees a year. That is a rate of 8 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 3500 times 8 times 3, divided by 100, is 840. That is our interest.
So for the rate: amount minus principal gives the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
Three dozen mangoes cost 1800 rupees. How much would 26 mangoes cost?
Careful with the units: the price is for dozens, but we are asked about single mangoes. A dozen is 12. So how many mangoes are in three dozen?

ask.ifNot: Three dozen means 3 lots of 12. And 3 times 12 is 36.

beats.say: 3 times 12 is 36. So 36 mangoes cost 1800 rupees.
Find one first. One mango costs 1800 divided by 36. Now, 36 times 5 is 180, so 36 times 50 is 1800. One mango costs 50 rupees.
And 26 mangoes?

ask.ifNot: 26 mangoes, at 50 rupees each. 26 lots of 50 means multiply.

beats.say: 26 times 5 is 130, so 26 times 50 is 1300.
So 26 mangoes cost 1300 rupees.
Check. 26 is 10 fewer than 36. Those 10 mangoes would cost 10 times 50, which is 500 rupees. And 1800 minus 500 is 1300.
The trap is to stop at the price of a dozen. Go all the way down to one mango, then build back up.

board.text: Rectangle: same perimeter. L and B = ?

beats.say: An equilateral triangle has a side of 12 centimetres. A rectangle has the same perimeter as the triangle. We have to pick the length and breadth it could have.

ask.ifNot: The walk goes along all 3 sides, so we add 12 three times. That is the same as 3 times 12.

beats.say: Equilateral means all 3 sides are equal. Which sum gives the walk all the way round the triangle?

spec.note: Perimeter = 36 cm

beats.say: 3 times 12 is 36. The triangle's perimeter is 36 centimetres, and so is the rectangle's.

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth take us exactly halfway round. So together they make half of 36.

beats.say: The walk round a rectangle is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. So what must one length and one breadth add up to?
Half of 36 is 18. So we are looking for a pair that adds up to 18.
Test the pairs. 10 plus 5 is 15: too small. 14 plus 6 is 20: too big.
8 plus 6 is 14: too small. And 13 plus 5 is 18. That is the one.

spec.note: Perimeter = 36 cm

beats.say: So the rectangle can have a length of 13 centimetres and a breadth of 5 centimetres.
Check the whole walk: 2 times 18 is 36, the same as the triangle.
The trap is to look for a pair that makes 36. Each side of a rectangle is walked twice, so the pair only makes half of the perimeter.
Which is the greatest: 15 over 17, 11 over 13, 9 over 19 or 10 over 21?
Two of these are less than one half. Which two?

ask.ifNot: A fraction is less than one half when its top is less than half of its bottom. Half of 19 is 9 and a half, and half of 21 is 10 and a half.

beats.say: 9 is less than half of 19, and 10 is less than half of 21. So those two are small, and they are out.
That leaves 15 over 17 and 11 over 13. Both are close to 1. So let's ask: how far from a whole is each one?
15 over 17 is missing 2 seventeenths. 11 over 13 is missing 2 thirteenths.
Which gap is smaller, 2 over 17 or 2 over 13?

ask.ifNot: Same top, so look at the size of the pieces. Seventeenths are smaller pieces than thirteenths, so 2 of them make the smaller gap.

beats.say: 2 over 17 is the smaller gap. That puts 15 over 17 closest to 1, so it is the greatest.
Use landmarks. Throw out anything below one half, then compare how far the rest are from 1. The smallest gap wins.
2000 is divided by a mystery number, giving 29 with 57 left over. We need that divisor, and then its square.
Write the division the other way round: divisor times quotient, plus remainder. What do the equal groups add up to, without the leftover?

ask.ifNot: The 57 is what was left after the groups were made. Take it away from 2000 and we have exactly the groups.

beats.say: 2000 minus 57 is 1943. So the mystery number times 29 is 1943.
How many 29s are in 1943? 29 times 60 is 1740. That leaves 203, and 203 is 29 times 7.
60 and 7 make 67. So the divisor is 67. And that fits: the remainder, 57, is smaller than 67.
Are we finished?

ask.ifNot: 67 is the divisor. But the question asks for the square of the divisor, so one more step.

beats.say: 67 times 67. 67 times 60 is 4020, and 67 times 7 is 469. Together, 4489.
Take the remainder off, divide by the quotient to get the divisor, and then do whatever the question asks with it.
A train leaves London at 6 45 p m and reaches Paris at 9 15 p m. Its speed is 32.5 metres per second. How far is it from London to Paris?

spec.note: The train leaves at 6:45 pm

beats.say: First, the journey time. Count on from 6 45 in friendly jumps: up to 7 o'clock, on to 9 o'clock, then the last bit to 9 15. How long is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Careful: 6 45 is nearly 7 o'clock, so it is less than 3 hours to 9 15. Jump 15 minutes to 7, then 2 hours to 9, then 15 minutes more.

beats.say: 15 minutes takes us to 7 o'clock. 2 hours takes us to 9 o'clock. 15 more minutes takes us to 9 15. That is 2 hours and 30 minutes.
The speed is in metres per second, but our time is in hours and minutes. Those do not mix. What is a good way to fix it?

choices: find how far it goes in 1 hour
ask.ifNot: 32.5 metres is what the train does in 1 second, so we cannot multiply it by hours. First let's find what it does in a whole hour.

beats.say: 1 hour is 60 times 60 seconds, which is 3600. So in one hour the train goes 32.5 times 3600 metres.
3600 is 4 times 9 times 100, so we can multiply in easy steps. 32.5 times 4 is 130. 130 times 9 is 1170. Times 100 gives 117000 metres.
1000 metres make 1 kilometre, so 117000 metres is 117 kilometres. The train's speed is 117 kilometres per hour.
Now the units match. 2 hours at 117 kilometres per hour is 234 kilometres. Half an hour is half of 117, which is 58.5 kilometres.
234 plus 58.5 is 292.5. So London to Paris is 292.5 kilometres.
Check with the whole time at once. 2 and a half hours, times 117, is 292.5. It matches.
So: count on to find the time, make the speed and the time use the same units, then distance is speed times time.
A dealer buys 26 cricket bats at 1250 rupees each. He sells 14 of them at 1800 rupees each, and the rest at 825 rupees each. Profit or loss, and what per cent?

board.text: Sold 14 at Rs.1800, the rest at Rs.825.

beats.say: First the cost. 26 bats at 1250 rupees each. 26 times 1000 is 26000, and 26 times 250 is 6500. Together, 32500 rupees.
He sold 14 bats at 1800 rupees. How many were left to sell at 825 rupees?

ask.ifNot: He had 26 bats and sold 14 of them at the higher price. The rest is 26 minus 14, which is 12 bats.

beats.say: Now his sales, as a bill. 14 bats at 1800 rupees is 25200. And the other 12 bats at 825 rupees is 9900.
Add the two lines of the bill. 25200 plus 9900 is 35100 rupees. That is the total selling price.
He paid 32500 and got 35100. More came in than went out, so it is a profit. 35100 minus 32500 is 2600 rupees.
For the profit per cent, the 2600 rupees is compared with which amount?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, all the money he paid. That is 32500 rupees.

beats.say: 1 per cent of 32500 is 325. How many 325s make 2600? 8 times 325 is 2600. So the profit is 8 per cent.
Check with a rough guess. 10 per cent of 32500 is 3250. Our profit, 2600, is a bit less than that, so 8 per cent is sensible.
So: total cost price, total selling price, the gap between them, and then the per cent on the cost price.

board.text: 2-digit primes with digit sum more than 10

beats.say: We go through the 2 digit primes and keep the ones whose digits add up to more than 10.

board.text: digit sum must be 11 or more

beats.say: More than 10 means 11 or bigger. Keep that in mind.
Small primes have small digit sums, so the first ones that pass are these. 29 gives 11, 47 gives 11, 59 gives 14 and 67 gives 13.
Carrying on: 79 gives 16, 83 gives 11, 89 gives 17 and 97 gives 16.

ask.ifNot: The question says more than 10. A sum of exactly 10 is not more than 10, so these three stay out.

beats.say: What about 19, 37 and 73? Each has a digit sum of exactly 10. Do they count?
So cross them out. This is the trap in the question.
Count the ones we kept: 4 in the first row and 4 in the second. That makes 8.
So there are 8 such primes. Read the words 'more than' carefully: they shut the door on exactly 10.
Mishti has marks in four subjects. Three are out of 50 and one is out of 100. We want her overall percentage.
Let us make a mark sheet. For the overall percentage we need two totals: the marks she scored, and the marks they were out of.
Add up what she scored, one line at a time. 44 plus 50 is 94. Add 42 to get 136. Add 84 to get 220.
Now the marks they were out of. 50 plus 50 plus 50 is 150, and 100 more makes 250.
She scored 220 marks. For the overall percentage, that is 220 out of what?

ask.ifNot: Three papers were out of 50 and one was out of 100. Altogether that is 250 marks, so we compare 220 with 250.

beats.say: So she has 220 out of 250. Per cent means out of 100, so shrink the 250 down to 100. Divide both by 5: 44 out of 50. Then double both: 88 out of 100.
88 out of 100 is 88 per cent.
Careful with a tempting shortcut: finding the per cent for each subject and averaging them. That does not work here, because Social Science carries more marks than the others.
Check: she lost 250 minus 220, which is 30 marks. 10 per cent of 250 is 25, so she lost a bit more than 10 per cent. 88 per cent is sensible.
So for an overall percentage: total scored, over total marks, then turn it into out of 100.
One division fact is given, and a second division is asked. The digits are the same, so we will reuse the fact.
The new sum divides by 6.8, which looks like the 68, not like the 12.75. So first swap the fact around. 867 divided by 68 is what?

ask.ifNot: In a division fact, the divisor and the answer can swap places. 867 divided by 12.75 gives 68, so 867 divided by 68 gives 12.75.

beats.say: 867 divided by 68 is 12.75. Now look at the decimal points.
867 became 8.67, so it was divided by 100. And 68 became 6.8, divided by 10.
The first number is 100 times smaller, which makes the answer 100 times smaller. But the divisor is 10 times smaller, which makes the answer 10 times bigger. Overall: 10 times smaller.
So take 12.75 and make it 10 times smaller. The point moves one place to the left: 1.275.
Does it feel right? 8.67 is a little more than 6.8, so the answer should be a little more than 1. And it is.
Reuse the given fact. Then track each decimal point: a smaller first number shrinks the answer, a smaller divisor grows it.
This series is going down: 405, 363, 321, 279, 237. We want the 9th term.
By how much does it drop each time?

ask.ifNot: 405 minus 363 is 42. And 363 minus 321 is 42 again.

beats.say: It drops by 42 every time.
We can see 5 terms. How many more drops take us from the 5th term to the 9th?

ask.ifNot: From the 5th to the 6th is 1 drop. To the 7th is 2, to the 8th is 3, and to the 9th is 4.

beats.say: 4 drops of 42. 4 times 42 is 168.
Start from the 5th term, 237, and take away 168. That leaves 69. So the 9th term is 69.
Check by stepping down one drop at a time: 237, 195, 153, 111, 69. Four drops, and we land on 69.
From the very start it is 8 drops. 8 times 42 is 336, and 405 minus 336 is 69 as well.
111 is among the choices, but it is only the 8th term. Count the drops carefully. The 9th term is 69.
Four sums of squares, and only one is true. For each, we work out the left side, then the right side, and see if they match.
The first one. 8 squared is 64 and 12 squared is 144. Together, 208. But 15 squared is 225. They do not match.
For the big ones, a shortcut: compare last digits only. In the third, 11 squared ends in 1. 59 squared ends in 1 too, because 9 times 9 is 81. So the left side ends in 2.
The left side ends in 2. The right side, 60 squared, ends in 0. Can the two sides be equal?

ask.ifNot: Equal numbers have the same last digit. One side ends in 2 and the other ends in 0, so they cannot be the same number.

beats.say: So the third is out. The fourth: 13 squared ends in 9, and 84 squared ends in 6, because 4 times 4 is 16. So the left side ends in 5. But 87 squared ends in 9, because 7 times 7 is 49. Out too.
So it should be the second one. Let's prove it. 12 squared is 144. For 35 squared: 3 times 4 is 12, then write 25. That is 1225.
What is 144 plus 1225?

ask.ifNot: Add the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds, carrying carefully.

beats.say: 144 plus 1225 is 1369. Now the right side: 37 thirties are 1110, and 37 sevens are 259. Together, 1369 as well!
Both sides are 1369. So the true one is 12 squared plus 35 squared equals 37 squared.
Last digits can knock out a false sum quickly. Then do the full working only for what is left.
Two equal fractions. 52 over 68 equals something over 153. We need the missing top number.
68 does not go neatly into 153, so we cannot jump straight across. Let's make 52 over 68 simpler first. What is the biggest number that divides both 52 and 68?

ask.ifNot: 2 works, but we can go bigger. Both 52 and 68 are in the 4 times table.

beats.say: 52 divided by 4 is 13, and 68 divided by 4 is 17. So 52 over 68 is 13 over 17.
Now 13 over 17 must equal something over 153. What was 17 multiplied by to make 153?

ask.ifNot: Try the 17 times table. 17 times 9 is 153.

beats.say: 17 times 9 is 153. So the top must be multiplied by 9 as well.
13 times 9. 10 times 9 is 90, and 3 times 9 is 27. Together that is 117.
So the missing number is 117.
Let's check. 117 and 153 both divide by 9, and that gives 13 over 17 again. It works.
If you cannot jump straight across, simplify first. Then multiply the top and the bottom by the same number.
The L C M of two numbers is 168 and their H C F is 7. One number is 56. We need the other number, and then its square.
Use the rule that links them: H C F times L C M equals the first number times the second number.

board.text: HCF × LCM = first number × second number

beats.say: So 7 times 168 equals 56 times the other number.
56 is 7 times 8. So the 7s cancel, and the other number is 168 divided by 8.
8 times 20 is 160, and one more 8 makes 168. So 168 divided by 8 is 21.
The other number is 21. Are we finished?

choices: No: the question wants its square
ask.ifNot: Read the question once more. It asks for the square of the other number, so there is one more step.

beats.say: 21 times 21. 21 times 20 is 420, and one more 21 makes 441.
Check the rule: 7 times 168 is 1176, and 56 times 21 is 1176 as well.
Two lessons here. The product rule finds the missing number. And always read to the end: this question wanted the square.

board.text: Sides become 5/4 and 3/5 of 30. Area difference = ?

beats.say: A square has a side of 30 centimetres. One side is stretched to 5 quarters of its length, and another is shrunk to 3 fifths. That makes a rectangle. How different are the two areas?
The square's area first. Side times side: 3 times 3 is 9, so 30 times 30 is 900 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 4 quarters make the whole. 5 quarters is one quarter more than the whole, so it is bigger than 30.

beats.say: Now the stretched side: 5 quarters of 30. Before we work it out, will it be bigger or smaller than 30?
It is bigger. One quarter of 30 is 30 divided by 4, which is 7.5. So 5 quarters is 5 times 7.5, which is 37.5 centimetres.
Now the shrunk side: 3 fifths of 30. One fifth of 30 is 6, so 3 fifths is 3 times 6, which is 18 centimetres.
The rectangle's area is 37.5 times 18. Here is a neat trick: double one number and halve the other, and the product stays the same. So it is 75 times 9.
75 times 9: 70 times 9 is 630, and 5 times 9 is 45. Together that is 675 square centimetres.

ask.ifNot: Difference means how much bigger one is than the other. So we take the smaller area away from the larger one.

beats.say: The square covers 900 and the rectangle covers 675. Which sum gives the difference?
900 take away 675 is 225. The difference is 225 square centimetres.
So: find each new side, then each area, then subtract. One side grew and one shrank, but the area did not stay the same.
Shraddha is facing East. She turns 135 degrees clockwise, and then 315 degrees anticlockwise. Which way is she facing at the end?
The compass has 8 points, spaced evenly round a full turn of 360 degrees. 360 divided by 8 is 45. So each step from one point to the next is 45 degrees.

ask.ifNot: Clockwise from East goes to South-East, then South, then South-West. Count all 3 steps.

beats.say: The first turn is 135 degrees, and 3 times 45 is 135. So it is 3 steps clockwise from East. Where does that take her?
South-East, South, South-West. After the first turn she is facing South-West.
Now the second turn: 315 degrees anticlockwise. That is a big one, nearly a full turn. How far short of a full turn is it? 360 take away 315 is 45.

ask.ifNot: She is turning anticlockwise and stops before she gets all the way back. So she is still 45 degrees on the clockwise side of South-West.

beats.say: A full turn would bring her right back to South-West. She stops 45 degrees short of that. So where does she end up, compared with South-West?
So turning 315 degrees anticlockwise ends in the same place as turning 45 degrees clockwise. And 1 step clockwise from South-West is West.
So Shraddha is facing West.
So take one turn at a time, in steps of 45 degrees. And for a very big turn, it is quicker to ask how far short of a full turn it is.
A fraction on each side this time. 4 x minus 5, over 5, equals 2 x plus 3, over 3. First we clear the bottoms.
Multiply both sides by 5 and by 3. On the left the 5 cancels and the 3 stays. On the right the 3 cancels and the 5 stays. That is cross multiplying.
Open the left bracket. The 3 multiplies the 4 x, and it multiplies the minus 5. What is 3 times minus 5?

ask.ifNot: 3 times 5 is 15, and the minus sign stays with it. So we get minus 15.

beats.say: So the left side is 12 x minus 15. On the right, 5 times 2 x is 10 x, and 5 times 3 is 15.
Take the smaller lot of x, 10 x, from both sides. 12 x take away 10 x leaves 2 x.
What clears the minus 15?

ask.ifNot: Adding undoes taking away. So we add 15, and we add it to both sides.

beats.say: Add 15 to both sides. 15 plus 15 is 30, so 2 x equals 30.
Divide both sides by 2. Half of 30 is 15. So x equals 15.
Check with 15. Left: 4 times 15, minus 5, is 55, and 55 over 5 is 11. Right: 2 times 15, plus 3, is 33, and 33 over 3 is 11. Both sides are 11.
With a fraction on each side: cross multiply, open the brackets, then solve it like any other equation.
Three boxes to fill with signs, so that the line comes to 16. We will test each set of signs.
First set: times, minus, divide. That would need 3 divided by 14, which is not a whole number. So it cannot land exactly on 16.
Second set: minus, divide, plus. Which part of this goes first?

ask.ifNot: Divide comes before plus and minus. So 6 divided by 3 goes first, though it sits in the middle.

beats.say: 6 divided by 3 is 2. Then 12 minus 2, plus 14, is 24. Not 16.
Third set: times, divide, plus. 12 times 6 is 72, divided by 3 is 24, and adding 14 gives 38. Not 16 either.
Fourth set: plus, times, minus. Times first: 6 times 3 is 18. Then 12 plus 18 is 30, and 30 minus 14 is 16. That is the one!
So the signs are plus, times, minus. Test every set, and each time do times and divide before plus and minus.
4250 rupees earns simple interest for 5 years, at 8 per cent per annum. We want the simple interest.

board.text: Rs.4250 for 5 years at 8% per annum

beats.say: 8 per cent per annum means every 100 rupees earns 8 rupees in a year. But 4250 is not a whole number of hundreds, so we go through 10 per cent.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.8 in 1 year

beats.say: 10 per cent of 4250 is 425. And 1 per cent is 42.5, so 2 per cent is double that: 85.
We have 10 per cent and 2 per cent. How do we make 8 per cent from them?

ask.ifNot: 8 is 2 less than 10. So 8 per cent is 10 per cent, with 2 per cent taken off.

beats.say: 425 minus 85 is 340. So one year earns 340 rupees.
Simple interest earns the same each year, for 5 years. 5 times 300 is 1500, and 5 times 40 is 200. Together, 1700.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. It gives 1700 as well.
So the simple interest is 1700 rupees.
So: the interest for one year first, then times the number of years. And an awkward per cent can be built from easy ones.
We want every one digit factor of 72, added together. A factor of 72 is a number that divides 72 exactly.
Test each one digit number, 1 to 9.

ask.ifNot: 9 times 8 is 72. So 9 is a factor, and so is its partner 8.

beats.say: Does 9 divide 72?
72 does not end in 0 or 5, so 5 is out. And 72 is not in the 7 times table, so 7 is out. Everything else divides 72.
Now add the ones left: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 9. Make it easy. 1 and 9 are 10, 2 and 8 are 10. That is 20.
Then 3, 4 and 6 make 13. And 20 plus 13 is 33.
So the sum is 33.
List, test, cross out, then add in friendly pairs that make 10.
A recipe with three steps: add, multiply, then look at the hundreds place of the answer.
The one digit odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Together they make 25.

ask.ifNot: 99 can be divided by 9, and 95 by 5. 97 cannot be divided by anything, so it is the one.

beats.say: And which is the greatest 2 digit prime?
So we need 25 times 97. 97 is 3 less than 100. 25 hundreds is 2500. Take away 25 threes, which is 75, and we get 2425.
Now the hundreds place of 2425. Units, tens, hundreds: the digit there is 4.
4 hundreds: 4 times 100 is 400.
So the place value of the hundreds digit is 400.
Careful with the last step: the question wants the place value, 400, and not just the digit 4.

spec.note: Area = 616 sq. cm

beats.say: A circle has an area of 616 square centimetres. Its circumference is the same as the perimeter of a square. We want the area of that square.

board.text: Area of circle = π × r × r, with π = 22/7

beats.say: It is a chain: the circle's area gives its radius, the radius gives the circumference, and that gives the square. The area of a circle is pi times the radius times the radius, and for pi we use 22 over 7.
So 22 over 7, times r times r, is 616. To undo that, divide by 22 and multiply by 7. 616 divided by 22 is 28, and 28 times 7 is 196.

ask.ifNot: We need a number that multiplies by itself to make 196, not half of 196. 14 times 14 is 196.

beats.say: r times r is 196. So what is r?
14 times 14 is 196, so the radius is 14 centimetres.
Now the circumference, the walk round the circle: 2 times pi times the radius. 14 divided by 7 is 2, so it is 2 times 22 times 2, which is 88 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 equal sides, and together they make 88. So one side is 88 shared into 4 equal parts.

beats.say: The square's perimeter is the same: 88 centimetres. How do we get one side of the square?
88 divided by 4 is 22. Each side of the square is 22 centimetres.
Last step: the square's area, side times side. 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44. Together that makes 484.
So the area of the square is 484 square centimetres.
A long chain, but each link is small: area to radius, radius to circumference, circumference to side, side to area. Write each link down before starting the next.
One gross of cricket balls costs 32,400 rupees. What will 85 cricket balls cost?
The word to unlock is gross. A dozen is 12, and a gross is a dozen dozens: 12 times 12, which is 144.
So 144 balls cost 32,400 rupees, and we want 85 balls. What do we find first?

ask.ifNot: 85 is not a neat number of dozens. So we go all the way down to 1 ball, and build up from there.

beats.say: One ball costs 32,400 divided by 144, which is 225 rupees. We can be sure by multiplying back: 144 times 225 is 32,400.
And how do we get the cost of 85 balls?

ask.ifNot: 85 balls, at 225 rupees each. 85 lots of 225 means multiply.

beats.say: Split the 85 into 80 and 5. 80 times 225 is 18,000. And 5 times 225 is 1125.
So 85 cricket balls cost 19,125 rupees.
Does it look right? 85 balls is a bit more than half a gross. And 19,125 rupees is a bit more than half of 32,400. Good.
So unlock the special word, find the cost of one, then find the cost of many.
We multiply all the one-digit odd numbers together, divide by 18, and want to know what is left over.
Which are the one-digit odd numbers?

ask.ifNot: One-digit numbers go up to 9. The odd ones among them are 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Don't leave out the 1 or the 9.

beats.say: Multiply them a step at a time. 1 times 3 times 5 is 15. Then 15 times 7 is 105. Then 105 times 9 is 945.
Now divide 945 by 18, in chunks. 18 times 50 is 900. That leaves 45.
18 times 2 is 36. That leaves 9. And 9 is smaller than 18, so we stop.
So 945 is 52 lots of 18, with 9 left over. The remainder is 9.
A neat sense check. 945 is odd, and any number of 18s is even. So the leftover has to be odd. That fits our 9.
For a remainder, take out the divisor in big easy chunks until what is left is smaller than the divisor.
We start with 80. Some per cent of 80 is added to it, and the sum must equal the square of 12. Which per cent?
First the target. The square of 12 is 12 times 12. 12 tens are 120, and 12 twos are 24. Together, 144.
We start at 80 and must reach 144. How do we find what has to be added?

ask.ifNot: We want the gap between where we are, 80, and where we must get to, 144. A gap is found by subtracting.

beats.say: 144 minus 80 is 64. So 64 must be added.
Careful: 64 is not the answer yet. The question asks what per cent of 80 that 64 is.
Use 10 per cent of 80, which is 8. How many 8s make 64? 8 times 8 is 64.
So 64 is 8 lots of 10 per cent. That is 80 per cent of 80.
Check: 80 per cent of 80 is 64, and 80 plus 64 is 144, the square of 12.
So: find the target, find the gap, then ask what per cent of the starting number the gap is.
An article is sold at a loss of 80 rupees. Had it been sold at 375 rupees, the profit would have been twice the loss. What was it really sold for?

board.text: Sold at a loss of Rs.80.
At Rs.375, the profit would be twice the loss.

beats.say: Everything here hangs on the cost price, the middle bar. The real sale is 80 rupees shorter than it. The sale at 375 is longer than it.
The profit would be twice the loss, and the loss is 80 rupees. So what would the profit be?

ask.ifNot: Twice means 2 times. 2 times 80 is 160.

beats.say: 2 times 80 is 160. So at 375 rupees, the profit would be 160 rupees.
A profit means 375 is above the cost price, by 160. So the cost price is 375 minus 160, which is 215 rupees.
Careful now. Is 215 our answer?

choices: No: take off the loss of 80
ask.ifNot: 215 rupees is the cost price. The article was really sold at a loss of 80, so the selling price is 80 below the cost price.

beats.say: 215 minus 80 is 135. So the article was sold for 135 rupees.
Check: from 135 up to 375 should be the loss and the profit together, 80 plus 160, which is 240. And 375 minus 135 is 240. It fits.
So find the cost price first. A profit sits above it, a loss sits below it.
28500 rupees amounts to 38760 rupees in 3 years, at simple interest. We want the rate of interest, as a per cent per annum.

board.text: Rs.28500 amounts to Rs.38760 in 3 years

beats.say: 38760 rupees is called the amount. It is the 28500 rupees that was put in, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 38760 minus 28500 is 10260. So the interest is 10260 rupees, for all 3 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 3. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 10260 divided by 3, which is 3420.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 28500 divided by 100 is 285, so the money is 285 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 285 hundreds earn 3420 rupees a year. 10 times 285 is 2850, and 2 times 285 is 570. Together that is 3420, so each hundred earns 12 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 12 rupees a year. That is a rate of 12 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 28500 times 12 times 3, divided by 100, is 10260. That is our interest.
So for the rate: amount minus principal gives the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
A train running at 108 kilometres per hour crosses a pole in 28 seconds. We want the length of the train.

board.text: Speed 108 km/hr, crosses a pole in 28 seconds

beats.say: While the train crosses the pole, from its front reaching the pole to its back end clearing it, how far does it travel?

ask.ifNot: The pole stands still while the whole train slides past. So the train moves forward by exactly one train length.

beats.say: So the length of the train is the distance it covers in 28 seconds. But the speed is per hour, and our time is in seconds. Let's change the speed into metres per second.
In 1 hour the train goes 108 kilometres. 1 kilometre is 1000 metres, so that is 108000 metres.
An hour has 60 minutes, and 108000 shared over 60 is 1800 metres each minute. A minute has 60 seconds, and 1800 shared over 60 is 30 metres each second.
Now the units match. 30 metres every second, for 28 seconds. What do we work out?

ask.ifNot: Every second adds another 30 metres, so 28 seconds means 28 lots of 30. And we use 30, the speed in metres per second, so that the units match.

beats.say: 3 times 28 is 84, so 30 times 28 is 840. The train is 840 metres long.
Check it. 840 metres, at 30 metres each second, takes 840 divided by 30, which is 28 seconds. That matches.
So when a train crosses a pole, the distance is the train's own length. Get the speed into metres per second, then multiply by the seconds.
How many three-digit numbers can be divided by 5, by 2 and by 8? Such a number is in all three tables.

board.text: 3-digit numbers divisible by 5, 2 and 8: how many?

beats.say: One of the three takes care of itself. 8 is 2 times 2 times 2, so anything in the 8 times table is already even. We only need 8 and 5.
Here is the 8 times table. Which is the first number in it that is also in the 5 times table?

ask.ifNot: A number in the 5 times table ends in 0 or 5. Look along the list: the first one that does is 40.

beats.say: 40 it is. So the L C M is 40, and we count three-digit multiples of 40.
The first three-digit one: 40 times 2 is 80, too small. 40 times 3 is 120.
The last one: 40 times 25 is 1000, which has four digits. One step back is 960, which is 40 times 24.
From number 3 in the table to number 24. How many numbers is that?

ask.ifNot: Out of 24 multiples, the first 2, which are 40 and 80, are too small. 24 take away 2 is 22.

beats.say: 24 minus 3, plus 1 for counting both ends, is 22.
Find the L C M, then its first and last multiple in the range. Subtract their places in the table, and add 1.
Two numbers. Add them and we get 92. Subtract them and we get 14. We want the square of the greater one.
Here is a neat trick: add the two lines together. What happens to the smaller number?

ask.ifNot: In the first line the smaller number is added. In the second it is taken away. Plus smaller and minus smaller cancel each other.

beats.say: So adding the lines leaves 2 lots of the greater number. And that equals 92 plus 14, which is 106.
Half of 106 is 53. So the greater number is 53.
Quick check. The smaller one is 92 minus 53, which is 39. And 53 minus 39 is 14. Good.
Is 53 our answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for the square of the greater number. Square means the number times itself.

beats.say: 53 times 53. Split it into two easier parts: 53 times 50 is 2650, and 53 times 3 is 159.
Add them: 2650 plus 159 is 2809. So 53 squared is 2809.
When you know a sum and a difference: add them and halve to get the greater number. Then do exactly what the question asks.

board.text: Clock at 9:33. Angle between the hands = ?

beats.say: The clock shows 9:33. We want the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand.
We measure how far each hand has turned from the 12 at the top, one hand at a time. The whole clock face is a full turn, 360 degrees.
The minute hand first. It goes all the way round, 360 degrees, in 60 minutes, so it turns 6 degrees every minute.
At 33 minutes it has turned 33 times 6. 30 times 6 is 180, and 3 times 6 is 18. Together, 198 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The hour hand never stops. 33 minutes is a little more than half an hour, so the hand is a little more than halfway from the 9 to the 10.

beats.say: Now the hour hand. At 9:33, where exactly is it pointing?
Take the 9 first. Each hour is 360 divided by 12, which is 30 degrees. So from the 12 round to the 9 is 9 times 30, which is 270 degrees.
Now the creep. The hour hand moves 30 degrees in 60 minutes, so half a degree each minute. In 33 minutes that is half of 33, which is 16.5 degrees.
So the hour hand is at 270 plus 16.5, which is 286.5 degrees.

ask.ifNot: The angle between the hands is the gap between their two positions, so we subtract. And we use 286.5, not 270, because the hour hand has moved past the 9.

beats.say: The hour hand is at 286.5 degrees and the minute hand is at 198 degrees. How do we get the angle between them?
To take away 198, take away 200 and then give 2 back. 286.5 take away 200 is 86.5, and 2 more makes 88.5.
The angle between the hands is 88.5 degrees.
So work the two hands separately: 6 degrees a minute for the minute hand, and 30 degrees an hour plus half a degree a minute for the hour hand. Then subtract.
A rectangle has an area of 468 square centimetres, and its breadth is 18 centimetres. We want its perimeter.

ask.ifNot: Area is length times breadth. So to get back from the area to the length, we divide by the breadth.

beats.say: For the perimeter we need both sides, and we only have the breadth. The area will give us the length. How?
We need 468 divided by 18: how many 18s make 468? Start with a big chunk. 20 lots of 18 make 360. That leaves 468 take away 360, which is 108.
And 6 lots of 18 make 108. So altogether that is 20 lots and 6 lots: 26. The length is 26 centimetres.

ask.ifNot: 26 plus 18 is only one length and one breadth, which is halfway round. We double it for the whole walk.

beats.say: Now the perimeter, the walk all the way round. Which sum gives it?
26 plus 18 is 44, and that is halfway. Double it: 2 times 44 is 88.

spec.note: Perimeter = 88 cm

beats.say: So the perimeter is 88 centimetres.
Check the length by multiplying back: 26 times 18 is 468, the area we were given.
So: divide the area by the side you know to find the other side, then add the two sides and double.
We add up every two-digit odd number that is less than 40. First we need to know where the list starts and stops.

board.text: Sum of all two-digit odd numbers less than 40

beats.say: Which is the first number in our list?

ask.ifNot: It must have two digits and be odd. 10 is even, so the first one is 11.

beats.say: The first is 11, and the last odd number below 40 is 39. They go up in 2s.
How many numbers is that? From 11 up to 39 is a climb of 28. In jumps of 2, that is 14 jumps.
14 jumps. So how many numbers?

ask.ifNot: 1 jump joins 2 numbers. 2 jumps join 3 numbers. There is always 1 more number than jumps.

beats.say: 15 numbers. Now pair them from the outside in. 11 plus 39 is 50. 13 plus 37 is 50 as well.
Every pair makes 50. 15 numbers give 7 pairs, with one number left alone in the middle. That middle number is 25. 7 pairs of 50 is 350.

board.text: 7 pairs, and 25 alone in the middle

beats.say: We have 350 from the pairs. What must we still add?

ask.ifNot: 15 is an odd count, so one number has no partner. It is the middle one, 25, and it still has to be added.

beats.say: 350 plus 25 is 375. So the sum is 375.
A neat check: the average of an evenly spaced list is its middle number, 25. And 15 lots of 25 is 375.
Find the first and last, count the numbers, pair the ends, and don't forget a middle one left on its own.
Three fractions: three quarters, 5 over 6 and 4 over 5. We want the greatest, the smallest, and the difference between those two.
Look closely. Each one is exactly one piece short of a whole.
The greatest fraction is missing the smallest piece. Which piece is the smallest?

ask.ifNot: The more pieces a bar is cut into, the smaller each piece is. Sixths are the smallest pieces here.

beats.say: So 5 over 6 is the greatest, because it is missing only a sixth. And three quarters is the smallest, because it is missing the biggest piece.
Now the difference: 5 over 6 take away three quarters. Sixths and quarters are different sizes. What is the smallest number that 6 and 4 both go into?

ask.ifNot: 24 works, but there is a smaller one. 6 times 2 is 12, and 4 times 3 is 12.

beats.say: In twelfths: 5 over 6 is 10 over 12, and three quarters is 9 over 12.
10 twelfths take away 9 twelfths is 1 twelfth. So the difference is 1 over 12.
Put them in order first, then subtract. And to subtract fractions, always make the pieces the same size.
Two hunts and then an addition: the 12th even number after 99, and the 18th even number before 99.
Start with the even numbers after 99. The first one is 100, and they go up in jumps of 2.

ask.ifNot: The 1st needs no jump at all. So the 12th needs one fewer than 12, which is 11 jumps.

beats.say: 100 is the 1st. How many jumps of 2 take us to the 12th?
11 jumps of 2 is 22. And 100 plus 22 is 122.
Now go backwards from 99. The first even number before it is 98. For the 18th we need 17 jumps back.
17 jumps of 2 is 34. And 98 minus 34 is 64.
Add the two: 122 plus 64 is 186.
So the sum is 186. The 1st one costs no jumps, so always use one fewer jump than the position.
Two numbers have L C M 672 and H C F 12. One of them is 84. Let's track down the other one.
The key is the product rule. H C F times L C M equals the first number times the second number.

board.text: HCF × LCM = first number × second number

beats.say: So 12 times 672 equals 84 times the other number.
The H C F always divides both numbers. So how many 12s are in 84?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 7 is 84. You can count up in 12s to see it land there.

beats.say: 84 is 12 times 7. So the 12s cancel, and the other number is 672 divided by 7.
7 times 90 is 630, which leaves 42. And 7 times 6 is 42. So 90 plus 6 makes 96.
So the other number is 96.
Check with the rule: 12 times 672 is 8064, and 84 times 96 is 8064 as well.
Product rule, then cancel the H C F before you multiply. The numbers stay small and the answer drops out.
p is 7, and q is built from p. Then there are four expressions, and we want the one with the greatest value.
First q. It is 2 p minus 9. What is 2 p when p is 7?

ask.ifNot: A number next to a letter means times. 2 p is 2 times 7, which is 14.

beats.say: So q is 14 minus 9, which is 5.
Now the first expression. 2 p is 14 and 3 q is 15. 14 minus 15 dips 1 below zero, and plus 5 brings us up to 4.
The second. 4 q is 20 and 2 p is 14. 20 minus 14 is 6.
The third. 7 plus 5 is 12, and 12 minus 12 is 0.
The last one. 7 q is 35, and 5 p is also 35. They cancel each other, and 3 is left.
The four values are 4, 6, 0 and 3. Which expression wins?

ask.ifNot: The greatest of 4, 6, 0 and 3 is 6. And 6 came from 4 q minus 2 p.

beats.say: So 4 q minus 2 p has the greatest value, 6.
Find the missing letter first, work out each expression carefully, and only then compare.
Three fractions in a chain, all equal: 12 over 52, y over 13, and m over 39. We want m take away y.
Start with y. From 52 down to 13, the bottom got smaller. What was 52 divided by?

ask.ifNot: 13 times 4 is 52. So going from 52 down to 13, the bottom was divided by 4.

beats.say: 52 divided by 4 is 13. So the top is divided by 4 as well: 12 divided by 4 is 3.
So y is 3.
Now m. Use the simple fraction, 3 over 13. From 13 up to 39, what was the bottom multiplied by?

ask.ifNot: 13 times 3 is 39. So the bottom was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: 13 times 3 is 39, so the top is multiplied by 3 too. 3 times 3 is 9. So m is 9.
Careful: the question wants m take away y, not just m. 9 take away 3 is 6.
Check the chain: 12 over 52, 3 over 13 and 9 over 39 are all the same amount.
In a chain of equal fractions, move from one to the next by multiplying or dividing the top and the bottom by the same number.
Four decimals, with minus and plus signs mixed together.
Going left to right, we would start by taking 14.659 from 2.007, and dip below zero. There is a friendlier way. Which two numbers are being taken away?

ask.ifNot: Each number owns the sign in front of it. The minus signs sit in front of 14.659 and 2.042.

beats.say: So gather them into two teams. The ones we add, and the ones we take away.
The adding team: 2.007 plus 16.317 is 18.324.
The taking-away team: 14.659 plus 2.042 is 16.701.
Now one subtraction. 18.324 minus 16 is 2.324, and taking away the other 0.701 leaves 1.623.
A rough check with whole numbers: 2 minus 15, plus 16, minus 2 is 1. Our answer is a bit more than 1. Good.
When plus and minus are mixed, add up everything with a plus, add up everything with a minus, and subtract once.
Here is a line with two per cents and a hidden number, M. We want M.
First we turn each per cent into a plain number. Start on the left, with 6.5 per cent of 800.
1 per cent of 800 is 8. So 6 per cent is 6 times 8, which is 48. And half a per cent is half of 8, which is 4.
6.5 per cent is 6 per cent and half a per cent together. 48 plus 4 is 52.
Now 8 per cent of 250. 1 per cent of 250 is 2.5, and 8 times 2.5 is 20.
So the line now says: 52 equals 20 plus M. Here it is on a balance.
20 plus M makes 52. How do we find M?

ask.ifNot: 20 and M together make 52. Take the 20 away from the 52, and what is left is M.

beats.say: 52 minus 20 is 32. So M is 32.
Check: 20 plus 32 is 52, and 52 is 6.5 per cent of 800. Both sides balance.
So with a line like this, turn each per cent into a plain number first. Then it is a simple missing number sum.
We add 97 to one of these numbers and get a square number. Let's add 97 to each and see.
Adding 97 is nearly adding 100: add 100, then take 3 back. 852 plus 97 is 949. 768 plus 97 is 865.
489 plus 97 is 586. And 927 plus 97 is 1024.
Which total is a square? Start with 949. 30 times 30 is 900, and 31 times 31 is 961. Is 949 a square?

choices: no, it is in the gap
ask.ifNot: 900 and 961 are squares next door to each other. A number between them cannot be a square.

beats.say: 949 is out. Next, 865. 29 times 29 is 841, and the next square is 900. 865 is in that gap, so it is out too.
586. 24 times 24 is 576, and 25 times 25 is 625. In a gap again.
That leaves 1024. We know 31 times 31 is 961. What is the next square, 32 times 32?

ask.ifNot: To step to the next square, add the two numbers: 961 plus 31 plus 32.

beats.say: 961 plus 31 plus 32 is 1024. So 1024 is 32 times 32. A square!
So 97 must be added to 927.
Try each choice, then test the total by trapping it between squares you know.
The series starts 7, 11, 15, 19. We want the sum of its first 8 terms.
What is the jump from each number to the next?

ask.ifNot: 11 minus 7 is 4. 15 minus 11 is 4. 19 minus 15 is 4.

beats.say: Plus 4 each time. We need 8 terms and have only 4, so keep adding 4: 23, 27, 31, 35.
Adding 8 numbers one by one is slow. Try pairing the ends instead. First and last: 7 plus 35 is 42. Next pair in: 11 plus 31 is 42 too.
15 with 27, and 19 with 23, also make 42. So how many pairs of 42 do we have?

ask.ifNot: There are 8 numbers, with 2 in each pair. 8 divided by 2 is 4 pairs.

beats.say: 4 pairs of 42. 4 times 42 is 168. So the sum is 168.
Check it in two halves. The first four add up to 52, the last four add up to 116, and 52 plus 116 is 168.
To add evenly spaced numbers, pair the ends. Every pair gives the same total, so one multiplication finishes the job.
A bracket in the middle and a little chain of times and divide on the end.
Where do we start?

ask.ifNot: Brackets come before everything else. So we work out the inside of the bracket first.

beats.say: Inside the bracket, times and divide go before the plus. 20 times 7 is 140. 150 divided by 3 is 50.
140 plus 50 is 190. So the whole bracket is worth 190.
The bracket is gone. What comes next?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide still come before plus and minus. So the 8 times 2 divided by 8 at the end is next.

beats.say: 8 times 2 is 16, and 16 divided by 8 is 2. Times 8 and divide by 8 undo each other, so only the 2 is left.
Now left to right. 200 minus 190 is 10, and 10 plus 2 is 12.
Bracket first. Then times and divide. Then plus and minus, from left to right.
An article sold for 78 rupees makes a loss of 35 per cent. We want the selling price that would give a profit of 15 per cent.

board.text: Sold for Rs.78: a loss of 35%.

beats.say: The bridge between the two sales is the cost price. Call the cost price 100 per cent.
With a loss of 35 per cent, the 78 rupees is what per cent of the cost price?

ask.ifNot: A loss takes 35 per cent away from the cost price. 100 minus 35 leaves 65 per cent.

beats.say: 100 minus 35 is 65. Careful: 78 rupees is not the 35 per cent. It is the 65 per cent that is left.
Here is a neat stepping stone. 65 per cent is 13 lots of 5 per cent. And 78 divided by 13 is 6. So 5 per cent of the cost price is 6 rupees.
The cost price is 100 per cent, which is 20 lots of 5 per cent. 20 times 6 is 120 rupees.
Now the new sale. A profit of 15 per cent is 3 lots of 5 per cent. 3 times 6 is 18 rupees.
The cost price is 120 and the profit is 18. What is the new selling price?

ask.ifNot: The profit is added on top of the cost price, 120, not on top of the old selling price.

beats.say: 120 plus 18 is 138. So it should be sold for 138 rupees.
Check the first sale. 35 per cent is 7 lots of 5 per cent, 7 times 6 is 42, and 120 minus 42 is 78. It fits.
So to move from a loss sale to a profit sale, go back to the cost price first. Then build the new selling price from it.
15 men can do a job in 28 days. If it must be done in 20 days, how many more men are needed?

board.text: 15 men do the work in 28 days
To finish in 20 days: how many MORE men?

beats.say: Read the last words slowly: how many more men. Not how many men in all. Let's underline that, so we don't forget.
First, how big is the whole job? 15 men, each working 28 days. How do we count the days of work?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 15 men puts in 28 days. So the whole job is 15 lots of 28 days of work.

beats.say: 10 times 28 is 280, and 5 times 28 is 140. Together, 420. The whole job is 420 days of work for one man.
Now those 420 days of work must fit into 20 days. 420 divided by 20 is 21. So 21 men are needed.
Is 21 our answer?

ask.ifNot: The question asks how many more men. 15 are already there, so we want only the extra ones: 21 minus 15.

beats.say: 21 minus 15 is 6.
So 6 more men are needed.
Check. 21 men for 20 days is 420 days of work, the same as 15 men for 28 days. The job matches.
Two things to keep. Fewer days needs more men. And answer the question that was asked: here, the extra men, not the total.
We want to earn 280 rupees of simple interest every month. The rate is 15 per cent per annum. How much must we invest?

board.text: Interest Rs.280 every month at 15% per annum

beats.say: The interest is given per month, but the rate is per annum, per year. What must we do first?

ask.ifNot: The rate, 15 per cent, is for a whole year. So the interest must be for a whole year too: 12 months of 280 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, that is the trap in this question. A year has 12 months, so we need 12 times 280. 10 times 280 is 2800, and 2 times 280 is 560. Together, 3360.
So in one year the interest is 3360 rupees. And that is 15 per cent of the money invested.
15 per cent is 3 lots of 5 per cent. So 5 per cent is 3360 divided by 3, which is 1120.
The whole is 100 per cent, which is 20 lots of 5 per cent. 20 times 1120 is 22400. So we must invest 22400 rupees.
Check: 10 per cent of 22400 is 2240, and 5 per cent is 1120. Together that is 3360 a year. Shared over 12 months, it is 280 a month.
So match the time to the rate first: monthly interest becomes yearly interest. Then build from the known per cent up to 100 per cent.
We need to cover 432 kilometres, travelling at 24 metres per second. How much time will that take?
Look at the units before anything else. The distance is in kilometres, but the speed is in metres per second. What should we do first?

ask.ifNot: 432 divided by 24 would mix kilometres with metres, and the answer would mean nothing. First we make the units match.

beats.say: The choices are in hours, so let's turn the speed into kilometres per hour. That means: how far does it go in one hour? 1 hour is 60 times 60 seconds, which is 3600.
Each second it goes 24 metres, so we need 24 times 3600. 20 times 36 is 720, 4 times 36 is 144, and together 864. With the two zeros, 86400 metres.
1000 metres make 1 kilometre, so 86400 metres is 86.4 kilometres. The speed is 86.4 kilometres per hour.
Now both are in kilometres and hours. Each hour covers 86.4 kilometres, and we have 432 to go. Have a guess: roughly how many hours?

ask.ifNot: Round both numbers to something friendly, and see how many of the smaller one fit into the bigger one. Then we test the guess by multiplying.

beats.say: Let's test 5. 80 times 5 is 400, and 6.4 times 5 is 32. Together, 432. Exactly right.
So the journey takes 5 hours.
Now the choices: 4 hours 40 minutes, 5.5 hours, and 4 hours. 5 hours is not there, so the right choice is none of these.
So: match the units first, then time is distance divided by speed. And trust careful working, even when the answer is not on the list.
Here is what we know: 4 x, plus 3, equals 22. Here is what we want: 12 x, plus 3. Let's see how to get from one to the other.
Start with the fact. How do we get the 4 x on its own?

ask.ifNot: The 4 x has a plus 3 with it. To undo plus 3 we do the opposite, and we do it to both sides.

beats.say: To undo plus 3 we take away 3, on both sides. 22 minus 3 is 19. So 4 x equals 19.
We could divide by 4 now to find x. But look at what we need: 12 x. How is 12 x related to 4 x?

ask.ifNot: 12 is 3 times 4. So 12 x is 3 lots of 4 x. We do not even need to find x.

beats.say: So 12 x is 3 times 19, which is 57.
Do not stop there! The question wants 12 x, plus 3. 57 plus 3 is 60.
We can check by finding x after all. 4 x is 19, so x is 19 divided by 4, which is 4.75. And 12 times 4.75, plus 3, gives 60 again.
The plan: find 4 x first, scale it up to 12 x, then finish with the plus 3. No need for x on its own.
Our angle is 58 degrees. It has two partners: a complementary angle and a supplementary angle. We want the two partners added together.

ask.ifNot: A right angle is a quarter turn, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. 180 is for a straight line, which comes next.

beats.say: Take the complementary angle first. It fits with 58 degrees inside a square corner, a right angle. So what do the two of them make together?
A right angle is 90 degrees. So the complementary angle is 90 take away 58.
Let's take 58 away in two easy hops. First the 50: 90 take away 50 leaves 40.
Now the 8 that is left: 40 take away 8 leaves 32. So 90 minus 58 is 32.
Now the supplementary angle. It fits with 58 degrees on a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn: 180 degrees. So it is 180 take away 58.
Let's take 58 away in two easy hops. First the 50: 180 take away 50 leaves 130.
Now the 8 that is left: 130 take away 8 leaves 122. So 180 minus 58 is 122.

ask.ifNot: The question asks for the sum, and sum means add. So we add the two partner angles: 32 and 122.

beats.say: The complement is 32 degrees and the supplement is 122 degrees. What does the question want us to do with them?
32 plus 122 is 154. The sum is 154 degrees.
So: complement from 90, supplement from 180, and then read the question again to see what it wants. Here it wanted the two added together.
Two jobs here. Multiply 7.2 by 3.9, then see how much more that is than the smallest 2-digit prime number.
First the product. Forget the points for a moment and do 72 times 39. 72 times 40 is 2880, and one 72 less is 2808.
Now put the point back. 7.2 and 3.9 have one decimal place each. How many decimal places does the product have?

ask.ifNot: One decimal place in each number makes two altogether. So the product has two decimal places.

beats.say: So 2808 becomes 28.08. That feels right, because 7 times 4 is 28.
Next, what is the smallest 2-digit prime number?

ask.ifNot: 10 is the smallest 2-digit number, but it divides by 2 and by 5, so it is not prime. The next one, 11, divides only by 1 and itself.

beats.say: It is 11. And 28.08 minus 11 is 17.08.
To multiply decimals, multiply as whole numbers, then count the decimal places to put the point back.
Four statements, and only one is correct. We work out each left side ourselves and compare.
The first. 7 squared is 49 and 11 squared is 121. 49 plus 121 is 170, not 150.
The second. 9 squared is 81 and 16 squared is 256. 81 plus 256 is 337, not 327. So close! Only the tens digit is off.
The third. 19 squared is 361, and 27 squared is 729. What is 361 plus 729?

ask.ifNot: Add the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds, and watch the carry. It comes to 1090, not 1190.

beats.say: 361 plus 729 is 1090. The statement says 1190, so that one is out as well.
Three are out, so it should be the last one. But we prove it. 18 squared: 18 tens are 180 and 18 eights are 144, so 324.
23 squared: 23 twenties are 460 and 23 threes are 69, so 529. What is 324 plus 529?

ask.ifNot: Add the ones first and carry into the tens. Then the tens, then the hundreds.

beats.say: 324 plus 529 is 853. That matches! 18 squared plus 23 squared is 853.
To check a statement, work out the left side yourself and compare. Near misses, like 337 and 327, are the ones to watch.
This series goes down: 197, 193, 185, 173, 157. We want the 8th term.
From 197 to 193 it drops 4. What is the drop from 193 to 185?

ask.ifNot: 193 minus 185 is 8. So this drop is 8, not 4 again.

beats.say: It drops 8. Then from 185 to 173 it drops 12, and from 173 to 157 it drops 16.
The drops are 4, 8, 12, 16. What is happening to them?

ask.ifNot: 4 to 8 looks like doubling, but 8 to 12 is not double. Each drop is 4 more than the one before: it is the 4 times table.

beats.say: Each drop is 4 bigger than the last. So the next drops are 20, 24 and 28.
The 6th term: 157 minus 20 is 137. The 7th term: 137 minus 24 is 113.
And the 8th term: what is 113 minus 28?

ask.ifNot: Take away 28 in two steps: the 2 tens first, then the 8 ones.

beats.say: 113 minus 28 is 85. So the 8th term is 85.
Here is the whole list. Count along it: 8 terms, ending on 85.
113 is among the choices, but it is only the 7th term. When the drops change, find the pattern in the drops. The 8th term is 85.
Two three-digit numbers, one ending in 7 and one ending in 6. Stars hide the rest. Which choice can be their product?
Start with what we can see: the last digits, 7 and 6. What must the product end in?

ask.ifNot: Multiply the two last digits, 7 and 6, and look at the digit that answer ends in. That is the last digit of the product.

beats.say: 7 times 6 is 42, so the product ends in 2. That removes 457647, which ends in 7.
Three are left, all ending in 2. So test the size. The smallest numbers that fit are 107 and 106, and 107 times 106 is 11342.
11332 is just below that. So close, but too small. Out.
The biggest numbers that fit are 997 and 996, and 997 times 996 is 993012. So 994312 is just too big. Out.
Only 353362 is left. And it does work: 547 times 646 is 353362.
Notice how close the decoys were to the limits. Work out the smallest and the biggest exactly, and you cannot be tricked.

board.text: Rectangle ABCD: 4 times the area. Sides = ?

beats.say: Square P Q R S has an area of 196 square centimetres. Rectangle A B C D has an area 4 times as big. We have to pick the sides the rectangle could have.

ask.ifNot: 4 times as big means multiply by 4. Adding 4 would only make it 4 square centimetres bigger.

beats.say: First, the rectangle's area. Which sum gives it?
4 times 196. 196 is 4 less than 200, so do 4 times 200, which is 800, and take away 4 times 4, which is 16. That leaves 784.
So the two sides of the rectangle must multiply to make 784. Here is a quick test: 784 ends in a 4, so the last digits of the two sides must multiply to give something ending in 4.
Try 52 and 18. 2 times 8 is 16, which ends in 6. Out. Try 28 and 36. 8 times 6 is 48, which ends in 8. Out as well.
That leaves 44 and 16, and 56 and 14. Work out the first. 44 times 10 is 440, and 44 times 6 is 264. Together 704. Not 784.
Now 56 and 14. 56 times 10 is 560, and 56 times 4 is 224. Together 784. That is the one.
So the sides of the rectangle can be 56 centimetres and 14 centimetres.
And here is why it works so neatly. 14 times 14 is 196, so the square's side is 14. Put 4 of those squares in a row, and you get a rectangle 56 long and 14 tall.
So: find the area you need, then test the pairs. Checking the last digit first saves a lot of multiplying.
This line is not true yet. One pair of brackets, in the right place, makes it equal 19.
As it stands: 192 divided by 12 is 16, times 3 is 48, and then minus 4 plus 13 gives 57. Far too big.
Think backwards from 19. If the plus 13 comes last, then just before it we had 6. So 192 divided by something is 6. Divided by what?

ask.ifNot: Try 6 times 32. It comes to exactly 192. So 192 divided by 32 is 6.

beats.say: We need to divide by 32. Can we build 32 from the 12, the 3 and the 4? 12 times 3 is 36, and 36 minus 4 is 32. Yes!
So the brackets go round 12 times 3 minus 4. Brackets first gives 32, and 192 divided by 32 is 6.
And 6 plus 13 is 19. The line is true now.
The shorter bracket, round 12 times 3 only, would mean dividing 192 by 36, and that does not come out whole. The longer one is needed.
To place brackets, work backwards from the answer, and build the number you need from the ones that are there.
Three letters, but only a is given. b is built from a, and c is built from b. So we find them in that order.
b first. a minus 1 is 17 minus 1, which is 16. Half of 16 is 8. So b is 8.
Then c is b plus 3. 8 plus 3 is 11.
Now the squares. What does a squared mean, when a is 17?

ask.ifNot: Squared means the number times itself. So 17 squared is 17 times 17, not 17 times 2.

beats.say: 17 times 17 is 289. 11 times 11 is 121. And 8 times 8 is 64.
So we have 289, minus 121, plus 64. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Plus and minus are done from left to right. Adding 121 and 64 first would take away too much.

beats.say: 289 minus 121 is 168. Then 168 plus 64 is 232.
So: find the letters in order, square each one, then work from left to right. The answer is 232.
16000 rupees is invested for 18 months, at 8 per cent per annum. We want the simple interest.

board.text: Rs.16000 for 18 months at 8% per annum

beats.say: Per annum means every year. 8 per cent means every 100 rupees earns 8 rupees in one year. And 16000 is 160 hundreds.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.8 in 1 year

beats.say: So one year earns 160 times 8. 16 times 8 is 128, so 160 times 8 is 1280 rupees.
The rate is for a year, but the money is invested for 18 months. How long is 18 months?

ask.ifNot: A year has 12 months. 18 months is 12 months and 6 more. That is 1 year, and half a year.
