How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 3 equal sides together make 23.1. To get back to one side, we share 23.1 equally among 3, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 23.1 by 3, split it into 21 and 2.1. 21 divided by 3 is 7, and 2.1 divided by 3 is 0.7.
7 plus 0.7 is 7.7. Each side is 7.7 centimetres.
Don't drop the decimal part. A side of just 7 would give a perimeter of only 21, and ours is 23.1.
Check: 3 sides of 7.7 make 23.1. That is the perimeter we were given.
The rule to keep: count the equal sides, then divide the perimeter by that number.
An isosceles triangle with a perimeter of 26 centimetres. Each of its two equal sides is 8 centimetres, and we want the third side.

board.text: Equal sides 8 cm each. Third side = ?

beats.say: Isosceles means two sides are equal, and congruent is just another word for equal. So the sides are 8, 8, and one we do not know yet.
What should we work out first?

ask.ifNot: There are two equal sides, and both are part of the perimeter. So first find how much the two of them make together.

beats.say: 8 plus 8 is 16. That is how much of the perimeter the two equal sides use up.
The rest belongs to the third side. 26 minus 16 is 10 centimetres.
The trap is taking away only one 8. That gives 18, but there are two equal sides to take off, not one.
Check by adding all three sides. 8 plus 8 plus 10 is 26. It matches the perimeter.
The plan to keep: perimeter, minus all the sides you already know, leaves the side you want.
Here is a square, and each side is 4.6 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.
How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 4.6 centimetres, 4 times over. A quicker way to write that is 4 times 4.6.
To multiply, split 4.6 into 4 and 0.6. 4 times 4 is 16, and 4 times 0.6 is 2.4.
Put the two pieces together. 16 plus 2.4 is 18.4, so the perimeter is 18.4 centimetres.
Now look at the units. A perimeter is a length, so it stays in centimetres. Square centimetres are for area, and nothing here was changed to millimetres.
Check by sharing it back out. 18.4 divided by 4 is 4.6, the side we started with.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
This is an equilateral triangle with every side 5.4 centimetres long. The perimeter is how far it is all the way round.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, each side 5.4 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 5.4 centimetres, 3 times over. A quicker way to write that is 3 times 5.4.
To multiply, split 5.4 into 5 and 0.4. 3 times 5 is 15, and 3 times 0.4 is 1.2.
Put the two pieces together. 15 plus 1.2 is 16.2, so the perimeter is 16.2 centimetres.
Two things to watch. A triangle has 3 sides, not 4. And a perimeter is a length, so it is in centimetres, not square centimetres.
Let's check. Share 16.2 equally among the 3 sides, and each one gets 5.4. That is our side.
So for any shape with equal sides, the perimeter is the number of sides times one side.
A square has a perimeter of 24.4 centimetres. We want the length of one side.
The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 24.4?

ask.ifNot: A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are the same length.

beats.say: So 4 equal sides, put end to end, make 24.4 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides together make 24.4. To get back to one side, we share 24.4 equally among 4, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 24.4 by 4, split it into 24 and 0.4. 24 divided by 4 is 6, and 0.4 divided by 4 is 0.1.
6 plus 0.1 is 6.1. Each side is 6.1 centimetres.
Now the units. The perimeter was in centimetres, so the side is in centimetres too. Not millimetres, and not square units, which are for area.
Let's check by going back round. 4 times 6.1 is 24.4, the perimeter. It works.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 48 centimetres and a length of 14 centimetres. We need its breadth.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 48 cm, length 14 cm. Breadth = ?

beats.say: Walk round a rectangle and you pass a length, a breadth, another length and another breadth. So the perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths.
So what does half of the perimeter give us?

ask.ifNot: Half of the walk round takes you along one length and one breadth. So half the perimeter is length plus breadth.

beats.say: Half of 48 is 24. So the length and the breadth together make 24.
The length is 14. So the breadth is 24 minus 14, which is 10 centimetres.
Here is the trap. Take both lengths off the 48 and you get 20. But that is two breadths, so it still has to be halved. And keep the unit: centimetres, like the question.
Check: 14 plus 10 is 24, and twice 24 is 48. It matches the perimeter.
So to find a missing side of a rectangle, halve the perimeter, then take away the side you know.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 72 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 72 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 72?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides, put end to end, make 72 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 6 equal sides together make 72. To get back to one side, we share 72 equally among 6, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: 72 divided by 6. Well, 6 times 12 is 72, so each side is 12 centimetres.
Careful with the 6 times table. 6 times 10 is 60, and 2 more sixes take us up to 72. So each side is 12.
Check: 6 sides of 12 make 72. That is the perimeter we were given.
So when all the sides are equal, one side is the perimeter divided by the number of sides.
A square with a perimeter of 36 centimetres. We want its area.
Area needs the side, and all we have is the perimeter. So this takes two steps: first the side, then the area.
A square has 4 equal sides. How do we get one side from the perimeter?

ask.ifNot: The 4 equal sides add up to the perimeter. So one side is the perimeter shared among 4.

beats.say: 36 divided by 4 is 9. Each side is 9 centimetres.
Now for the area of the square. Which sum is it?

ask.ifNot: Area counts the little squares inside: 9 rows, with 9 in each row. That is side times side. 4 times the side only takes us back to the perimeter.

beats.say: 9 times 9 is 81. The area is 81 square centimetres.
Careful not to do something quick with the 36, like doubling it. The area always comes from the side, and 9 times 9 is exactly 81.
Check the first step: 4 sides of 9 make 36, the perimeter we were given.
So from perimeter to area in a square: divide by 4 for the side, then multiply the side by itself.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 40 centimetres, and its length is 8 centimetres more than its breadth. We want the area, so first we need both sides.

board.text: Rectangle: perimeter 40 cm, length = breadth + 8 cm

beats.say: Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 40 is 20.
The length is a breadth with 8 extra. If we take that extra 8 away from the 20, what is left?

ask.ifNot: Without its extra 8, the length is exactly as long as the breadth. So what is left is one breadth, and another breadth.

beats.say: 20 minus 8 is 12, and that is two breadths.
So one breadth is half of 12, which is 6. And the length is 6 plus 8, which is 14.
Now the area, which is length times breadth. 14 times 6 is 84 square centimetres.
Careful not to multiply the numbers in the question. 40 is a perimeter and 8 is a difference, so 40 times 8 means nothing here. We need the two sides first.
Check: 14 plus 6 is 20, and twice 20 is 40. And 14 is 8 more than 6. Both clues fit.
So: halve the perimeter, take off the extra, and halve again for the shorter side. Then it is length times breadth.
A square with an area of 676 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 676.
Let's get close first. 25 times 25 is 625. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 625 is smaller than 676. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 25.

beats.say: 676 ends in 6, and 6 times 6 ends in 6. So let's try 26. 26 times 26 is 676, so the side is 26 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 26, so it is 4 times 26.

beats.say: 4 times 26 is 104. The perimeter is 104 centimetres.
Mind the units. Area is in square centimetres, but a perimeter is a length. So the answer is 104 centimetres, plain centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 104 divided by 4 is 26, and 26 times 26 is 676, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
The length of this rectangle is twice its breadth, and the perimeter is 78 centimetres. We need the length and the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 2 parts, because it is 2 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 3 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 3 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 2 plus 1 plus 2 plus 1 is 6 parts. And those 6 parts together are the whole perimeter, 78 centimetres.
So one part is 78 divided by 6, which is 13. That is the breadth: 13 centimetres.
The length is 2 parts. 2 times 13 is 26 centimetres.
The trap is to share 78 among 3 parts only. That makes both sides twice too big, because we pass every side twice on the way round.
Check: 26 plus 13 is 39, and twice 39 is 78. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
So when one side is so many times the other, count the parts all the way round, find one part, and build the sides from it.
An equilateral triangle has a perimeter of 29.1 centimetres. We want the length of one side.

board.text: Equilateral triangle, perimeter 29.1 cm. Each side = ?

beats.say: The perimeter is all the sides added together. How many equal sides share this 29.1?

ask.ifNot: Equilateral means all the sides are equal, and a triangle has 3 sides.

beats.say: So 3 equal sides, put end to end, make 29.1 centimetres.
How do we get back to just one side?

ask.ifNot: The 3 equal sides together make 29.1. To get back to one side, we share 29.1 equally among 3, and sharing is dividing.

beats.say: To divide 29.1 by 3, split it into 27 and 2.1. 27 divided by 3 is 9, and 2.1 divided by 3 is 0.7.
9 plus 0.7 is 9.7. Each side is 9.7 centimetres.
Careful with the whole part. 3 times 9 is 27, so the side starts with 9, not with 8 or 7.
Let's check by going back round. 3 times 9.7 is 29.1, the perimeter. It works.
The rule to keep: count the equal sides, then divide the perimeter by that number.
A regular hexagon has a perimeter of 42 centimetres. We want the total of just 5 of its sides.

board.text: Regular hexagon, perimeter 42 cm. Sum of 5 sides = ?

beats.say: First, how many equal sides does a regular hexagon have?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So 6 equal sides make 42. One side is 42 divided by 6, which is 7 centimetres.
We want 5 of the sides, not all 6. What is the quickest way to get that?

ask.ifNot: 5 sides is all 6 sides with one side left out. So we can take one side, 7, away from the whole perimeter.

beats.say: 42 minus 7 is 35. The 5 sides add up to 35 centimetres.
We can also multiply. 5 sides of 7 centimetres is 35. Two ways, one answer.
The trap is dividing 42 by 5. The 42 belongs to all 6 sides, so we must find one side first.
So with a regular shape, always find one side first. After that you can build any number of sides you like.
Here is a regular hexagon, and each side is 6.1 centimetres. We want the perimeter, the distance all the way round.

board.text: Regular hexagon, each side 6.1 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: How many equal sides does it have?

ask.ifNot: Hex means 6. A hexagon has 6 sides, and regular means they are all the same length.

beats.say: So going round, we walk 6.1 centimetres, 6 times over. A quicker way to write that is 6 times 6.1.
To multiply, split 6.1 into 6 and 0.1. 6 times 6 is 36, and 6 times 0.1 is 0.6.
Put the two pieces together. 36 plus 0.6 is 36.6, so the perimeter is 36.6 centimetres.
Don't drop the little 0.1. It is on all 6 sides, so together it adds 0.6. The answer is 36.6, not just 36.
Check by sharing it back out. 36.6 divided by 6 is 6.1, the side we started with.
The rule to keep: when every side is equal, count the sides and multiply by the length of one.
A triangle with sides 3.2, 4.6 and 5.3 centimetres. The perimeter is the walk all the way round, so we add the three sides.

board.text: Triangle: sides 3.2 cm, 4.6 cm, 5.3 cm. Perimeter = ?

beats.say: Add the whole numbers first. 3 plus 4 plus 5 is 12.
Now the tenths: 2 tenths, 6 tenths and 3 tenths. How many tenths is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Add them like ordinary numbers. 2 plus 6 is 8, and 3 more makes 11. So there are 11 tenths.

beats.say: 11 tenths is more than one whole. It is 1 whole and 1 tenth, which we write as 1.1. This is the step that often gets dropped.
12 plus 1.1 is 13.1. The perimeter is 13.1 centimetres.
Check by adding in order. 3.2 plus 4.6 is 7.8, and 7.8 plus 5.3 is 13.1 again.
So with decimals, add the wholes, add the tenths, and when the tenths go past 10, carry a whole across.
Thrice means 3 times. So this rectangle is 3 times as long as it is wide, and its perimeter is 64 centimetres. We want the breadth.
Call the breadth 1 part. Then the length is 3 parts, because it is 3 times as long.
Going all the way round the rectangle, how many parts do we pass?

ask.ifNot: One length and one breadth make 4 parts. But the walk round passes two lengths and two breadths, so it is 4 parts, twice over.

beats.say: 3 plus 1 plus 3 plus 1 is 8 parts. And those 8 parts together are the whole perimeter, 64 centimetres.
So one part is 64 divided by 8, which is 8. And one part is the breadth: 8 centimetres.
The length is 3 parts, so 3 times 8 is 24 centimetres. We were not asked for it, but it helps us check.
Two traps here. Sharing 64 among 4 parts forgets we pass every side twice. And the question wants the breadth, not the length.
Check: 24 plus 8 is 32, and twice 32 is 64. That is the perimeter, so it all fits.
The plan to keep: turn the sides into parts, count the parts round the whole edge, and divide the perimeter by that.
An isosceles triangle with a perimeter of 32 centimetres. Each of its two equal sides is 9 centimetres, and we want the third side.

board.text: Equal sides 9 cm each. Third side = ?

beats.say: Isosceles means two sides are equal, and congruent is just another word for equal. So the sides are 9, 9, and one we do not know yet.
What should we work out first?

ask.ifNot: There are two equal sides, and both are part of the perimeter. So first find how much the two of them make together.

beats.say: 9 plus 9 is 18. That is how much of the perimeter the two equal sides use up.
The rest belongs to the third side. 32 minus 18 is 14 centimetres.
Don't stop at 18. That is the two equal sides together, not the third side. The third side is what is left of the perimeter.
Check by adding all three sides. 9 plus 9 plus 14 is 32. It matches the perimeter.
The plan to keep: perimeter, minus all the sides you already know, leaves the side you want.
A rectangle with a length of 1.2 metres and a breadth of 50 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Rectangle: length 1.2 m, breadth 50 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Before we multiply anything, look at the units. What do you notice?

choices: one is metres, one is centimetres
ask.ifNot: Read the two measurements again. The length is in metres, but the breadth is in centimetres. They do not match yet.

beats.say: The answer is wanted in square centimetres, so let's turn the length into centimetres. 1 metre is 100 centimetres.
So 1.2 metres is 1.2 times 100, which is 120 centimetres.
Now both sides are in centimetres, and area is length times breadth. 12 times 5 is 60, and the two zeros go on the end: 6000 square centimetres.
Here is the trap. Multiply 1.2 by 50 straight away and you get 60. But that mixes metres with centimetres, so it means nothing.
So before any area sum, make the units match. Then it is just length times breadth.
A square whose area and perimeter are the very same number. We have to find its side.
Write the two rules side by side. Area is side times side. Perimeter is 4 times the side.
Let's try a small square and watch. With side 2, the area is 2 times 2, which is 4. The perimeter is 4 times 2, which is 8. Not equal.
Look at the two rules again. Both multiply the side by something. When will they give the same answer?

ask.ifNot: One rule multiplies the side by the side, the other multiplies it by 4. They agree when those two are the same, so the side must be 4.

beats.say: Try 4. The area is 4 times 4, which is 16. The perimeter is 4 times 4, which is 16. Equal!
What about 0? The numbers do match, but a square with side 0 is no square at all. So we leave that one out.
And bigger squares? With side 5, the area is 25 but the perimeter is only 20. From here on the area runs ahead, so 4 is the only answer.
So when a question gives a rule but no numbers, write the formulas side by side and test small numbers.
A rectangle with a perimeter of 50 centimetres. Its length is 3 over 2 times its breadth, and we want the area.
3 over 2 times sounds hard, so let's make it easy. Cut the breadth into 2 equal parts. Then the length is 3 of those same parts.
Half of the perimeter is one length plus one breadth. Half of 50 is 25.
One length and one breadth together: how many parts is that?

ask.ifNot: The length is 3 parts and the breadth is 2 parts. Together that is 3 plus 2.

beats.say: 3 plus 2 is 5 parts, and they make 25. So one part is 25 divided by 5, which is 5 centimetres.
The breadth is 2 parts: 2 times 5 is 10. The length is 3 parts: 3 times 5 is 15.
Area is length times breadth. 15 times 10 is 150 square centimetres.
Check both clues. Twice 15 plus 10 is 50, the perimeter. And 15 is one and a half times 10. Everything fits.
So when one side is a fraction of the other, turn the sides into equal parts. Find one part, and the rest follows.
Two playgrounds. One is a rectangle, 25 metres by 20 metres. The other is a square with sides of 22 metres. Which one is bigger?
A bigger playground means more room to play. Which measurement tells us that?

ask.ifNot: Room to run about is the flat space inside the edges. That is the area.

beats.say: The rectangle first. 25 times 20 is 500 square metres.
Now the square, 22 times 22. Take it in two bites: 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44.
440 plus 44 is 484 square metres.
500 is more than 484. So the rectangular playground is the bigger one.
Don't judge by the side lengths. 22 looks big next to 20, but the rectangle has that long 25. Only working out both areas settles it.
So to compare two shapes for size, find the area of each one, then compare the two numbers.
A plot of land is 16 metres long and 10 metres wide. Each square metre costs 1000 rupees. What does the whole plot cost?

board.text: Plot 16 m × 10 m. 1 sq m costs Rs. 1000. Cost = ?

beats.say: The price is for each square metre. So what must we find first?

ask.ifNot: Square metres measure the flat surface of the plot, and that is its area.

beats.say: Area is length times breadth. 16 times 10 is 160 square metres.
Picture 160 squares, each one metre by one metre, and every one of them costs 1000 rupees. So the cost is 160 times 1000.
To multiply by 1000, write 160 and put three zeros after it. That makes 1,60,000 rupees.
Careful with the trap. 16 times 1000 is only 16000. That leaves out the breadth altogether.
Check by dividing back. 1,60,000 divided by 1000 is 160, the area we found.
So for a cost on land or floors, find the area first, then multiply by the price of one square metre.
A ground 30 metres long and 20 metres wide has to be levelled. The charge is 5 rupees for every square metre.

board.text: Ground 30 m × 20 m. Levelling: Rs. 5 per sq m. Cost = ?

beats.say: We pay for every square metre of ground. So which sum comes first?

ask.ifNot: The number of square metres is the area of the ground. For a rectangle, that is length times breadth.

beats.say: 30 times 20. 3 times 2 is 6, and the two zeros go on the end: 600 square metres.
Careful: 600 is the area, not the cost. Each of those 600 square metres costs 5 rupees.
6 times 5 is 30, so 600 times 5 is 3000. The levelling costs 3000 rupees.
Check by sharing the money back out. 3000 rupees divided by 5 rupees is 600 square metres, the area we found.
So it is always two steps: the area first, then area times the rate.
A square with an area of 144 square centimetres. We want its perimeter.
The perimeter needs the side. And the area of a square is side times side. So we want a number that, multiplied by itself, makes 144.
Let's get close first. 10 times 10 is 100. So what can we say about the side?

ask.ifNot: 100 is smaller than 144. So the side has to be a bit bigger than 10.

beats.say: 144 ends in 4, and 2 times 2 is 4. So let's try 12. 12 times 12 is 144, so the side is 12 centimetres.
Now the perimeter. A square has 4 equal sides, so which sum do we want?

ask.ifNot: The perimeter is the walk round all 4 sides. Each side is 12, so it is 4 times 12.

beats.say: 4 times 12 is 48. The perimeter is 48 centimetres.
Careful not to divide 144 by 4, and don't stop at 12. The side comes first, then all 4 sides. And the answer is a length, in centimetres.
Check by going backwards. 48 divided by 4 is 12, and 12 times 12 is 144, the area we were given.
Two steps to keep: the area tells you the side, and 4 times the side is the perimeter.
A triangle with an area of 5 square centimetres and a height of 2 centimetres. We want its base. It is isosceles, but that does not change the area rule.

board.text: Triangle: area 5 sq cm, height 2 cm. Base = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
Put in what we know. 5 equals half, times the base, times 2.
Look at the half and the 2 on that line. What is half of 2?

ask.ifNot: Half of 2 means 2 split into two equal parts. Each part is 1.

beats.say: So the half and the 2 together make just 1. And 1 times the base is simply the base.
That leaves 5 equals the base. The base is 5 centimetres.
Check it in the rule. Half of 5 times 2 is half of 10, which is 5. That is our area.
The trap is to forget the half and say 5 divided by 2. The steady way is: double the area, then divide by the height.
So for a missing base, double the area and divide by the height.
A room has a floor 5 metres long and 4 metres wide. Its four walls have a total area of 108 square metres. How high is the room?

board.text: Floor 5 m × 4 m. Four walls: 108 sq m. Height = ?

beats.say: Imagine unfolding the four walls and laying them flat in a row. They make one long rectangle, exactly as tall as the room.
How long is that strip of walls?

ask.ifNot: The walls stand on the edges of the floor, all the way round. So the strip is as long as the walk round the floor, its perimeter.

beats.say: The floor's perimeter is 2 lengths and 2 breadths. 5 plus 4 is 9, and twice 9 is 18 metres.
So the strip is 18 metres long, and its area is 108. Length times height gives area.
The height is 108 divided by 18. Now 18 times 6 is 108, so the room is 6 metres high.
Check wall by wall. Two walls are 5 by 6, which is 30 each. Two are 4 by 6, which is 24 each. And 30, 30, 24 and 24 make 108.
The trap is dividing 108 by the floor area, 20. The walls stand on the floor's edges, so it is the perimeter we need.
So the area of four walls is the perimeter of the floor times the height. Divide to get the height back.
One side of a square grows by 50 percent, and the other shrinks by 50 percent. It becomes a rectangle. Is its area bigger, smaller, or the same?

board.text: Square: one side + 50%, the other side − 50%
New area: bigger, smaller or the same?

beats.say: No numbers are given, so let's choose an easy square. Say each side is 10. Its area is 10 times 10, which is 100.
50 percent means half. So what is 50 percent of 10?

ask.ifNot: 50 percent is the same as half. And half of 10 is 5.

beats.say: One side grows by 5: 10 plus 5 is 15. The other shrinks by 5: 10 minus 5 is 5.
One side went up by 5 and the other came down by 5. What do you think happens to the area?

ask.ifNot: It feels as if up 5 and down 5 should cancel out. But area multiplies the sides, so let's work it out and see.

beats.say: The new rectangle is 15 times 5, which is 75. And 75 is less than 100.
So the rectangle's area is smaller than the square's.

board.text: The new area is smaller than the square

beats.say: That is the trap: the same percent up and down does not cancel. One side became one and a half times as long, but the other became only half. Together that makes just three quarters of the square.
So when a question gives no numbers, pick easy ones and try it. The sums will show you what really happens.
A hall is 5 metres long and 4 metres wide. It is covered with square tiles of side 25 centimetres. How many tiles are needed?

board.text: Hall 5 m × 4 m, square tiles of side 25 cm. Tiles = ?

beats.say: Metres and centimetres are mixed, so first we make them match. 1 metre is 100 centimetres, so the hall is 500 centimetres by 400 centimetres.
How many 25 centimetre tiles fit in one row along the 500 centimetre length?

ask.ifNot: Four 25s make 100. There are 5 hundreds in 500, so that is 4 times 5, which is 20 tiles.

beats.say: 500 divided by 25 is 20 tiles in a row. And across the breadth, 400 divided by 25 is 16 rows.
So the floor is a grid of tiles: 16 rows, with 20 tiles in each row. 20 times 16 is 320 tiles.
Check it with areas. The floor is 500 times 400, which is 200000 square centimetres. One tile is 25 times 25, which is 625.
And 200000 divided by 625 is 320. The same answer both ways.
The trap is using 5 and 4 with 25 without changing units. Metres and centimetres must never be mixed in one sum.
So for tiles: same units first, count how many fit along each side, then multiply.
A wire 100 centimetres long is bent into a square. Then the same wire makes a rectangle, 5 centimetres longer and 5 centimetres narrower than the square.

board.text: Wire 100 cm, bent into a square
Rectangle: length = side + 5 cm, breadth = side − 5 cm

beats.say: The wire goes all the way round the square, so 100 centimetres is its perimeter. One side is 100 divided by 4, which is 25.
The area of the square is 25 times 25, which is 625 square centimetres.
Now the rectangle. Its length is 5 more than 25, and its breadth is 5 less than 25. What are they?

ask.ifNot: Both sides change. 25 plus 5 is 30 for the length, and 25 minus 5 is 20 for the breadth.

beats.say: So the rectangle is 30 by 20, and 30 times 20 is 600 square centimetres.
The difference is 625 minus 600, which is 25 square centimetres.
Don't answer 625 or 600. Those are the two areas, and the question wants the gap between them.
Notice something. Both shapes use the same wire: twice 30 plus 20 is 100 too. Yet the square holds more, by exactly 5 times 5.
So: the perimeter gives the side, the side gives each area, and then we subtract.
A triangle with a base of 5.2 centimetres and a height of 2.9 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Triangle: base 5.2 cm, height 2.9 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
A smart move is to halve one of the numbers first. Which one halves more easily?

ask.ifNot: 5.2 ends in an even digit, so it halves neatly. 2.9 ends in an odd digit, so its half would be messier.

beats.say: Half of 5.2 is 2.6. So the area is 2.6 times 2.9.
Leave the decimal points out for a moment: 26 times 29. Now 26 times 30 is 780, and taking away one 26 leaves 754.
Time to put the point back. 2.6 and 2.9 have one decimal place each. So how many decimal places does the answer have?

ask.ifNot: Count the decimal places in both numbers: one, and one more. Together that makes 2 decimal places in the answer.

beats.say: So 754 becomes 7.54. The area is 7.54 square centimetres.
Does that look right? Half of 5 times 3 is 7 and a half, so 7.54 is sensible. And area is in square centimetres, not plain centimetres.
So for a triangle: halve the easy number, multiply, then count the decimal places.
A square with each side 6.1 centimetres. We want its area.
Which sum gives the area of a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk round the edge, which is the perimeter. Area is the space inside: side times side.

beats.say: That is the trap in this question. 4 times 6.1 is 24.4, but that is the perimeter, a length.
So we need 6.1 times 6.1. Leave the points out for now: 61 times 61. Well, 61 times 60 is 3660, and one more 61 makes 3721.
Each 6.1 has one decimal place. So where does the point go in 3721?

ask.ifNot: One decimal place and one more make two. So count two digits from the right, and put the point there.

beats.say: That gives 37.21. The area is 37.21 square centimetres.
A quick sense check: 6 times 6 is 36, and 6.1 is a little more than 6. So a little more than 36 is just right.
So for the area of a square, multiply the side by itself, then count the decimal places in the answer.
A rectangle with a length of 1.1 centimetres and a breadth of 30 centimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Rectangle: length 1.1 cm, breadth 30 cm. Area = ?

beats.say: Both sides are already in centimetres, so we can multiply straight away. Area is length times breadth.
1.1 is 1 whole and 1 tenth. What is 1 tenth of 30?

ask.ifNot: A tenth means divide by 10. And 30 divided by 10 is 3.

beats.say: So split the sum in two. 1 times 30 is 30, and 0.1 times 30 is 3.
30 plus 3 is 33. The area is 33 square centimetres.
Here is another way to see it. 11 times 30 is 330, and one decimal place brings that back to 33.
Watch the decimal point: it is 33, not 330. And we multiplied centimetres by centimetres, so the answer is in square centimetres.
So for an area with a decimal, split the decimal into its whole and its tenths, multiply each, and add.
A triangle with an area of 120 square centimetres and a base of 40 centimetres. We want its height.

board.text: Triangle: area 120 sq cm, base 40 cm. Height = ?

beats.say: The area of a triangle is half of base times height.
Put in what we know. Half of the base is half of 40, which is 20. So 20 times the height is 120.
20 times the height is 120. So how do we find the height?

ask.ifNot: 20 times something gives 120. To undo the times, we divide 120 by 20.

beats.say: 120 divided by 20 is 6. The height is 6 centimetres.
Now look at the choices: none of them says 6 centimetres. A height is a length, so which unit could be right?

ask.ifNot: Square units are for area. A height is a length, so it needs a plain length unit, like millimetres.

beats.say: 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. So 6 centimetres is 6 times 10, which is 60 millimetres.
Check it in the rule. Half of 40 is 20, and 20 times 6 is 120. And mind the trap: 120 divided by 40 gives 3, which forgets the half.
So for a missing height: halve the base, divide the area by that, and then check which unit the answer is wanted in.
A square with a perimeter of 52 millimetres. We want its area.

board.text: Triangle: base 20 cm, height 7 cm. Area = ?

spec.note: Area = ?

beats.say: Here is our triangle. Its base is 20 centimetres and its height is 7 centimetres. We want its area, the flat space inside.

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides is for the walk round the edge. The space inside a rectangle is its length times its breadth.

beats.say: Counting squares inside a triangle is awkward. So let me box it in: a rectangle around the triangle, with the same base and the same height. How do we find the area of that rectangle?
The area of a rectangle is its length times its breadth. Here that means base times height.
20 times 7 is 140.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing once more. The triangle covers only half of the dashed rectangle. So we need half of 140.

beats.say: Now look closely. The two corner pieces outside the triangle fit together to make another triangle, just the same size. So what do we do with 140?
So the rule for a triangle is: half of base times height.
Half of 140 is 70. And see how it is written: a half, times 20, times 7.

spec.note: Area = 70 sq. cm

beats.say: So the area of the triangle is 70 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area counts little squares.
A quick check: two triangles of 70 make 140, the whole rectangle. It fits.
The method in one line: half of base times height. If you stop at base times height, you have found the whole rectangle, not the triangle.

spec.note: Circumference = ?

beats.say: Here is our circle. Its radius, from the centre out to the edge, is 14 centimetres. We want the circumference, and we are told to use 22 over 7 for pi.
Circumference is the walk all the way round the circle. And here is a lovely fact: for every circle, that walk is a little more than 3 times the distance straight across. That number is pi.

ask.ifNot: The radius only goes from the centre to the edge. The diameter goes right across, through the centre. That is 2 radii, so 2 times 14.

beats.say: We were given the radius, 14. So what is the distance straight across, the diameter?
The diameter is 2 radii: 2 times 14 is 28 centimetres. That is why the rule is often written as 2 times pi times the radius.
Now we need 22 over 7, times 28. Divide by the 7 first, because 28 is in the 7 times table: 28 divided by 7 is 4.
Then multiply by the 22. 22 times 4 is 88.

spec.note: Circumference = 88 cm

beats.say: So the circumference is 88 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because it is a length, a walk round the edge.
Does that make sense? 3 times 28 is 84, and our answer, 88, is a little more than that. Just as pi promised.
So: circumference is 2 times pi times the radius. The slip to watch for is forgetting to double the radius, which gives only half the walk.

board.text: Rectangle: length 25 cm, breadth 5 cm. Perimeter = ?

spec.note: Perimeter = ?

ask.ifNot: 25 plus 5 only gets us halfway, along one length and one breadth. The walk goes along all 4 sides. And 25 times 5 would be the space inside, the area.

beats.say: Which sum takes us all the way round?
Let's walk it. One length and one breadth: 25 plus 5 is 30. That is halfway round.
The other two sides are the same again, so we double it: 30 plus 30 is 60.
That is where the rule comes from: add the length and the breadth, then double.

spec.note: Perimeter = 60 cm

beats.say: So the perimeter is 60 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because a perimeter is a length.
Check with the whole walk: 25 plus 5 plus 25 plus 5 makes 60.
The method in one line: perimeter is 2 times, length plus breadth. Do not stop after adding just two sides.
Here is 43 degrees, drawn on a straight line. Its supplementary angle is the other piece of that line, the one marked with a question mark.

ask.ifNot: Look at the drawing. The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a corner, a right angle.

beats.say: Stand at the point and turn from one end of the line to the other. That is a half turn. So how much do our two angles make together?
A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So 43 degrees, plus our missing angle, makes 180 degrees.

ask.ifNot: When we know the whole and one part, we take the part away from the whole. So it is 180 take away 43.

beats.say: We know the whole, 180, and one part, 43. How do we find the other part?
Let's take 43 away in two easy hops. First the 40: 180 take away 40 leaves 140.
Now the 3 that is left: 140 take away 3 leaves 137. So 180 minus 43 is 137.
So the supplementary angle is 137 degrees. Watch it go into the drawing.
Let's check by adding them back. 43 plus 137 makes 180. It fits exactly.
So for a supplementary angle, take the angle away from 180. To remember which is which: S for supplementary, S for straight line. C for complementary, C for corner.
Here is our triangle. Two of its angles are 41 degrees and 71 degrees. The third one, at the top, is our mystery.

ask.ifNot: A straight line is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees. So the 3 angles of a triangle always make 180 degrees.

beats.say: Here is something you can try with paper. Tear the 3 corners off any triangle and put them side by side. They always make a straight line. So how much do the 3 angles make together?

board.text: Angles of a triangle add up to 180°

beats.say: A straight line is a half turn, 180 degrees. So the 3 angles of any triangle add up to 180 degrees.
First, how much have the two angles we know used up? 41 plus 71 is 112.

ask.ifNot: Both known angles have to come off the 180, not just one of them. Together they are 112, so it is 180 take away 112.

beats.say: So 112 of the 180 degrees is gone. What sum finds the third angle?
Let's take 112 away in two easy hops. First the 110: 180 take away 110 leaves 70.
Now the 2 that is left: 70 take away 2 leaves 68. So 180 minus 112 is 68.
So the third angle is 68 degrees. Into the drawing it goes.
Check: 41 plus 71 plus 68 makes 180. All three together make the straight line.
So for any triangle: add the two angles you know, then take the total away from 180. The slip to watch for is taking away only one of them.

board.text: On a straight line: x° and 116°. x = ?

beats.say: Here is a straight line with two angles sitting on it. One is 116 degrees. The other is called x, and we want to know its size.

ask.ifNot: The two angles lie along a straight line, and a straight line is a half turn. That makes 180 degrees. 90 is for a square corner.

beats.say: Stand where the two angles meet. Facing along the line one way, then turning to face the other way, is a half turn. So how much do the two angles make together?
A half turn is 180 degrees. So x, plus 116, equals 180. Now it is an equation.

ask.ifNot: To undo plus 116, we take away 116. And to keep the two sides level, we take it from both sides.

beats.say: We want x on its own. What do we do about the plus 116?
To undo plus 116, we take 116 away, from both sides.
Let's take 116 away in two easy hops. First the 110: 180 take away 110 leaves 70.
Now the 6 that is left: 70 take away 6 leaves 64. So 180 minus 116 is 64.
So x equals 64. The other angle is 64 degrees.
Check: 64 plus 116 makes 180, a full straight line. It fits.
So angles on a straight line always make 180 degrees. Take the one you know away from 180, and you have the other.

board.text: Lines cross: one angle is 108°. Opposite angle = ?

beats.say: Two straight lines cross and make 4 angles. One of them is 108 degrees. We want the angle vertically opposite: the one straight across the crossing point.
I have called the two angles next door p and q. Now, here is what we know about a straight line: it is a half turn, and a half turn is 180 degrees.
Look at 108 degrees and its neighbour, p. They sit side by side on one straight line. Let's take 108 away in two easy hops. First the 100: 180 take away 100 leaves 80.
Now the 8 that is left: 80 take away 8 leaves 72. So 180 minus 108 is 72.

ask.ifNot: p and the mystery angle share a straight line, so together they make 180 degrees. We take p, which is 72, away from 180.

beats.say: So p is 72 degrees. Now look at p and our mystery angle. They sit side by side on the other straight line. So what is the mystery angle?
Let's take 72 away in two easy hops. First the 70: 180 take away 70 leaves 110.
Now the 2 that is left: 110 take away 2 leaves 108. So 180 minus 72 is 108.
108 degrees. Exactly the angle we started with! That always happens: angles straight across from each other are equal.
So next time you can say it straight away: the vertically opposite angle is equal, 108 degrees. The slip to watch for is giving 72, which is the neighbour on the line.

board.text: From 100 to 300: how many are divisible by 4?

beats.say: We are counting the numbers from 100 to 300 that 4 divides exactly, with nothing left over.
Divisible by 4 means the number is in the 4 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 4.

ask.ifNot: 300 itself is in the 4 times table, and it is inside our range. So 300 is the last one.

beats.say: Let's find the far end first. Which is the last multiple of 4 that does not go past 300?
4 times 75 is exactly 300. It lands right on the end of our range, so it counts.
Look at the 4 times table from its very start. 300 is multiple number 75. So up to 300 there are 75 multiples of 4.
Careful here: 100 itself is in the 4 times table, so it counts. The ones that are too small stop at 96, which is 4 times 24.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 96, and 96 is 4 times 24. So exactly 24 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 75 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
75 take away 24 leaves 51.
Check another way. From 100 to 300 is 200. That is 50 jumps of 4, and 50 jumps join 51 numbers.
So 51 numbers from 100 to 300 are divisible by 4.
The plan: find the last multiple, count from the start of the table, then take away the ones that are too small.

board.text: Odd numbers from 100 to 130: how many?

beats.say: We want to know how many odd numbers there are from 100 to 130. Both ends count, if they are odd.

ask.ifNot: 100 is even, so it does not count. The very next number, 101, is the first odd one.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first odd number in the range?
So we start at 101. And the last one is 129, because 130 is even.
Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 101, 103, 105 and so on, all the way to 129.
From 101 to 129 is 28. Each jump is 2, so that is 14 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 14 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
14 jumps join 15 numbers. The extra 1 is the number we started on.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 odd ones. From 100 up to 130 there are 3 runs of 10. The 130 left at the end is even, so it adds nothing. 15 again.
So there are 15 odd numbers from 100 to 130.
Find the two ends, count the jumps between them, then add 1 for the starting number. That works every time.

board.text: Even numbers from 100 to 120: how many?

beats.say: From 100 to 120, how many of the numbers are even? Let's count them without writing every one.

ask.ifNot: 100 itself is even, and it is inside the range, so it counts. Our list starts right at 100.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first even number in the range?
So we start at 100. And the last one is 120 itself, because 120 is even.
Even numbers go up in jumps of 2: 100, 102, 104 and so on, all the way to 120.
From 100 to 120 is 20. Each jump is 2, so that is 10 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 10 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
10 jumps join 11 numbers. The extra 1 is the number we started on.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 even ones. From 100 up to 120 there are 2 runs of 10, plus 120 itself, which is even. That gives 11 again.
So there are 11 even numbers from 100 to 120.
Find the two ends, count the jumps between them, then add 1 for the starting number. That works every time.

board.text: From 10 to 60: how many are divisible by 3?

beats.say: From 10 to 60, some numbers can be divided by 3 exactly. Our job is to count them.
Divisible by 3 means the number is in the 3 times table. So really, we are counting multiples of 3.

ask.ifNot: 60 itself is in the 3 times table, and it is inside our range. So 60 is the last one.

beats.say: Start at the top end. What is the biggest multiple of 3 that is not more than 60?
3 times 20 is exactly 60. It lands right on the end of our range, so it counts.
Look at the 3 times table from its very start. 60 is multiple number 20. So up to 60 there are 20 multiples of 3.
But our range only starts at 10. 3 times 3 is 9, still too small. The next one, 12, is the first one inside.

ask.ifNot: The too small ones run up to 9, and 9 is 3 times 3. So exactly 3 of them go.

beats.say: So out of the 20 multiples, how many are too small and have to go?
20 take away 3 leaves 17.
Check another way. From 12 to 60 is 48. That is 16 jumps of 3, and 16 jumps join 17 numbers.
So 17 numbers from 10 to 60 are divisible by 3.
The plan: find the last multiple, count from the start of the table, then take away the ones that are too small.

board.text: Odd numbers from 50 to 70: how many?

beats.say: We want to know how many odd numbers there are from 50 to 70. Both ends count, if they are odd.

ask.ifNot: 50 is even, so it does not count. The very next number, 51, is the first odd one.

beats.say: Where does our list start? Which is the first odd number in the range?
So we start at 51. And the last one is 69, because 70 is even.
Odd numbers go up in jumps of 2: 51, 53, 55 and so on, all the way to 69.
From 51 to 69 is 18. Each jump is 2, so that is 9 jumps.

ask.ifNot: Think of fence posts. 1 jump joins 2 numbers, and 2 jumps join 3. There is always one more number than jumps.

beats.say: 9 jumps. So how many numbers are on our list?
One more than the jumps: 9 plus 1 is 10. That extra 1 is our starting number.
Check another way. Any 10 numbers in a row hold 5 odd ones. From 50 up to 70 there are 2 runs of 10. The 70 left at the end is even, so it adds nothing. 10 again.
So there are 10 odd numbers from 50 to 70.
First one, last one, count the jumps of 2, and add 1. The add 1 is the step people forget.

board.text: Sum of the first 20 odd numbers = ?

beats.say: Add up the first 20 odd numbers: 1, 3, 5 and so on. Let's start small and hunt for a pattern.
The first odd number on its own is 1. The first 2 odd numbers, 1 plus 3, make 4. And 4 is 2 times 2.
The first 3 odd numbers: 1 plus 3 plus 5 makes 9. That is 3 times 3. Interesting!

ask.ifNot: Add them up: 1, 3, 5 and 7. Then compare with 4 times 4. They match.

beats.say: So what do you think the first 4 odd numbers, 1, 3, 5 and 7, add up to?
Yes, 4 times 4. Look at the picture: each new odd number wraps round the square like a letter L, and makes the next bigger square.
So the first 20 odd numbers must add up to 20 times 20.
20 times 20 is 400.
Check with pairs. The last odd number is 39. First plus last, 1 plus 39, is 40. Forwards and backwards gives 20 columns of 40, and half of that is 400.
So the sum of the first 20 odd numbers is 400.
So, count how many odd numbers there are, and multiply that count by itself. Isn't that neat?
Look at this. 6 x, plus 9, plus 8 x, minus 5. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's see which.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 6 x is 6 boxes, and 8 x is 8 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 6 x and 8 x together make 14 x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 9 minus 5, which is 4.
So we have 14 x and 4. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 14 x means 14 lots of a hidden number. 4 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 14 x plus 4. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 1. The long one is 6 plus 9 plus 8 minus 5, which is 18. The short one is 14 plus 4, also 18. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 5 and y is 1. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 1 y.
First, what does 5 x turn into when x is 5?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 5.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 5, and 1 y becomes 1 times 1.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 5 is 25. And 1 y is just one single y, so that is 1.
Now add them. 25 plus 1 is 26. So 5 x plus 1 y is worth 26.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 5 x is 5 times x, never the two digits side by side.
This one is a recipe. Start with 8, multiply it by 2, then add 9. We just have to follow it in the right order.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 2 comes before add 9. So first we work out 8 times 2.

beats.say: So we multiply. 8 times 2 makes 16.
Next the recipe says add 9. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 16.

beats.say: 16 plus 9 is 25. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 2 n plus 9. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 8 in for n. 2 times 8, plus 9, is 25. The same answer. Just never add the 2 and the 9 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 6. We want the value of 3 x, plus 13, minus 5.
Before we swap anything: when x is 6, what is 3 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 3 x means 3 times x, and here that is 3 times 6.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 6 in its place, with a times sign. 3 times 6, plus 13, minus 5.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 3 times 6 comes first.

beats.say: 3 times 6 is 18. So now we have 18, plus 13, minus 5.
Now we go left to right. 18 plus 13 is 31. Then 31 minus 5 is 26.
That gives 26. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
6 x, plus 6, plus 5 x, plus 8. That is quite a mouthful. Let's tidy it up, so it says the same thing in fewer pieces.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 6 x is 6 boxes, and 5 x is 5 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 6 x and 5 x together make 11 x.
Now the plain numbers. 6 plus 8 makes 14.
So we have 11 x and 14. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 11 x means 11 lots of a hidden number. 14 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 11 x plus 14. Same value, far fewer pieces.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 36. The short one, 11 times 2 plus 14, comes to 36 as well. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 8 and y is 5. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 2 y.
Before we swap anything: when x is 8, what is 5 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 8.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 8, and 2 y becomes 2 times 5.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 8 is 40. And 2 times 5 is 10.
Now add them. 40 plus 10 is 50. So 5 x plus 2 y is worth 50.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 5 x is 5 times x, never the two digits side by side.
A number game! Our number is 9. We multiply it by 3, and then we add 11. Let's take it one step at a time.
What do we work out first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 3 comes before add 11. So first we work out 9 times 3.

beats.say: 9 times 3 is 27.
Next the recipe says add 11. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 27.

beats.say: 27 plus 11 is 38. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 3 n plus 11. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 9 in for n. 3 times 9, plus 11, is 38. The same answer. Just never add the 3 and the 11 first, because that changes the recipe.
The plan for any number recipe: do the first step, keep the result, then do the next step to that result.
This time the hidden number is not hidden at all: x is 6. So we can work out what 8 x, plus 12, minus 6 is worth.
First, what does 8 x turn into when x is 6?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 8 x means 8 times x, and here that is 8 times 6.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 6 in its place, with a times sign. 8 times 6, plus 12, minus 6.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 8 times 6 comes first.

beats.say: 8 times 6 is 48. So now we have 48, plus 12, minus 6.
Now we go left to right. 48 plus 12 is 60. Then 60 minus 6 is 54.
That gives 54. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
Neha buys 4 pens at 10 rupees each, and hands over 50 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 4 pens at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.50.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 50 rupees pays for the pens, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the pens
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 4 pens, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 4 pens at 10 rupees each: that is 4 times 10. 4 times 10 is 40.
Careful: 40 is only the cost, not the answer. Neha paid 50. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 40 away from 50.

beats.say: Count up from 40 to 50. That is 10 more.
So Neha gets 10 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 40, plus the change, 10, should make the 50 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
The bag costs Nikhil 100 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 15 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 100 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 100 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
And here the cost price is exactly 100 rupees. So 15 out of every 100 is simply 15 rupees. That is the profit.
So the profit is 15 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 100 plus 15 is 115. So the selling price is 115 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 115 is 15 more than 100. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
Riya pays 300 rupees for a laptop. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 300 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 300 divided by 10 gives 30.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 30 is 15.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 30 plus 15 makes 45. That is the loss.
So the loss is 45 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 45 is 255. So the selling price is 255 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 255 is 45 below 300. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!
8 sharpeners cost 24 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one sharpener.
Picture the 24 rupees as one long bar, cut into 8 equal pieces, one piece for each sharpener. Every sharpener costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one sharpener?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 24 rupees equally among 8 sharpeners. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 8 times table. 8 times what makes 24? 8 times 3 is 24.
There it is: each sharpener costs 3 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 8 sharpeners at 3 rupees each: 8 times 3 is 24. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. You can do the next one yourself!
Here is a long expression. 2 x, plus 10, plus 7 x, plus 10. Simplify means write it shorter, without changing what it is worth.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family, and the plain numbers are another. Which two are like terms?

ask.ifNot: Like terms have the same letter part. 2 x and 7 x both have an x, so they are family. 10 has no x at all.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 2 x and 7 x together make 9 x.
Now the plain numbers. 10 plus 10 makes 20.
So we have 9 x and 20. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 9 x means 9 lots of a hidden number. 20 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 9 x plus 20. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 38. The short one, 9 times 2 plus 20, comes to 38 as well. They match.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart.
Two letters this time. x is 4 and y is 2. Our job is to find the value of 2 x plus 1 y.
First, what does 2 x turn into when x is 4?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 2 x means 2 times x, and here that is 2 times 4.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 2 x becomes 2 times 4, and 1 y becomes 1 times 2.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. And 1 y is just one single y, so that is 2.
Now add them. 8 plus 2 is 10. So 2 x plus 1 y is worth 10.
The plan: put the numbers in place of the letters, multiply, then add. A number next to a letter always means times.
A number game! Our number is 6. We multiply it by 3, and then we add 9. Let's take it one step at a time.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 3 comes before add 9. So first we work out 6 times 3.

beats.say: So we multiply. 6 times 3 makes 18.
Next the recipe says add 9. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 18.

beats.say: 18 plus 9 is 27. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 3 n plus 9. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 6 in for n. 3 times 6, plus 9, is 27. The same answer. Just never add the 3 and the 9 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 2. We want the value of 8 x, plus 2, minus 2.
First, what does 8 x turn into when x is 2?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 8 x means 8 times x, and here that is 8 times 2.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 2 in its place, with a times sign. 8 times 2, plus 2, minus 2.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 8 times 2 comes first.

beats.say: 8 times 2 is 16. So now we have 16, plus 2, minus 2.
Look closely: plus 2, and then minus 2. Those two undo each other. So we are left with 16.
That gives 16. Remember the order: number in for the letter, then the times, then the plus and minus from left to right.
Look at this. 7 x, plus 7, plus 2 x, plus 9. Four pieces, and some of them can be joined together. Let's see which.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family, and the plain numbers are another. Which two are like terms?

ask.ifNot: Like terms have the same letter part. 7 x and 2 x both have an x, so they are family. 7 has no x at all.

beats.say: So gather the x terms. 7 x and 2 x together make 9 x.
Now the plain numbers. 7 plus 9 makes 16.
So we have 9 x and 16. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 9 x means 9 lots of a hidden number. 16 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: That leaves 9 x plus 16. It cannot get any shorter than that.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 2. The long one comes to 34. The short one, 9 times 2 plus 16, comes to 34 as well. They match.
So to simplify: gather the x terms, gather the plain numbers, and keep the two families apart.
Two letters this time. x is 4 and y is 5. Our job is to find the value of 3 x plus 2 y.
Before we swap anything: when x is 4, what is 3 x?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 3 x means 3 times x, and here that is 3 times 4.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 3 x becomes 3 times 4, and 2 y becomes 2 times 5.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 3 times 4 is 12. And 2 times 5 is 10.
Now add them. 12 plus 10 is 22. So 3 x plus 2 y is worth 22.
The plan: put the numbers in place of the letters, multiply, then add. A number next to a letter always means times.
This one is a recipe. Start with 14, multiply it by 4, then add 5. We just have to follow it in the right order.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 4 comes before add 5. So first we work out 14 times 4.

beats.say: So we multiply. 14 times 4 makes 56.
Next the recipe says add 5. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 56.

beats.say: 56 plus 5 is 61. That is what we get.

Here is a shop sum with two parts. 8 erasers at 6 rupees each, and Vivek pays with 63 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 8 erasers at Rs.6 each. Pays Rs.63.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 63 rupees pays for the erasers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the erasers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 erasers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 erasers at 6 rupees each: that is 8 times 6. 8 times 6 is 48.
Careful: 48 is only the cost, not the answer. Vivek paid 63. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 48 away from 63.

beats.say: From 63, take off the 48. That leaves 15.
So Vivek gets 15 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 48, plus the change, 15, should make the 63 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. You can do the next one yourself!
The book costs Isha 50 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 20 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 50 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 50 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 50 divided by 10 is 5.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 5 makes 10. That is the profit.
So the profit is 10 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 50 plus 10 is 60. So the selling price is 60 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 60 is 10 above 50. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!

First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 200 divided by 10 gives 20.

Here is a shop sum with two parts. 7 rulers at 9 rupees each, and Riya pays with 83 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 7 rulers at Rs.9 each. Pays Rs.83.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 83 rupees pays for the rulers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the rulers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 7 rulers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 7 rulers at 9 rupees each: that is 7 times 9. 7 times 9 is 63.
Careful: 63 is only the cost, not the answer. Riya paid 83. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 63 away from 83.

beats.say: From 83, take off the 63. That leaves 20.
So Riya gets 20 rupees back.

The bag costs Aditya 75 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 40 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 75 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 40 per cent. But 40 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 75 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 75 divided by 10 is 7.5.
Now, 40 per cent is just 10 per cent, 4 times over. 4 times 7.5 makes 30. That is the profit.
So the profit is 30 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 75 plus 30 is 105. So the selling price is 105 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 105 is 30 more than 75. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!

Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 600 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 600 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 600 divided by 10 is 60.
20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 60 is 120. That is the loss.
So the loss is 120 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 600 take away 120 is 480. So the selling price is 480 rupees.

So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. You can do the next one yourself!
