Check by building it back up. 24 pens at 9 rupees each: 24 times 9 is 216. It fits.
Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. Now you try one!
Isha is at the shop, buying 7 pens. Each one costs 12 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one pen, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 7 pens costs 12 rupees. That is 12 rupees, 7 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 12 is 10 and 2. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 7 is 70.
And 2 times 7 is 14.
Put the two bites together. 70 plus 14 makes 84. So 7 times 12 is 84.
So Isha pays 84 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 84 rupees, in lots of 12 rupees, gives 7 pens. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 7 books at 6 rupees each, and Karan pays with 47 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 7 books at Rs.6 each. Pays Rs.47.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 47 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 7 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 7 books at 6 rupees each: that is 7 times 6. 7 times 6 is 42.
Careful: 42 is only the cost, not the answer. Karan paid 47. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 42 away from 47.

beats.say: Count up from 42 to 47. That is 5 more.
So Karan gets 5 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 42 plus 5 is 47. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. You can do the next one yourself!
Neha pays 40 rupees for a bag. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 40 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 40 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 40 divided by 10 is 4.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 4 is 2.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 4 plus 2 makes 6. That is the profit.
So the profit is 6 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 40 plus 6 is 46. So the selling price is 46 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 46 is 6 above 40. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
Nikhil pays 600 rupees for a tablet. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 10 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 600 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 10 per cent. But 10 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 600 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is a friendly one: it is one tenth. So we divide by 10. 600 divided by 10 is 60. That is the loss.
So the loss is 60 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 600 take away 60 is 540. So the selling price is 540 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 540 is 60 below 600. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. You can do the next one yourself!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 6 sharpeners for 42 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one sharpener.
Picture the 42 rupees as one long bar, cut into 6 equal pieces, one piece for each sharpener. Every sharpener costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one sharpener?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 42 rupees equally among 6 sharpeners. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 6 times table. 6 times what makes 42? 6 times 7 is 42.
So one sharpener costs 7 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 6 sharpeners at 7 rupees each: 6 times 7 is 42. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. You can do the next one yourself!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 3 pencils at 7 rupees each, and Ananya pays with 36 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 3 pencils at Rs.7 each. Pays Rs.36.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 36 rupees pays for the pencils, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the pencils
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 3 pencils, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 3 pencils at 7 rupees each: that is 3 times 7. 3 times 7 is 21.
Careful: 21 is only the cost, not the answer. Ananya paid 36. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 21 away from 36.

beats.say: From 36, take off the 21. That leaves 15.
So Ananya gets 15 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 21 plus 15 is 36. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
The pen set costs Siddharth 250 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 50 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 250 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 250 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
50 per cent is 50 out of every 100, and that is exactly one half. Half of 250 is 125. That is the profit.
So the profit is 125 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 250 plus 125 is 375. So the selling price is 375 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 375 is 125 more than 250. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!
Tara pays 800 rupees for a laptop. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 25 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 800 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 800 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
4 lots of 25 make 100, so 25 per cent is one quarter. A quarter is half of a half. First, half of 800 is 400.
And half of 400 is 200. So 25 per cent of 800 is 200 rupees. That is the loss.
So the loss is 200 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 800 take away 200 is 600. So the selling price is 600 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 600 is 200 below 800. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. You can do the next one yourself!
15 stickers cost 150 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one sticker.
Picture the 150 rupees as one long bar, cut into 15 equal pieces, one piece for each sticker. Every sticker costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one sticker?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 150 rupees equally among 15 stickers. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: 150 is exactly 15 tens. So 150 divided by 15 is 10.
There it is: each sticker costs 10 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 15 stickers at 10 rupees each: 15 times 10 is 150. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Now you try one!
3 bags of lentils, each one 3 kilograms 750 grams. Our job is to find what they weigh altogether, in grams.

board.text: 3 bags of lentils, each 3 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: One bag is written in two units at once, kilograms and grams, and those do not mix. We want grams, so let's turn the kilograms into grams. How many grams are in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 3 kilograms is 3 times 1000, which is 3000 grams.
Do not lose the 750 grams that came with it. 3000 plus 750 is 3750 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 3750 grams, and there are 3 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 3 bags, and each one is the full 3750 grams. So we need 3 lots of 3750: a multiplication.

beats.say: Let's multiply in two easy pieces. 3 times 3000 is 9000, and 3 times 750 is 2250.
Add the two pieces: 9000 plus 2250 is 11250. So the 3 bags together weigh 11250 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 9000 grams. Our 11250 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 750 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
A drum holds 20 litres of water, and each glass takes 300 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?
Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the drum, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: Each litre is 1000 millilitres. Smaller unit, so more of them: we multiply by 1000. 20 times 1000 gives 20000 millilitres in the drum.
Now both are in millilitres, so we want to know how many lots of 300 fit into 20000. Take two zeros off each to make it friendlier: how many lots of 3 fit into 200?
3 does not go into 200 exactly. 3 times 66 is 198, and that is as close as we can get without going over.
So 66 glasses use 19800 millilitres. Take that from 20000, and 200 millilitres are left over.
Here is the bit to think about. There are 200 millilitres left in the drum. Can we count one more glass?

ask.ifNot: A glass only counts when it is full, and a full one needs 300 millilitres. We have just 200 left, so that last bit stays in the drum.

beats.say: The leftover 200 millilitres is not enough for another glass. So 66 glasses can be filled.
Let's be sure. Glass number 67 would bring the total to 20100 millilitres, and that is more than the 20000 the drum holds. So 66 is right.
So the plan: same units first, then divide. And when something is left over, ask what the leftover means before you round.
Here is a rectangle, 17 centimetres long and 6 centimetres wide. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides takes you along the edges, and that is the perimeter, the walk around. For the space inside we count rows of squares: length times width.

beats.say: Picture little squares, 1 centimetre each way. Every row holds 17 of them, and there are 6 rows. 6 rows of 17 is 17 times 6.
Split 17 into 10 and 7. 10 times 6 is 60, and 7 times 6 is 42. Together that makes 102.
That gives an area of 102 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area counts squares that cover the shape.
Check by undoing it. 102 shared into 6 rows gives 17 in each row, and that is our length. It fits.
Remember: area means the space inside, so multiply length by width. Adding the sides is for the walk around the edge.
40 millimetres. Same length, new unit: we want it in centimetres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. You can see it on your ruler: 10 tiny gaps inside every centimetre.
A centimetre is bigger than a millimetre. So will the number of centimetres be bigger or smaller than 40?

ask.ifNot: It takes 10 millimetres to make just 1 centimetre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: Every 10 millimetres make 1 centimetre, so we count how many lots of 10 are in 40. 40 divided by 10 is 4.
So 40 millimetres is the same length as 4 centimetres.
Check by going back the other way. 4 centimetres, times 10, is 40 millimetres. Just what we started with.
Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.
Aditya has 2 bags of lentils, and each bag weighs 2 kilograms 500 grams. We want the weight of all the bags together, in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of lentils, each 2 kg 500 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 2 kg 500 g

beats.say: One bag is written in two units at once, kilograms and grams, and those do not mix. We want grams, so let's turn the kilograms into grams. How many grams are in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. A gram is much smaller than a kilogram, so we need many more of them: that is why we multiply. 2 times 1000 is 2000 grams.
Now put back the 500 grams that were already there. 2000 plus 500 makes 2500 grams. That is one bag, all in grams.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 2 kg 500 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 2500 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 2500 grams. So we need 2 lots of 2500: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 2000 is 4000, and double 500 is 1000.
Add the two pieces: 4000 plus 1000 is 5000. So the 2 bags together weigh 5000 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 4000 grams. Our 5000 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 500 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
We have a bucket with 15 litres of water in it, and glasses that hold 200 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.
Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the bucket, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: Each litre is 1000 millilitres. Smaller unit, so more of them: we multiply by 1000. 15 times 1000 gives 15000 millilitres in the bucket.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 200 millilitre glasses fit into 15000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

beats.say: Dividing by 200 is easy with one friendly fact: 5 glasses of 200 millilitres make exactly 1000. So every litre fills 5 glasses.
There are 15 litres, with 5 glasses from each one. 15 times 5 is 75. So 75 glasses can be filled.
Check by pouring it back. 75 glasses of 200 millilitres is 75 times 200, which is 15000 millilitres. That is the whole bucket, with nothing left over.
Remember the order. Same units first, here millilitres. Then divide the big amount by the size of one glass.
Here is a square, and each side is 18 centimetres. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk around the edge, and that is the perimeter. For the space inside we count rows of little squares: side times side.

beats.say: In a square every side is the same. So each row holds 18 little squares, and there are 18 rows as well. That is 18 times 18.
Split 18 into 10 and 8. 18 times 10 is 180, and 18 times 8 is 144. Together that makes 324.
So the area is 324 square centimetres. Careful: 18 times 18 means 18 rows of 18. It is not the same as doubling 18.
Check by undoing it. 324 shared into 18 rows gives 18 in each row. That is our side again.
Remember: area of a square is side times side. Rows of little squares, all the same length.
7000 metres. Same length, new unit: we want it in kilometres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 kilometre is 1000 metres. The clue is in the name: kilo means a thousand.
A kilometre is bigger than a metre. So will the number of kilometres be bigger or smaller than 7000?

ask.ifNot: It takes 1000 metres to make just 1 kilometre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: Every 1000 metres make 1 kilometre, so we count how many lots of 1000 are in 7000. 7000 divided by 1000 is 7.
So 7000 metres is the same length as 7 kilometres.
Check by going back the other way. 7 kilometres, times 1000, is 7000 metres. Just what we started with.
So, small unit to a bigger unit: divide by how many small ones make one big one. Bigger unit, smaller number.

board.text: 6 markers at Rs.12 each. Pays Rs.92.

Put the two bites together. 60 plus 12 makes 72. So 6 times 12 is 72.

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 72 away from 92.

beats.say: 92 take away 72 leaves 20.
So Vivek gets 20 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 72, plus the change, 20, should make the 92 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. You can do the next one yourself!

20 pens cost 60 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one pen.

9 pens, and every one costs 7 rupees. How much does Arjun pay altogether?
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One pen costs 7 rupees, and there are 9 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 9 pens costs 7 rupees. That is 7 rupees, 9 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 9 times, so it is a times sum. 9 times 7 is 63.
So Arjun pays 63 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 63 rupees, in lots of 7 rupees, gives 9 pens. It fits.
Remember it like this: price of one, times the number you buy, is the total cost. You can do the next one yourself!
Siddharth has 5 bags of rice, and each bag weighs 2 kilograms 750 grams. We want the weight of all the bags together, in grams.

board.text: 5 bags of rice, each 2 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 2 kg 750 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. A gram is much smaller than a kilogram, so we need many more of them: that is why we multiply. 2 times 1000 is 2000 grams.
Now put back the 750 grams that were already there. 2000 plus 750 makes 2750 grams. That is one bag, all in grams.

beats.say: Every bag weighs 2750 grams, and there are 5 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 5 bags, and each one is the full 2750 grams. So we need 5 lots of 2750: a multiplication.

beats.say: Let's multiply in two easy pieces. 5 times 2000 is 10000, and 5 times 750 is 3750.
Add the two pieces: 10000 plus 3750 is 13750. So the 5 bags together weigh 13750 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 10000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 750 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
We have a bottle with 8 litres of water in it, and glasses that hold 300 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.
Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the bottle, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 8 times 1000 is 8000 millilitres.
Now both are in millilitres, so we want to know how many lots of 300 fit into 8000. Take two zeros off each to make it friendlier: how many lots of 3 fit into 80?
3 does not go into 80 exactly. 3 times 26 is 78, and that is as close as we can get without going over.
So 26 glasses use 7800 millilitres. Take that from 8000, and 200 millilitres are left over.
Here is the bit to think about. There are 200 millilitres left in the bottle. Can we count one more glass?

ask.ifNot: A glass only counts when it is full, and a full one needs 300 millilitres. We have just 200 left, so that last bit stays in the bottle.

beats.say: The leftover 200 millilitres is not enough for another glass. So 26 glasses can be filled.
Let's be sure. Glass number 27 would bring the total to 8100 millilitres, and that is more than the 8000 the bottle holds. So 26 is right.
Remember: get both amounts into millilitres, see how many glasses fit, and never round up a glass that is not full.
Our shape is a square with sides of 5 centimetres. The question asks for its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk around the edge, and that is the perimeter. For the space inside we count rows of little squares: side times side.

beats.say: In a square every side is the same. So each row holds 5 little squares, and there are 5 rows as well. That is 5 times 5.
5 times 5 is 25. That is a tables fact worth knowing by heart.
So the area is 25 square centimetres. Careful: 5 times 5 means 5 rows of 5. It is not the same as doubling 5.
Check by undoing it. 25 shared into 5 rows gives 5 in each row. That is our side again.
Remember: area of a square is side times side. Rows of little squares, all the same length.
1400 centimetres. Same length, new unit: we want it in metres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 metre is 100 centimetres. Think of a metre stick: it has 100 centimetres marked along it.
A metre is bigger than a centimetre. So will the number of metres be bigger or smaller than 1400?

ask.ifNot: It takes 100 centimetres to make just 1 metre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: Every 100 centimetres make 1 metre, so we count how many lots of 100 are in 1400. 1400 divided by 100 is 14.
So 1400 centimetres is the same length as 14 metres.
Check by going back the other way. 14 metres, times 100, is 1400 centimetres. Just what we started with.
Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.
Siya buys 8 rulers at 8 rupees each, and hands over 79 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 8 rulers at Rs.8 each. Pays Rs.79.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 79 rupees pays for the rulers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the rulers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 rulers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 rulers at 8 rupees each: that is 8 times 8. 8 times 8 is 64.
Careful: 64 is only the cost, not the answer. Siya paid 79. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 64 away from 79.

beats.say: 79 take away 64 leaves 15.
So Siya gets 15 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 64, plus the change, 15, should make the 79 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Now you try one!
Arjun pays 60 rupees for a book. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 50 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 60 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 60 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
50 out of every 100 is one half. So we just halve it: half of 60 is 30. That is the profit.
So the profit is 30 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 60 plus 30 is 90. So the selling price is 90 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 90 is 30 more than 60. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!
Diya pays 250 rupees for a phone. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 250 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 250 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 250 divided by 10 is 25.
20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 25 is 50. That is the loss.
So the loss is 50 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 250 take away 50 is 200. So the selling price is 200 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 200 is 50 below 250. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. You can do the next one yourself!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 24 crayons for 120 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one crayon.
Picture the 120 rupees as one long bar, cut into 24 equal pieces, one piece for each crayon. Every crayon costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one crayon?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 120 rupees equally among 24 crayons. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: We need the number that, times 24, makes 120. Let us try 5. 24 is 20 and 4. 20 times 5 is 100, and 4 times 5 is 20.
Together, 100 plus 20 is 120. It fits exactly. So 120 divided by 24 is 5.
So one crayon costs 5 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 24 crayons at 5 rupees each: 24 times 5 is 120. It fits.
Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. Now you try one!
Here are 5 bags of rice. Every bag weighs 5 kilograms 500 grams, and Nikhil wants the total weight in grams.

board.text: 5 bags of rice, each 5 kg 500 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 5 kg 500 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 5 kilograms is 5 times 1000, which is 5000 grams.
Do not lose the 500 grams that came with it. 5000 plus 500 is 5500 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 5 kg 500 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 5500 grams, and there are 5 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 5 bags, and each one is the full 5500 grams. So we need 5 lots of 5500: a multiplication.

beats.say: A big multiplication is easier in two pieces. First 5 times 5000, which is 25000. Then 5 times 500, which is 2500.
Add the two pieces: 25000 plus 2500 is 27500. So the 5 bags together weigh 27500 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 25000 grams. Our 27500 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 500 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
That is the whole method. Change the kilograms into grams, add the loose grams, then multiply by how many bags there are.
We have a drum with 12 litres of water in it, and glasses that hold 200 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.
Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the drum, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 12 times 1000 is 12000 millilitres.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 200 millilitre glasses fit into 12000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

beats.say: Here is a friendly fact to help. 200 times 5 is exactly 1000, so each litre of water fills 5 glasses.
There are 12 litres, with 5 glasses from each one. 12 times 5 is 60. So 60 glasses can be filled.
Check by pouring it back. 60 glasses of 200 millilitres is 60 times 200, which is 12000 millilitres. That is the whole drum, with nothing left over.
Remember the order. Same units first, here millilitres. Then divide the big amount by the size of one glass.
Here is a square, and each side is 16 centimetres. We want its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round, like an ant walking along the edge. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: Side times side counts the squares inside, and that is the area. For the walk around, count the sides: a square has 4, all the same length.

beats.say: A square has 4 equal sides, and the ant walks along every one of them. So the perimeter is 4 times the side.
4 times 16 is easy if we double twice. Double 16 is 32, and double 32 is 64.
So the perimeter is 64 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because it is a distance along a line.
Check by walking round. 16, and 16, and 16, and 16. That adds up to 64.
Remember: perimeter is the walk around, and a square has 4 equal sides. So it is 4 times the side.
We have 800 centimetres, and we want to say the same length in metres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 metre is 100 centimetres. Think of a metre stick: it has 100 centimetres marked along it.
A metre is bigger than a centimetre. So will the number of metres be bigger or smaller than 800?

ask.ifNot: It takes 100 centimetres to make just 1 metre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

So 800 centimetres is the same length as 8 metres.
Check by going back the other way. 8 metres, times 100, is 800 centimetres. Just what we started with.
Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: Each litre is 1000 millilitres. Smaller unit, so more of them: we multiply by 1000. 20 times 1000 gives 20000 millilitres in the tank.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 200 millilitre glasses fit into 20000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

beats.say: Dividing by 200 is easy with one friendly fact: 5 glasses of 200 millilitres make exactly 1000. So every litre fills 5 glasses.
There are 20 litres, with 5 glasses from each one. 20 times 5 is 100. So 100 glasses can be filled.
Check by pouring it back. 100 glasses of 200 millilitres is 100 times 200, which is 20000 millilitres. That is the whole tank, with nothing left over.

Here is a rectangle, 6 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide. We want its perimeter.
Perimeter is the distance all the way round, like an ant walking along the edge. Which sides does the ant walk along?

ask.ifNot: Trace the edge with your finger: along the top, down the side, back along the bottom, up the other side. That is 2 lengths and 2 widths.

beats.say: One length and one width take the ant halfway round. So we add them, then double.
Halfway round first. 6 plus 3 is 9 centimetres.
Careful: 9 is only half the walk, and stopping here is the slip to watch for. Double it for the whole way round. 2 times 9 is 18.
So the perimeter is 18 centimetres. Plain centimetres, because it is a distance along a line.
Check by walking it side by side. 6, then 3, then 6, then 3. That adds up to 18.
So for the perimeter of a rectangle: add the length and the width, then double.
We have 6000 metres, and we want to say the same length in kilometres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 kilometre is 1000 metres. The clue is in the name: kilo means a thousand.
A kilometre is bigger than a metre. So will the number of kilometres be bigger or smaller than 6000?

ask.ifNot: It takes 1000 metres to make just 1 kilometre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: We are bundling the metres into groups of 1000, one group for each kilometre. 6000 divided by 1000 is 6.
So 6000 metres is the same length as 6 kilometres.
Check by going back the other way. 6 kilometres, times 1000, is 6000 metres. Just what we started with.
So, small unit to a bigger unit: divide by how many small ones make one big one. Bigger unit, smaller number.
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 4 books at 12 rupees each, and Isha pays with 98 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 4 books at Rs.12 each. Pays Rs.98.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 98 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 4 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 4 books at 12 rupees each: that is 4 times 12. 12 is 10 and 2. So we do it in two easy bites. 10 times 4 is 40.
And 2 times 4 is 8.
Put the two bites together. 40 plus 8 makes 48. So 4 times 12 is 48.
Careful: 48 is only the cost, not the answer. Isha paid 98. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 48 away from 98.

beats.say: From 98, take off the 48. That leaves 50.
So Isha gets 50 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 48 plus 50 is 98. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Now you try one!
Vivek pays 50 rupees for a pen set. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 50 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 50 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 50 rupees.

50 per cent is 50 out of every 100, and that is exactly one half. Half of 50 is 25. That is the profit.
So the profit is 25 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 50 plus 25 is 75. So the selling price is 75 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 75 is 25 more than 50. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
12 erasers cost 108 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one eraser.
Picture the 108 rupees as one long bar, cut into 12 equal pieces, one piece for each eraser. Every eraser costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one eraser?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 108 rupees equally among 12 erasers. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Try 10 lots first. 12 times 10 is 120. That is a little too much.
Take one lot of 12 off: 120 minus 12 is 108. So it is 9 lots, one fewer than 10.
There it is: each eraser costs 9 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 12 erasers at 9 rupees each: 12 times 9 is 108. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Now you try one!
Karan is at the shop, buying 12 notebooks. Each one costs 20 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One notebook costs 20 rupees, and there are 12 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 12 notebooks costs 20 rupees. That is 20 rupees, 12 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 20 is 2 tens. So first double the 12: that is 24.
Then 10 times 24 is 240. So 12 times 20 is 240.
So the total cost is 240 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 240 rupees, in lots of 20 rupees, gives 12 notebooks. It fits.
Remember it like this: price of one, times the number you buy, is the total cost. You can do the next one yourself!
Aarav buys 3 books at 4 rupees each, and hands over 17 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 3 books at Rs.4 each. Pays Rs.17.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 17 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 3 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 3 books at 4 rupees each: that is 3 times 4. 3 times 4 is 12.
Careful: 12 is only the cost, not the answer. Aarav paid 17. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 12 away from 17.

beats.say: Count up from 12 to 17. That is 5 more.
So Aarav gets 5 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 12 plus 5 is 17. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Now you try one!
Priya pays 150 rupees for a watch. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 10 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 150 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.

Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. You can do the next one yourself!
Siddharth buys 6 crayons at 10 rupees each, and hands over 85 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 6 crayons at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.85.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 85 rupees pays for the crayons, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the crayons
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 6 crayons, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 6 crayons at 10 rupees each: that is 6 times 10. 6 times 10 is 60.
Careful: 60 is only the cost, not the answer. Siddharth paid 85. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 60 away from 85.

beats.say: 85 take away 60 leaves 25.
So Siddharth gets 25 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 60, plus the change, 25, should make the 85 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. You can do the next one yourself!
Tara pays 50 rupees for a toy. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 50 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 50 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 50 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
50 per cent is 50 out of every 100, and that is exactly one half. Half of 50 is 25. That is the profit.
So the profit is 25 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 50 plus 25 is 75. So the selling price is 75 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 75 is 25 above 50. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
The tablet costs Aditya 1000 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a loss of 20 per cent. What is the selling price?
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 1000 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 1000 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 1000 divided by 10 is 100.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 100 makes 200. That is the loss.
So the loss is 200 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 1000 take away 200 is 800. So the selling price is 800 rupees.
Does that make sense? A loss should drop the selling price below the cost price, and 800 is 200 less than 1000. It fits.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 10 pencils for 50 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one pencil.
Think of the 50 rupees as a bar shared into 10 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one pencil.
So which sum finds the cost of one pencil?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 50 rupees equally among 10 pencils. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 10 times table. 10 times what makes 50? 10 times 5 is 50.
There it is: each pencil costs 5 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 10 pencils at 5 rupees each: 10 times 5 is 50. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 9 erasers at 3 rupees each, and Neha pays with 37 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 9 erasers at Rs.3 each. Pays Rs.37.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 37 rupees pays for the erasers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the erasers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 9 erasers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 9 erasers at 3 rupees each: that is 9 times 3. 9 times 3 is 27.
Careful: 27 is only the cost, not the answer. Neha paid 37. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 27 away from 37.

beats.say: Count up from 27 to 37. That is 10 more.
So Neha gets 10 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 27, plus the change, 10, should make the 37 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Now you try one!
Nikhil pays 80 rupees for a bag. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 80 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 80 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 80 divided by 10 is 8.
20 per cent is 2 lots of 10 per cent. 2 times 8 is 16. That is the profit.
So the profit is 16 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 80 plus 16 is 96. So the selling price is 96 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 96 is 16 above 80. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Riya pays 600 rupees for a tablet. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 600 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 600 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 600 divided by 10 is 60.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 60 makes 120. That is the loss.
So the loss is 120 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 600 take away 120 is 480. So the selling price is 480 rupees.
Does that make sense? A loss should drop the selling price below the cost price, and 480 is 120 less than 600. It fits.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 15 notebooks for 135 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one notebook.
Think of the 135 rupees as a bar shared into 15 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one notebook.
So which sum finds the cost of one notebook?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 135 rupees equally among 15 notebooks. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Try 10 lots first. 15 times 10 is 150. That is a little too much.
Take one lot of 15 off: 150 minus 15 is 135. So it is 9 lots, one fewer than 10.
So one notebook costs 9 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 15 notebooks at 9 rupees each: 15 times 9 is 135. It fits.
Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. Your turn next!
2 bags of lentils, each one 3 kilograms 750 grams. Our job is to find what they weigh altogether, in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of lentils, each 3 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 3 kilograms is 3 times 1000, which is 3000 grams.
Do not lose the 750 grams that came with it. 3000 plus 750 is 3750 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 3750 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 3750 grams. So we need 2 lots of 3750: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 3000 is 6000, and double 750 is 1500.
Add the two pieces: 6000 plus 1500 is 7500. So the 2 bags together weigh 7500 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 6000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 750 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
Remember the order: get everything into one unit first, then do the multiplying. Units first, sums second.
A tank holds 8 litres of water, and each glass takes 300 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?
Look at the units first. The tank is in litres, the glass is in millilitres, and those two do not mix. Which shall we change?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 8 times 1000 is 8000 millilitres.
Now both are in millilitres, so we want to know how many lots of 300 fit into 8000. Take two zeros off each to make it friendlier: how many lots of 3 fit into 80?
3 does not go into 80 exactly. 3 times 26 is 78, and that is as close as we can get without going over.
So 26 glasses use 7800 millilitres. Take that from 8000, and 200 millilitres are left over.
Here is the bit to think about. There are 200 millilitres left in the tank. Can we count one more glass?

ask.ifNot: A glass only counts when it is full, and a full one needs 300 millilitres. We have just 200 left, so that last bit stays in the tank.

beats.say: The leftover 200 millilitres is not enough for another glass. So 26 glasses can be filled.
Let's be sure. Glass number 27 would bring the total to 8100 millilitres, and that is more than the 8000 the tank holds. So 26 is right.
Remember: get both amounts into millilitres, see how many glasses fit, and never round up a glass that is not full.
Our shape is a square with sides of 8 centimetres. The question asks for its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk around the edge, and that is the perimeter. For the space inside we count rows of little squares: side times side.

beats.say: In a square every side is the same. So each row holds 8 little squares, and there are 8 rows as well. That is 8 times 8.
8 times 8 is 64. That is a tables fact worth knowing by heart.
So the area is 64 square centimetres. Careful: 8 times 8 means 8 rows of 8. It is not the same as doubling 8.
Check by undoing it. 64 shared into 8 rows gives 8 in each row. That is our side again.
So for the area of a square, multiply the side by itself. 4 times the side is a different question, the perimeter.
We have 90 millimetres, and we want to say the same length in centimetres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. You can see it on your ruler: 10 tiny gaps inside every centimetre.
A centimetre is bigger than a millimetre. So will the number of centimetres be bigger or smaller than 90?

ask.ifNot: It takes 10 millimetres to make just 1 centimetre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: We are bundling the millimetres into groups of 10, one group for each centimetre. 90 divided by 10 is 9.
So 90 millimetres is the same length as 9 centimetres.
Check by going back the other way. 9 centimetres, times 10, is 90 millimetres. Just what we started with.
Remember the idea, not just the rule. Bigger units mean fewer of them, so going up to a bigger unit we divide.
Dev buys 8 sharpeners at 10 rupees each, and hands over 105 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 8 sharpeners at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.105.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 105 rupees pays for the sharpeners, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the sharpeners
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 sharpeners, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 sharpeners at 10 rupees each: that is 8 times 10. 8 times 10 is 80.
Careful: 80 is only the cost, not the answer. Dev paid 105. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 80 away from 105.

beats.say: From 105, take off the 80. That leaves 25.
So Dev gets 25 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 80, plus the change, 25, should make the 105 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Now you try one!
Kavya pays 40 rupees for a book. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 50 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 40 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 40 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
50 per cent is 50 out of every 100, and that is exactly one half. Half of 40 is 20. That is the profit.
So the profit is 20 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 40 plus 20 is 60. So the selling price is 60 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 60 is 20 more than 40. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Sahil pays 200 rupees for a phone. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 20 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 200 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 200 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 200 divided by 10 is 20.
Now, 20 per cent is just 10 per cent, 2 times over. 2 times 20 makes 40. That is the loss.
So the loss is 40 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 200 take away 40 is 160. So the selling price is 160 rupees.
Does that make sense? A loss should drop the selling price below the cost price, and 160 is 40 less than 200. It fits.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 6 pencils for 48 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one pencil.
Think of the 48 rupees as a bar shared into 6 equal pieces. Each piece is the price of one pencil.
So which sum finds the cost of one pencil?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 48 rupees equally among 6 pencils. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 6 times table. 6 times what makes 48? 6 times 8 is 48.
So one pencil costs 8 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 6 pencils at 8 rupees each: 6 times 8 is 48. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. Your turn next!
3 x, plus 8, plus 3 x, minus 2. That is quite a mouthful. Let's tidy it up, so it says the same thing in fewer pieces.
Think of x as a box with a secret number of sweets inside. 3 x is 3 boxes, and 3 x is 3 more boxes. The plain numbers are loose sweets. What can we count together?

choices: a box and some loose sweets
ask.ifNot: Boxes go with boxes, and loose sweets go with loose sweets. We cannot add a box to a loose sweet, because we do not know how many are inside the box.

beats.say: First the x family. 3 lots of x and 3 more lots of x make 6 lots of x.
Now the plain numbers. Careful: the sign in front of a number belongs to that number. So this is 8 minus 2, which is 6.
So we have 6 x and 6. Here is where people slip. Can we squash those two into one term?

choices: No, they are not like terms
ask.ifNot: 6 x means 6 lots of a hidden number. 6 is a plain number. They are different families, so they stay side by side.

beats.say: So the short form is 6 x plus 6. Same value, far fewer pieces.
Let's test it with a number. Say x is 1. The long one is 3 plus 8 plus 3 minus 2, which is 12. The short one is 6 plus 6, also 12. They match.
The plan every time: x terms with x terms, numbers with numbers, and each sign stays with its own term.
Two letters this time. x is 3 and y is 6. Our job is to find the value of 5 x plus 1 y.
First, what does 5 x turn into when x is 3?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 5 x means 5 times x, and here that is 5 times 3.

beats.say: So we swap each letter for its number. 5 x becomes 5 times 3, and 1 y becomes 1 times 6.
Now we have two multiplications and one addition. Which do we do first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 5 times 3 is 15. And 1 y is just one single y, so that is 6.
Now add them. 15 plus 6 is 21. So 5 x plus 1 y is worth 21.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 5 x is 5 times x, never the two digits side by side.
A number game! Our number is 20. We multiply it by 5, and then we add 11. Let's take it one step at a time.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 5 comes before add 11. So first we work out 20 times 5.

beats.say: 20 times 5 is 100.
Next the recipe says add 11. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 100.

beats.say: 100 plus 11 is 111. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 5 n plus 11. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 20 in for n. 5 times 20, plus 11, is 111. The same answer. Just never add the 5 and the 11 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 6. We want the value of 4 x, plus 11, minus 5.
First, what does 4 x turn into when x is 6?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 4 x means 4 times x, and here that is 4 times 6.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 6 in its place, with a times sign. 4 times 6, plus 11, minus 5.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 4 times 6 comes first.

beats.say: 4 times 6 is 24. So now we have 24, plus 11, minus 5.
Now we go left to right. 24 plus 11 is 35. Then 35 minus 5 is 30.
So when x is 6, the whole thing is worth 30. The plan: swap the letter for its number, multiply first, then work left to right.
Find the square root of 484. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 484?

beats.say: Yes. The same number goes in both boxes: something times itself makes 484. Think of 484 tiles laid out as a perfect square. How long is one side?
484 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 20 times 20 is 400. 30 times 30 is 900.
484 sits between 400 and 900. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 484 is more than 400 and less than 900. So its root is more than 20 and less than 30.

beats.say: Now the clever clue: the last digit. 484 ends in 4. 2 times 2 is 4, and 8 times 8 is 64: both end in 4.
So our number ends in 2 or 8: it is 22 or 28. Now, 484 is closer to 400 than to 900. Which one shall we try?

ask.ifNot: 400 is the square of 20, and 484 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 20, and that is 22.

beats.say: Let's test 22. Break the second 22 into 20 and 2. 22 times 20 is 440, and 22 times 2 is 44.
440 plus 44 is 484. That is our number exactly!
So the square root of 484 is 22.
That is the plan every time: squeeze it between two tens, read the last digit, and test your best guess by multiplying.
Which of these is a perfect square: 144, 150, 147 or 145? Let's remember what a perfect square is first.
A perfect square is a number of tiles that makes a full square, with nothing left over. Like 9 tiles, in 3 rows of 3.
Let's walk up the squares until we reach our numbers. 11 times 11 is 121: too small.
The next square is 12 times 12. What does that make?

ask.ifNot: 12 times 12 is 12 lots of 12. From the 12 times table, that is 144.

beats.say: 12 times 12 is 144, and there it is in our list! 144 tiles make a square with 12 on each side.
What about the others? The very next square is 13 times 13, which is 169. So 150, 147 and 145 are stuck in the gap between two squares.
So the perfect square is 144.
To test for a perfect square, walk up the squares and see whether you land exactly on the number.
Let's read it together. The square root of x, plus 12, equals 18. Under that root sign sits x, and we want it.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 12 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: Plus 12 is undone by minus 12. Whatever we do on the left, we do on the right as well.
On the left, only the root of x is left. On the right, 18 minus 12 is 6.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 6 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 6 times 6, not 6 times 2.

beats.say: Picture a square of tiles, 6 rows with 6 tiles in each row. The side of the square is the root. All the tiles together are x.
6 times 6 is 36. So x is 36. There is our hidden number!
Let's check it. The square root of 36 is 6, and 6 plus 12 is 18. It fits perfectly.
So the plan for a puzzle like this: first get the root on its own, then square it to find x.
We want the square of 9. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.
Look at this square of tiles: 9 rows, with 9 tiles in each row. Count all the tiles, and you have the square of 9.
So which sum gives us the square of 9?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tiles. There are 9 rows, and each row has 9 tiles. That is 9 lots of 9, so 9 times 9.

beats.say: Careful with that little 2 up in the air. It never means times 2. It tells us to multiply the number by itself.
And what is 9 times 9? Use your tables.

ask.ifNot: Count up in lots of 9, 9 times over. You land on 81.

beats.say: 9 times 9 is 81. So the square of 9 is 81.
A quick check, going backwards: the square root of 81 is 9, because 9 times 9 is 81.
Remember: the square of a number is that number times itself, like the tiles in a square.
Find the square root of 196. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 196?

beats.say: So we need one number for both boxes. Picture 196 tiles arranged in a perfect square: the square root is the length of its side.
196 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 10 times 10 is 100. 20 times 20 is 400.
196 sits between 100 and 400. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 196 is more than 100 and less than 400. So its root is more than 10 and less than 20.

beats.say: Now the clever clue: the last digit. 196 ends in 6. 4 times 4 is 16, and 6 times 6 is 36: both end in 6.
So our number ends in 4 or 6: it is 14 or 16. Now, 196 is closer to 100 than to 400. Which one shall we try?

ask.ifNot: 100 is the square of 10, and 196 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 10, and that is 14.

beats.say: Let's test 14. Break the second 14 into 10 and 4. 14 times 10 is 140, and 14 times 4 is 56.
140 plus 56 is 196. That is our number exactly!
So the square root of 196 is 14.
That is the plan every time: squeeze it between two tens, read the last digit, and test your best guess by multiplying.
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 15, equals 22. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.
Think of the square root of x as one closed box. The box plus 15 makes 22. So what do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 15 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: To undo plus 15, we take away 15. And to keep the balance level, we take it from both sides.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 22 minus 15 gives us 7.
Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 7. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 7 times 7, not 7 times 2.

beats.say: Picture a square of tiles, 7 rows with 7 tiles in each row. The side of the square is the root. All the tiles together are x.
From our tables, 7 times 7 is 49. So x equals 49.
Let's check it. The square root of 49 is 7, and 7 plus 15 is 22. It fits perfectly.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Find the square of 8. That little word, square, is a big clue. So let's draw one.
Here is a square made of tiles. It has 8 rows, and 8 tiles in every row. The square of 8 is the number of tiles in it.
Which sum counts all the tiles in that square?

ask.ifNot: Look at the tiles. There are 8 rows, and each row has 8 tiles. That is 8 lots of 8, so 8 times 8.

beats.say: Careful with that little 2 up in the air. It never means times 2. It tells us to multiply the number by itself.
And what is 8 times 8? Use your tables.

ask.ifNot: Count up in lots of 8, 8 times over. You land on 64.

We want the square root of 36. Before we hunt for it, what does a square root mean?
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 36?

beats.say: So we need one number for both boxes. Picture 36 tiles arranged in a perfect square: the square root is the length of its side.
Let's test some numbers. 5 times 5 is 25. That is too small.
Too small, so we go one bigger. What is 6 times 6?

ask.ifNot: 6 times 6 means 6 lots of 6. Count up in lots of 6 and you land on 36.

beats.say: 6 times 6 is exactly 36. Look: 36 tiles make a square with 6 on each side.
So the square root of 36 is 6.

We want the square root of 900. Before we hunt for it, what does a square root mean?
Which of these is the square root asking for?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 900?

beats.say: Yes. The same number goes in both boxes: something times itself makes 900. Think of 900 tiles laid out as a perfect square. How long is one side?
900 ends in two zeros. Cover them for a moment and we see 9. Which number, times itself, makes 9?

ask.ifNot: Try your tables: 3 times 3 is 9.

beats.say: 3 times 3 is 9. So 3 tens times 3 tens is 9 hundreds: 30 times 30 is 900.
So the square root of 900 is 30. There it is!
Picture it: 30 rows with 30 tiles in each row is 900 tiles. A perfect square.
So when a number ends in two zeros, find the root of the front part, then put one zero back.
Look at this one. The square root of x, plus 9, makes 20. Our job is to find x itself.
The root of x is not alone on the left. Something is sitting next to it. What should we move out of the way first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 9 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: Plus 9 is undone by minus 9. Whatever we do on the left, we do on the right as well.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 20 minus 9 gives us 11.

Good mathematicians always check. Put 121 in place of x: its square root is 11, and 11 plus 9 is 20. It works.

We want the square of 11. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.

Which sum counts all the tiles in that square?

Here is a long expression. 11 x, plus 3, plus 3 x, plus 5. Simplify means write it shorter, without changing what it is worth.
Some of these pieces belong together. The ones with an x are one family, and the plain numbers are another. Which two are like terms?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 5 comes before add 14. So first we work out 7 times 5.

beats.say: 7 times 5 is 35.
Next the recipe says add 14. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 35.

ask.ifNot: Multiplying comes before adding. So we work out each times first, and only then add the two answers.

beats.say: 4 times 8 is 32. And 4 times 6 is 24.
Now add them. 32 plus 24 is 56. So 4 x plus 4 y is worth 56.
So for any question like this: swap each letter for its number, do the times first, then add. And 4 x is 4 times x, never the two digits side by side.
This one is a recipe. Start with 14, multiply it by 2, then add 8. We just have to follow it in the right order.
Which step comes first?

ask.ifNot: Read the recipe again: multiply it by 2 comes before add 8. So first we work out 14 times 2.

beats.say: 14 times 2 is 28.
Next the recipe says add 8. What do we add it to?

ask.ifNot: We add it to the number we are holding now, not the one we started with. Right now we are holding 28.

beats.say: 28 plus 8 is 36. That is what we get.
Here is the clever bit. If we call the starting number n, the whole recipe is 2 n plus 8. That is all algebra is: a recipe, with a letter standing for the number.
Put 14 in for n. 2 times 14, plus 8, is 36. The same answer. Just never add the 2 and the 8 first, because that changes the recipe.
So: follow the steps in the order they are given, one at a time, and always carry on from the number you have reached.
We know that x is 5. We want the value of 7 x, plus 12, minus 6.
First, what does 7 x turn into when x is 5?

ask.ifNot: When a number sits right next to a letter, there is a hidden times sign between them. So 7 x means 7 times x, and here that is 7 times 5.

beats.say: So we rub out the x and write 5 in its place, with a times sign. 7 times 5, plus 12, minus 6.
Three jobs here: a times, a plus and a minus. Which one goes first?

ask.ifNot: Multiplying always goes before adding and taking away. So 7 times 5 comes first.

beats.say: 7 times 5 is 35. So now we have 35, plus 12, minus 6.
Now we go left to right. 35 plus 12 is 47. Then 47 minus 6 is 41.
So when x is 5, the whole thing is worth 41. The plan: swap the letter for its number, multiply first, then work left to right.
Let's read it together. The square root of x, plus 19, equals 31. Under that root sign sits x, and we want it.
Before we touch the root sign, we want the root of x standing by itself. What is in its way?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 19 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: So we subtract 19. Both sides, remember, or the balance tips.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 31 minus 19 gives us 12.
Don't put your pencil down yet. 12 is only the root of x. Which sum takes us from the root back to x?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 12 times 12, not 12 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 12 rows of 12 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.
12 times 12 is a big one, so we split it. 12 times 10 is 120, and 12 times 2 is 24.
120 plus 24 is 144. So x is 144. There is our hidden number!
Let's check it. The square root of 144 is 12, and 12 plus 19 is 31. It fits perfectly.
Two moves, in order: undo the plus, then undo the root by squaring. Your turn next!
Let's read it together. The square root of x, plus 18, equals 24. Under that root sign sits x, and we want it.
Think of the square root of x as one closed box. The box plus 18 makes 24. So what do we clear away first?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 18 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

beats.say: So we subtract 18. Both sides, remember, or the balance tips.
Now the root of x stands alone. And 24 minus 18 gives us 6.
Now the trap. We have found the square root of x, and that is 6. We have not found x yet! What undoes a square root?

ask.ifNot: A square root is the number that multiplies by itself to make x. So we go back the other way: x is 6 times 6, not 6 times 2.

beats.say: Here is why. Build a square with 6 rows of 6 tiles. Its side is the square root, and the number of tiles in it is x.

Good mathematicians always check. Put 36 in place of x: its square root is 6, and 6 plus 18 is 24. It works.
Remember the two steps. Clear away what is added, then multiply the root by itself.
Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 9, equals 23. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.

Here is our puzzle. The square root of x, plus 7, equals 16. We are hunting for x, the number hiding under the root sign.

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side again. The root of x has a plus 7 hanging on to it. That goes first, and the root sign waits until the end.

Find the square root of 361. First, let's be sure what that is asking.
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 361?

beats.say: So we need one number for both boxes. Picture 361 tiles arranged in a perfect square: the square root is the length of its side.
361 is too big for our tables, so we trap it between two squares we know. 10 times 10 is 100. 20 times 20 is 400.
361 sits between 100 and 400. So where is our number?

ask.ifNot: Look at the two lines. 361 is more than 100 and less than 400. So its root is more than 10 and less than 20.

So our number ends in 1 or 9: it is 11 or 19. Now, 361 is closer to 400 than to 100. Which one shall we try?

ask.ifNot: 400 is the square of 20, and 361 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 20, and that is 19.

beats.say: Let's test 19. Break the second 19 into 10 and 9. 19 times 10 is 190, and 19 times 9 is 171.
190 plus 171 is 361. That is our number exactly!
So the square root of 361 is 19.
So for a big square root: trap it between two tens, let the last digit pick the candidates, then multiply to make sure.

Find the square of 25. That little word, square, is a big clue. So let's draw one.
A 25 by 25 square is too big for our board, so here is a baby one: 3 rows of 3 tiles. 3 times 3 is 9 tiles, so the square of 3 is 9.
Our square is the same idea, only bigger: 25 rows, with 25 tiles in each row. So which sum gives the square of 25?

ask.ifNot: Think of the square: 25 rows, and 25 tiles in every row. That is 25 lots of 25, so 25 times 25.

25 times 20 is 500. And 25 times 5 is 125. What do they make together?

ask.ifNot: Take it slowly. Add the ones first, then the tens, then the hundreds. 500 plus 125 comes to 625.

And if we go backwards, the square root of 625 brings us home to 25. Square and square root undo each other.

We want the square of 12. It gets its name from a shape, so let's start with the shape.

beats.say: 120 plus 24 is 144. So the square of 12 is 144.

We want the square root of 729. Before we hunt for it, what does a square root mean?
What is a square root question really asking?

ask.ifNot: A square root is not a half. It asks: which number, multiplied by itself, makes 729?

ask.ifNot: 900 is the square of 30, and 729 is close to it. So we want the one nearer to 30, and that is 27.

beats.say: Let's test 27. Break the second 27 into 20 and 7. 27 times 20 is 540, and 27 times 7 is 189.
540 plus 189 is 729. That is our number exactly!
