Rohan buys 5 crayons at 10 rupees each, and hands over 70 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 crayons at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.70.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 70 rupees pays for the crayons, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the crayons
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 crayons, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 5 crayons at 10 rupees each: that is 5 times 10. 5 times 10 is 50.
Careful: 50 is only the cost, not the answer. Rohan paid 70. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 50 away from 70.

beats.say: From 70, take off the 50. That leaves 20.
So Rohan gets 20 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 50 plus 20 is 70. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
Priya pays 200 rupees for a bag. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 200 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 200 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 200 divided by 10 is 20.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 20 is 10.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 20 plus 10 makes 30. That is the profit.
So the profit is 30 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 200 plus 30 is 230. So the selling price is 230 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 230 is 30 more than 200. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!

Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 800 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.

First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 800 divided by 10 gives 80.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 80 is 40.

Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the bottle, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 20 times 1000 is 20000 millilitres.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 500 millilitre glasses fit into 20000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

beats.say: Dividing by 500 is easy with one friendly fact: 2 glasses of 500 millilitres make exactly 1000. So every litre fills 2 glasses.
There are 20 litres, with 2 glasses from each one. 20 times 2 is 40. So 40 glasses can be filled.
Check by pouring it back. 40 glasses of 500 millilitres is 40 times 500, which is 20000 millilitres. That is the whole bottle, with nothing left over.
So the plan: get both amounts into the same unit first, then divide to see how many fit.
Here is a square, and each side is 13 centimetres. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that for a square?

ask.ifNot: 4 times the side is the walk around the edge, and that is the perimeter. For the space inside we count rows of little squares: side times side.

beats.say: In a square every side is the same. So each row holds 13 little squares, and there are 13 rows as well. That is 13 times 13.
Split 13 into 10 and 3. 13 times 10 is 130, and 13 times 3 is 39. Together that makes 169.
So the area is 169 square centimetres. Careful: 13 times 13 means 13 rows of 13. It is not the same as doubling 13.
Check by undoing it. 169 shared into 13 rows gives 13 in each row. That is our side again.
Remember: area of a square is side times side. Rows of little squares, all the same length.
Here are 2 bags of lentils. Every bag weighs 6 kilograms 250 grams, and Tara wants the total weight in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of lentils, each 6 kg 250 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 6 kg 250 g

beats.say: One bag is written in two units at once, kilograms and grams, and those do not mix. We want grams, so let's turn the kilograms into grams. How many grams are in 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 6 kilograms is 6 times 1000, which is 6000 grams.
Now put back the 250 grams that were already there. 6000 plus 250 makes 6250 grams. That is one bag, all in grams.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 6 kg 250 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 6250 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 6250 grams. So we need 2 lots of 6250: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 6000 is 12000, and double 250 is 500.
Add the two pieces: 12000 plus 500 is 12500. So the 2 bags together weigh 12500 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 12000 grams. Our 12500 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 250 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
That is the whole method. Change the kilograms into grams, add the loose grams, then multiply by how many bags there are.
Tara buys 7 erasers at 4 rupees each, and hands over 38 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 7 erasers at Rs.4 each. Pays Rs.38.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 38 rupees pays for the erasers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the erasers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 7 erasers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 7 erasers at 4 rupees each: that is 7 times 4. 7 times 4 is 28.
Careful: 28 is only the cost, not the answer. Tara paid 38. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 28 away from 38.

beats.say: Count up from 28 to 38. That is 10 more.
So Tara gets 10 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 28 plus 10 is 38. It works.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. You can do the next one yourself!
The pen set costs Siddharth 120 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 40 per cent. What is the selling price?
Picture two bars, one under the other. The cost price, 120 rupees, is on top. The selling price is below, with a question mark for now.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 40 per cent. But 40 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 120 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 per cent is the easy one: it is one tenth. 120 divided by 10 is 12.
40 per cent is 4 lots of 10 per cent. 4 times 12 is 48. That is the profit.
So the profit is 48 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 120 plus 48 is 168. So the selling price is 168 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 168 is 48 more than 120. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Now you try one!
The camera costs Ananya 300 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a loss of 15 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 300 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 300 divided by 10 is 30.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 30 is 15.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 30 plus 15 makes 45. That is the loss.
So the loss is 45 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 45 is 255. So the selling price is 255 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 255 is 45 below 300. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. You can do the next one yourself!
Here we know the price of the whole lot: 12 erasers for 36 rupees. Our job is to find the price of one eraser.
Picture the 36 rupees as one long bar, cut into 12 equal pieces, one piece for each eraser. Every eraser costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one eraser?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 36 rupees equally among 12 erasers. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Count in lots of 12. 12, and 12 more, and 12 more, makes 36. That is 3 lots.
There it is: each eraser costs 3 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 12 erasers at 3 rupees each: 12 times 3 is 36. It fits.
Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. Now you try one!
Here are 5 bags of rice. Every bag weighs 4 kilograms 250 grams, and Siddharth wants the total weight in grams.

board.text: 5 bags of rice, each 4 kg 250 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 4 kg 250 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. A gram is much smaller than a kilogram, so we need many more of them: that is why we multiply. 4 times 1000 is 4000 grams.
Do not lose the 250 grams that came with it. 4000 plus 250 is 4250 grams, so now one bag is written in a single unit.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 4 kg 250 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 4250 grams, and there are 5 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 5 bags, and each one is the full 4250 grams. So we need 5 lots of 4250: a multiplication.

beats.say: A big multiplication is easier in two pieces. First 5 times 4000, which is 20000. Then 5 times 250, which is 1250.
Add the two pieces: 20000 plus 1250 is 21250. So the 5 bags together weigh 21250 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 20000 grams. Our 21250 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 250 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
Remember the order: get everything into one unit first, then do the multiplying. Units first, sums second.
A drum holds 10 litres of water, and each glass takes 300 millilitres. How many glasses can we fill?
Look at the units first. The drum is in litres, the glass is in millilitres, and those two do not mix. Which shall we change?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: 1 litre is 1000 millilitres. A millilitre is much smaller, so we need many more of them, and that means multiply. 10 times 1000 is 10000 millilitres.
Now both are in millilitres, so we want to know how many lots of 300 fit into 10000. Take two zeros off each to make it friendlier: how many lots of 3 fit into 100?
3 does not go into 100 exactly. 3 times 33 is 99, and that is as close as we can get without going over.
So 33 glasses use 9900 millilitres. Take that from 10000, and 100 millilitres are left over.
Here is the bit to think about. There are 100 millilitres left in the drum. Can we count one more glass?

ask.ifNot: A glass only counts when it is full, and a full one needs 300 millilitres. We have just 100 left, so that last bit stays in the drum.

beats.say: The leftover 100 millilitres is not enough for another glass. So 33 glasses can be filled.
Let's be sure. Glass number 34 would bring the total to 10200 millilitres, and that is more than the 10000 the drum holds. So 33 is right.
So the plan: same units first, then divide. And when something is left over, ask what the leftover means before you round.
Here is a rectangle, 6 centimetres long and 5 centimetres wide. We want its area.
Area is the space inside the shape: how many little squares would cover it. Which rule gives us that?

ask.ifNot: Adding the sides takes you along the edges, and that is the perimeter, the walk around. For the space inside we count rows of squares: length times width.

beats.say: Picture little squares, 1 centimetre each way. Every row holds 6 of them, and there are 5 rows. 5 rows of 6 is 6 times 5.
6 times 5 is 30. You can count the little squares in the picture to be sure.
That gives an area of 30 square centimetres. Square centimetres, because area counts squares that cover the shape.
Check by undoing it. 30 shared into 5 rows gives 6 in each row, and that is our length. It fits.
So for the area of a rectangle, multiply the length by the width. If you catch yourself adding the sides, stop: that is the perimeter.
We have 700 centimetres, and we want to say the same length in metres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 metre is 100 centimetres. Think of a metre stick: it has 100 centimetres marked along it.
A metre is bigger than a centimetre. So will the number of metres be bigger or smaller than 700?

ask.ifNot: It takes 100 centimetres to make just 1 metre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: We are bundling the centimetres into groups of 100, one group for each metre. 700 divided by 100 is 7.
So 700 centimetres is the same length as 7 metres.
Check by going back the other way. 7 metres, times 100, is 700 centimetres. Just what we started with.
So, small unit to a bigger unit: divide by how many small ones make one big one. Bigger unit, smaller number.
3 bags of wheat, each one 3 kilograms 250 grams. Our job is to find what they weigh altogether, in grams.

board.text: 3 bags of wheat, each 3 kg 250 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 250 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: 1 kilogram is 1000 grams. A gram is much smaller than a kilogram, so we need many more of them: that is why we multiply. 3 times 1000 is 3000 grams.
Now put back the 250 grams that were already there. 3000 plus 250 makes 3250 grams. That is one bag, all in grams.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 250 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 3250 grams, and there are 3 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 3 bags, and each one is the full 3250 grams. So we need 3 lots of 3250: a multiplication.

beats.say: A big multiplication is easier in two pieces. First 3 times 3000, which is 9000. Then 3 times 250, which is 750.
Add the two pieces: 9000 plus 750 is 9750. So the 3 bags together weigh 9750 grams.
Quick sense check. The kilograms on their own came to 9000 grams. Our 9750 is a bit bigger, thanks to the extra 250 grams in every bag. Leaving those out is the classic slip.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
We have a bottle with 10 litres of water in it, and glasses that hold 250 millilitres each. Let's find how many glasses it fills.
Before any sums, check the units. Litres for the bottle, millilitres for the glass. They do not mix, so one of them has to change. Which one?

ask.ifNot: We can only compare amounts that are in the same unit. Changing the litres into millilitres keeps every number whole, so that is the friendly choice.

beats.say: Each litre is 1000 millilitres. Smaller unit, so more of them: we multiply by 1000. 10 times 1000 gives 10000 millilitres in the bottle.
Now both amounts are in millilitres. How do we find how many 250 millilitre glasses fit into 10000 millilitres?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing the water out into equal glasses. Finding how many equal groups fit is a division.

beats.say: Here is a friendly fact to help. 250 times 4 is exactly 1000, so each litre of water fills 4 glasses.
There are 10 litres, with 4 glasses from each one. 10 times 4 is 40. So 40 glasses can be filled.
Check by pouring it back. 40 glasses of 250 millilitres is 40 times 250, which is 10000 millilitres. That is the whole bottle, with nothing left over.
So the plan: get both amounts into the same unit first, then divide to see how many fit.
We have 400 centimetres, and we want to say the same length in metres.
Start with the fact that links the two units. 1 metre is 100 centimetres. Think of a metre stick: it has 100 centimetres marked along it.
A metre is bigger than a centimetre. So will the number of metres be bigger or smaller than 400?

ask.ifNot: It takes 100 centimetres to make just 1 metre. A bigger unit means fewer of them, so the number goes down: we divide.

beats.say: We are bundling the centimetres into groups of 100, one group for each metre. 400 divided by 100 is 4.
So 400 centimetres is the same length as 4 metres.
Check by going back the other way. 4 metres, times 100, is 400 centimetres. Just what we started with.
So, small unit to a bigger unit: divide by how many small ones make one big one. Bigger unit, smaller number.
2 bags of lentils, each one 3 kilograms 750 grams. Our job is to find what they weigh altogether, in grams.

board.text: 2 bags of lentils, each 3 kg 750 g

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Look at how one bag is written: kilograms and grams mixed together. The answer must be in grams, so we change the kilograms. How many grams make 1 kilogram?

ask.ifNot: Kilo means a thousand. So 1 kilogram is 1000 grams.

beats.say: Grams are tiny next to kilograms, so the number has to grow: we multiply by 1000. 3 kilograms is 3 times 1000, which is 3000 grams.
Now put back the 750 grams that were already there. 3000 plus 750 makes 3750 grams. That is one bag, all in grams.

spec.note: Each bag weighs 3 kg 750 g

beats.say: Every bag weighs 3750 grams, and there are 2 of them. What shall we work out?

ask.ifNot: There are 2 bags, and each one is the full 3750 grams. So we need 2 lots of 3750: a multiplication.

beats.say: Doubling is easiest in two pieces. Double 3000 is 6000, and double 750 is 1500.
Add the two pieces: 6000 plus 1500 is 7500. So the 2 bags together weigh 7500 grams.
Does that make sense? The kilograms alone gave 6000 grams, and our answer is a little more, because every bag has 750 extra grams. Forgetting those extra grams is the slip to watch for.
So the plan for mixed units: first write one bag in a single unit, here grams. Then multiply by the number of bags.
Which is greater, 2 over 5 or 5 over 6? Let's find out.
A picture first. Two equal bars: the top one cut into 5 with 2 shaded, the bottom one cut into 6 with 5 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 2 and 5?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Fifths and sixths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 5 and 6 both go into, and the smallest one is 30.
For 2 over 5, the bottom was multiplied by 6, so the top must be too. 2 times 6 is 12, so 2 over 5 is 12 over 30.
And for 5 over 6, the bottom was multiplied by 5, so the top must be too. 5 times 5 is 25, so 5 over 6 is 25 over 30.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all thirtieths. Which is greater, 12 over 30 or 25 over 30?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 25 pieces is more than 12 pieces.

beats.say: 25 pieces beat 12 pieces. And 25 over 30 is only another name for 5 over 6, so 5 over 6 is the greater fraction.
The picture agrees. The bar for 5 over 6 has more of it shaded.
So to compare fractions: make the pieces the same size, then compare the tops.
Here is our sum. 3 over 9, plus 4 over 9.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 9 equal pieces. The first has 3 shaded, and the second has 4.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all ninths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, this is the classic slip. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, ninths. Adding more ninths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 9.

beats.say: So adding is just counting. 3 pieces, and 4 pieces more, is 7 pieces.
Can we make 7 over 9 simpler? 7 and 9 share no factor except 1, so it is already in its simplest form.
So 3 over 9 plus 4 over 9 is 7 over 9.
Let's check against the picture. 3 shaded pieces, and 4 more, is 7 pieces. Just what we wrote.
Remember it like this. Same size pieces? Just count them: add the tops, and the bottom stays as it is.
Here is our story. Rohan has 80 marbles, and 5 over 8 of them go to a friend. How many does Rohan keep?
Let's draw all 80 marbles as one long bar. The bottom number is 8, so we cut it into 8 equal parts.
How many marbles are in each part?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 80 marbles equally into 8 parts. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 80 divided by 8.

beats.say: 80 divided by 8 is 10. So each part holds 10 marbles.
Rohan gives away 5 of those parts. 5 times 10 is 50 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 50?

ask.ifNot: 50 is how many marbles went to the friend. Rohan started with 80, so what is left is 80 take away 50.

beats.say: 80 take away 50 leaves 30. Rohan keeps 30 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. 3 parts were not given away, and 3 times 10 is 30. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
Two equal fractions, but one top number is hiding. One quarter equals something over 12.
Here is one quarter as a bar: 4 pieces, 1 shaded. Underneath is the very same bar, cut into 12 smaller pieces.
Start with the bottoms. What was 4 multiplied by to make 12?

ask.ifNot: Use the 4 times table. 4 times 3 is 12, so the bottom was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: 4 times 3 is 12. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 3 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 3 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 3.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 1 times 3 is 3.
So one quarter equals 3 over 12. The missing number is 3.
Check with the picture. The same amount of bar is shaded in both. Only the size of the pieces changed.
So for equal fractions: whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by the same number.
Which is greater, two thirds or 1 over 6? Let's find out.
Let's draw them as two bars, both the same length. One has 3 pieces with 2 shaded, and the other has 6 pieces with 1 shaded.
Is it fair to compare the tops, 2 and 1, straight away?

choices: Yes, the bigger top always wins
No, the pieces are different sizes
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Thirds and sixths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. 3 goes into 6, so we can turn the thirds into sixths.
For two thirds, the bottom was multiplied by 2, so the top must be too. 2 times 2 is 4, so two thirds is 4 over 6. And 1 over 6 stays as it is.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all sixths. Which is greater, 4 over 6 or 1 over 6?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 4 pieces is more than 1 pieces.

beats.say: 4 is more than 1, so 4 over 6 is greater. And 4 over 6 is just two thirds cut into smaller pieces.
The picture agrees. The bar for two thirds has more of it shaded.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
Here is our story. Karan has 24 marbles, and 5 over 6 of them go to a friend. How many does Karan keep?
Let's draw the 24 marbles. The bottom number is 6, so we share them into 6 equal groups.
So how many marbles does one group hold?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 24 marbles equally into 6 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 24 divided by 6.

beats.say: 24 shared into 6 equal groups gives 4 in each. So one group is 4 marbles.
The top number is 5, so 5 groups go to the friend. 5 times 4 is 20 marbles.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 20?

ask.ifNot: 20 is how many marbles went to the friend. Karan started with 24, so what is left is 24 take away 20.

beats.say: 24 minus 20 is 4. So Karan has 4 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 group was not given away, and one group is 4 marbles. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
Two equal fractions, but one top number is hiding. One half equals something over 8.
Here is one half as a bar: 2 pieces, 1 shaded. Underneath is the very same bar, cut into 8 smaller pieces.
Start with the bottoms. What was 2 multiplied by to make 8?

ask.ifNot: Use the 2 times table. 2 times 4 is 8, so the bottom was multiplied by 4.

beats.say: 2 times 4 is 8. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 4 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 4 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 4.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 1 times 4 is 4.
So one half equals 4 over 8. The missing number is 4.
Check with the picture. The same amount of bar is shaded in both. Only the size of the pieces changed.
So for equal fractions: whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by the same number.
We need 4 over 7 of 42. Let's work it out together.
A picture helps. These are 42 counters, and the bottom number, 7, says share them into 7 equal groups.
What do we do to the 42 first?

ask.ifNot: The bottom number, 7, tells us how many equal groups to make. Sharing into 7 equal groups means dividing by 7.

beats.say: 42 divided by 7 is 6. So each group holds 6.
Now the top number, 4. It tells us how many of those groups to take. So what is 4 over 7 of 42?

ask.ifNot: One group is 6, and the top number says take 4 of them. So we need 4 times 6.

beats.say: 4 groups of 6. 4 times 6 is 24.
There it is. 4 over 7 of 42 is 24.
Let's check our groups were fair. 7 groups of 6 should give back 42, and 7 times 6 is 42. They were.
Here is the plan to keep. Share into the bottom number of groups, then take the top number of them.
Which is greater, three quarters or 5 over 6? Let's find out.
Here they are as two bars of the same length. The first is cut into 4 pieces with 3 shaded. The second is cut into 6 pieces with 5 shaded.
Can we just compare the top numbers, 3 and 5?

choices: No, the pieces are different sizes
Yes, the bigger top always wins
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Quarters and sixths are different sizes, so counting pieces is not fair yet. First the pieces must be the same size.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 4 and 6 both go into, and the smallest one is 12.
For three quarters, the bottom was multiplied by 3, so the top must be too. 3 times 3 is 9, so three quarters is 9 over 12.
And for 5 over 6, the bottom was multiplied by 2, so the top must be too. 5 times 2 is 10, so 5 over 6 is 10 over 12.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all twelfths. Which is greater, 9 over 12 or 10 over 12?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 10 pieces is more than 9 pieces.

beats.say: 10 pieces beat 9 pieces. And 10 over 12 is only another name for 5 over 6, so 5 over 6 is the greater fraction.
The picture agrees. The bar for 5 over 6 has more of it shaded.
So to compare fractions: make the pieces the same size, then compare the tops.
Here is our sum. 10 over 12, plus 10 over 12. And we must give the answer in its simplest form.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 12 equal pieces. The first has 10 shaded, and the second has 10.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all twelfths. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, this is the classic slip. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, twelfths. Adding more twelfths does not change their size, so the bottom stays 12.

beats.say: So adding is just counting. 10 pieces, and 10 pieces more, is 20 pieces.
20 over 12. The top is bigger than the bottom, and that is fine. It means more than 1 whole: one full bar, and 8 more pieces.
20 over 12 is right, but we can make it simpler. What is the biggest number that divides both 20 and 12?

ask.ifNot: Try the times tables. 4 goes into 20, and 4 goes into 12, and nothing bigger goes into both.

beats.say: So we divide the top and the bottom by 4. 20 divided by 4 is 5, and 12 divided by 4 is 3.
So 10 over 12 plus 10 over 12 is 5 over 3, in its simplest form.
Let's check against the picture. 10 shaded pieces, and 10 more, is 20 pieces. Just what we wrote.
So when the bottom numbers match: add the tops, keep the bottom, and then simplify if you can.
Rohan has 36 marbles and gives away three quarters of them. We want to know how many are left.
Let's draw the 36 marbles. The bottom number is 4, so we share them into 4 equal groups.
So how many marbles does one group hold?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 36 marbles equally into 4 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 36 divided by 4.

beats.say: 36 shared into 4 equal groups gives 9 in each. So one group is 9 marbles.
The top number is 3, so 3 groups go to the friend. 3 times 9 is 27 marbles.
Careful now. Read the question again: it asks how many are left. So what do we do with the 27?

ask.ifNot: 27 is how many marbles went to the friend. Rohan started with 36, so what is left is 36 take away 27.

beats.say: 36 minus 27 is 9. So Rohan has 9 marbles left.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 group was not given away, and one group is 9 marbles. It matches.
So: find the fraction of the amount first. Then read the question once more, to see if it wants what was given or what is left.
Three quarters equals something over 24. Let's find the missing top number.

So how many marbles does one group hold?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 36 marbles equally into 4 groups. Sharing equally is dividing, so we need 36 divided by 4.

beats.say: 36 divided by 4 is 9. So each group holds 9 marbles.
Aarav gives away 3 of those groups. 3 times 9 is 27 marbles.
Here is the trap. The question asks how many are left, not how many were given. What do we do with the 27?

ask.ifNot: 27 is how many marbles went to the friend. Aarav started with 36, so what is left is 36 take away 27.

beats.say: 36 take away 27 leaves 9. Aarav keeps 9 marbles.
Let's check with the picture. Just 1 group was not given away, and one group is 9 marbles. It matches.
The plan: divide by the bottom number, multiply by the top, and then check what the question is really asking for.
7 over 8 equals something over 48. Let's find the missing top number.
Here is 7 over 8 as a bar: 8 equal pieces, with 7 shaded. To get 48 pieces, each one has to be cut into smaller pieces.
Start with the bottoms. What was 8 multiplied by to make 48?

ask.ifNot: Use the 8 times table. 8 times 6 is 48, so the bottom was multiplied by 6.

beats.say: 8 times 6 is 48. In the picture, that means every piece was cut into 6 smaller pieces.
So to keep the two fractions equal, what must happen to the top?

ask.ifNot: Every shaded piece was cut into 6 as well. So the top must be multiplied by the same number, 6.

beats.say: The top gets the same treatment. 7 times 6 is 42.
So 7 over 8 equals 42 over 48. The missing number is 42.
Check it backwards. Divide 42 and 48 by 6, and we are back at 7 over 8.
The rule to keep: top and bottom always get multiplied by the same number.
Two fractions, two thirds and 2 over 7. We want the greater one.
Let's draw them as two bars, both the same length. One has 3 pieces with 2 shaded, and the other has 7 pieces with 2 shaded.
Both tops are 2. Does that mean the two fractions are equal?

choices: Yes, same top means same amount
No, the pieces are different sizes
ask.ifNot: Look at the bars. Thirds and sevenths are different sizes, so 2 of one is not the same as 2 of the other.

beats.say: So let's cut both bars into the same size of piece. We need a number that 3 and 7 both go into, and the smallest one is 21.
For two thirds, the bottom was multiplied by 7, so the top must be too. 2 times 7 is 14, so two thirds is 14 over 21.
And for 2 over 7, the bottom was multiplied by 3, so the top must be too. 2 times 3 is 6, so 2 over 7 is 6 over 21.
Now every piece is the same size: they are all twenty-firsts. Which is greater, 14 over 21 or 6 over 21?

ask.ifNot: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them. 14 pieces is more than 6 pieces.

beats.say: 14 pieces beat 6 pieces. And 14 over 21 is only another name for two thirds, so two thirds is the greater fraction.
Did you notice? Both tops were 2, but thirds are bigger pieces than sevenths. Same top, smaller bottom, greater fraction.
Keep this plan. Same bottom number first, and only then compare the tops.
We are adding two fractions. One quarter, plus 2 over 4.
Let's draw them. Two bars, each cut into 4 equal pieces. The first has 1 shaded, and the second has 2.
Every piece here is the same size. They are all quarters. So when we add, what happens to the bottom number?

ask.ifNot: Careful, this is the classic slip. The bottom number is only the name of the pieces, quarters. Adding more quarters does not change their size, so the bottom stays 4.

beats.say: So adding is just counting. 1 piece, and 2 pieces more, is 3 pieces.
Can we make 3 over 4 simpler? 3 and 4 share no factor except 1, so it is already in its simplest form.
So one quarter plus 2 over 4 is three quarters.
Let's check against the picture. 1 shaded pieces, and 2 more, is 3 pieces. Just what we wrote.
Remember it like this. Same size pieces? Just count them: add the tops, and the bottom stays as it is.

Priya buys 7 books at 9 rupees each, and hands over 83 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 7 books at Rs.9 each. Pays Rs.83.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 83 rupees pays for the books, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the books
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 7 books, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 7 books at 9 rupees each: that is 7 times 9. 7 times 9 is 63.
Careful: 63 is only the cost, not the answer. Priya paid 83. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 63 away from 83.

beats.say: From 83, take off the 63. That leaves 20.

A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 800 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Loss per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 800 divided by 10 is 80.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 80 is 40.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 80 plus 40 makes 120. That is the loss.
So the loss is 120 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 800 take away 120 is 680. So the selling price is 680 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 680 is 120 below 800. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!

Check by building it back up. 12 erasers at 12 rupees each: 12 times 12 is 144. It fits.
Cost of many, and you want the cost of one? Divide the total cost by the number of things. Now you try one!

6 x, plus 14, equals 32. Someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 6, then added 14, and got 32. Let's work backwards and find that number.
The two sides are worth the same, like a level see-saw. To get x alone we undo things, last one first. The plus 14 was done last. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 14, we take away 14.

beats.say: And here is the rule of the balance: whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So 14 comes off both sides.
On the left, plus 14 and minus 14 cancel each other out. On the right, 32 minus 14 makes 18.
It is tempting to stop here and say 18. But that is 6 x, and we want just x. 6 x means 6 times x. What undoes times 6?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 6, we divide by 6.

beats.say: We divide the left by 6 and, to keep it fair, the right by 6 too.
18 divided by 6 is 3. So x equals 3. There is our hidden number!
Does it really work? Swap the x for 3. 6 times 3 is 18, and 18 plus 14 is 32. Both sides match.
We undid things in reverse: first the plus, then the times. Keep the balance level, and the hidden number always comes out.

Diya is sharing out 39 toffees in the ratio 1 is to 2. Our job is to find the larger group.

board.text: 39 toffees in the ratio 1 : 2. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 39 to share. The ratio is 1 is to 2. And the question only wants the larger group.
A ratio of 1 is to 2 means this. One side gets 1 equal part, and the other gets 2 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 1 and 2 together make 3 parts.

beats.say: 1 plus 2 is 3. So the whole 39 is cut into 3 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 39 fills all 3 parts, not just the 2 parts of one bar. So we divide 39 by 3.

beats.say: 39 divided by 3 is 13. So every single part is worth 13 toffees.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 13

beats.say: The larger group has 2 of these parts. 2 times 13 is 26.
So 26 toffees are in the larger group.
Let's check. The smaller group is just 1 part, which is 13. And 13 plus 26 is 39, the number we started with.
That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
Read it with me: 2 is to 10, equals 8 is to x. It says the two ratios are the same, and it hides one number behind x.
Before any sum, look at what is given. The first ratio is whole: 2 is to 10. The second has its first number, 8, and a gap where x sits.
Compare the two first numbers, 2 and 8. What happened to 2 to turn it into 8?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 2 times 4 gives 8, so it was multiplied by 4.

beats.say: 8 divided by 2 is 4. So the first number was multiplied by 4.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 10?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 2 was multiplied by 4, so 10 is multiplied by 4 as well.

beats.say: So 10 times 4, which is 40. Notice we multiply, we never add, to keep a ratio the same.
So x is 40. There is our missing number!
Let's check. Divide 8 and 40 by 4, and we get 2 and 10 again. The two ratios match.
That is the trick for any proportion. Spot the multiplier between the first numbers, and use it on the second numbers.

That is the whole method. Total parts first, then one part, then the share the question asks for.
Here is our story. 48 marbles, split into two groups in the ratio 3 is to 5. How many marbles land in the larger group?

board.text: 48 marbles in the ratio 3 : 5. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 48 to share. The ratio is 3 is to 5. And the question only wants the larger group.
Let's draw the ratio. 3 is to 5: one bar with 3 equal parts, and one bar with 5. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 3 and 5 together make 8 parts.

beats.say: 3 and 5 make 8. That means the 48 is spread over 8 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 48 fills all 8 parts, not just the 5 parts of one bar. So we divide 48 by 8.

beats.say: 48 divided by 8 is 6. So every single part is worth 6 marbles.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 6

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 5 parts. 5 times 6 makes 30.
So the larger group has 30 marbles. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is 3 times 6, which is 18. And 18 plus 30 is 48, just what we started with.
Remember the three moves. Add the parts, divide to find one part, then multiply for the share you want.
Read it with me: 5 is to 6, equals 25 is to x. It says the two ratios are the same, and it hides one number behind x.
Before any sum, look at what is given. The first ratio is whole: 5 is to 6. The second has its first number, 25, and a gap where x sits.
Compare the two first numbers, 5 and 25. What happened to 5 to turn it into 25?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 5 times 5 gives 25, so it was multiplied by 5.

beats.say: 25 divided by 5 is 5. So the first number was multiplied by 5.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 6?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 5 was multiplied by 5, so 6 is multiplied by 5 as well.

beats.say: So 6 times 5, which is 30. Notice we multiply, we never add, to keep a ratio the same.
That makes x equal to 30.
Let's check. Divide 25 and 30 by 5, and we get 5 and 6 again. The two ratios match.
That is the trick for any proportion. Spot the multiplier between the first numbers, and use it on the second numbers.

Here is a puzzle. 5 numbers, average 52. We can see 4 of them, but the last one is missing.

spec.note: Levelled out, each of the 5 would be 52

beats.say: An average of 52 means that if we levelled all 5 numbers out, each one would be 52. So what do all 5 add up to?

ask.ifNot: Picture 5 equal bars, each one 52. The total is 5 lots of 52, so we multiply.

beats.say: 5 times 52 is 260. So all 5 numbers together must make 260.
Now add up the 4 we know. 39 plus 40 is 79. 42 plus 49 is 91. And 79 plus 91 makes 170.
All 5 must make 260. The 4 we know make 170. How do we find the hidden one?

ask.ifNot: The hidden number is whatever is still needed to climb from 170 up to 260. We find that gap by taking away.

beats.say: 260 minus 170 is 90. So the missing number is 90.
Let's check. 170 plus 90 is 260, and 260 shared among 5 is 52. Just what the question told us.
The key idea: average times count gives the total. Once you have the total, the missing number is just what is left.
Here is the story. 6 numbers, average 48. Along comes one more number, 76. What happens to the average?
We are not told what the 6 numbers are. But we can still find what they add up to. How?

ask.ifNot: An average of 48 means the 6 numbers, levelled out, would each be 48. So their total is 6 lots of 48.

beats.say: Split 48 into 40 and 8. 6 times 40 is 240, 6 times 8 is 48, and together that is 288. That is what the 6 numbers add up to.
Now the new number joins in. 288 plus 76 is 364.
Here comes the trap. How many numbers are we sharing among now?

ask.ifNot: There were 6 numbers and one more has joined, so now there are 7. The new total is shared among all 7.

beats.say: 364 divided by 7 is 52. We can check: 7 times 52 is 364. So the new average is 52.
The newcomer was bigger than the old average, so it pulled the average up, from 48 to 52. But only a little: one number against 6 cannot drag it all the way to 76.
So: find the old total, add the newcomer, then share among the new count.
We have 6 numbers and we want their average. Look at them as bars. They are not all the same height.

beats.say: Adding first, then. The first 3 make 156. The last 3 make 186. And 156 plus 186 is 342.

ask.ifNot: Count the numbers in the list. There are 6 of them, so the total is shared into 6 equal parts.

beats.say: 342 divided by 6 is 57. We can be sure of that, because 6 times 57 is 342. So the average is 57.

beats.say: Does 57 make sense? An average always lands between the smallest number and the biggest. Ours run from 20 up to 77, and 57 sits in between.

Find the L C M of 16 and 15. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: The first number in both tables: that is our target. Counting up in 16s and 15s would take a while. So we build the L C M from prime factors instead, the building blocks of each number.
Take 16. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 three times, and 2 is left. So 16 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 2.
Take 15. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 3, and 5 is left. So 15 is 3 times 5.
Here is the important part. Both 16 and 15 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 16 and all of 15, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: four 2s from 16, and the 3 and the 5 from 15. These two share no prime at all, so every prime goes in.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 5 is 240. So the L C M is 240.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 240 divided by 16 is 15, and 240 divided by 15 is 16, with nothing left over.
So for an L C M with bigger numbers: split both into primes, then take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Multiply, and you are done!
Which of these numbers is divisible by 12? We could do four long divisions. But there is a quicker way: a divisibility rule.
12 is 4 times 3. So what must be true of a number that 12 divides?

ask.ifNot: 2 and 6 overlap, because 6 already has a 2 inside it. But 4 and 3 share nothing, so passing both of those tests means 12 divides the number.

beats.say: Two tests, then. For 4, the last two digits must be in the 4 times table. For 3, the digits must add up to a multiple of 3.

board.text: Rule for 12: pass the 4 test and the 3 test

beats.say: First, 3596. Its last two digits make 96, and 96 is 4 times 24. So it passes the test for 4.
Now the test for 3. 3 plus 5 plus 9 plus 6 makes 23. 23 is 3 times 7, plus 2 left over, so 3596 is out.
Next, 1452. Its last two digits make 52, and 52 is 4 times 13. So it passes the test for 4.
Now the test for 3. 1 plus 4 plus 5 plus 2 makes 12. Is 12 in the 3 times table?

ask.ifNot: 12 is 3 times 4, so yes, it is in the 3 times table.

beats.say: So 1452 passes both tests. Ring it!
A careful mathematician tests the rest too. Now 8879. It ends in 9, so it is odd. 4 will not go into an odd number, so 12 cannot either.
Last one: 1799. It ends in 9, so it is odd. 4 will not go into an odd number, so 12 cannot either.
Only 1452 passed, so that is our answer. And the division agrees: 1452 divided by 12 is 121, with nothing left over.
So for 12, run two tests: the last two digits for 4, and the digit sum for 3. It must pass both.
Find the H C F of 75 and 45. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 75 and 45 exactly.

beats.say: The biggest number that divides both 75 and 45: that is our target. To find it, we split each number into its prime factors.
75 is odd, so 2 will not go in. Try 3 next, and 3 does go in. Keep splitting, and 75 is 3 times 5 times 5.
45 is odd, so 2 will not go in. Try 3 next, and 3 does go in. Keep splitting, and 45 is 3 times 3 times 5.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 75 and 45 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Ring them on the board. Both lines have a 3 and a 5. Careful: 45 has two 3s, but 75 has only one 3. So only one 3 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 3 times 5 is 15. So the H C F is 15.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 75 divided by 15 is 5, and 45 divided by 15 is 3. Both divide exactly, and 5 and 3 have nothing more in common.
Remember the three moves: split into primes, ring what is shared, multiply. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.

Now the key idea. The L C M must contain all of 18 and all of 10. So we take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Which of these builds the L C M?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 18 and all of 10, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: the 2 and two 3s from 18, and the 5 from 10. Careful: we do not add the 2 in 10 on top, because the 2 from 18 already covers it.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 3 times 3 times 5 is 90. So the L C M is 90.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Let's check. 90 divided by 18 is 5, and 90 divided by 10 is 9. Both divide exactly, so 90 is a multiple of each.
So for an L C M with bigger numbers: split both into primes, then take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Multiply, and you are done!
We need the L C M of 18 and 15. That is the lowest common multiple: the first number that is in the 18 times table and in the 15 times table.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the L C M be smaller than 18?

choices: No, 18 has to fit into it
ask.ifNot: A multiple of 18 is 18 or something bigger. So the L C M can never be smaller than 18, the bigger of our two numbers.

beats.say: With small numbers like these we can just write out both tables and watch for a match. First the 18s: 18, 36, 54, 72, 90, 108.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 18 and 15?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 90 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 90 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 90.
Let's check. 90 divided by 18 is 5, and 90 divided by 15 is 6. Both divide exactly, so 90 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 18 by 15 gives 270, which is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 90 gets there first.
So for small numbers: count up in both tables, and the first number in both is the L C M. Your turn next!
Which of these numbers is divisible by 11? We could do four long divisions. But there is a quicker way: a divisibility rule.
The rule for 11 is a neat one. Add the 1st and 3rd digits. Then add the 2nd and 4th digits.

board.text: Add the 1st and 3rd digits. Add the 2nd and 4th.

beats.say: If the two totals are equal, or exactly 11 apart, then 11 divides the number.

board.text: Totals equal, or 11 apart: divisible by 11

beats.say: First, 5753. The 1st and 3rd digits, 5 and 5, make 10. The 2nd and 4th, 7 and 3, make 10 as well. Does 5753 pass?

choices: Yes, the totals fit the rule
ask.ifNot: The totals are 10 and 10. The rule wants them equal, or exactly 11 apart, and these fit.

beats.say: The two totals match, so 5753 passes. Ring it!
A careful mathematician tests the rest too. Next, 9810. The 1st and 3rd digits make 10, and the 2nd and 4th make 8. Not equal, and not 11 apart, so 9810 is out.
Now 2190. The 1st and 3rd digits make 11, and the 2nd and 4th make 1. Not equal, and not 11 apart, so 2190 is out.
Last one: 9906. The 1st and 3rd digits make 9, and the 2nd and 4th make 15. Not equal, and not 11 apart, so 9906 is out.
Only 5753 passed, so that is our answer. And the division agrees: 5753 divided by 11 is 523, with nothing left over.
So for 11, add every other digit to make two totals. Equal totals, or totals 11 apart, mean 11 divides the number.
Find the H C F of 84 and 70. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 84 and 70 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both 84 and 70. The plan: break each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
Take 84. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2 twice, then 3, and 7 is left. So 84 is 2 times 2 times 3 times 7.
70 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 70 is 2 times 5 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 84 and 70 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Let's ring them. Both lines have a 2 and a 7. Careful: 84 has two 2s, but 70 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 7 is 14. So the H C F is 14.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 84 divided by 14 is 6, and 70 divided by 14 is 5. Both divide exactly, and 6 and 5 have nothing more in common.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.
Find the L C M of 20 and 7. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: The first number in both tables: that is our target. We could count up both tables, but with 20 and 7 that is a long walk. Prime factors get us there faster.
20 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 20 is 2 times 2 times 5.
7 is a prime number already. It cannot be split, so we leave it just as it is.
Here is the important part. Both 20 and 7 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 20 and all of 7, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: two 2s and the 5 from 20, and 7 itself. These two share no prime at all, so every prime goes in.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 2 times 5 times 7 is 140. So the L C M is 140.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Let's check. 140 divided by 20 is 7, and 140 divided by 7 is 20. Both divide exactly, so 140 is a multiple of each.
Remember the difference. For an H C F we keep only the shared primes. For an L C M we take every prime, the most times it appears.
Siya has 55 stickers and shares them into two groups, in the ratio 2 is to 3. We want to know how many are in the larger group.

board.text: 55 stickers in the ratio 2 : 3. Larger group = ?

beats.say: First, what are we given? A total of 55, and a ratio, 2 is to 3. And what are we asked for? Just the larger group.
Let's draw the ratio. 2 is to 3: one bar with 2 equal parts, and one bar with 3. Every piece is the same size.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 2 and 3 together make 5 parts.

beats.say: 2 plus 3 is 5. So the whole 55 is cut into 5 equal parts.
Now for the step where slips happen. How do we find what one part is worth?

ask.ifNot: The 55 fills all 5 parts, not just the 3 parts of one bar. So we divide 55 by 5.

beats.say: 55 divided by 5 is 11. Now we can write 11 on every piece of both bars.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 11

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 3 parts. 3 times 11 makes 33.
So 33 stickers are in the larger group.
Let's check. The smaller group is 2 times 11, which is 22. And 22 plus 33 is 55, just what we started with.
So, to share in a ratio: count the parts, find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as you need.
Read it with me: 7 is to 12, equals 42 is to x. It says the two ratios are the same, and it hides one number behind x.
What do we have? A complete ratio, 7 is to 12. The second ratio shows only its first number, 42. We must find its partner.
Compare the two first numbers, 7 and 42. What happened to 7 to turn it into 42?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 7 times 6 gives 42, so it was multiplied by 6.

beats.say: 42 divided by 7 is 6. So the first number was multiplied by 6.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 12?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 7 was multiplied by 6, so 12 is multiplied by 6 as well.

beats.say: 12 times 6 is 72. Careful: we multiply here. Adding would break the ratio.
So x is 72. There is our missing number!
Let's check. Divide 42 and 72 by 6, and we get 7 and 12 again. The two ratios match.
So in a proportion, find what the first number was multiplied by, then do the very same to the second.

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 2 times 3 gives 6, so it was multiplied by 3.

Let's write it on the board. 4 x, minus 3, equals 9. The x is a mystery number, and our job is to work out what it is.
The two sides are worth the same, like a level see-saw. To get x alone we undo things, last one first. The minus 3 was done last. How do we undo it?

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo minus 3, we add 3.

beats.say: So 3 goes on. But if we only did that on the left, the balance would tip. So we add 3 to both sides.
On the left, minus 3 and plus 3 cancel each other out. On the right, 9 plus 3 makes 12.
It is tempting to stop here and say 12. But that is 4 x, and we want just x. 4 x means 4 times x. What undoes times 4?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 4, we divide by 4.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide both by 4.
12 divided by 4 is 3. So x equals 3. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 3 back in place of x. 4 times 3 is 12, and 12 minus 3 is 9. It works.
We undid things in reverse: first the minus, then the times. Keep the balance level, and the hidden number always comes out.
Look at this one. 5 x, plus 11, equals 41. We want x standing all on its own, so we can see what it is worth.
Both sides of an equation weigh the same, like a balance, and every move has to keep it level. So what is our first move?

ask.ifNot: If we divided first, the 11 would have to be divided as well, and that gets messy. It is easier to clear the plus 11 first, by doing the opposite.

beats.say: We take 11 from both sides. Minus is the opposite of plus, so that clears the plus 11 away.
On the left the plus 11 has gone, and only 5 x is there. On the right, 41 minus 11 is 30. So 5 x equals 30.
It is tempting to stop here and say 30. But that is 5 x, and we want just x. 5 x means 5 times x. What undoes times 5?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 5, we divide by 5.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 5.
30 divided by 5 is 6. So x equals 6. There is our hidden number!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 6 back in place of x. 5 times 6 is 30, and 30 plus 11 is 41. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Here is our equation. 7 x, minus 10, equals 67. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 7 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 7 x has a minus 10 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo minus 10, we add 10. And to keep the balance level, we add it to both sides.
On the left, minus 10 and plus 10 cancel each other out. On the right, 67 plus 10 makes 77.
Careful, we are not finished. 77 is what 7 x is worth, not x. How do we get from 7 lots of x down to one x?

ask.ifNot: 7 x is 7 equal lots of x. To find one lot, we share 77 into 7 equal parts. That is dividing by 7.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 7.
77 divided by 7 is 11. So x equals 11. Found it!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 11 back in place of x. 7 times 11 is 77, and 77 minus 10 is 67. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Here is our equation. 2 x, minus 9, equals 15. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 2 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 2 x has a minus 9 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: To undo minus 9, we add 9. And to keep the balance level, we add it to both sides.
On the left, minus 9 and plus 9 cancel each other out. On the right, 15 plus 9 makes 24.
It is tempting to stop here and say 24. But that is 2 x, and we want just x. 2 x means 2 times x. What undoes times 2?

ask.ifNot: Times and divide are partners. Whatever times does, divide undoes. So to undo times 2, we divide by 2.

beats.say: So we divide both sides by 2.
24 divided by 2 is 12. So x equals 12. Found it!
Let's test it in the equation we started with. 2 times 12 is 24. Then 24 minus 9 gives 15, just as it should.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is taken off. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
5 x, plus 17, equals 57. Someone took a secret number, multiplied it by 5, then added 17, and got 57. Let's work backwards and find that number.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So, what is in the way of the 5 x?

ask.ifNot: Look at the left side once more. The 5 x has a plus 17 hanging on to it. That is the first thing to clear away.

beats.say: The opposite of plus 17 is minus 17. Whatever we do to one side we do to the other, so I write it under both.
On the left the plus 17 has gone, and only 5 x is there. On the right, 57 minus 17 is 40. So 5 x equals 40.
Careful, we are not finished. 40 is what 5 x is worth, not x. How do we get from 5 lots of x down to one x?

ask.ifNot: 5 x is 5 equal lots of x. To find one lot, we share 40 into 5 equal parts. That is dividing by 5.

beats.say: So a bar goes under each side, and we divide both by 5.
40 divided by 5 is 8. So x equals 8. Found it!
Good mathematicians always check. Put 8 back in place of x. 5 times 8 is 40, and 40 plus 17 is 57. It works.
Remember the order: undo the plus 17 first, then undo the times 5. And every move is made on both sides.

board.text: 48 stickers in the ratio 1 : 2. Larger group = ?

beats.say: Let's read it like detectives. There is 48 to share. The ratio is 1 is to 2. And the question only wants the larger group.
A ratio of 1 is to 2 means this. One side gets 1 equal part, and the other gets 2 parts of the very same size. Here they are as two bars.

spec.note: Every piece is the same size

beats.say: Count the pieces in both bars. How many equal parts are there altogether?

ask.ifNot: Count every piece, in both bars. 1 and 2 together make 3 parts.

beats.say: 1 and 2 make 3. That means the 48 is spread over 3 equal parts.
Careful with this next step, it is the one that trips people up. What is one part worth?

ask.ifNot: The 48 fills all 3 parts, not just the 2 parts of one bar. So we divide 48 by 3.

beats.say: 48 divided by 3 is 16. So every single part is worth 16 stickers.

spec.note: Each piece is worth 16

beats.say: We want the larger group, and that is 2 parts. 2 times 16 makes 32.
So the larger group has 32 stickers. There it is!
Let's check. The smaller group is just 1 part, which is 16. And 16 plus 32 is 48, the number we started with.
So, to share in a ratio: count the parts, find what one part is worth, then take as many parts as you need.
This says 7 is to 11, equals 21 is to x. So the second ratio is the first one in disguise, and x is its missing number.
Before any sum, look at what is given. The first ratio is whole: 7 is to 11. The second has its first number, 21, and a gap where x sits.
Compare the two first numbers, 7 and 21. What happened to 7 to turn it into 21?

ask.ifNot: Ratios grow by multiplying, not by adding. 7 times 3 gives 21, so it was multiplied by 3.

beats.say: 21 divided by 7 is 3. So the first number was multiplied by 3.
For the two ratios to stay equal, what must we do to the second number, 11?

ask.ifNot: Whatever was done to the first number must be done to the second. 7 was multiplied by 3, so 11 is multiplied by 3 as well.

beats.say: 11 times 3 is 33. Careful: we multiply here. Adding would break the ratio.
So x is 33. There is our missing number!
Let's check. Divide 21 and 33 by 3, and we get 7 and 11 again. The two ratios match.
That is the trick for any proportion. Spot the multiplier between the first numbers, and use it on the second numbers.
Find the L C M of 10 and 9. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: The first number in both tables: that is our target. We could count up both tables, but with 10 and 9 that is a long walk. Prime factors get us there faster.
10 is even, so 2 comes out first. That leaves 5, so 10 is 2 times 5.
9 is odd, so 2 will not go in. Try 3 next, and 3 does go in. That leaves 3, so 9 is 3 times 3.
Here is the important part. Both 10 and 9 must fit inside the L C M. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in either number. Which of these does that?

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 10 and all of 9, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: the 2 and the 5 from 10, and two 3s from 9. These two share no prime at all, so every prime goes in.
In the picture, the L C M is everything, counted once. 2 times 3 times 3 times 5 is 90. So the L C M is 90.

spec.note: The L C M uses every prime in the picture, once each.

beats.say: Let's check. 90 divided by 10 is 9, and 90 divided by 9 is 10. Both divide exactly, so 90 is a multiple of each.
So for an L C M with bigger numbers: split both into primes, then take each prime the most times it appears in one number. Multiply, and you are done!
Which of these numbers is divisible by 6? We could do four long divisions. But there is a quicker way: a divisibility rule.
6 is 2 times 3. So what must be true of a number that 6 divides?

choices: It is even AND 3 divides it
It is even OR 3 divides it
ask.ifNot: If 6 goes into a number, then 2 and 3 both go into it. One of them alone is not enough: the number must pass both tests.

beats.say: So we run two tests. The number must be even, and its digits must add up to a multiple of 3.

board.text: Rule for 6: even, and digit sum a multiple of 3

beats.say: First, 7190. It ends in 0, so it is even. Now the test for 3: 7 plus 1 plus 9 plus 0 makes 17. 17 is 3 times 5, plus 2 left over, so 7190 is out.
Next, 1741. It ends in 1, so it is odd. 2 will not go into it, so 6 cannot either.
Now 1623. It ends in 3, so it is odd. 2 will not go into it, so 6 cannot either.
Last one: 5574. It ends in 4, so it is even. Now the test for 3: 5 plus 5 plus 7 plus 4 makes 21. Is 21 in the 3 times table?

ask.ifNot: 21 is 3 times 7, so yes, it is in the 3 times table.

beats.say: So 5574 passes both tests. Ring it!
Only 5574 passed, so that is our answer. And the division agrees: 5574 divided by 6 is 929, with nothing left over.
So for 6, run two quick tests: is it even, and do the digits add up to a multiple of 3? It must pass both.
We need the H C F of 120 and 45. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both of them with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 45?

choices: No, it has to fit into 45
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 45, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: So how do we find it? We split each number into its prime factors, the smallest building blocks it is made of.
120 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 120 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3 times 5.
Take 45. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 3 twice, and 5 is left. So 45 is 3 times 3 times 5.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 120 and 45 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Let's ring them. Both lines have a 3 and a 5. Careful: 45 has two 3s, but 120 has only one 3. So only one 3 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 3 times 5 is 15. So the H C F is 15.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 120 divided by 15 is 8, and 45 divided by 15 is 3. Both divide exactly, and 8 and 3 have nothing more in common.
Remember the three moves: split into primes, ring what is shared, multiply. And the H C F is never bigger than the smaller number.

ask.ifNot: The L C M has to hold all of 8 and all of 3, but nothing twice over. So each prime goes in the most times it shows up in one number.

beats.say: Box our picks: three 2s from 8, and 3 itself. These two share no prime at all, so every prime goes in.

beats.say: Let's check. 24 divided by 8 is 3, and 24 divided by 3 is 8. Both divide exactly, so 24 is a multiple of each.

Find the L C M of 6 and 15. L C M is short for lowest common multiple. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A multiple of a number is anything in its times table. So the lowest common multiple is the first number that is in both tables.

beats.say: With small numbers like these we can just write out both tables and watch for a match. First the 6s: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36.
Now count up in 15s: 15, 30, 45.
Look along both lists. What is the L C M of 6 and 15?

ask.ifNot: We want the first number that shows up in both lists. Run a finger along each one: 30 is in both, and nothing before it is.

beats.say: There it is. 30 is the first number in both lists, so the L C M is 30.
Let's check. 30 divided by 6 is 5, and 30 divided by 15 is 2. Both divide exactly, so 30 really is a multiple of each.
One trap to watch for. Multiplying 6 by 15 gives 90, which is a common multiple, but not the lowest one. 30 gets there first.
So for small numbers: count up in both tables, and the first number in both is the L C M. Your turn next!
Find the H C F of 24 and 42. H C F is short for highest common factor. So what are we hunting for?

choices: The first number in both tables
ask.ifNot: A factor is a number that divides exactly. So the highest common factor is the biggest number that divides both 24 and 42 exactly.

beats.say: So we want the biggest number that goes into both 24 and 42. The plan: break each number into prime factors, its building blocks.
24 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 24 is 2 times 2 times 2 times 3.
Take 42. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 3, and 7 is left. So 42 is 2 times 3 times 7.
Here comes the important part. A common factor can only use primes that are in both numbers. So which of these do 24 and 42 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have a 2 and a 3. Careful: 24 has three 2s, but 42 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 3 is 6. So the H C F is 6.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Let's check. 24 divided by 6 is 4, and 42 divided by 6 is 7, with nothing left over. And 4 and 7 share no factor, so nothing bigger would work.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 15, the smaller of our two numbers.

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

Here is our equation. 4 x, plus 22, equals 102. Somewhere behind that x a number is hiding, and we are going to find it.

ask.ifNot: Adding and taking away are partners: each one undoes the other. So to undo plus 22, we take away 22.

beats.say: And here is the rule of the balance: whatever we do to one side, we do to the other. So 22 comes off both sides.

Good mathematicians always check. Put 20 back in place of x. 4 times 20 is 80, and 80 plus 22 is 102. It works.
So here is the plan for any equation like this. First clear away what is added. Then undo the times. Your turn next!
Let's write it on the board. 2 x, plus 27, equals 67. The x is a mystery number, and our job is to work out what it is.

Let's write it on the board. 2 x, plus 30, equals 54. The x is a mystery number, and our job is to work out what it is.

We need the H C F of 12 and 18. That is the highest common factor: the biggest number that goes into both of them with nothing left over.
Before we start, a quick thought. Could the H C F be bigger than 12?

choices: No, it has to fit into 12
ask.ifNot: A factor has to fit inside the number it divides. So the H C F can never be bigger than 12, the smaller of our two numbers.

beats.say: So how do we find it? We split each number into its prime factors, the smallest building blocks it is made of.
12 is even, so 2 comes out first. Keep splitting, and 12 is 2 times 2 times 3.
Take 18. Keep pulling out the smallest prime that fits: 2, then 3, and 3 is left. So 18 is 2 times 3 times 3.
Now the key idea. The H C F is built only from the primes that both numbers have. Which of these is exactly what 12 and 18 share?

ask.ifNot: Look for the primes that sit on both lines. A prime that only one number has cannot divide the other one, so it stays out.

beats.say: Circle them on both lines. Both lines have a 2 and a 3. Careful: 12 has two 2s, but 18 has only one 2. So only one 2 is shared.
The overlap in the picture shows what they share. Multiply those together: 2 times 3 is 6. So the H C F is 6.

spec.note: The overlap holds the primes both numbers share.

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 12 divided by 6 is 2, and 18 divided by 6 is 3. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 3 have nothing more in common.
So the plan for any H C F: break both numbers into primes, keep only the primes they share, and multiply those. Your turn next!

beats.say: Good mathematicians always check. 14 divided by 7 is 2, and 49 divided by 7 is 7. Both divide exactly, and 2 and 7 have nothing more in common.
That is the whole method. Split both numbers into primes, ring the ones on both lines, and multiply what you ringed.

Someone puts 500 rupees in a bank at 12 per cent simple interest, and leaves it for 5 years. How much is there at the end? That is called the amount.

board.text: Rs.500 at 12% simple interest for 5 years

beats.say: 12 per cent means 12 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 12 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.12 in 1 year

beats.say: So how many hundreds are in 500? 500 divided by 100 is 5. That is 5 hundreds.

spec.note: Each 100 earns Rs.12 in a year

beats.say: Each of the 5 hundreds earns 12 rupees in a year. So which sum gives the interest for one year?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 5 hundreds earns 12 rupees. So that is 12 rupees, 5 times over: 5 times 12.

beats.say: 5 times 12 is 60. That is what one year earns: 60 rupees of interest.
Simple interest is steady. It earns the same 60 rupees every single year. Look at the table, one year at a time.
So we need 60, 5 times over. 5 times 60 is 300. That is the interest for all 5 years.
Grown-ups write this as a formula. The starting money is the principal. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time in years, divided by 100.
Put our numbers in. 500 times 12 times 5, divided by 100, comes to 300. The same answer, so we can trust it.
Now, careful. The question asks for the amount after 5 years. Is 300 the amount?

choices: No: take it away from Rs.500
ask.ifNot: 300 rupees is only the interest, the extra money. The amount is everything in the bank: the 500 rupees put in at the start, plus the interest.

beats.say: 500 plus 300 is 800. So the amount after 5 years is 800 rupees.
So: find what one year earns, multiply by the number of years, and for the amount, add the interest back on to the money at the start. Now you try one!
